parts.overview: Ostra is one Rust program with 15 crates that runs software tasks as sessions of AI agents. A user describes a task in a React console in the browser, and Ostra moves the task through research, specification, plan, implementation, review, test, and documentation stages. Each session is an append-only event log, and a pure planner reads the state that the log produces to choose the next step. Executors run each agent on a model API with an API key or inside an installed harness command-line tool. A policy engine and an operating system sandbox check every tool call of every agent. Ostra reaches outside services through model APIs, harness tools, MCP servers, git remotes, and Web Push.

sections.title: Architecture and crate map
sections.summary: Ostra is one binary built from 15 Rust crates. This page shows what each crate owns, which way dependencies point, and which traits keep the engine independent.
sections.body:
## The problem the layout solves

Ostra runs a long pipeline. One session reads code, calls models, waits for people, and runs commands in a sandbox. If one crate knew all of these parts, a change to a model provider would force a change in the planner. A test of the planner would also need a network and a real model.

The workspace avoids this with layers. Each of the 15 crates owns one concern. The engine depends on traits, not on the crates that implement them. This page covers:

- the one binary that the crates build
- what each crate owns and which crates it depends on
- the rule for the direction of dependencies and the traits that enforce it
- the path of one agent run through the crates
- where the browser code and the state on disk fit

The terms in this page are defined in Core concepts and terms. The commands to build the crates are in Build, run, and format.

## One binary: `ostra`

[`crates/ostra-server`](crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs) builds the only binary of the workspace. Its manifest sets `[[bin]] name = "ostra"`. The binary holds the HTTP and WebSocket server, the web console, and the agent assets. At compile time, `rust_embed` copies `web/dist` into the binary (see [`assets.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/assets.rs)). The `ostra-agents` crate embeds the `assets/` folder in the same way.

The executable is also its own helper program. Harness CLIs call `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio`. The sandbox starts `ostra sandbox-init` inside the sandbox. The function `main` registers the executable as the helper with `ostra_sandbox::set_helper`.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ostra` or `ostra serve` | Starts the server. Flags: `--port`, `--no-open`, `--dev`, `--bind`, `--allow-host`. |
| `ostra hook` | Hook bridge for harness executions. A harness CLI calls it. You do not. |
| `ostra mcp-stdio` | MCP stdio shim for harness executions. A harness CLI calls it. You do not. |
| `ostra config` | Prints the config path. Writes the default config if none exists. |
| `ostra url` | Prints a fresh sign-in URL for a running server. |
| `ostra sessions` | Lists the browsers signed in to Ostra. `ostra sessions revoke <id>` or `--all` revokes sign-ins. |
| `ostra signout` | Signs out every browser. It does the same as `ostra sessions revoke --all`. |
| `ostra stop <session>` | Stops a pipeline session while the server is not running. |
| `ostra sandbox-init` | Hidden from `--help`. Runs inside a sandbox before the async runtime starts. |

The word `sessions` in `ostra sessions` means browser sign-ins. A pipeline session is a different thing.

## The 15 crates

Each crate lives in `crates/ostra-<concern>`. The root `Cargo.toml` uses `members = ["crates/*"]`, so a new folder under `crates/` joins the workspace.

| Crate | Owns | Internal dependencies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra-core` | Ids, agents, settings, pipeline enums, the event log types, submit schemas, API types for the browser, and the `Executor` and `ExecutionHost` traits. | none |
| `ostra-sandbox` | The kernel sandbox under agent commands: profiles, the bubblewrap and Seatbelt backends, the egress proxy, and decoy files. | core |
| `ostra-store` | SQLite storage: the workspace database, the machine registry, and each project's lesson memory. | core |
| `ostra-policy` | The policy engine: layer 1 guards, layer 2 permissions, and the Bash command parser. | core |
| `ostra-providers` | Model providers behind one chat interface: the Anthropic Messages API, the OpenAI Responses API, and a scripted provider for tests. | core |
| `ostra-agents` | The embedded assets (prompts, judges, references, skills), prompt rendering per executor, the typed spawn contract, and the repo brief. | core |
| `ostra-mcp` | An MCP client for the external MCP servers of a workspace: stdio and streamable HTTP transports, and OAuth. | core |
| `ostra-notify` | Web Push without OpenSSL: RFC 8291 encryption and RFC 8292 VAPID authentication. | core |
| `ostra-tools` | The native tool implementations. Names and input shapes follow the tools of Claude Code. | core, sandbox, store |
| `ostra-code` | Code navigation: the tokenizer, the per-project index, language servers, and code providers. | core, sandbox |
| `ostra-exec-harness` | Harness executors: run one agent inside an installed CLI under a PTY, with a hook bridge and an MCP shim. | core, sandbox |
| `ostra-engine` | Event-sourced sessions, the pure planner, judge calls, and the runner that performs steps. | core, sandbox, store, agents |
| `ostra-exec-native` | The native agent loop: one execution of one agent on an API key. | core, sandbox, providers, tools, policy, store |
| `ostra-workspace` | Settings validation, projects, trust approvals, create and delete, and the runtime of an open workspace. | core, sandbox, store, engine, agents, policy |
| `ostra-server` | The `ostra` binary: bootstrap, auth, the REST and WebSocket API, the embedded web build, and the glue between the crates. | all 14 other crates |

The dependencies above come from the `[dependencies]` tables of the manifests. Dev-dependencies add `ostra-code` and `ostra-tools` to `ostra-exec-harness` tests. Three crates (`ostra-providers`, `ostra-exec-native`, and `ostra-exec-harness`) enable the `test-prices` feature of `ostra-core` in their tests. That feature exposes `install_test_prices()` in [`pricing.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/pricing.rs).

### Ranks of the crates

A crate has the rank of its longest path down to `ostra-core`. A crate depends only on crates of a lower rank.

| Rank | Crates |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | `ostra-core` |
| 1 | `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store`, `ostra-policy`, `ostra-providers`, `ostra-agents`, `ostra-mcp`, `ostra-notify` |
| 2 | `ostra-tools`, `ostra-code`, `ostra-exec-harness`, `ostra-engine` |
| 3 | `ostra-exec-native`, `ostra-workspace` |
| 4 | `ostra-server` |

## The rule for the direction of dependencies

The engine reaches executors, providers, and the server only through traits. The engine manifest lists `ostra-core`, `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store`, and `ostra-agents`. It does not list `ostra-exec-native`, `ostra-exec-harness`, `ostra-providers`, `ostra-tools`, `ostra-policy`, `ostra-workspace`, or `ostra-server`. The crate `ostra-workspace` reaches the server only through the `WorkspaceHost` trait.

Only `ostra-server` knows every crate. It builds the real parts and gives them to the engine through the traits.

The rules for a change:

- Add a method to a trait when the engine needs a new capability.
- Do not add an executor, provider, or server crate to the manifest of `ostra-engine`.
- Keep `ostra-core` free of internal dependencies.

The reason: the engine tests use fakes for the traits. A direct dependency on a real executor removes that fake from the test. A dependency on `ostra-server` also creates a cycle, because the server already depends on the engine. Cargo refuses a cycle.

### The traits that carry the boundary

| Trait | Defined in | What it gives | Real implementation | Test fakes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Executor` | [`crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs) | `run(spec, host, cancel)` returns an `ExecutionResult`. | `NativeExecutor`, `HarnessExecutor` | `Scripted` and `Hanging` in the engine tests |
| `ExecutionHost` | [`crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs) | The callbacks of an executor: `emit`, `ask_permission`, `record_message`. | `EngineHost` in `runner.rs` | `FakeHost` in the native executor tests |
| `Services` | [`crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs) | The view of the engine on the outside: settings, `executor(kind)`, `factory()`, `judge(...)`, `notify`, `protected_paths`, `command_approved`. | `ServerServices` in `ostra-server` | `Fake` in the engine tests |
| `SpawnFactory` | [`crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs) | `agent_meta`, `build`, and `judge_prompt`. | `AgentsFactory` in `factory.rs`, which uses `ostra-agents` | none |
| `WorkspaceHost` | [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/host.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/host.rs) | The registry, the global config, the environment, provider and harness status, and `services(id, root)`. | `Shared` in `ostra-server` | none |

## The path of one agent run

### Flowchart: how the crates connect at run time

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Browser["Browser console (web/)"] -->|"REST /api, WebSocket /ws"| Server["ostra-server: axum API"]
  Server -->|"WorkspaceRt::open"| Rt["WorkspaceRt (ostra-workspace)"]
  Rt --> Engine["Engine (ostra-engine)"]
  Engine -->|"append_event"| Store[("workspace.db (ostra-store)")]
  Engine -->|"Services::executor, Services::judge"| Svc["ServerServices (ostra-server)"]
  Svc --> Native["NativeExecutor (ostra-exec-native)"]
  Svc --> Harness["HarnessExecutor (ostra-exec-harness)"]
  Svc -->|"judge call"| Providers["ostra-providers"]
  Native --> Providers
  Native --> Policy["ExecutionPolicy (ostra-policy)"]
  Native --> Tools["ostra-tools"]
  Tools --> Sandbox["ostra-sandbox"]
  Harness -->|"ostra hook to /internal/policy"| Server
```

The browser sends requests to the server. The server finds the `WorkspaceRt` of the workspace. The `WorkspaceRt` owns one `Engine` and one `WorkspaceDb`. The engine writes every state change as an event and asks `ServerServices` for an executor or a judge call.

The two executors check policy in different places. `NativeExecutor` calls `ExecutionPolicy::check` in its own process. A harness CLI runs outside Ostra, so its hook runs `ostra hook`, which posts the tool call to `/internal/policy`. The server then runs `ExecutionPolicy` for it (see [`bridge.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs)).

### Sequence: one execution

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant E as Engine
  participant S as Services
  participant X as Executor
  participant H as EngineHost
  E->>S: executor(kind)
  S-->>E: Some(executor)
  E->>X: run(spec, host, cancel)
  X->>H: emit(delta)
  X->>H: ask_permission(call, reason, rule)
  H-->>X: PermissionAnswer
  X-->>E: ExecutionResult
```

The engine passes the `ExecutionSpec`, the `EngineHost`, and a `CancellationToken` to the executor. The executor streams `ExecutionDelta` values through `emit`. When policy returns an ask, the executor waits in `ask_permission` for the answer. The executor returns one `ExecutionResult`, and the engine records it as an event.

## Browser code and state on disk

The browser code is one npm workspace. The root `package.json` lists `design`, `web`, and `site`. The `design` folder holds `@ostra/design`, which has the tokens and React components. The `web` folder holds the console that the binary embeds. The `site` folder holds the homepage and the docs. The `site` folder is absent from this checkout.

`web` and `site` import the design system from `@ostra/design` and never import each other. The console calls the server on `/api` and `/ws`. Its API types are generated from `ostra-core` (see Build, run, and format).

Ostra keeps state in three places. The data directory (`OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, else the OS local data directory plus `ostra`) holds `registry.db` and `server.json`. Each workspace has a `.ostra/` folder with `workspace.toml`, `workspace.db`, and `sessions/<session id>/`. Each project has its own `.ostra/` folder with `project.toml`, `INVENTORY.md`, and `memory/knowledge.sqlite3`. The topic Stores, workspaces, and trust explains these files.

### What happens when

- **A developer adds `ostra-server` to the engine manifest.** Cargo refuses the dependency cycle.
- **A developer adds `ostra-exec-native` to the engine manifest.** Cargo accepts it, but the engine now links a real executor. Add a method to `Services` instead.
- **The server does not run.** The commands `ostra config`, `ostra sessions`, and `ostra stop` still work. The command `ostra url` needs a running server.
- **A harness execution needs a policy decision.** The hook calls `/internal/policy`. The server accepts `/internal/` only from local peers. It refuses a request that has an `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` header, because only Ostra clients call these routes.
- **An executor needs the user to answer.** It calls `ExecutionHost::ask_permission` and waits for the browser answer. Under YOLO, `ExecutionPolicy::check` turns an ask into an allow and a denial stays a denial.

The `Services` and `SpawnFactory` traits through which the engine reaches the outside.
The trait through which `ostra-workspace` reaches the server.

`Shared` implements `WorkspaceHost`. `App` holds the open workspaces.
The CLI subcommands and the hidden `sandbox-init` mode.
The hook bridge routes `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp` for harness executions.

sections.title: Core concepts and terms
sections.summary: Defines workspace, project, session, category, lane, stage, phase, execution, agent, gate, judge, and YOLO. Lists the id prefixes and the role of each of the 14 agents.
sections.body:
## Why the terms need fixed meanings

Ostra uses common words with one fixed meaning each. A session, a stage, a phase, and an execution are four different things. If a reader mixes them, the pipeline reads like a different system. This page defines each term once. Other pages use the term with the meaning given here.

Ostra runs an engineering pipeline for a request: research, spec, fact-check, plan, build, review, test, and docs. Code drives the pipeline and holds every gate. Models do the work inside a stage and answer a small set of named questions.

## How the terms relate

### Entity diagram: the main terms

```mermaid
erDiagram
  WORKSPACE ||--o{ PROJECT : "registers"
  WORKSPACE ||--o{ SESSION : "holds"
  SESSION }o--o{ PROJECT : "has in scope"
  SESSION ||--o{ EVENT : "is the fold of"
  SESSION ||--o{ EXECUTION : "spawns"
  SESSION ||--o{ GATE : "opens"
  SESSION ||--o{ DECISION : "records"
  EXECUTION }o--|| AGENT : "runs one"
  EXECUTION }o--|| EXECUTOR : "runs on"
```

A workspace holds projects and sessions. A session is the fold of its events. The events record each execution, gate, and decision.

## The terms

| Term | Meaning | In code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace | A folder that holds one or more projects and one `.ostra/` state folder. The registry lists it. One `Engine` runs for each open workspace. | `WorkspaceId`, `WorkspaceRt` |
| Project | A code folder in a workspace. A key names it: a lowercase slug that matches `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`. It has its own `.ostra/project.toml`, `INVENTORY.md`, skills, and lesson memory. | `ProjectEntry`, `is_project_key` |
| Session | One run of the pipeline for one request. Its kind is `Pipeline`, or `Init { project }` for the setup of a project. Its folder is `<workspace>/.ostra/sessions/<session id>/`. | `SessionId`, `SessionKind` |
| Request | The text that the user types, with the options `tests`, `docs`, `yolo`, and an optional `track`. | `SessionOptions` |
| Category | The kind of work that the Classify judge picks for a request. There are 10 values. | `Category` |
| Track | `light` or `full`. It sets how much of the pipeline an `IMPLEMENT` request runs. | `Track` |
| Stage | One kind of node in the pipeline. A stage instance carries a project key, a phase, and a round. There are 38 stage kinds. | `StageKind` |
| Lane | One of 9 columns of the session board. Each stage kind belongs to one lane. | `Lane`, `StageKind::lane` |
| Phase | One unit of build work from the Phase Index of the plan. It has an id, a project, a complexity, a test policy, and the phases it depends on. If the plan is skipped, the phase is synthetic and inline. | `PhaseInfo` |
| Agent | A leaf model worker with its own prompt and definition. It ends its run by calling `submit_<agent>`. There are 14 agents. | `AgentName` |
| Execution | One run of one agent on one executor. | `ExecutionId`, `ExecutionStatus` |
| Executor | The part that runs an execution: `native` or `harness:<name>`. | `ExecutorKind` |
| Harness | An installed agent CLI: Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Antigravity. The names in settings are `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. | `HarnessKind` |
| Gate | A point where the session waits for an answer. There are 14 gate kinds. | `GatePayload`, `GateId` |
| Judge | One model call that answers one named question of the pipeline. The call returns JSON that matches a schema. There are 10 judges. | `JudgeKind` |
| Decision | The stored result of a judge call, with a reason. The user can override some decisions. | `DecisionId`, `SessionState::can_override` |
| YOLO | A session option. The engine answers the gates in place of the user. | `SessionOptions::yolo` |
| Event | One record of the append-only log of a session. The state of a session is the fold of its events. | `SessionEvent`, `StoredEvent` |
| Book | The documentation book that the docs stage writes for a workspace. | `ostra_core::book` |
| Sign-in | One signed-in browser. The CLI command `ostra sessions` lists sign-ins. A sign-in is not a session. | `si_` ids in `auth.rs` |
| Tier | A model class: `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, or `frontier`. Settings map a tier to a model for each executor. | `Tier` |
| Effort | The reasoning effort: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`. | `Effort` |
| Complexity | The `low`, `medium`, or `high` value of a phase. It routes the tier of the `implementer` and `write-test` agents. | `Complexity` |

### Categories

The Classify judge picks one of these values for each request: `RESEARCH`, `SPEC`, `PLAN`, `IMPLEMENT`, `VERIFY`, `TEST`, `DOCS`, `PROMPT`, `QUICK_CHANGE`, and `QUICK_ANSWER`. Three of them have a fixed meaning in the code:

- `TEST` runs the test stage alone on existing code. Logs from before the rename say `UNIT_TEST`.
- `DOCS` runs the docs stage alone on existing code. It writes a documentation book and changes no code.
- `QUICK_CHANGE` is a small edit that the request fully describes. It runs one implementer pass on the native executor.

The topic How a session runs from request to completion shows which stages each category runs.

### Lanes

The nine lanes, in order, are `research`, `requirements`, `verification`, `design`, `build`, `review`, `test`, `docs`, and `done`. A lane is a display group. `StageKind::lane` in [`pipeline.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/pipeline.rs) maps each stage kind to a lane. For example, `Implement`, `Autofix`, `Handoff`, and `Rescue` belong to `build`. `Review`, `Staging`, `Format`, and `ImplementationReview` belong to `review`.

### Gates and judges

A gate stops the session until someone answers. The 14 gate kinds are `open_questions`, `spec_approval`, `plan_approval`, `fact_check_recurring`, `review_cap`, `stuck`, `phase_blocked`, `closing_gate`, `permission`, `harness_failure`, `skill_approval`, `execution_failed`, `budget_reached`, and `implementation_review`. The topic Gates: the 14 kinds, their answers, and YOLO explains each one.

A judge is the only place where a model makes an orchestration decision. The 10 judges are `classify`, `sufficiency`, `stakes`, `track`, `route-answer`, `feedback`, `rescue`, `resolve-review`, `yolo-answer`, and `completion`. Each judge has a prompt in `assets/judges/<name>.md`. The topic Judges: what each one decides and how a call runs explains them.

## YOLO

YOLO is a session option. The user sets it in the New task form, or the workspace default `yolo.default` sets it. A `YoloSet` event can change it during a session. When YOLO is on, the planner emits a `Step::YoloAnswer` for each open gate, and the engine answers the gate. The engine records each answer with a reason. The completion report lists them under "Decided for you" with a link to undo each one.

YOLO does not remove every stop. These limits hold:

- YOLO never answers the `budget_reached` gate, because spending more is the decision of the user.
- YOLO does not answer an `execution_failed` gate for an execution that the user stopped.
- The review loop budget rises from `REVIEW_CAP` (3 passes) to `YOLO_REVIEW_BUDGET` (10 passes).
- Layer 1 guards of the policy engine stay on. No permission, user answer, or YOLO setting overrides a guard.
- `ExecutionPolicy::check` turns an ask into an allow under YOLO. A denial stays a denial.

The `yolo` default is a registry-only setting. A folder file cannot set it, because a repository could otherwise change its own safety limits (Rule A2).

## Id prefixes

Each id type is a string with a prefix and a UUIDv7 in 32 lowercase hex digits without hyphens. UUIDv7 is time ordered, so the lexical order of ids matches the order of creation. The macro `id_type!` in [`ids.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/ids.rs) makes the six id types.

| Prefix | Type | Names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ws_` | `WorkspaceId` | A workspace |
| `s_` | `SessionId` | A pipeline session |
| `x_` | `ExecutionId` | One agent run |
| `g_` | `GateId` | One gate |
| `d_` | `DecisionId` | One judge decision |
| `m_` | `MessageId` | One message between agents, a question or an answer |
| `si_` | none (a string in `auth.rs`) | One signed-in browser. It uses random bytes in hex. |

A project key is not an id. The user chooses it, and `is_project_key` checks it.

## The 14 agents

An agent is a leaf worker. It does not start other agents. Each agent has a folder `assets/agents/<name>/` with `prompt.md` and `agent.toml`. The kebab-case name of the agent is the folder name. The tool that ends a run is `submit_<name in snake case>`, for example `submit_code_reviewer`.

| Agent | Role | Default tier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | Researches one task and writes one research document. It is the only agent that searches the web for the pipeline. | advanced |
| `generate-spec` | Reads every research document and writes one spec: requirements in EARS notation with acceptance criteria. | advanced |
| `fact-check` | Checks a spec or a plan for claims that break the implementer. Ostra refuses approval without a recorded PASS. | advanced |
| `plan` | Turns the approved spec into a master plan and one file for each phase. | advanced |
| `implementer` | Writes the code for one phase or one inline change. It never writes tests. | balanced |
| `code-reviewer` | Reviews the working-tree changes and runs a security scan on every changed file. It submits findings. | balanced |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | Traces the execution paths of the changed code and writes the EPA report that assigns a test level to each check. | balanced |
| `write-test` | Writes the tests that the EPA report assigns and runs them with the regression suites. It writes only test code. | balanced |
| `documentation` | Writes the part of the documentation book for one project. | advanced |
| `system-architecture` | Writes the architecture of a book that covers two or more projects. | advanced |
| `prompt-generation` | Writes or edits prompts, skills, and agent definitions for a `PROMPT` request. | advanced |
| `initializer` | Bootstraps a project in six modes: `detect`, `scout`, `propose`, `generate-skill`, `generate-inventory`, and `adopt`. | balanced |
| `quick-answer` | Answers one question in the side panel. It is read-only. | balanced |
| `advisor` | Reads a failed or stuck step and tells the engine how to continue. It is read-only. | advanced |

The tier comes from `default_tier` in `agent.toml`. Routing settings can change it. Nine agents are confined to the session folder and the OS temp folder by the write-scope guard: `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `advisor`, `documentation`, and `system-architecture` (`AgentName::is_session_only`). Only `implementer` can create projects (`AgentName::manages_projects`).

The old agent name `module-documentation` is retired. `AgentName` and `StageKind` accept it as an alias for `documentation`, so old logs and databases still load.

### What happens when

- **A name has the prefix `ostra:` or `ultracode:`.** `AgentName::from_str` removes the prefix before it looks up the agent.
- **A workspace file names a retired agent.** Settings validation ignores the name and does not refuse the file (`RETIRED_AGENTS`).
- **An agent name is unknown.** `from_str` returns the error `unknown agent` with the name.
- **An executor string is not `native` or `harness:<name>`.** `ExecutorKind::from_str` returns an error that lists the valid forms. For example, `harness:vim` fails.

sections.title: Build, run, and format
sections.summary: Gives the cargo commands, the pinned toolchain, and the order of the web build before the release build. Explains the web dev server, mock mode, Biome, and ts-rs types.
sections.body:
## The problem: two build systems that depend on each other

Ostra has a Rust workspace and a web console. The release binary contains the compiled console. If a developer compiles the Rust crates before the console exists, the compile fails. If a developer changes a Rust type and does not run the tests, the TypeScript types stay old. This page gives the commands and the order that avoid both problems.

This page covers the toolchain, the commands, the release build, the web dev server and mock mode, Biome, and the generation of TypeScript types. The install scripts and Docker are in the topic Run, install, and extend the server.

## Prepare a fresh checkout

Do these steps in order:

1. Install `rustup`.
2. Run `rustup toolchain install` in the repo root. The command reads `rust-toolchain.toml` and installs `1.98.1` with `rustfmt` and `clippy`.
3. Install Node 24. The `Dockerfile` installs Node 24.
4. Run `npm ci --no-audit --no-fund` in the repo root. The root `package.json` lists the workspaces `design`, `web`, and `site`.
5. Run `cd web && npm run build`.
6. Run `cargo build --workspace`.

Build the console before any command that compiles `ostra-server`. The `RustEmbed` derive in [`assets.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/assets.rs) reads `web/dist` at compile time. If the folder is missing, the compile stops with the error `#[derive(RustEmbed)] folder '...' does not exist`. The folder `web/dist` is in `.gitignore`, so every fresh checkout has this problem.

Commands that do not compile `ostra-server` work without `web/dist`. For example, `cargo test -p ostra-engine` does not need it, because the engine does not depend on the server.

## Rust commands

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Compile every crate | `cargo build --workspace` |
| Run every Rust test | `cargo test --workspace` |
| Format every crate | `cargo fmt --all` |
| Lint with warnings as errors | `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` |
| Test one crate | `cargo test -p ostra-engine` |
| Run one integration test file | `cargo test -p ostra-engine --test recover` |
| Run the planner conformance suite | `cargo test -p ostra-engine --test conformance` |
| Regenerate the TypeScript types | `cargo test -p ostra-core export_bindings` |

The `cargo test --workspace` command skips the live evals. Those tests carry `#[ignore]` because they call real models and cost money. The topic Unit, integration, and conformance tests explains each suite.

The clippy command comes from the maintainer guide of the last commit (see Conventions and common changes). The workspace has no `[lints]` table and no `clippy.toml`. Four `#[allow(clippy::...)]` attributes exist in the crates. The workspace has no `rustfmt.toml`, so `cargo fmt --all` uses the rustfmt defaults.

The folder `tests/windows-probes` is not a workspace member (`exclude` in `Cargo.toml`). Cargo commands at the repo root never build it. Run its commands from inside that folder.

## Toolchain and build profiles

| Item | Value | File |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Toolchain channel | `1.98.1` | `rust-toolchain.toml` |
| Toolchain components | `rustfmt`, `clippy` | `rust-toolchain.toml` |
| Minimum Rust version | `rust-version = "1.98"` | `Cargo.toml` |
| Edition | `2024` | `Cargo.toml` |
| Resolver | `"3"` | `Cargo.toml` |
| Dev profile | `debug = "line-tables-only"`, dependencies at `opt-level = 1` | `Cargo.toml` |
| Release profile | `debug = false`, `strip = true` | `Cargo.toml` |

Every crate takes `version`, `edition`, and `license` from `[workspace.package]`. Every crate takes third-party versions from `[workspace.dependencies]` with `name.workspace = true`. Pin a new third-party dependency once in the root manifest.

## Build the release binary

Run `./build.sh` to build the release binary at `target/release/ostra`. The script does these steps:

1. It changes to the repo root.
2. If `node_modules` is missing, it runs `npm ci --no-audit --no-fund`.
3. If `web/dist/index.html` is missing or any watched path is newer, it runs `npm run -s build` in `web/`.
4. It runs `cargo build --release -p ostra-server`.

The watched paths are `web/src`, `web/public`, `web/index.html`, `web/package.json`, `design/src`, and `design/package.json`. The script checks them with `find ... -newer web/dist/index.html`.

The script does not watch `web/vite.config.ts`, `web/tsconfig.json`, or `package-lock.json`. If you change only one of them, `build.sh` prints `Web UI is up to date` and embeds the old console. Delete `web/dist/index.html` to force a rebuild.

The `Dockerfile` uses the same order in three stages: web, Rust, and runtime.

### Start Ostra with `run.sh`

`./run.sh [ostra flags]` builds and then starts Ostra. It passes the flags to the binary, for example `./run.sh --bind 0.0.0.0`. The script reads two environment variables:

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `SKIP_BUILD=1` | Starts the existing binary and skips `build.sh`. |
| `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` | Names a credentials file. The script applies only the lines that start with `export NAME=`. |

Put only trusted lines in the file that `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` names. The script filters lines with `grep` and then passes each matching line to `eval`, so the shell runs the full text of that line.

The script ends with `exec ./target/release/ostra "$@"`. With no subcommand, the binary runs `ostra serve`. The port is `--port`, else `server.port` of the config, else `7878`. The server binds `127.0.0.1` unless you set `--bind` or `server.bind`. The topic Startup sequence, request guard, and sign-in explains the start and the sign-in.

## Work on the web console

The console is a Vite and React app in `web/`. All commands below run in `web/`.

| Command | What it runs |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run dev` | `vite` on port `5173`. |
| `npm run dev:mock` | `vite --mode mock`. No server is needed. |
| `npm run build` | `vite build` into `web/dist`. |
| `npm run typecheck` | `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json`. |
| `npm test` | `vitest run` with jsdom. |
| `npm run lint` | `biome lint`. |
| `npm run format` | `biome format --write`. |
| `npm run check` | `biome check`. |
| `npm run check:fix` | `biome check --write`. |

### Develop against a real server

Start the server with `cargo run -p ostra-server -- serve --dev --no-open`. Then run `npm run dev` in `web/`. The flag `--dev` makes the server accept the hosts `localhost:5173` and `127.0.0.1:5173`.

The Vite server proxies `/api`, `/ws`, and `/mcp/oauth` to the address in `OSTRA_DEV_SERVER`. The default is `http://127.0.0.1:7878`. If the server runs on another port, set `OSTRA_DEV_SERVER` to its address. The OAuth redirect for an MCP server returns to the origin of the page, so `/mcp/oauth` must go through the proxy.

### Develop in mock mode

Run `npm run dev:mock` to work on the console without a server. The command loads `web/.env.mock`, which sets `VITE_MOCK=1`. In [`web/src/api/index.ts`](web/src/api/index.ts), `isMock` selects `mockApi` instead of `httpApi`. The fixtures are in `web/src/api/mock/`.

The code loads `mockApi` with a dynamic `import()`. A static import would keep the fixtures in the production bundle, even when the branch never runs. The unit tests also run in mock mode, because `vite.config.ts` sets `VITE_MOCK` to `"1"` in the `test.env` block.

The file `web/.env.shot` sets `VITE_MOCK=1` and `VITE_SHOT=1` for the console shot on the homepage. Set variables through Vite modes. Do not put them inline in npm scripts, because npm runs scripts through `cmd.exe` on Windows.

### Biome and the TypeScript compiler

Biome lints and formats the JavaScript and TypeScript workspaces. The root `biome.json` holds the settings. The version is pinned to `2.5.14` in `web/package.json`.

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Indent | 2 spaces |
| Line width | 120 |
| Quotes | double |
| Semicolons | always |
| Trailing commas | all |
| Organize imports | on |
| Accessibility rules | off |
| Linter preset | `recommended`, with `useExhaustiveDependencies` as a warning |
| Ignored paths | `**/dist`, `web/src/api/gen`, `**/.vitest`, `**/.shots`, `site/public/console`, `tests/browser` |

Biome skips `web/src/api/gen` because ts-rs writes those files. The `tsconfig.json` of `web/` turns on `strict`, `noUnusedLocals`, `noUnusedParameters`, and `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`.

Before you finish a console change, run `npm run typecheck`, `npm run check`, and `npm test` in `web/`. The `design/` workspace has the same `typecheck`, `test`, `lint`, and `check` scripts.

## How TypeScript types are generated

Rust types that the browser uses are the source of truth. The tool ts-rs writes their TypeScript form. All `#[ts(export)]` types are in `ostra-core` (329 attributes). The generated files are in `web/src/api/gen/` (332 files).

The mechanism has these steps:

1. A type derives `TS` and carries `#[ts(export)]`.
2. For each such type, ts-rs generates a test named `export_bindings_<type>`.
3. `cargo test` runs the generated tests. Each test writes `web/src/api/gen/<Type>.ts`.
4. Cargo sets two environment variables from [`.cargo/config.toml`](.cargo/config.toml): `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` is `web/src/api/gen` relative to the repo root, and `TS_RS_LARGE_INT` is `number`.
5. The developer runs `cd web && npm run typecheck`. TypeScript reports each place where a changed shape breaks code. Fix only what breaks.

The filter `export_bindings` in `cargo test -p ostra-core export_bindings` matches every generated test by name. It also matches the empty test `export_bindings` in [`api.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs). That test exists so that the command stays stable. Generation is a side effect of a test run. `cargo build` never writes these files.

The generated files are committed. A Rust change that alters a shape shows up as a diff in the same change.

Ts-rs needs help for types it does not know:

| Attribute | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `#[ts(type = "string")]` | A `PathBuf` field, or an id type. |
| `#[ts(optional)]` | An `Option<T>` field that can be absent. |
| `#[ts(as = "...")]` | A field that has a different shape in TypeScript. |

The `ts-rs` features in `Cargo.toml` are `serde-json-impl`, `uuid-impl`, `chrono-impl`, and `no-serde-warnings`. The last feature silences warnings about serde attributes that ts-rs does not support.

### The barrel file

[`web/src/api/types.ts`](web/src/api/types.ts) is a hand-written list of `export type * from "./gen/<Type>"` lines. It has 232 lines of re-exports, and 100 of the 332 generated files are not in it. The `*Submit` types and `Book` are examples. Nothing checks the barrel against the folder. Add a line to the barrel when you want a new type there. Otherwise import it from `api/gen/<Type>` directly.

### What happens when

- **`web/dist` is missing.** Any compile of `ostra-server` fails with the `RustEmbed` error. Run `cd web && npm run build`.
- **A developer changes only `web/vite.config.ts`.** `build.sh` does not rebuild the console. Delete `web/dist/index.html`.
- **A developer adds a Rust field and does not run the tests.** The file in `web/src/api/gen/` stays old. The console can compile against a wrong shape.
- **A Rust field is `i64` or `u64`.** TypeScript sees `number`. Values above 2^53 lose precision. The repo has no test for this.
- **`site/` is missing.** `build.sh` still works. The site spec of the browser suite cannot build the site.
- **A new exported type has a `PathBuf` field and no `#[ts(type = "string")]`.** ts-rs generates a type that does not match the JSON that serde writes. Add the attribute.

## Limits and defaults

| Name | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default server port | `7878` | `ostra serve`, `server.port` |
| Vite dev port | `5173` | `web/vite.config.ts` |
| Default `OSTRA_DEV_SERVER` | `http://127.0.0.1:7878` | `web/vite.config.ts` |
| `chunkSizeWarningLimit` | `4000` (KB) | `web/vite.config.ts` |
| Build output | `web/dist`, `emptyOutDir`, no source maps | `web/vite.config.ts` |
| Vendor chunks | `react`, `router`, `icons`, `markdown-lib` | `web/vite.config.ts` |
| Web test files | 48 (`src/**/*.test.ts` and `.tsx`) | `web/src` |

code_refs.note: Pins the toolchain channel `1.98.1` with `rustfmt` and `clippy`.
Sets `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` and `TS_RS_LARGE_INT` for ts-rs.
Builds the web console when it is stale, then the release binary.
Builds, loads exported variables from `OSTRA_ENV_FILE`, and starts `ostra`.
The `RustEmbed` derive that reads `web/dist` at compile time.
Dev proxy, build chunks, and the vitest settings.
Chooses the mock API when `VITE_MOCK=1`.
Biome format and lint settings for the npm workspaces.
The empty test that gives a stable command to regenerate the bindings.
The hand-written barrel of generated type re-exports.

sections.title: Conventions and common changes
sections.summary: States the crate layout rules, error types, rule IDs, and prose rules. Lists the files that each common change touches, and notes that the maintainer guide is absent from the working tree.
sections.body:
## The problem: rules that a change can break without a failed test

Some rules of this codebase have no compiler check. A change can break one of them and all tests still pass. Examples are a second place that appends events, or a guard that a user setting can override. This page states those rules with their reasons. It then lists the files that each common change touches, so a developer does not forget one.

## The maintainer guide is absent

The files `CLAUDE.md`, `HANDOVER.md`, `README.md`, and the `docs/` folder are deleted in the working tree. The command `git status` shows them as deleted. They exist in the last commit (`efc7938`). The folder `site/` is also absent, although `package.json`, `build.sh`, and `Dockerfile` name it.

This page takes the rules from the maintainer guide of the last commit and checks each one against the code. Read the guide with `git show HEAD:CLAUDE.md`. Comments in the code cite sections of `HANDOVER.md`, for example `HANDOVER 10.1` in `ostra-exec-native`. Those sections are not in the working tree. Read the comments and the tests of the code instead.

The recipe to add a docs page needs `docs/` and `site/src/docs/pages.ts`. It cannot run in this checkout.

## Layout rules for crates and files

- Put each concern in its own crate at `crates/ostra-<concern>`.
- Declare the crate in `[workspace.dependencies]` of the root `Cargo.toml` by path. Refer to it with `name.workspace = true`.
- Pin each third-party version once, in the root manifest.
- Start `lib.rs` (or `main.rs` for the server) with a `//!` comment. State the concern of the crate in one to three sentences.
- Name source files by concern. For example, the engine has `state.rs`, `plan.rs`, `runner.rs`, `judge.rs`, `judge_input.rs`, `factory.rs`, `init.rs`, `services.rs`, and `view.rs`.
- Give a module a folder only when it has sub-parts. Examples are `ostra-core/src/doc`, `ostra-sandbox/src/sys`, `ostra-exec-harness/src/adapters`, `ostra-server/src/files`, and `ostra-code/src/lsp`.
- Keep the OS-specific code of the sandbox in `sys/`. Choose the `Os` implementation only in `sys/mod.rs`.
- Put embedded assets at the repo root: `assets/agents/<name>/{prompt.md,agent.toml}`, `assets/judges`, `assets/refs`, `assets/skills`, and `assets/tool-mapping.toml`.
- Split long files with banner comments: a line of dashes, a title line, and a line of dashes.

## Code conventions

- Use Rust edition 2024 with the toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml`.
- Keep `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean. Four `#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]` or `type_complexity` attributes exist.
- Write no comment by default. Write one short line only for a hidden constraint, an invariant, or a workaround. Rule citations always stay.
- Do not handle cases that cannot happen. Validate at the boundaries: API input, model output, and files.

### Error types

Each library crate has its own `thiserror` enum. The enums are `StoreError`, `EngineError`, `ProviderError`, `McpError`, `NotifyError`, `AgentsError`, `ConfigError`, and `RouteError`. Only `ostra-server` depends on `anyhow`.

At the HTTP boundary, `ApiErr` in [`api.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) turns an error into a status and the JSON body `ApiError { error, issues }`. The generated TypeScript type has the same name.

| Error | HTTP status |
| --- | --- |
| `EngineError::NotFound` | `404` |
| `EngineError::Invalid` | `409` |
| `EngineError::Ended` | `409` |
| `EngineError::Store` and `StoreError` | `500` |
| Settings validation (`ApiErr::invalid`, `invalid_request`) | `422` |

```rust
impl From<EngineError> for ApiErr {
    fn from(e: EngineError) -> Self {
        match e {
            EngineError::NotFound(m) => ApiErr::not_found(m),
            EngineError::Invalid(m) => ApiErr::new(StatusCode::CONFLICT, m),
            EngineError::Ended => ApiErr::new(StatusCode::CONFLICT, e.to_string()),
            EngineError::Store(e) => ApiErr::new(StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, e.to_string()),
        }
    }
}
```

## Rule IDs in comments

The design brief gave each behavior rule an ID, such as `D3a`, `T4`, `H2`, or `O5`. Code that implements a rule cites its ID in a one-line comment. The form is `// Rule D3: ...` or `/// Rule O5: ...`. The crates hold 283 such `// Rule` comments. The letter groups rules of one area. It does not name a crate. For example, `B` rules cover documentation books, `T` rules cover the test stage, and `A2` covers settings that only the registry can hold.

Three conventions keep rule IDs useful:

- Cite the rule ID in the comment of the code that implements it.
- Add or change a fixture in `tests/conformance/main.rs` in the same change as a new or changed planner rule. The suite has one fixture group for each rule.
- Keep every rule ID in the prompts. The test `rule_id_sets_survive_the_port` in `ostra-agents` checks that the spec prompt keeps its `K1` to `K8` and `S1` to `S8` IDs.

The reason: a rule ID links the code, the test, and the prompt. When the ID is gone, a reader cannot find the other two.

## Patterns that every change follows

1. **Every state change is an event.** The state of a session is `SessionState::fold(events)` in [`state.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs). Only `SessionState::apply` changes the state. Only `Inner::append` in [`runner.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs) appends events. Keep the fold a pure function of the log. If a fact from outside the log changes how an event folds, record the fact in the event. For example, the review execution carries the auto-fixable rule IDs in its `params` (`AUTO_FIXABLE_PARAM`), because the fold cannot read `project.toml`.
2. **The planner is pure.** `next_steps(&SessionState, &PlanCtx) -> Vec<Step>` in [`plan.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs) decides what happens next. The runner performs the steps and appends what happened. Settings reach the planner only through `PlanCtx`. Each `Step` has a `key()`, so the engine never starts one step twice. Add new behavior as fold state plus a planner rule. Do not add logic to the runner.
3. **Agents return structured data.** Every agent ends with a `submit_<agent>` call. Its schema is the struct in [`submit.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/submit.rs). `validate_submit` checks the shape. The engine reads only that payload and never a final message. The prompt in `assets/agents/<name>/prompt.md` must describe the same fields.
4. **Spawns are typed.** The `Label: value` block of each agent is a struct in `crates/ostra-agents/src/spawn.rs`. Required parameters are non-`Option` fields. `factory.rs` in the engine maps planner `SpawnInputs` onto them.
5. **Every tool call passes the policy.** Native and harness executions call `ExecutionPolicy::check` on a canonical `ToolCall`. Layer 1 guards cannot be overridden by permissions, users, or YOLO.
6. **Settings are read fresh and validated at save.** Global config, workspace settings, and project profiles are read again for each execution. A route that does not resolve is an error at save time (`validate_workspace`), not a silent fallback at spawn time.
7. **Spend has limits.** `limits.max_parallel_executions` (default `3`) caps the executions of a workspace that run at the same time. `limits.session_budget_usd` (default `25.0`) turns a spawn into a `budget_reached` gate. Fan-out stages have caps, for example `init::MAX_SCOUTS` (`6`) and `init::MAX_DEFAULT_GENERATE` (`8`). Give each new fan-out a cap and send it through the slot limiter.

## Add a gate kind

Do these steps in order:

1. Add the variant to `GatePayload` in [`event.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/event.rs).
2. Add its arms to `GatePayload::stage()` and `GatePayload::kind_str()` in the same file.
3. Fold it in `on_gate_opened` and `on_gate_answered` in `state.rs`.
4. Open the gate from the planner in `plan.rs`.
5. Add its arm to `yolo_plan` in [`judge_input.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/judge_input.rs). Return `YoloPlan::Fixed`, `YoloPlan::Judge`, or `None` for a gate that YOLO must not answer.
6. Accept its answer shape in `validate_answer` in `runner.rs`.
7. Add the kind to `ANSWER_KIND` in [`web/src/lib/gateAnswers.ts`](web/src/lib/gateAnswers.ts) and add a form in `web/src/features/gates/`.
8. Add a fixture to `tests/conformance/main.rs`.
9. Regenerate the TypeScript types and run `npm run typecheck` in `web/`.

The Rust `match` statements in steps 2 and 5 have no default arm, so the compiler reports a missing arm. `ANSWER_KIND` is a `Record` over all gate kinds, so TypeScript reports a missing key.

## Add or change a judge

1. Add the variant to `JudgeKind` and its name to `JudgeKind::as_str` in `event.rs`.
2. Add the output struct and its schema to [`judge.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/judge.rs) (`output_schema`).
3. Add the input builder to `judge_input.rs`.
4. Write the prompt in `assets/judges/<name>.md`. `prompt_name` returns `JudgeKind::as_str`, so the file name must match.
5. Add the planner step that asks the judge.
6. Add the fold that applies the decision.
7. Decide whether the user can override the decision (`SessionState::can_override`).
8. Add a case to `tests/evals/judges.toml` and run the live eval for the judge.

## Change an agent

1. Edit `assets/agents/<name>/prompt.md` and `agent.toml`. The file `agent.toml` holds the default tier, the effort for each executor, the capabilities, and the timeout.
2. If the return changes, change the submit struct in `submit.rs` and the fold that reads it.
3. Keep every rule ID in the prompt.
4. Run `cargo test -p ostra-agents`. The test `every_prompt_renders_for_every_executor_with_no_unresolved_token` renders each prompt for each executor.

## Add a native tool

1. Implement the tool in `ostra-tools`. Add its name to the `match` in `execute` in [`lib.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/lib.rs).
2. Add its definition to `definitions` in `defs.rs`. Model the description on the tool description of Claude Code. Use no em dash.
3. Add a `Capability` variant and its `native_tool` name in [`agent.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs).
4. Add a row for each executor to `assets/tool-mapping.toml`.
5. Classify the tool in `family` in `crates/ostra-policy/src/perms.rs`: `Read`, `Edit`, `Bash`, `WebFetch`, or `Other`.

The tool crate does not check permissions or guards. The policy layer runs before `execute`. If you skip step 5, the policy treats the tool as `Family::Other`.

## Add a guard

1. Port the guard into `crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs`.
2. Cite its Ultracode source in a one-line comment on the function.
3. Add a test in `crates/ostra-policy/tests/`.
4. Write the denial so that the correction comes first. Grok clips reasons to 256 characters.

Guards are layer 1. No permission, user answer, or YOLO setting overrides a guard.

## Add an endpoint

1. Write the handler in [`api.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) and register it with `.route(...)` in `router`.
2. Return `ApiErr` for errors, so the client gets `{ error, issues }`.
3. Add a TypeScript client call in `web/src/api/client.ts` and a mock in `web/src/api/mock/mockApi.ts`.

Every path under `/api` passes `guard`, which checks the host, the origin, and the cookie. The path `/internal/*` is for harness callbacks and accepts local peers only. The browser suite reads each `.route(` of `api.rs` in `tests/browser/lib/routes.ts`, so it covers a new route without a change. The helper throws if it parses fewer than 60 routes.

## Change an API type

1. Add or edit the type in `ostra-core`. Keep `#[derive(TS)]` and `#[ts(export)]` on it.
2. Run `cargo test -p ostra-core` to regenerate `web/src/api/gen/`.
3. Run `cd web && npm run typecheck` and fix only what breaks.
4. Commit the generated files with the Rust change.

## Add a setting

1. Add the field to `WorkspaceSettings` in [`config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs). Every settings struct uses `#[serde(default)]`, so a missing key takes the default.
2. Add the dotted key and a one-line description to `SETTING_KEYS`. The test `setting_keys_name_fields` fails when a key does not name a field.
3. Check the value at save time in `validate_workspace`.
4. Decide where the value lives. A repository can change `workspace.toml`. If that would let a repository lift its own limits, store the value in the registry (Rule A2). Add it to `trust::overlay` in `ostra-workspace`.

## Prose rules

Text that users or models read follows the writing rules of the design brief. This covers prompts, judge prompts, UI copy, and error messages. The rules are:

- Use no em dash.
- Write headings in sentence case.
- Write the instruction first, then the reason.
- Use no metaphor and no superlative.
- Keep the `because` clauses.

Only the em dash rule has tests. `no_em_dashes_in_any_asset` in `ostra-agents` scans every embedded asset. `descriptions_follow_writing_rules` in `ostra-tools` scans the tool descriptions.

### What happens when

- **A change appends an event outside `Inner::append`.** The state is not folded, the clients get no broadcast, and the driver does not wake. Tests can still pass.
- **The fold reads a file.** A restart can fold the same log to a different state. Put the fact in the event.
- **A new gate kind has no `yolo_plan` arm.** The code does not compile.
- **A new native tool has no entry in `tool-mapping.toml`.** A prompt that names the tool cannot render for that executor.
- **A new setting is not in `SETTING_KEYS`.** The settings search does not find it.
- **A repository file sets a registry-only value.** The server ignores the file value, because `overlay` replaces it from the registry.

code_refs.note: `SessionState::fold` and `apply`, the only code that changes session state.
`EngineError`, `Inner::append`, and `validate_answer`.
The pure planner and `Step::key`.
`GatePayload::stage`, `kind_str`, and `JudgeKind`.
The YOLO answer for each gate kind.
Error mapping, the `guard` function, and the `router`.
Layer 1 guards.
Classifies a tool name as Read, Edit, Bash, WebFetch, or Other.
The dispatch from a tool name to its implementation.
Settings keys and the test that checks them.
Registry-only settings (Rule A2).
The planner fixtures, one group for each rule ID.
The answer kind of each gate, which mirrors `validate_answer`.

sections.title: How a session runs from request to completion
sections.summary: Follows one session from the request through classify, explore, the flow of each category, review, closing stages, and the final report. Defines the stage, lane, and category words and shows how the console derives a status and a stage label.
sections.body:
## Why a session has a fixed order of stages

A session is one user request that the engine carries to a completion report. The order of the work is fixed in code. The function `next_steps` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs) holds every stage order and every gate. A model never chooses the next stage. Judges are model calls that answer only the questions that the planner asks, and the engine stores each answer as an event.

A fixed order makes a session predictable. The same event history always gives the same next step. Because of this, a restart can continue a session and a test can check the order without a model. The page "The event log and the fold" explains the mechanism.

This page covers:

- The words that name the pipeline: category, track, stakes, stage, lane, phase, and gate.
- How a session starts.
- The classify and explore stages that most categories share.
- The flow of each of the 10 categories.
- The `IMPLEMENT` flow from spec to completion.
- How the console derives a status and a stage label.

The loops inside a phase, the judges, and the gate catalog have their own pages. See "The implement, review, autofix, and rescue loop", "Judges: what each one decides and how a call runs", and "Gates: the 14 kinds, their answers, and YOLO".

## The vocabulary of the pipeline

The pipeline types live in [`crates/ostra-core/src/pipeline.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/pipeline.rs). Each term has one meaning in this book.

| Term | Code | Values | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Category | `Category` | 10 | The kind of request. The classify judge picks it. |
| Track | `Track` | `light`, `full` | How much of the pipeline an `IMPLEMENT` request runs. |
| Stakes | `Stakes` | `low`, `medium`, `high` | The result of the stakes judge. `low` skips the plan. |
| Stage | `StageKind` | 38 | One node kind of the pipeline. Each execution, gate, and command belongs to one stage. |
| Lane | `Lane` | 9 | One column of the session board. Each stage belongs to one lane. |
| Phase | `PhaseInfo` | numbered | One unit of build work, from the plan or created inline when no plan exists. |
| Gate | `GatePayload` | 14 | A point where the session waits for an answer from the user or from YOLO. |

The 10 categories are `RESEARCH`, `SPEC`, `PLAN`, `IMPLEMENT`, `VERIFY`, `TEST`, `DOCS`, `PROMPT`, `QUICK_CHANGE`, and `QUICK_ANSWER`. The log format also accepts the old name `UNIT_TEST` for `TEST`.

The function `StageKind::lane` assigns each of the 38 stages to a lane. The lanes follow the order of the software lifecycle.

| Lane | Stages |
| --- | --- |
| Research | `Intake`, `Classify`, `Explore`, `Sufficiency`, `Track`, `QuickAnswer`, `Detect`, `Scout` |
| Requirements | `Spec`, `OpenQuestions`, `Propose`, `SkillApproval` |
| Verification | `FactCheckSpec`, `FactCheckPlan`, `SpecApproval` |
| Design | `Stakes`, `Plan`, `PlanApproval` |
| Build | `Implement`, `Autofix`, `Handoff`, `Rescue`, `Verify`, `PromptGen`, `GenerateSkill`, `GenerateInventory` |
| Review | `Review`, `Staging`, `Format`, `ImplementationReview` |
| Test | `ClosingGate`, `Epa`, `WriteTest`, `TestReview` |
| Docs | `Documentation`, `Architecture`, `BookWrite` |
| Done | `Completion` |

A gate has no stage of its own. The function `GatePayload::stage` maps each gate to a stage, and the console shows the gate in that lane. Five gates map to `Implement`: `PhaseBlocked`, `Permission`, `HarnessFailure`, and `ExecutionFailed`, and so on for the work loop. The gate `BudgetReached` maps to `Intake`. The gate `ReviewCap` maps to `Review` or `TestReview`. The gate `FactCheckRecurring` maps to `FactCheckSpec` or `FactCheckPlan`. The gate `Stuck` maps to `Rescue`.

### The name closing gate

The words closing gate name one gate only: `GatePayload::ClosingGate`, titled `Tests and documentation`, in stage `ClosingGate` and lane Test. This gate does not end the session. The session ends at stage `Completion` in lane Done.

## How a session starts

The server calls `Engine::create_session` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs). This function calls `start_session`. The steps run in this order:

1. Reject an empty request with the message `Describe the task first.` Reject a documentation book id that is not valid.
2. Read the workspace settings. If `yolo.default` is true, set `options.yolo` to true.
3. Keep only the projects that have an inventory file (`.ostra/INVENTORY.md`). If none remains, return an error, because every agent routes its work by the inventory of its project.
4. If the user pinned projects, reject a key that is unknown or not initialized. Then keep only the pinned projects (Rule O6).
5. Check the attached files (at most 50) and the staged uploads (at most 20).
6. Create the session folder under `.ostra/sessions/<session id>`, a `.gitignore` that holds `*`, and one subfolder for each project. Move the uploads into the session folder.
7. Insert the session row, create the in-memory `Live` record, append `SessionCreated`, and start the driver task.

The event `SessionCreated` carries the request, the options, the projects, the attached files, the uploads, the pinned keys, and the book id. The page "Uploads, attached files, and context added during a session" explains the files and uploads.

A session of kind `Init` runs the initializer flow (`init_flow`) and not the flow on this page. This page covers sessions of kind `Pipeline`.

Before the first event, the planner returns no step. It also returns no step when the session is terminal or paused (Rule P1).

## Classify and explore: the shared start

### Classify

1. The planner returns `Step::Judge` with `JudgeKind::Classify` when the session has no category and no classify decision.
2. The runner appends `DecisionMade`. The fold method `apply_classify` then sets the category, the title (cleaned to at most 60 characters), the project scope, and `opts_in` (the tests and docs choices of the judge).
3. For `RESEARCH`, `SPEC`, `PLAN`, and `IMPLEMENT`, the fold queues one explore task for each task that the judge listed. If the judge lists no task, the fold queues one task for each scoped project. That task holds the whole request (Rule D1).
4. For `VERIFY`, `DOCS`, `TEST`, `QUICK_CHANGE`, and `PROMPT`, the fold creates inline phases and queues no explore task.

Pinned projects always win over the projects that the judge picked. A project that an agent created stays in scope (Rule O3). The user can override a classify decision only until dependent work starts.

### Explore

- The planner spawns every ready `explore` execution at once (Rule M1). The explore agent only reads, so parallel tasks cannot conflict. The execution slot limit still applies. See "Engine limits and constants".
- The function `explore_complete` returns true only when every task that is not bound to a loop has finished.
- An explore result can list `not_covered` items. For each unjudged result, the planner returns `Step::Judge` with `JudgeKind::Sufficiency`. The judge marks which items are needed. Each needed item becomes a new explore task. A task with the same project and text as an unfinished task is not queued again. The planner calls the sufficiency judge at most `SUFFICIENCY_ROUNDS` times (3).
- If no research document exists after the tasks end, the planner returns `Step::Fail` with this error: `Every research task failed or was abandoned, so there is no research document to write a spec from.` This rule applies to `RESEARCH`, `SPEC`, `PLAN`, and `IMPLEMENT` (Rule D1).

## The flow of each category

The method `Planner::flows` chooses the flow with one `match` on the category. This table shows what each category runs after classify.

| Category | What runs | The session ends when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RESEARCH` | Explore and sufficiency. | Explore is complete, then the completion step runs. |
| `SPEC` | Explore, then the spec flow. The spec needs a fact-check PASS but no approval gate. | The spec passes its fact-check, then completion runs. |
| `PLAN` | Explore, the spec flow with the `SpecApproval` gate, then the plan flow with the `PlanApproval` gate. | The plan is approved, then completion runs. |
| `IMPLEMENT` | Explore, track, optional spec and plan, phases, review, closing stages. | Every closing stage ends, then completion runs. |
| `VERIFY` | One inline phase for each project. The implementer runs the project test command and reports. No review and no `git add`. | Every implement loop is terminal and nothing runs. |
| `PROMPT` | One inline phase in the first scoped project. The work agent is `prompt-generation`. A review runs only if code changed. | The same as `VERIFY`. |
| `QUICK_CHANGE` | One inline phase for each project, one implementer pass, no review. The executor is native. | The same as `VERIFY`. |
| `QUICK_ANSWER` | No explore. One `quick-answer` execution on the native executor. | The answer exists. The answer becomes the report, and no completion judge runs. |
| `TEST` | The phase starts as done, with a synthetic request report. Only the test stage runs. The closing gate and the format command are skipped. | The closing stages end, then completion runs. |
| `DOCS` | The same as `TEST`, with the docs stage only. | The closing stages end, then completion runs. |

For `TEST` and `DOCS`, the fold sets the closing choice to tests only or docs only, and it records format as already done. The runner writes the synthetic request report when the first agent needs it.

## The IMPLEMENT category from spec to completion

The `IMPLEMENT` category uses all the stages. The next diagram shows the order.

### Order of the IMPLEMENT stages

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[SessionCreated] --> B[classify judge]
  B --> C[explore tasks]
  C --> D[sufficiency judge when items are not covered]
  D --> E[track judge]
  E -->|light| H[inline phases]
  E -->|full| F[spec flow with approval]
  F --> G[stakes judge]
  G -->|low| H
  G -->|medium or high| P[plan flow with approval]
  P --> H
  H --> I[implementation review gate]
  I --> J[format then closing gate then tests and docs]
  J --> K[book]
  K --> L[completion judge]
  L --> M[SessionCompleted]
```

The planner code for this order is short. This excerpt shows the arm for `IMPLEMENT`.

```rust
Category::Implement => {
    if !self.explore_complete() { return; }
    let Some(track) = s.track else {
        self.push(Step::Judge { judge: JudgeKind::Track, subject: None });
        return;
    };
    if track == Track::Full {
        if !self.spec_flow(true) { return; }
        ...
        if stakes != Stakes::Low && !self.plan_flow() { return; }
    }
    self.phases();
    if !self.implementation_review() { return; }
    self.closing_stages();
    if self.all_implement_done() { self.completion(); }
}
```

Each flow method returns false until its stage is done. The planner then returns without a later step. Thus a later stage never starts before an earlier stage ends.

### Track and stakes

1. The track judge picks `light` or `full`. The New task form can set the track. If it does, the track judge does not run.
2. On the light track, the fold creates one inline phase for each project. The implementer gets the request and the research documents. No spec and no plan exist.
3. On the full track, the spec flow runs first. Then the stakes judge runs. If the stakes are `low`, the plan is skipped and the fold creates inline phases. Otherwise the plan flow runs.

### The spec flow

1. Spawn `generate-spec` (purpose `Spec { round }`).
2. If the spec has open questions that the user has not seen for this version, open the `OpenQuestions` gate (Rule D3). The fact-check waits for the answers. The gate text says that each answer is written back into the spec first, so the fact-check reads the final text.
3. Spawn `fact-check` (purpose `FactCheck { target, pass }`). The `source_check` input is `refetch` only on the first pass of a spec that has External Evidence rows. Otherwise it is `citations` (Rule D3b).
4. If the verdict is FAIL, the findings go back to `generate-spec`. After 3 FAILs in a row, the `FactCheckRecurring` gate opens.
5. If the verdict is PASS and the flow needs approval, open the `SpecApproval` gate. An approval needs a PASS on the current spec version. The method `Engine::answer_gate` rejects an approval without a PASS, and the fold also ignores it.

### The plan flow

1. Spawn `plan`. The plan agent reads the spec and its own earlier plan and nothing else (Rule D4).
2. If the plan has clarifying questions, open an `OpenQuestions` gate for the plan. The answers change requirements, so they go into the spec first, and the plan is written again (Rule D10).
3. Spawn `fact-check` for the plan. The source check is always `citations` (Rule D5).
4. Open the `PlanApproval` gate with the Phase Index. When the user approves, the fold calls `adopt_plan_phases`, which replaces the phase set.

### Phases

The method `Planner::phases` starts an idle phase only when two rules allow it:

- No other phase of the same project is busy (Rule M2).
- Every dependency has a finished implement loop (`deps_passed`). A phase with an unreadable `depends_on` value depends on every earlier phase (Rule M5).

Each phase runs a work loop of implement, review, fix, and `git add`. A blocked phase removes the idle phases that depend on it, and independent phases continue (`removed_phases`).

### Implementation review

When every phase that is not removed is terminal and nothing runs, the planner calls the feedback judge for each feedback round without a route. Then it opens the `ImplementationReview` gate (Rule F1). The runner writes the session context file before it appends this gate (Rule F2). The user answers `done` or `feedback` with text. A `feedback` answer creates revision phases and the flow goes back to the phases. A `done` answer sets `feedback.accepted`.

### Closing stages

The method `closing_stages` checks each project whose code is done and that has at least one passed phase:

1. Run the `Format` command once for the project. No gate guards it (Rule D8).
2. If the request set both `tests` and `docs`, either in the options or in the classify result, the gate is skipped (Rule T3). Otherwise the planner collects the projects that reach this point together into one `ClosingGate` gate (Rule T6). The answer is `GateAnswer::Closing` with one `tests` and `docs` choice for each project.
3. If tests are on, run the test stage. One `execution-path-analyzer` runs for each covered phase, in parallel. A phase is covered when it has no plan file or its test policy is `Required` (Rule T4). Then `write-test` runs for each covered phase, one after the other in phase order, and each has its own review loop (stage `TestReview`).
4. If docs are on and the tests are done, run the docs stage. One `documentation` execution runs for each project, at most `MAX_DOCS_WRITERS` (4) at the same time (Rule B7). An open BLOCKER finding blocks this stage (Hard rule 21).
5. After every part is written, a book of two or more projects gets one `system-architecture` execution (Rule B4). Then the planner returns `Step::WriteBook`. The engine writes the book files and no agent does (Rule B5).

### Completion

The method `completion` returns a step only when three conditions hold: nothing runs and only `Permission` gates are open, every created project has finished its init, and no coordination ask is open (Rule H9).

1. With no completion decision, the planner returns `Step::Judge` with `JudgeKind::Completion`.
2. With a decision, the planner returns `Step::Complete`. Its text is the `report_markdown` of the judge, plus a `Projects created` section when agents created projects (Rule O3).
3. The runner writes the report to `ostra-completion.md` in the session folder and appends `SessionCompleted`. The summary is the first non-empty line of the report, without the leading `#`.
4. The fold sets `completed`. The method `is_terminal` is now true, the driver task ends, and the console gets the push notice `Session complete`.

## How the console shows status and stage

The function `view::summary` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/view.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/view.rs) derives the session status. The first rule that matches wins.

| Order | Status | Condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `Completed` | `completed` is set. |
| 2 | `Failed` | `failed` is set. |
| 3 | `Paused` | `paused` is true. |
| 4 | `Waiting` | At least one gate is open and no execution runs. |
| 5 | `Running` | None of the above. |

The API type `SessionStatus` also has the value `stalled`. The function `summary` never returns it.

The function `inferred_stage` derives the lane and the label. The first rule that matches wins.

| Order | Condition | Lane | Label |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The session is completed. | Done | `Complete` |
| 2 | The session failed. | Done | `Stopped: ` and the first line of the error, at most 120 characters |
| 3 | Containment signals paused the session. | Lane of the execution stage | `Paused: read the <agent> execution's Activity, because it tripped 3 containment signals` |
| 4 | A gate is open. The last open gate counts. | Lane of the gate stage | `Waiting: ` and the gate title |
| 5 | An execution runs. The last one counts. | Lane of its stage | `Implementing phase N`, `Reviewing phase N, pass K`, `Reviewing tests of phase N, pass K`, `Writing tests for phase N`, or the stage label |
| 6 | A format or `git add` command runs. | Review | `Formatting <project>` or `Staging reviewed files in <project>` |
| 7 | The session has no category. | Research | `Classifying the request` |
| 8 | None of the above. | Research | `Working` |

A pause by the user sets the status to `Paused` but does not match rule 3. The label then comes from the later rules. The cost in the summary is the sum of the finished executions plus the cost of the judge calls.

The runner recomputes the summary after every event and stores it in the session row. The console reads the session list from these rows. You can also read the whole log with `GET /api/sessions/{id}/events`.

## What happens when

- **The classify judge returns output that does not match its schema.** The fold fails the session with `The Classify judge returned output that does not match its schema.`
- **The user sends context while the session runs.** Added context waits for the route-answer judge before any step starts. The page "Uploads, attached files, and context added during a session" explains this rule.
- **A rule ID in a code comment is unknown to you.** The comments cite rule IDs such as `Rule P1` and `Rule D3`. This repository does not contain the rule list. The comment next to each rule states it, and the conformance fixtures in [`tests/conformance/main.rs`](tests/conformance/main.rs) name tests by rule ID.

## Test the order of the stages

The fixtures in [`tests/conformance/main.rs`](tests/conformance/main.rs) build an event history, fold it, and compare the summaries of `next_steps`. Run them with `cargo test --workspace`. The test `d1_explore_leads_to_spec_never_plan` and the test `stakes_low_skips_plan` check the flow on this page.
