sections.title: Settings files and every setting
sections.summary: Ostra reads three TOML files and one database. The page lists every key of `config.toml`, `workspace.toml`, and `project.toml` with its default, unit, and storage place.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra has three settings files

A machine, a workspace, and a project need different choices. The machine holds provider keys and sandbox rules. The workspace holds routes, limits, and project folders. The project holds build commands. One file cannot serve all three scopes.

Trust is the second problem. A repository can carry `.ostra/` files into a clone. If those files could set the budget, the sandbox, or the guards, a repository could lift its own limits. Ostra keeps those settings in a database that no folder file can write.

This page covers:

- the three files and the database that hold settings
- every key of `config.toml`, with its default
- every key of `workspace.toml`, with its default
- the settings that Ostra keeps only in the registry
- every field of `project.toml`

The page *Save-time validation and when a change takes effect* lists the checks and the time of effect. The page *Routes: choosing executor, tier, model, and effort* explains the `routing` keys.

## The three files and the registry

The Rust types for all three files are in [`crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs). The registry is the SQLite database `registry.db`. It is not a settings file, but it holds the settings that a folder file cannot set.

| Name | Path | Rust type | Scope | Written by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Global config | `$OSTRA_CONFIG`, else `<config dir>/ostra/config.toml` | `GlobalConfig` | One machine | The user. Ostra writes the default file when none exists. |
| Workspace settings | `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.toml` | `WorkspaceSettings` | One workspace | Ostra on each save, or the user by hand |
| Project profile | `<project>/.ostra/project.toml` | `ProjectProfile` | One project | The initializer agent |
| Registry | `registry.db` in the data dir | none | One machine | Ostra |

The data dir is `$OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, else `<data local dir>/ostra`. The command `ostra config` prints the path of the global config. It writes the default file first when none exists. The server does the same when it starts (`ensure_global_config`). The default file lists every key, so the user can edit it in place.

### Environment variables that move or switch settings

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_CONFIG` | Path of the global config file |
| `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` | Data dir that holds `registry.db` and the price cache |
| `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` | Master key file. No agent can read it. |
| `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` | Price catalog URL. An empty value turns the fetch off. |
| `OSTRA_LOG` | Log filter. The default is `info`. |

### How Ostra loads and saves a file

Every settings struct has `#[serde(default)]`. A key that is absent from the file takes its default from the struct. Ostra ignores a misspelled key without an error, so check each key name against this page.

- `load_toml` returns the default value when the file does not exist. It returns a `ConfigError` when the file cannot be read or parsed.
- `load_toml_required` returns an error when the file does not exist.
- `save_toml` writes `<name>.toml.tmp` and renames it over the target. A reader never sees a half-written file.

### What happens when a file is missing or broken

- **The global config is missing at start.** The server writes the default file.
- **The global config cannot be parsed at start.** `build` fails and the server does not start.
- **The `[sandbox]` table fails its checks at start.** The server does not start and names the key.
- **The global config breaks after the server runs.** `Shared::global()` logs a warning and returns the last good copy.
- **`workspace.toml` cannot be read or parsed.** Ostra logs a warning and uses `WorkspaceSettings::seeded("workspace")`. The registry values still apply on top.
- **`project.toml` is missing or invalid.** The callers use an empty profile, so the repo brief has no commands.

> Back up `workspace.toml` before you edit it by hand. When the file does not parse, Ostra replaces your settings with the seeded defaults, and your routes and projects stop applying.

## Global config: `config.toml`

The global config holds what is true for the whole machine. Ostra reads it again on every call, so most edits apply without a restart. The page *Save-time validation and when a change takes effect* lists the exceptions.

> Write every table that you change in full. When the file has a `tiers`, `providers`, `harness`, or `permissions` table, Ostra uses the file value and does not merge the default. A file with only `[tiers.native]` has no `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy` table, and a route to those executors then fails.

### Top-level key

| Key | Default | Choices | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tool_enforcement` | `disabled` | `disabled`, `enabled` | Rule G1. A workspace can replace it. |

The value `enabled` adds four layer-1 checks: write scope, the report path, self-protection, and the shell and interpreter checks behind them. The value `disabled` lets an agent reach files by any route, such as one script that edits many files. These guards stay on in both modes: secret reads, git metadata, state ownership, artifact ownership, and the no-tests guard. The workflow gates, the permission rules, and the sandbox also stay on. The page *Two layers and the guard catalog* explains each guard.

### Providers: `[providers.<name>]`

A provider table tells Ostra where to find the key and the base URL of a native model provider.

| Key | Default for `anthropic` | Default for `openai` | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_key_env` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | Variable that holds the API key |
| `auth_token_env` | `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` | none | Variable that holds a bearer token. Ostra uses it when no API key is set. |
| `keychain_service` | none | none | OS keychain service that holds the key |
| `base_url` | none | none | Fixed base URL. It wins over every other source. |
| `base_url_env` | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | Variable that holds the base URL |

Ostra looks for a key in this order and stops at the first hit:

1. The variable that `api_key_env` names. The status source is `env:NAME`.
2. The variable that `auth_token_env` names. Ostra sends it as `Authorization: Bearer`.
3. The saved API key, then the saved bearer token. The status source is `saved`.
4. The OS keychain entry of `keychain_service`. The status source is `keychain`.

The base URL follows a similar order: `base_url`, then the `base_url_env` variable, then the saved URL, then the provider default. The saved values are the credentials that a user enters in the browser. Ostra keeps them in the registry as `SavedCredentials`, and the variables override them. The `Debug` output of `SavedCredentials` prints `***` in place of a secret.

### Tier tables: `[tiers.<table>]`

A tier table maps the four tier names to a model for one executor. The table name is `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`. The page *Routes: choosing executor, tier, model, and effort* explains how a route reads these tables.

| Table | `fast` | `balanced` | `advanced` | `frontier` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `native` | `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` | `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-fable-5-1` |
| `claude` | `haiku` | `sonnet` | `opus` | `fable` |
| `codex` | `gpt-5.6-luna` | `gpt-5.6-terra` | `gpt-5.6-sol` | `gpt-5.6-sol` |
| `grok` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` |
| `agy` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` |

A `native` entry must have the form `provider:model`. A harness entry is the model name that the harness CLI accepts.

### Harness commands: `[harness.<name>]`

The name is `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`. The default `command` is the harness name, and the default `args` list is empty. Ostra adds `args` to every launch of that CLI. When `command` is empty, Ostra uses the harness name (`GlobalConfig::harness_command`). Set `command` to an absolute path when the CLI is not on `PATH`.

### Permission rules: `[permissions]`

The keys `allow`, `ask`, and `deny` hold rule strings such as `Bash(git push *)`. The default is `deny = ["Bash(rm -rf /*)"]`, and the other two lists are empty. For each execution, Ostra joins the global rules and the workspace rules into one list. The global rules come first (`PermissionRules::merged`). The page *Permission modes, rules, and approvals* explains how a rule matches a call.

### Server: `[server]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `port` | none | Fixed port. When absent, Ostra tries the ports 7878 to 7897, then asks the OS for a free port. |
| `bind` | none, so `127.0.0.1` | Listen address. It accepts an IP address, `localhost`, `all`, or `*`. The values `all`, `*`, `0.0.0.0`, and `::` listen on every interface. |
| `allowed_hosts` | `[]` | More host names that the browser can use, such as the domain of a reverse proxy |
| `use_ip_host` | `false` | Sign in at `127.0.0.1` in place of a private `ostra-....localhost` name |

The command-line flags `--port`, `--bind`, and `--allow-host` override or extend these keys. The server reads this table only when it starts, so restart the server after a change.

> Set `use_ip_host` to `true` only for a browser that cannot resolve `*.localhost`. The session cookie then reaches every other port on the machine, because cookies are not scoped to a port.

A `bind` address that is not a loopback address makes the server print a warning. The traffic is plain HTTP, and anyone with a sign-in link can run commands as the user.

### Sandbox: `[sandbox]`

This table sets the sandbox profile for agent commands: the native Bash tool, harness CLIs, and programs that Ostra starts for a project.

| Key | Default | Choices or format | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | `required` on Linux and macOS, `auto` on Windows | `auto`, `required`, `off` | `auto` sandboxes when the machine can and runs unsandboxed with a warning otherwise. `required` refuses to start an execution that cannot be sandboxed. |
| `network` | `allowlist` | `none`, `allowlist`, `public`, `host` | What sandboxed programs reach |
| `allowed_hosts` | `[]` | `host`, `*.domain`, or either with `:port` | More hosts that the egress proxy lets through under `allowlist` |
| `upstream_proxy` | none | `http://host:port` | An HTTP proxy that the egress proxy connects through |
| `extra_writable` | `[]` | Absolute path or `~/...` | More paths that agent commands can write |
| `extra_hidden` | `[]` | Absolute path or `~/...` | More paths that agent commands cannot see |

The default for `mode` is `auto` on Windows because Windows has no sandbox backend yet. A default of `required` there would refuse every execution.

The four `network` choices:

- `none` gives no network. A harness CLI still reaches its own model API.
- `allowlist` allows package registries, source hosts, the model API of a harness, and `allowed_hosts`.
- `public` allows any public address. Loopback, private, and link-local addresses stay refused.
- `host` uses the host network without a filter.

Every choice except `host` gives each sandbox its own network namespace. Traffic then leaves only through the egress proxy of Ostra. The `loopback` and `blocked_ports` fields of `SandboxConfig` have `#[serde(skip)]`. Ostra never reads them from `config.toml` because they are workspace settings. The page *Sandbox settings, modes, and failure cases* explains the behavior.

## Workspace settings: `workspace.toml`

The workspace file holds the choices of one workspace. Ostra writes it on every save from the console. The user can also edit it. The constructor `WorkspaceSettings::seeded(name)` makes the defaults for a new workspace.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `workspace` | Workspace name. Validation refuses an empty name. |
| `projects` | `[]` | `[[projects]]` entries. See the table below. |
| `routing.executor` | empty, so every agent is native | Executor per agent, with `byAgent` and `byPhaseComplexity` |
| `routing.model` | seeded tiers | Tier or model per agent, with `byAgent` and `byPhaseComplexity` |
| `routing.effort` | empty | Reasoning effort per agent, with `byAgent` and `byPhaseComplexity` |
| `instructions.all` | none | Text that every agent receives |
| `instructions.agents.<agent>` | `{}` | Text that one agent receives |
| `permissions.allow`, `.ask`, `.deny` | `[]` | Workspace permission rules |
| `notifications.push` | `true` | Push notifications for gates and finished sessions |
| `mcp_servers` | `[]` | `[[mcp_servers]]` entries. See the table below. |

The `instructions` text goes into the first message of each agent. For one agent, Ostra sends `instructions.all` first and then the entry of that agent. Blank text is ignored. An instruction can name an artifact with a tag, and validation refuses a tag that names a hidden or missing artifact (Rule W3).

The `permissions.mode` key is also part of the settings JSON, but Ostra stores it in the registry. See the next section.

### Project entries: `[[projects]]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | required | Project key. Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes, with a letter or digit first. |
| `path` | required | Absolute folder of the project |
| `stack` | none | Free text of at most 64 characters, such as `rust` or `elixir-phoenix`. It seeds skills for an empty folder. |
| `code_provider` | none | A program that answers code navigation for the Files view. It has `command` (a list) and `timeout_secs`. |
| `language_servers` | `[]` | Language servers for code navigation. Each has `command`, `languages`, `timeout_secs`, and `initialization_options`. |

The `timeout_secs` of a code provider and of a language server defaults to 10 seconds and must be from 1 to 120 seconds (`MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT`). When a request takes longer, Ostra answers with the built-in code index. The order of the three code sources is: `code_provider`, then the language server of the file language, then the built-in index.

### MCP servers: `[[mcp_servers]]`

An MCP server entry names an external server whose tools every executor can call. Set `command` for a local server over stdio, or `url` for a remote server over streamable HTTP. Do not set both.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | required | Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. At most 24 characters. |
| `enabled` | `true` | Switch for the server |
| `command` | `[]` | Program and arguments of a local server, run in the workspace root |
| `env` | `{}` | Environment of a local server |
| `url` | none | Address of a remote server |
| `headers` | `{}` | Request headers of a remote server |
| `oauth` | none | OAuth client settings: `client_id`, `client_secret_env`, `scopes` |
| `disabled_tools` | `[]` | Tools that agents do not get |
| `agents` | `[]` | Agents that get the tools. An empty list means every agent. |
| `timeout_secs` | `120` | Seconds that one tool call can take. The range is 1 to 600. |

A value of `env` or `headers` can name the server environment as `${VAR}`, so a secret stays out of the file. The page *External MCP client, OAuth, and Web Push* explains the connection.

### Excerpt of a `workspace.toml`

```toml
name = "shop"

[[projects]]
key = "backend"
path = "/home/me/code/shop-backend"
stack = "rust"

[routing.executor.byAgent]
implementer = "harness:codex"

[routing.model.byAgent]
plan = "advanced"
quick-answer = { native = "anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5" }

[permissions]
allow = ["Bash(./mvnw *)"]
deny = ["Bash(git push *)"]
```

An excerpt like this one is not a complete file. A complete file has a model route for every agent, and validation reports each missing route.

## Registry-only settings

Ten settings never go into `workspace.toml`. Ostra keeps them in the registry as one JSON record under the key `workspace_access:<canonical workspace root>`. This is Rule A2.

| Setting | Default | Choices or unit | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `permissions.mode` | `default` | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `bypass` | `default` asks for edits and unlisted commands. `acceptEdits` allows edits inside the project. `plan` is read-only. `bypass` asks nothing. |
| `yolo.default` | `false` | `true`, `false` | New sessions start in YOLO mode |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | `3` | Count of executions, at least 1 | Executions that run at the same time in the workspace |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | `25.0` | US dollars. `0` means no limit. | Spend at which a session pauses for a decision |
| `sandbox_mode` | none, so follow the global config | `auto`, `required`, `off` | Replaces `[sandbox] mode` |
| `tool_enforcement` | none, so follow the global config | `disabled`, `enabled` | Replaces the global `tool_enforcement` |
| `sandbox_network` | none, so follow the global config | `none`, `allowlist`, `public`, `host` | Replaces `[sandbox] network` |
| `sandbox_allowed_hosts` | `[]` | Same format as the global list | Added to the global hosts |
| `sandbox_decoys` | `[]` | `~/` file paths. At most 32. | Added to the built-in decoy credential files |
| `sandbox_loopback` | `open` | `open`, `listed` | Loopback ports that sandboxed commands on macOS can reach |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` | `[]` | Ports 1 to 65535. At most 64. | Loopback ports that sandboxed commands on macOS never reach |

The reason for Rule A2 is in the code comment: without it, a repository could lift its own budget, turn off its own guards, open its own sandbox, or plant decoys that pause every session.

The mechanism has three parts:

1. `trust::set_access` writes the ten values to the registry when Ostra saves the workspace.
2. `trust::write_file` removes the ten keys from the TOML before it writes `workspace.toml`.
3. `trust::overlay` copies the registry values over the file values each time Ostra loads the settings.

Because of step 3, a hand-written value in `workspace.toml` for one of these keys has no effect. The console shows and saves the ten values as normal fields of the settings JSON. When no registry record exists, Ostra uses the defaults in the table.

### How a workspace value combines with the global value

`SandboxConfig::for_workspace` and `WorkspaceSettings::enforces_tool_calls` build the effective values:

- **Mode and network:** the workspace value replaces the global value when the workspace sets one.
- **Allowed hosts:** the workspace hosts are added to the global hosts. A workspace never removes a global host or a built-in host.
- **Decoys:** the workspace decoys are added to the built-in decoys. A workspace cannot remove a built-in decoy.
- **Loopback choice and blocked ports:** these come from the workspace only.
- **Tool enforcement:** the workspace value, else the global value.

The page *Trust approvals and registry-only settings* explains the approval of commands that a folder file names. The page *Sandbox settings, modes, and failure cases* explains the effect of each sandbox value.

## Project profile: `project.toml`

The initializer agent writes `project.toml` when it initializes a project. The profile tells later agents how to build, test, and format the project. Ostra checks the file at the last step of an init: the `generate-inventory` submit calls `check_profile`, so the agent can fix the file while it still runs.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | number | Write `1` |
| `generated_at` | string | Time of generation |
| `stack` | string | The name of the stack, such as `rust` or `python-django` |
| `build_tool` | string | Build tool, such as `cargo` |
| `[commands]` | table | `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `format`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `run` |
| `test_framework` | string | Test framework name |
| `[test_types.<name>]` | tables | `command`, `command_one`, `matches` (globs), `note`, `reports` |
| `[[module_map]]` | rows | `glob` and `area` |
| `[[skills]]` | rows | `name`, `kind`, `path`, `component_type`, `source` |
| `[conventions]` | table | `immutability_keyword`, `naming`, `notes` |
| `[[review_rules]]` | rows | `id`, `rule`, `severity`, `auto_fixable` |

The `kind` of a skill is `convention`, `creation`, `test`, or `other`. The `source` is `generated`, `reused`, `adopted`, or `user`. The `severity` of a review rule is `H`, `M`, or `L`.

```toml
schema_version = 1
stack = "rust"
build_tool = "cargo"

[commands]
build = "cargo build --workspace"
test = "cargo test --workspace"
format = "cargo fmt --all"
```

### Who reads the profile

- **The repo brief** lists the commands, test types, skills, conventions, review rules, and the module map for the agent. `Commands::entries` drops a command that is empty or that holds the placeholder `—` (U+2014).
- **The native executor** builds its policy inputs from the profile. The build commands are `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `lint`, and `typecheck`. The test commands are `test` and `test_one`.
- **The review spawn** receives the ids from `ProjectProfile::auto_fixable_ids`. A rule id that starts with `SEC-BLOCK` or `PHASE-REQ` is never auto-fixable, even when the profile says it is.
- **The console** shows the profile in `ProjectView.profile`.

A project `[commands].format` command runs only after the user approves it. The approval is a trust topic, and the page *Trust approvals and registry-only settings* explains it.

### Shapes that `check_profile` corrects

Models often copy JSON shapes into TOML. `check_profile` returns a fix for each of these before it returns the parser text, because some harnesses clip a long tool error:

- `key = null`: TOML has no null. Omit the key.
- `[[conventions]]`: write `[conventions]`, because `conventions` is one table.
- `[stack]` or `[[stack]]`: write `stack = "rust"` and put `build_tool` at the top level.
- `schema_version = "1"`: write the number `1`.

Older projects can still carry a `[stack]` table with `language`, `frameworks`, and `build_tool`. The reader folds it into `stack` as `language/framework1,framework2`. A `build_tool` inside that table is used when the top level has none.

code_refs.note: Global config types and the defaults in `GlobalConfig::default`.
Workspace settings, `seeded` defaults, `SETTING_KEYS`, and `instructions_for`.
Project profile types, `check_profile`, and `auto_fixable_ids`.
`load_toml`, `load_toml_required`, and the atomic `save_toml`.
Registry-only settings: `Access`, `set_access`, `overlay`, and `write_file`.
`bind_addr`, `access`, and `Shared::global`, which keeps the last good config.

sections.title: Save-time validation and when a change takes effect
sections.summary: Ostra refuses a workspace save that has any problem and reports every problem at once. The page lists each rule, the missing-route fixes, and the time at which each setting takes effect.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra validates at save time

A route that does not resolve is a settings error. If Ostra found it at spawn time, the execution would end as `denied` in the middle of a session. The module comment of `config.rs` states the rule: Ostra shows the error at save time. The sandbox validator states the same rule: a value that the sandbox cannot enforce is an issue at save time and never a silent fallback at spawn time.

This page covers:

- the save flow and the shape of an issue
- every validation rule, with its limit
- the fixes that Ostra applies on its own
- the time at which each setting takes effect

The page *Settings files and every setting* lists the keys. The page *Routes: choosing executor, tier, model, and effort* explains the route rules.

## The save flow

The console saves settings with `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}`. The route `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/validate` runs the same checks and saves nothing.

### Sequence of a settings save

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant API as patch_workspace
    participant RT as WorkspaceRt
    participant VAL as validate_settings
    participant TRUST as trust
    Browser->>API: PATCH workspace settings
    API->>RT: save_settings
    RT->>VAL: validate
    VAL-->>RT: list of ValidationIssue
    alt the list has issues
        RT-->>API: Err with the issues
        API-->>Browser: 422 ApiError with issues
    else the list is empty
        RT->>TRUST: save_workspace
        TRUST-->>RT: file and registry written
        RT->>RT: sync_projects
        API-->>Browser: 200 WorkspaceDetail
    end
```

`WorkspaceRt::save_settings` collects the issues. If the list is not empty, it writes nothing and returns the whole list. After a successful write, `sync_projects` mirrors the project list to the `projects` table of `workspace.db`. A write failure returns one issue with an empty `path`.

The API answers an invalid save with status 422. The body is `ApiError`: the text `The settings have problems. Fix them and save again.` and the list `issues`.

### The shape of an issue

A `ValidationIssue` has two fields: `path` and `message`. The `path` is a dotted settings path, such as `routing.model.byAgent.plan` or `projects[0].key`. Ostra sorts the issues by `path` and then by `message`, and it removes duplicates. Each message starts with the correction, such as `Write ... as ...`, and then gives the reason after `because`. The console shows the message next to the field.

## Validation rules

Three functions run the checks: `validate_workspace` in `ostra-core`, and `validate_settings` and `WorkspaceRt::validate` in `ostra-workspace`. `validate_settings` also calls `ostra_sandbox::validate::workspace`, the permission rule parser, and the MCP checks.

### Identity and projects

| Path | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Not empty after trimming |
| `projects[i].key` | Matches `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`. Each key is used once. |
| `projects[i].path` | Absolute, or rooted. A rooted path without a drive counts as absolute so that configs stay portable across systems. |
| `projects[i].path` | An absolute path must be an existing folder |
| `projects[i].stack` | After trimming, at most 64 characters (`MAX_STACK_LEN`) and no control character. An empty stack is valid. |
| `projects[i].code_provider.command` | The first item is not empty |
| `projects[i].code_provider.timeout_secs` | From 1 to 120 |
| `projects[i].language_servers[j].command` | The first item is not empty |
| `projects[i].language_servers[j].languages` | Not empty. Each id is in `NAV_LANGUAGES`. One server per language in a project, because each file asks one server. |
| `projects[i].language_servers[j].timeout_secs` | From 1 to 120 |

### Routing

| Path | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `routing.executor.byAgent.<key>` | The key is a route key or a retired agent name |
| `routing.model.byAgent.<key>` | The key is a route key or a retired agent name |
| `routing.effort.byAgent.<key>` | The key is an agent name (not `judge`) or a retired agent name |
| `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity.<key>` | The agent must route by complexity: `implementer` or `write-test` |
| `routing.executor.byAgent.judge` | Refused, because judge calls always run natively |
| `routing.executor.byAgent.quick-answer` | Only `native`, because quick answers run on the native executor only |
| every route key on every complexity | `resolve_route` must succeed |
| `routing.executor.byAgent.<key>` | A harness route needs the harness installed on this machine |
| `routing.model.byAgent.<key>` | A native route needs a provider with a usable key. The provider `mock` is exempt. |

A route key is an agent name or `judge`. The check runs `resolve_route` for each of the 15 route keys. The two agents that route by complexity run it for `low`, `medium`, and `high`, so the check makes 19 resolutions. A resolution error gets the suffix ` (low)`, ` (medium)`, or ` (high)` in its message.

> The validator does not check the agent names under `routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity` and `routing.model.byPhaseComplexity`. A misspelled name never matches. Ostra then falls back to `byAgent` without an error.

### Limits

| Path | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | At least 1 |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | A finite number, 0 or more. `0` means no limit. |

### MCP servers

| Path | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `mcp_servers[i].name` | Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. A letter first. At most 24 characters (`MAX_SERVER_NAME`). Not `ostra`. Used once. |
| `mcp_servers[i].command`, `.url` | Set exactly one. The first item of `command` is not empty. |
| `mcp_servers[i].url` | Starts with `http://` or `https://` |
| `mcp_servers[i].headers`, `.oauth` | Only with `url`. Pass secrets to a local server in `env`. |
| `mcp_servers[i].agents` | Each entry is an agent name |
| `mcp_servers[i].timeout_secs` | From 1 to 600 (`MAX_TIMEOUT_SECS`) |

The name rule has a reason: the double underscore (`__`) splits the server name from the tool name, so a server name cannot hold one.

### Sandbox entries

| Path | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `sandbox_allowed_hosts[i]` | A host name, `*.domain`, or an IP address, with an optional `:port`. A URL is not a host. A loopback host needs a port, because programs connect to loopback directly and the sandbox forwards only the listed ports. |
| `sandbox_decoys[i]` | A file path that starts with `~/`. It is not the sign-in file of a harness CLI, because a decoy there would sign that CLI out in the sandbox. |
| `sandbox_decoys` | At most 32 entries (`MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS`), because each is a watched file and a mount in every agent sandbox |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports[i]` | A port from 1 to 65535 |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` | At most 64 ports (`MAX_BLOCKED_PORTS`), because each is a rule in every sandbox policy |

### Permission rules and instructions

| Path | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `permissions.allow[i]`, `.ask[i]`, `.deny[i]` | `validate_rule` parses the rule. A path pattern of an Edit or Read rule must compile. A WebFetch rule must have the form `WebFetch(domain:example.com)`. |
| `instructions.all`, `instructions.agents.<agent>` | An artifact tag must name an artifact that every agent can read (Rule W3) |

### Global config checks

Ostra validates only the `[sandbox]` table of `config.toml`, with `ostra_sandbox::validate::global`:

- Each path of `extra_writable` and `extra_hidden` must be absolute or start with `~/`, and must not hold a NUL character. A relative path would depend on where an execution starts.
- Each `allowed_hosts` entry follows the host rule above.
- `upstream_proxy` must have the form `http://host:port`, without a path or credentials, because the egress proxy connects to it with plain HTTP CONNECT.

## Missing routes and their fixes

A new release can add an agent. A workspace saved before that release has no model route for it. `keys_without_route` finds each route key that has no model route. For an agent that routes by complexity, the key is listed when any of the three complexities has no route.

Three functions turn the finding into a fix:

1. `settings_fixes` makes one `SettingsFix` for each key: `path` is `routing.model.byAgent.<key>`, and `value` is `default`. The label is ``Route `key` to its default tier (tier)``.
2. `WorkspaceDetail.fixes` carries the list to the console, which shows a button.
3. `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/settings/fix` calls `WorkspaceRt::apply_fixes`. It inserts each value and saves the file.

`apply_fixes` does not validate the other settings. An unrelated problem must not block a fix. The value `default` is safe because every agent has a default tier in its `agent.toml`.

## What happens when

- **A save has three problems.** Ostra returns all three in one 422 answer and writes nothing.
- **The machine changes after a save.** A harness is uninstalled, or a provider key is removed. The saved file is unchanged, but `WorkspaceDetail.validation` lists the new issue, because Ostra computes it for each `detail()` call. The next save is refused until the user fixes it.
- **A save passes, but the global config changes later.** A route can fail at spawn time. The engine then records an execution with the status `denied` and the error `route: ...`.
- **A save arrives while the file waits for approval.** The file keeps waiting. A save cannot approve commands that the user did not see. The page *Trust approvals and registry-only settings* explains this.
- **`workspace.toml` is edited by hand.** Ostra does not validate the file at load time. Validation runs when the user saves or when `detail()` builds the validation list.

## When a change takes effect

Ostra has no settings cache for a workspace. `WorkspaceRt::settings()` and `ServerServices::settings()` read `workspace.toml` and the registry on each call. The global config is also read again on each call. The table shows when each setting reaches running work.

| Setting | Read by | Takes effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Any `config.toml` key, except those below | `Shared::global()` | On the next call. No restart. A broken file keeps the last good copy. |
| `[server]` | `run` and `access` | When the server starts |
| `[providers]` | `Providers::from_config`, `reload_providers` | When the server starts, and after the user saves provider credentials in the browser |
| `[harness]` | The harness executor at spawn | At the next spawn |
| `routing.*` | `resolve_route` and `resolve_effort` at spawn | At the next spawn. A running execution keeps its route. |
| `instructions.*` | The spawn factory | At the next spawn |
| `yolo.default` | Session start | For sessions that start later. A running session keeps its own flag, and the `SetYolo` call changes it. |
| `permissions.*`, `tool_enforcement`, `sandbox_*` | `ExecContext` built at execution start | At the next execution start. A running execution does not change. |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | `acquire_slot` | Within 2 seconds for waiting spawns. Running executions are not cancelled. |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | `plan_ctx` | At the next planning pass. A value of `0` turns the limit off. |
| `notifications.push` | `notify` | At the next notice |
| `projects` | `sync_projects` | On open and on each save |

The spend that the budget compares with counts finished executions only. A running execution is counted when it finishes (`SessionState::spent_usd`).

The slot limit follows this rule: a waiting spawn checks the limit again when a slot becomes free and at least every 2 seconds. If you increase the limit, waiting spawns start within 2 seconds. If you decrease it, Ostra cancels nothing, and new spawns wait until the count is below the new limit. The page *Failure, restart, stop, pause, and concurrency* explains slots in full.

### Test the settings from the command line

Use these commands to check the behavior that this page describes:

- Run `cargo test -p ostra-core` to run the validation and route tests.
- Run `cargo test -p ostra-workspace` to run the tests of `agent_infos` and the trust overlay.

sections.title: Routes: choosing executor, tier, model, and effort
sections.summary: `resolve_route` turns an agent name into an executor and a model. The page explains each step, the tier tables, complexity routing, effort, the overrides, and the fixes for a missing route.
sections.body:
## The problem a route solves

Ostra has 14 agents, 5 executors, and 4 tiers. Each execution needs one executor, one model, and one reasoning effort. A user wants to change them without a code change, for example to run the implementer on Codex with a cheap model for easy phases. A wrong route that Ostra finds at spawn time stops a session in the middle. The route rules therefore live in one function, and the settings validation runs the same function at save time.

This page covers:

- the terms of a route
- the steps of `resolve_route`, with the reason for each
- complexity routing for the implementer and the test writer
- effort
- overrides that the engine applies
- the seeded routes, and the fixes for a missing route

## Terms

- **Route key:** the name that the route settings use for an execution. It is an agent name or `judge`. There are 15 route keys (`route_keys`).
- **Executor:** what runs the execution: `native` (the loop of Ostra) or `harness:<name>` for the CLI `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`.
- **Tier:** a model class. The four tiers are `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, and `frontier`.
- **Tier table:** the table `[tiers.<table>]` of the global config. It maps each tier to a model for one executor. The table name is `executor.tier_table()`: `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`.
- **Complexity:** the `**Complexity:**` value of a plan phase: `low`, `medium`, or `high`. Work with no phase file counts as `low`.
- **Route:** the result, a `ResolvedRoute` with `executor`, `model`, and `tier`. The `model` is `provider:model` for native and the CLI model name for a harness. The `tier` is empty when the route names a concrete model.

## The three route settings

The `routing` table of `workspace.toml` has three parts. Each has the keys `byAgent` and `byPhaseComplexity`.

| Setting | Value of an entry | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `routing.executor` | `native` or `harness:<claude\|codex\|grok\|agy>` | Empty. Every agent runs native. |
| `routing.model` | A tier name, `default`, a concrete model, or a per-executor table | Seeded. See below. |
| `routing.effort` | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max` | Empty. The agent definition decides. |

The `byAgent` table maps a route key to a value. The `byPhaseComplexity` table maps a route key and a complexity to a value, such as `routing.model.byPhaseComplexity.implementer.high`. An entry in `byPhaseComplexity` wins over the `byAgent` entry for the same key.

A model value has four forms:

- A tier name, such as `advanced`. Ostra reads the model from the tier table of the executor.
- `default`. Ostra uses the default tier of the agent from its `agent.toml`.
- A concrete model, such as `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5` or `gpt-5.6-sol`.
- A per-executor table, such as `{ native = "anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5", codex = "gpt-5.6-terra" }`. The key is the tier table name.

## How `resolve_route` works

The caller passes a `RouteQuery`: the route key, the default tier of the agent, the complexity, an optional `tier_override`, and an optional `executor_override`.

### Decision steps of `resolve_route`

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["RouteQuery"] --> B{"executor_override set?"}
    B -->|yes| D["Use the override"]
    B -->|no| C["resolve_executor"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["Select the tier table of the executor"]
    E --> F{"tier_override set?"}
    F -->|yes| G["from_tier with the override"]
    F -->|no| H{"Model route found?"}
    H -->|no| X["RouteError: no model route"]
    H -->|yes| I{"Kind of value"}
    I -->|default| J["from_tier with default_tier"]
    I -->|tier name| K["from_tier with that tier"]
    I -->|model text| L["Use the text as the model"]
    I -->|per-executor table| M["Read the entry of the table name"]
    G --> N["check_model, then ResolvedRoute"]
    J --> N
    K --> N
    L --> N
    M --> N
```

The steps in order:

1. **Executor.** `executor_override` wins. Otherwise `resolve_executor` runs. It returns `native` for the key `judge`, because the judge is an engine call and not an agent execution. For other keys it reads `routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity[key][complexity]`, then `routing.executor.byAgent[key]`, then falls back to `native`.
2. **Tier table.** Ostra selects `[tiers.<table>]` from the global config with the executor name.
3. **Tier override.** If the query has a `tier_override`, Ostra reads that tier from the table and stops. The model route is not read.
4. **Model route.** Ostra reads `routing.model.byPhaseComplexity[key][complexity]`, then `routing.model.byAgent[key]`. If neither exists, the result is an error.
5. **Value.** A tier name or `default` reads the tier table. Other text is the model. A per-executor table must have an entry for the tier table name. That entry is a tier name or a model.
6. **Model check.** `check_model` refuses an empty model. For the native executor, the model must have the form `provider:model` with the provider `anthropic`, `openai`, or `mock`.

The tier name is trimmed before the match, and the match is exact. `default` has no special meaning in a per-executor table. Ostra treats it as a model name there.

### Reasons for the rules

- `byPhaseComplexity` wins over `byAgent` so that a user can set a general route and then override one complexity.
- The `judge` always runs natively because it is a call that the engine makes, not an agent with tools.
- The settings validation calls `resolve_route` for each key, so an error appears at save time.
- The native check exists because the native executor needs a provider name to pick the client.
- A harness model is not checked, because Ostra does not know the model names of a CLI.

### Example from the tests

The test `parses_sample_and_routes` uses this workspace excerpt. The implementer runs on Codex for `low` and `medium`, and natively for `high`.

```toml
[routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity.implementer]
low = "harness:codex"
medium = "harness:codex"
high = "native"

[routing.model.byPhaseComplexity.implementer]
low = "fast"
medium = "fast"
high = "balanced"
```

With the default global config, `low` resolves to the Codex `fast` entry: `gpt-5.6-luna`. The `high` case resolves to the native `balanced` entry: `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5`.

## Tier tables

The default tier tables are in the page *Settings files and every setting*. Two facts matter for routing. First, the table name comes from the executor and not from the agent, so one tier name gives a different model on each executor. Second, a tier that is missing from the table gives this error: ``key routes to tier `balanced` on `native`, but `[tiers.native]` in the global config has no `balanced` entry``.

The `RoutingPreset` choices of the setup wizard use this design. `RoutingPreset::apply` replaces only the executor routes. The preset `codex` or `claude` puts `implementer` and `write-test` on that harness. The model routes stay, because the same tier names resolve per executor. The preset `native` clears the executor routes.

## Complexity routing

Two agents route by complexity: `implementer` and `write-test` (`AgentName::routes_by_complexity`). The plan gives each phase a `**Complexity:**` line, and the engine passes it as `RouteQuery.complexity`. Work with no phase file has no complexity, and Ostra treats it as `low` (`Complexity::default`).

The seeded model routes for these agents are:

| Complexity | Tier |
| --- | --- |
| `low` | `fast` |
| `medium` | `fast` |
| `high` | `balanced` |

The reason is cost. A phase that the plan marks as easy runs on a cheaper tier, and a hard phase gets a stronger one. The `default_tier` of both agents in `agent.toml` is `balanced`.

A `byAgent` entry covers all three complexities, because the lookup falls back to it. The validator and `keys_without_route` need a route on all three complexities for these two agents. A seeded workspace has all three.

## Effort

Effort is the reasoning level of a run. `resolve_effort` reads it from the settings:

1. `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity[key][complexity]`
2. `routing.effort.byAgent[key]`
3. If neither exists, the result is empty.

When the result is empty, the spawn factory calls `effort_for(agent, executor)`. That function reads the `[effort]` table of the `agent.toml` of the agent with the key of the tier table name. If the table has no entry, it reads the `native` entry. If that is also missing, the effort is `high`. The implementer, for example, has `high` on every executor.

The five effort values, from low to high, are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max`. An older settings file can hold a flat table, such as `[routing.effort]` with `plan = "high"`. Ostra reads a flat table as `byAgent`. Ostra always writes the split form. A value that is not one of the five values makes the file fail to parse with this error: `routing.effort takes byAgent and byPhaseComplexity tables of low, medium, high, xhigh, or max`.

The validator refuses `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity.<key>` for an agent that does not run per phase. The error says to set the effort under `byAgent`. The judge call always uses `low` effort, and no setting changes it.

## Overrides that the engine applies

The engine can force a part of the route, whatever the settings say:

- **Tier override.** The initializer in the `generate-skill` mode runs on `advanced`.
- **Native after a harness failure.** `SessionState::forced_executor` returns `native` for an agent that is in `native_fallback`.
- **Quick change.** A session of the category `QuickChange` runs on `native`, because that skips the start cost of a harness.
- **Quick answer.** The `quick-answer` agent runs on `native`, because it serves the side panel.
- **Continuation.** A paused run and a run that continues another run keep the executor and model of the earlier run. This keeps the prompt cache.

The forced executor is an `executor_override`. It changes the tier table, so the same tier name gives the native model in that case.

## Seeded routes

`WorkspaceSettings::seeded` gives each route key a model route. Settings of a new workspace have these `routing.model.byAgent` entries:

| Tier | Route keys |
| --- | --- |
| `advanced` | `explore`, `generate-spec`, `plan`, `fact-check`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`, `prompt-generation`, `judge`, `advisor` |
| `balanced` | `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `initializer`, `quick-answer` |

The agents `implementer` and `write-test` use the `byPhaseComplexity` entries above. The test `seeded_defaults_validate` checks that the seeded settings have no issue.

## Missing routes and the fix

A workspace that was saved before a new agent shipped has no route for it. `keys_without_route` finds the keys. `settings_fixes` offers `routing.model.byAgent.<key> = default`, and `apply_fixes` writes it. The page *Save-time validation and when a change takes effect* explains the flow. The value `default` resolves to the tier in the `agent.toml` of the agent.

## The settings screen view

`agent_infos` builds one `AgentInfo` for each agent. The field `resolved` is the route under the current settings. It is `null` when the route does not resolve. The field `default_route` is the route that `Agent default` gives: the same executor with `tier_override` set to the default tier. The field `default_effort` is `effort_for` for the executor of the agent.

## What happens when

- **No model route at spawn.** The engine records an execution with status `denied` and the error `route: <message>`. The message names the key and the table to edit.
- **A tier is missing from the table.** The route fails with the tier error above.
- **A native model has no `provider:` prefix.** The route fails. The message says that native models are written `anthropic:<model>` or `openai:<model>`.
- **A per-executor table lacks the entry of the executor.** The route fails. The message names the table name and the executor.
- **The executor is not available.** The engine records a `denied` execution with the text `The <executor> executor is not available.`
- **A harness is not installed.** Save-time validation refuses the settings with an issue at `routing.executor.byAgent.<key>`.
- **A native provider has no key.** Save-time validation refuses the settings with an issue at `routing.model.byAgent.<key>`.
- **A route changes while an execution runs.** The execution keeps its route. The next spawn uses the new route.

## Add a route key for a new agent

1. Add the agent to `AgentName` and to `AgentName::ALL` in `crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`. `route_keys` then includes it.
2. Add `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml` with a `default_tier` and an `[effort]` table.
3. Add the agent to the list in `WorkspaceSettings::seeded`.
4. Run `cargo test -p ostra-core`. The test `seeded_defaults_validate` fails when a key has no seeded route.

Older workspaces then show a fix for the new key, because they have no route for it.

sections.title: Shared types: ids, names, usage, and wire shapes
sections.summary: The `ostra-core` crate holds the ids, agent and executor names, `Usage`, `ExecutionStatus`, and the wire types that ts-rs exports to TypeScript. The page explains each and the steps to add a wire type.
sections.body:
## Why the shared types live in one crate

The server, the engine, the executors, the policy layer, and the browser must agree on the same names and shapes. The crate `ostra-core` holds them. Its module comment names the purpose: ids, agents, settings, pipeline enums, events, and the contracts between the engine, the executors, the policy layer, and the browser. A change to a shared type then fails to compile in every crate that uses it, and the Rust compiler finds each user.

[`crates/ostra-core/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/lib.rs) declares the modules and re-exports these names: `AgentName`, `Capability`, `InitializerMode`, `ExecutorKind`, `HarnessKind`, the six id types, `Complexity`, `Effort`, and `Tier`.

This page covers:

- the six id types
- the names of agents, capabilities, executors, tiers, effort, and complexity
- `Usage` and `ExecutionStatus`
- the wire types and how ts-rs exports them

The page *Path layout and credential paths* covers `paths.rs`. The page *Pricing: the cost formula and the catalog lookup* covers `pricing.rs`. The page *Executor contract: spec, context, result, and deltas* covers the rest of `exec.rs`.

## Id types

The macro `id_type!` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/ids.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/ids.rs) makes six newtypes. Each wraps a `String` that starts with a prefix.

| Type | Prefix | Names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WorkspaceId` | `ws_` | A registered workspace |
| `SessionId` | `s_` | A session. The session folder carries this name. |
| `ExecutionId` | `x_` | One run of an agent |
| `GateId` | `g_` | One gate, a question that waits for the user |
| `DecisionId` | `d_` | One decision of a judge |
| `MessageId` | `m_` | One question from a subagent to another subagent |

The `new` function builds the id from the prefix and `Uuid::now_v7().simple()`. A UUID v7 starts with a timestamp, so the lexical order of ids matches the creation order. A sort of ids lists the oldest first, and the store can use the id as an ordering key.

> Do not write `..Default::default()` in a struct that has an id field if you want an empty id. `Default` for an id type calls `new()`. It makes a fresh id, not an empty one.

The ids have `#[ts(export, type = "string")]`, so the TypeScript type of each id is `string`. The types also have `From<String>` and `From<&str>`, so tests can build an id from a literal.

## Agent names

`AgentName` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs) lists the 14 leaf agents. The serialized form is kebab-case, and it matches the folder `assets/agents/<name>/`.

| Group | Agents |
| --- | --- |
| Research and plan | `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan` |
| Code | `implementer`, `write-test` |
| Review | `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer` |
| Documentation | `documentation`, `system-architecture` |
| Support | `prompt-generation`, `initializer`, `quick-answer`, `advisor` |

The methods of `AgentName` give the data that other parts need:

- `as_str` gives the kebab-case name. `label` gives the sentence-case name, such as `Code reviewer`. `snake` and `submit_tool_name` give `code_reviewer` and `submit_code_reviewer`.
- `is_session_only` is true for `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `advisor`, `documentation`, and `system-architecture`. The write-scope guard confines these agents to their session folder and the OS temp folder.
- `routes_by_complexity` is true for `implementer` and `write-test`.
- `manages_projects` is true for `implementer` only (Rule O2), because only a phase of an approved plan starts a project.

`FromStr` trims the text and removes the prefixes `ostra:` and `ultracode:`. It also maps the retired name `module-documentation` to `Documentation`. The serde alias does the same for logs that were written before books existed. `RETIRED_AGENTS` lists `module-documentation`, so a saved workspace that still names it passes validation.

`route_keys()` returns the 14 agent names and `judge` (`JUDGE_ROUTE`). The page *Routes: choosing executor, tier, model, and effort* explains why `judge` is a route key but not an agent.

`InitializerMode` has six values: `detect`, `scout`, `propose`, `generate-skill`, `generate-inventory`, and `adopt`.

### Capabilities

An agent definition lists capabilities. Each capability names one native tool, and the names follow Claude Code.

| Capability | Native tool |
| --- | --- |
| `read`, `write`, `edit` | `Read`, `Write`, `Edit` |
| `shell` | `Bash` |
| `search_text`, `glob` | `Grep`, `Glob` |
| `skill`, `report`, `document` | `Skill`, `Report`, `Document` |
| `web_search`, `web_fetch` | `WebSearch`, `WebFetch` |
| `memory`, `memory_recall` | `Memory`, `MemoryRecall` |
| `docs_search` | `DocsSearch` |
| `code` | The eight tools of `CODE_TOOLS`: `CodeOutline`, `CodeFind`, `CodeCallers`, `CodeCallees`, `CodeImplementations`, `CodeNeighbors`, `CodeImpact`, `CodeMap` |
| `manage_projects` | The tools of `PROJECT_TOOLS` |
| `coordinate` | The tools of `COORD_TOOLS` |

`Capability::writes` is true for `write` and `edit`. Ostra uses it to derive read-only runs.

## Executors, tiers, effort, and complexity

`HarnessKind` has four values: `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. The display names are Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, and Antigravity. The text `antigravity` parses as `agy`.

`ExecutorKind` is `Native` or `Harness(HarnessKind)`. It serializes as the string `native` or `harness:<name>`. The type has a hand-written `Serialize` and `Deserialize`, and its TypeScript type is `string`. A text that is not one of the five forms gives the error `unknown executor ... use native or harness:<claude|codex|grok|agy>`. Its methods are:

- `tier_table()` gives the table name for `[tiers.<table>]`.
- `all()` lists the five executors.
- `stream()` gives `ExecStream::Activity` for native and `ExecStream::Terminal` for a harness. This is what the browser shows for a running execution: the Activity feed or a terminal.

`Tier` has four values from `fast` to `frontier`. `Effort` has five values from `low` to `max`. `Complexity` has `low`, `medium`, and `high`. `Complexity` parses without regard to letter case, and its default is `low`.

## Usage

`Usage` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs) is the count of one execution. Each field has a default of zero, so an older record that lacks a field still loads.

| Field | Unit | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `input_tokens` | tokens | Input tokens, without cache reads and cache writes |
| `output_tokens` | tokens | Output tokens |
| `cache_read_tokens` | tokens | Tokens that the provider read from its cache |
| `cache_write_tokens` | tokens | Every cache write, with the 5-minute and 1-hour TTL together |
| `cache_write_1h_tokens` | tokens | The part of `cache_write_tokens` that has the 1-hour TTL, which costs more |
| `cost_usd` | US dollars | The cost that `pricing::cost` computes |
| `tool_calls` | count | Tool calls of the execution |
| `build_ms` | milliseconds | Wall time in build and test commands, for the build-loop metric |
| `context_tokens` | tokens | The size of the latest request context: its prompt plus its output |

`Usage::add` adds every field except `context_tokens`. For `context_tokens`, the latest value wins. A zero value does not replace it. The reason is that the next request sends the context again, so a sum would count the same tokens many times.

The cost formula needs `input_tokens` to exclude cache reads and cache writes. Every provider and harness transcript is normalized to that form before the cost is computed.

## ExecutionStatus

`ExecutionStatus` is the state of one execution. It serializes in lowercase.

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `running` | The execution runs. This is the only value that is not terminal. |
| `ok` | The agent submitted a result |
| `stuck` | The agent hit its retry ceiling on one failure and reports a diagnostic and a need |
| `handoff` | The agent needs the `prompt-generation` specialist before it can continue |
| `waiting` | The run asked another subagent and waits for the answer (Rule H2) |
| `error` | The execution failed |
| `denied` | The engine did not start the execution, for example because the route did not resolve |
| `interrupted` | The engine stopped the run, for example for a pause. The stage can start again. |
| `cancelled` | The run was cancelled |

`is_terminal` returns true for every value except `running`. That includes `waiting`. The values `ok`, `stuck`, and `handoff` match `SubmitStatus` in `submit.rs`, the status field of the submit call of an agent.

## Wire types and ts-rs

The browser and the server exchange JSON. The Rust types in `ostra-core` define the shapes, and the crate ts-rs writes a TypeScript file for each exported type. The browser then cannot disagree with the server about a field name.

### How the export works

1. A type has `#[derive(TS)]` and `#[ts(export)]`.
2. ts-rs generates a test for each exported type. When `cargo test -p ostra-core` runs, each test writes `<Type>.ts`.
3. The file `.cargo/config.toml` sets `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` to `web/src/api/gen`, relative to the repo root.
4. The same file sets `TS_RS_LARGE_INT = "number"`, so `u64` and `i64` fields become `number`.
5. The web code imports a type with a line such as `import type { Usage } from "../api/gen/Usage"`.

The generated files are in git. The folder `web/src/api/gen/` holds 332 files. Each file starts with the line `This file was generated by ts-rs. Do not edit this file manually.`

The command `cargo test -p ostra-core export_bindings` regenerates the files. The test `export_bindings` in `api.rs` is empty. It makes the command stable, and the filter also matches the generated tests.

### Attributes that change the TypeScript type

| Attribute | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `#[ts(type = "string")]` | A `PathBuf` field, an id type, and `ExecutorKind` |
| `#[ts(optional)]` | A field that can be absent |
| `#[ts(as = "Option<T>", optional)]` | A field that Rust stores as text, such as a `String` that holds an enum value |
| `#[ts(rename = "byAgent")]` | A field that has a different name in JSON |
| `#[ts(type = "unknown")]` | A field with a free JSON value, such as the `submit` payload |

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, TS)]
#[ts(export)]
pub struct WorkspaceSummary {
    pub id: WorkspaceId,
    pub name: String,
    #[ts(type = "string")]
    pub root: PathBuf,
    pub projects: u32,
    pub active_sessions: u32,
    pub available: bool,
}
```

### Casing of enums and tags

The serde attribute of each type sets the casing. Check it before you write a value in JSON or TOML.

| Casing | Types |
| --- | --- |
| kebab-case | `AgentName`, `InitializerMode` |
| lowercase | `HarnessKind`, `Tier`, `Effort`, `Complexity`, `ExecutionStatus`, `ToolEnforcement`, `SandboxMode`, `SandboxNetwork`, `LoopbackAccess` |
| camelCase | `PermissionMode`, `PendingKind` |
| snake_case | `Capability`, `ExecStream`, `SessionStatus`, `StageStatus`, `PhaseStatus`, `InitStatus`, `RoutingPreset` |
| tag `type`, snake_case | `ClientMsg`, `ServerMsg` |
| tag `kind`, snake_case | `ExecutionDelta` |

### Groups in `api.rs`

[`crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs) holds about 100 REST and WebSocket types.

| Group | Main types |
| --- | --- |
| Workspace and project | `WorkspaceSummary`, `CreateWorkspace`, `WorkspaceDetail`, `ProjectView`, `ImportProject`, `CloneProject`, `AgentInfo`, `SettingsFix` |
| Approvals | `PendingCommands`, `PendingCommand`, `PendingKind`, `ApproveCommands` |
| Git | `GitRepoStatus`, `GitChange`, `GitBranch`, `GitCommitRequest`, `GitCheckoutRequest`, `GitOpResult`, `GitCredentialView`, `GitCredentialEdit` |
| Machine status | `HarnessStatus`, `ProviderStatus`, `EnvironmentStatus`, `ShellStatus`, `SandboxStatus` |
| Setup | `CreatePermissions`, `CreateYolo`, `CreateNotifications`, `RoutingPreset`, `OnboardingState` |
| Console layout | `WorkspaceUiState`, `UiTab` |
| Sessions | `CreateSession`, `SessionStatus`, `SessionSummary`, `StageCard`, `PhaseView`, `ExecutionView`, `GateView`, `DecisionView`, `SessionDetail` |
| Cost | `CostRow`, `CostReport` |
| Errors | `ApiError` with `error` and `issues`, and `ValidationIssue` |
| Skills and MCP | `SkillView`, `ProjectSkills`, `McpServerStatus`, `McpToolInfo` |

Two rules in this file come from comments in the code:

- `CreateWorkspace` takes enum values as strings. An unknown value then becomes a validation issue on its own field, and not a parse error that names no field.
- The types that carry a secret implement `Debug` by hand. `ProviderCredentialsEdit` prints only the base URL, and `GitCredentialEdit` hides its secret. A log line then cannot leak a key.

The constants of this file are `UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES` (64 KB of JSON for the console layout) and `SUMMARY_CHARS` (120 characters for the one-line summary of an execution).

### WebSocket messages

The socket at `/ws` carries JSON text frames of `ClientMsg` and `ServerMsg`. The channels are `session:<id>`, `execution:<id>`, `term:<execution>`, `workspace:<id>`, and `home`.

| Direction | Messages |
| --- | --- |
| Browser to server | `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `term_input`, `term_resize`, `code_complete`, `code_signature`, `code_navigate` |
| Server to browser | `session_event`, `execution_delta`, `execution_status`, `session_updated`, `workspace_updated`, `harness_status`, `subscribed`, `error`, `project_fs_changed`, `git_progress`, `tree_patch`, `code_completion`, `code_signature_help`, `code_navigation`, `activity` |

The socket also carries binary frames for the terminal. A frame has one byte that holds the length `n` of the execution id, then `n` bytes of execution id, then the raw terminal bytes. The page *REST routes, errors, and the WebSocket protocol* explains the behavior of each message.

## Add a wire type

1. Add the struct or enum to `crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs`. Derive `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq`, `Serialize`, `Deserialize`, and `TS`.
2. Add `#[ts(export)]` to the type.
3. Add `#[ts(type = "string")]` to each `PathBuf` field, so the TypeScript type is `string`.
4. Run `cargo test -p ostra-core`.
5. Commit the new file in `web/src/api/gen/` with the Rust change. The web build reads that folder.

Do not edit a generated file by hand. The next export overwrites your change.

## What happens when

- **You rename a field in Rust and do not run the export.** The old TypeScript file stays in git. The browser then reads a field that the server no longer sends.
- **A client sends an unknown enum value in `CreateWorkspace`.** The server returns an issue on that field.
- **A record from an older version lacks a `Usage` field.** The field loads as zero because of `#[serde(default)]`.
- **A log line prints `SavedCredentials`.** The key shows as `***`.

Agent names, the properties of each agent, `route_keys`, and `RETIRED_AGENTS`.
String form, `tier_table`, and `stream` of an executor.
`Tier`, `Effort`, and `Complexity`.
`ExecutionStatus`, `Usage`, and `Usage::add`.
WebSocket message types.
`TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` and `TS_RS_LARGE_INT` for the export.

sections.title: Path layout and credential paths
sections.summary: `paths.rs` derives every path that Ostra uses. The page shows the layout on disk, the owner-only file rules, the credential paths that the guards hide, and the path resolution that follows links like the OS.
sections.body:
## The problem that one path module solves

Many parts of Ostra read and write the same files: the server, the engine, the policy layer, the sandbox, and the tools. If each part built its own path, two parts could disagree about where a file is. A second problem is safety. A guard that compares path text can be fooled by a link, a `..` segment, or a Windows spelling. The module comment of `paths.rs` states the rule: Ostra addresses state by session and project key, and every reader and writer resolves it the same way, so all derivations live in one file.

This page covers:

- the layout of files on disk
- the names of reports
- the owner-only file helpers
- the credential paths that guards hide
- the path resolution functions

## Layout on disk

The file is [`crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs). The constant `RUNTIME_DIR` is `.ostra`.

```text
<config dir>/ostra/config.toml            global_config_path (or $OSTRA_CONFIG)
<data dir>/                               data_dir (or $OSTRA_DATA_DIR)
  registry.db                             registry_db_path
  models-dev.json                         price cache
  assets/                                 materialized agent assets
  decoys/                                 decoy credential files
<workspace>/.ostra/
  workspace.toml                          workspace_toml
  workspace.db                            workspace_db
  uploads/                                upload_staging
  sessions/<session id>/                  session_root
    <project key>/                        session_project_dir
    uploads/                              session_uploads
    .state/                               session_state_dir
      harness/<execution id>/terminal.log harness_execution_dir, terminal_transcript
<project>/
  .ostra/INVENTORY.md                     project_inventory
  .ostra/project.toml                     project_profile
  .ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3         project_memory_db
  .agents/skills/                         project_skills_dir
```

These facts explain the layout:

- **Session root.** Artifacts that cover many projects, such as the spec and the plan, are in the session root.
- **Project folder in the session.** Reports of one project are in `<session root>/<project key>/`.
- **Engine state.** The `.state` folder belongs to the engine. No agent can write there.
- **Terminal transcript.** A harness execution keeps its raw terminal bytes in `terminal.log`, so an ended run can be replayed.
- **Project memory.** The memory database of a project is inside the project, in `.ostra/memory/`.

### Skills and instruction files

Ostra writes every new skill to `.agents/skills` (`SKILLS_DIR`), the cross-harness standard. It still reads the older folder `.ostra/skills` (`LEGACY_SKILLS_DIR`) and never writes there. `find_project_skill` looks in `.agents/skills` first, so a skill with the same name in both folders resolves to the new one.

`project_instruction_files` finds `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md` at the project root. The match ignores letter case, and the result is in that order. The test `instruction_files_match_any_case` checks that `claude.MD`, `Agents.md`, and `AGENT.md` match and that a folder named `agents.md.d` does not.

### Report names

The engine names every report, so later stages can predict the file name. The functions are in the module `paths::report`.

| Function | File name |
| --- | --- |
| `implementer(phase)` | `ostra-implementer-phase-<phase>.md` |
| `implementer_progress(phase)` | `ostra-implementer-progress-phase-<phase>.md` |
| `epa(phase)` | `ostra-epa-phase-<phase>.md` |
| `write_test(phase)` | `ostra-write-test-phase-<phase>.md` |
| `review_ledger(phase)` | `ostra-review-ledger-phase-<phase>.md`, or `ostra-review-ledger.md` |
| `prompt_gen(n)` | `ostra-prompt-gen-<n>.md` |
| `docs_request()` | `ostra-docs-request.md` |
| `docs_parts()` | `ostra-docs-parts.json` |
| `completion()` | `ostra-completion.md` |
| `test_request()` | `ostra-test-request.md` |
| `session_context()` | `ostra-session-context.md` |
| `security_sentinel()` | `ostra-security-block.json` |

The prefix is `ostra-` (`ARTIFACT_PREFIX`). `review_ledger` uses the phase name form only when the value is a number, or a number with the suffix `-tests`. Any other value, such as `none` or `-tests`, gives `ostra-review-ledger.md`.

## Owner-only files and folders

The data dir holds the registry with the saved credentials. SQLite creates its `-wal` and `-shm` files with world-readable permissions. Ostra therefore tightens the folder itself:

- `ensure_data_dir` creates the data dir, or tightens an existing one, to mode `0700` on Unix.
- `create_private_dir_all` and `create_private_dir` create folders with mode `0700` on Unix.
- `private_file_options` creates files with mode `0600` on Unix.
- `restrict_to_owner` tightens an existing file to `0600` or a folder to `0700`.

On Windows, a new folder or file inherits the access list of its parent. Under the profile folder, that list grants only the user, the system, and the administrators. The server calls `ensure_data_dir` at start.

## Credential paths that guards hide

`HOME_CREDENTIALS` lists 56 files and folders under the home folder that no agent reads. Each entry is a `HomeCredential` with a `path` and an optional `harness`.

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Keys and cloud sign-in | `.ssh`, `.gnupg`, `.aws`, `.azure`, `.config/gcloud`, `.kube`, `.docker` |
| Tokens of tools | `.netrc`, `.git-credentials`, `.config/gh/hosts.yml`, `.cargo/credentials`, `.pypirc`, `.vault-token`, `.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json` |
| Key stores | `.local/share/keyrings`, `.password-store`, `.Xauthority` |
| Browsers | `.mozilla`, `.config/google-chrome`, `.config/chromium`, `.config/BraveSoftware` |
| macOS | The `Library` folders for keychains, cookies, browsers, mail, messages, and the TCC database |
| Windows | `_netrc`, and folders under `AppData` for credentials, browsers, and the PowerShell history |
| Sign-in files of harness CLIs | `.claude/.credentials.json`, `.codex/auth.json`, `.grok/auth.json`, `.gemini/oauth_creds.json`, `.gemini/google_accounts.json` |

The last group is the five entries that have a `harness` value. The harness is the one CLI that signs in with the file, and it is the only program that can see it.

`secret_paths(home)` returns the list that the guards use: the data dir, the file that `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` names, and every `HOME_CREDENTIALS` entry under the home folder. Three parts of Ostra use these paths:

- **The policy layer** refuses a tool call that names one of them (`guards.rs`).
- **The sandbox** hides them. For a harness run, it does not hide the sign-in file of that harness (`profile.rs` filters on `own`). That CLI needs the file to sign in.
- **Grep and Glob** skip them (`SecretFilter` in `ostra-tools/src/search.rs`). The folder of the agent assets inside the data dir stays visible.

`decoy::invalid` uses the `harness` value too. A workspace cannot add the sign-in file of a harness as a decoy, because a decoy there would sign that CLI out in the sandbox.

## Resolve paths the way the OS does

A guard must judge the file that the OS opens, not the text of the path. Five functions do this work.

| Function | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `normalize(path)` | Applies `.` and `..` without touching the file system |
| `resolve(cwd, target)` | Resolves one component at a time and follows each link, including a link that points to nothing, before a later `..` applies |
| `canonical(path)` | `std::fs::canonicalize` without the `\\?\` prefix that Windows adds |
| `is_inside(outer, inner)` | True when `inner` is `outer` or is below it. It compares whole components, so `/a/bc` is not inside `/a/b`. |
| `fold(path)` | The form that guards compare. On Windows it folds letter case and separators. On Unix it changes nothing. |

The reason for `resolve` is in its comment: a link must not make a path look inside a root when the write lands outside it. This test in `paths.rs` shows the case:

```rust
std::os::unix::fs::symlink(&outside, repo.join("link")).unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    resolve(&repo, Path::new("link/../x")),
    root.join("outside/x")
);
```

The link `repo/link` points to `outside/deep`. The text `link/../x` looks like `repo/x`, but the kernel opens `outside/x`. `normalize` would give the wrong answer, and `resolve` gives the right one. On Unix, `resolve` follows at most 40 links.

### Windows rules

Windows needs more rules, because one file has many spellings. These functions return their normal answer only on Windows. On Unix, they return false, `None`, or the input.

- `windows_path_problem` names a path that is not a plain file path: a share (`\\host\share`), a device or object namespace, a path that is relative to the working folder of a drive (`C:foo`), or an alternate data stream (`file:stream`). Guards compare drive paths only, so each of these could name a protected file under a spelling that the guard misses.
- `is_reserved_device` is true for a last component that is a device name, such as `CON`, `COM1.txt`, or `lpt1 .log`. The name `NUL` is excepted.
- `dot_dot_after_link` is true when a `..` follows a junction or symlink. Win32 programs apply the `..` to the folder of the link, and Git Bash applies it to the target. A guard cannot judge both, so it refuses.
- `strip_verbatim` removes the `\\?\` prefix, and `canonical` calls `dunce` to do the same.
- `from_msys` turns a Git Bash path such as `/c/Users/me` into `C:\Users\me`. It maps `/tmp` to the temp folder.
- `link` makes a symlink on Unix. On Windows it makes a junction for a folder. For a file it tries a symlink, then a hard link, then a copy.

The resolver on Windows loops at most 40 times while it follows links.

## What happens when

- **A path has a link before `..`.** `resolve` gives the real target, and the guard judges that file.
- **A link points to a file that does not exist yet.** `resolve` follows it. The write would land at the target, so the guard judges the target.
- **More than 40 links are in one path.** The resolver stops following links. The path is then judged as it stands.
- **A tool call names a file below the data dir.** The guard refuses it, because `secret_paths` starts with the data dir.
- **The home folder is unknown.** The home value is empty, and the home-relative entries do not match real files.
- **`OSTRA_CONFIG` places the config file in a shared folder.** The sandbox hides only that file, and not the whole folder.
