sections.title: Embedded assets and prompt rendering
sections.summary: How Ostra embeds agent assets, loads agent.toml, looks up effort, copies assets to disk, and renders each prompt for the native executor or for one of four harness CLIs.
sections.body:
This page explains how Ostra stores the text of its agents and how it renders that text for one executor. It covers the embedded assets, the fields of `agent.toml`, the effort lookup, the copy of the assets on disk, strict prompt rendering, the 28 tool tokens, and the tool vocabulary for harnesses. The page "Spawn contract and repo brief" covers the other inputs of an execution.

## The problem: one prompt, five tool vocabularies

An execution is one run of one agent. An executor is the component that runs an execution. The native executor calls a model API with a key. A harness executor starts an installed CLI in a terminal. The harness CLIs are Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, and Antigravity. Ostra has these 5 executor kinds.

Every agent prompt names tools such as `Read`, `Bash`, and `submit_implementer`. Each executor names its tools in a different way. For example, Codex has no `Read` tool. A prompt that names only Claude Code tools gives a false instruction to Codex.

Ostra solves the problem with 3 rules:

- Ostra keeps one prompt template for each agent.
- Ostra maps each capability to a tool name for each executor in `assets/tool-mapping.toml`.
- Ostra renders the template in strict mode, so a wrong token fails at render time and not in the middle of a run.

## Assets that the binary embeds

The `ostra-agents` crate embeds the whole `assets/` folder with `rust-embed`. The struct `Assets` in [`crates/ostra-agents/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-agents/src/lib.rs) has the attribute `#[folder = "../../assets"]`. The function `asset_text(path)` returns the text of one file. It returns `AgentsError::Missing` for an unknown path and `AgentsError::Parse` for text that is not valid UTF-8.

| Path under `assets/` | Count | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `agents/<name>/agent.toml` | 14 | Tier, timeout, capabilities, and effort of one agent. |
| `agents/<name>/prompt.md` | 14 | The prompt template of one agent. |
| `judges/<name>.md` | 10 | System prompts of the judges: `classify`, `completion`, `feedback`, `rescue`, `resolve-review`, `route-answer`, `stakes`, `sufficiency`, `track`, `yolo-answer`. |
| `refs/*.md` | 7 | 5 stack references (`_generic`, `go`, `java-spring`, `python`, `typescript-node`) and 2 guides for the initializer (`inventory-and-profile`, `skill-archetypes`). |
| `skills/meta-author/SKILL.md` | 1 | The only skill that ships with Ostra. It holds the 16 writing laws for instruction files. |
| `code-tools.md` | 1 | Guide to the 8 code navigation tools. |
| `coordination.md` | 1 | Guide to the subagent tools. |
| `output-rules.md` | 1 | The output rule that Ostra puts at the top of every prompt. |
| `tool-mapping.toml` | 1 | The map from capability to tool name for each executor. |

The workspace does not enable the `debug-embed` feature of `rust-embed`. In `rust-embed` version 8, a debug build then reads the files from the `assets/` folder at run time. A release build embeds the files in the binary.

## Fields of agent.toml

Each agent has one file `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml`. The private struct `AgentToml` has no default values. Because of this, every field is required and the `[effort]` table must exist.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | string | What the agent does and when it runs. |
| `default_tier` | `Tier` | The model tier of the agent: `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, or `frontier`. |
| `timeout_seconds` | integer | The time budget of one execution, in seconds. It becomes `ExecutionSpec.timeout_secs`. |
| `capabilities` | list of `Capability` | The tools of the agent, in snake_case. The page "Agent catalog and submit payloads" lists them for each agent. |
| `[effort]` | table | The reasoning effort for each executor table: `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy`. Values: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`. |

This file is the whole definition of `quick-answer`, with the description shortened:

```toml
description = "Answers one question about the workspace's projects in the side panel ..."
default_tier = "balanced"
timeout_seconds = 300
capabilities = ["read", "search_text", "glob", "web_search", "web_fetch", "memory_recall", "code", "docs_search"]

[effort]
native = "medium"
claude = "medium"
codex = "medium"
grok = "medium"
agy = "medium"
```

The function `load_defs` reads the file of each name in `AgentName::ALL`. The function `agent_def(agent)` returns a `&'static AgentDef`. Ostra loads all definitions once, at the first call, and keeps them in a `OnceLock`. The engine reads a definition through `AgentsFactory::agent_meta`. That function returns `default_tier`, `capabilities`, and `timeout_secs` in an `AgentMeta`.

### What happens when an agent.toml is wrong

- **A file is missing or has a wrong value, for example `default_tier = "huge"`:** the first call to `agent_def` panics with the text `embedded agent definitions are invalid`. The crate comment calls this a build defect, because the tests load every definition.
- **`capabilities` names a value that `Capability` does not define:** the parse fails and the same panic follows.
- **The `[effort]` table lacks the key of an executor:** `effort_for` uses the `native` key. The test `every_agent_definition_loads_with_the_handover_tiers` requires all 5 keys, but it checks only the 13 agents in its list. The `advisor` is not in that list.

## Effort lookup for an execution

Effort is the reasoning level of the model. The type `Effort` has 5 values, from low to high: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`. Two functions decide the effort of an execution:

1. `ostra_core::config::resolve_effort(settings, agent, complexity)` reads the workspace settings. It reads `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity[agent][complexity]` first and `routing.effort.byAgent[agent]` second. The value `complexity` is `low` when the phase gives none.
2. `effort_for(agent, executor)` reads `agent.toml`. Ostra calls it only when the first function returns nothing.

```rust
pub fn effort_for(agent: AgentName, executor: ExecutorKind) -> Effort {
    let def = agent_def(agent);
    def.effort
        .get(executor.tier_table())
        .or_else(|| def.effort.get("native"))
        .copied()
        .unwrap_or(Effort::High)
}
```

The method `tier_table()` returns `native` for the native executor and the CLI name for a harness: `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`. The lookup falls back to `native`, and then to `high`.

12 agents use `high` for every executor. The agent `quick-answer` uses `medium` for every executor, because it answers in the side panel and has a 300-second budget. The agent `initializer` differs by executor:

| Executor table | Effort of `initializer` |
| --- | --- |
| `native` | `high` |
| `claude` | `high` |
| `codex` | `xhigh` |
| `grok` | `xhigh` |
| `agy` | `max` |

The `native` value is lower than the original value `max`. A test comment states the reason: a self-initialization spent about $240 on Opus at `max` effort. Each harness executor also caps the effort at the ceiling of its CLI. The page "Launching a harness CLI: plans, terminal, and sandbox wrap" gives the ceilings.

## Copy of the assets on disk

Agents read stack references and skills as files with their read tool. The advisor reads the instructions of a failed agent. Embedded assets have no path on disk, so Ostra copies the needed ones to a folder.

The server does this at startup in [`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs):

1. It calls `ostra_agents::set_assets_dir(<data dir>/assets)`.
2. It calls `ostra_agents::materialize_assets(<data dir>/assets)`. If this call fails, startup stops with the text `writing assets: ...`.

The function `materialize_assets(dir)` builds a list of files and writes each one:

1. For each embedded file under `refs/` and `skills/`, it replaces `{{assets_dir}}` and `{{ assets_dir }}` with `dir`. It keeps the relative path.
2. For each of the 14 agents, it renders the prompt for the native executor with `dir`. It writes the result to `agents/<name>.md`. Rule O5 gives the reason: the advisor must see what a failed step can write and must return.
3. It compares each target file with the new text. It writes the file only when the text differs. It returns the list of files that it wrote.

A second call with the same assets returns an empty list. The test `materialize_writes_refs_and_skills_with_the_assets_dir_filled` checks this.

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `assets_dir()` | The folder from `set_assets_dir`. If none is set, `<data dir>/assets`. The data dir is `$OSTRA_DATA_DIR` or the local data folder plus `ostra`. |
| `instructions_path(agent)` | `<assets dir>/agents/<name>.md`. |
| `reference_path(name)` | `<assets dir>/refs/<name>.md`. The factory uses it for the `Stack reference:` line. |
| `reference(name)` | The text of one reference, with the assets folder filled in. |
| `reference_names()` | The names of all 7 references. |
| `stack_names()` | The stacks that have a seed reference: `go`, `java-spring`, `python`, `typescript-node`. |
| `embedded_skill(name)` | The text of a skill that ships with Ostra. |
| `judge_prompt(name)` | The system prompt of a judge, or `None` for an unknown name. |

The function `stack_names()` takes each reference whose first line starts with `# Stack Reference:`. It leaves out names that start with `_`, so the `_generic` fallback is not a stack. An empty project stack lets the initializer detect the stack.

### What happens when assets are copied

- **`set_assets_dir` runs twice:** the second call returns `false` and the first folder stays.
- **Nobody calls `set_assets_dir`:** `assets_dir()` returns `<data dir>/assets`.
- **`reference` or `embedded_skill` runs before `set_assets_dir`:** each function caches its text at the first call, with the folder at that time. Call `set_assets_dir` first.
- **A person edits a file in the assets folder:** the next startup overwrites it, because the text differs from the embedded text. Edit the files under `assets/` in the repository.
- **A file leaves the embedded assets:** the old copy stays on disk, because `materialize_assets` never deletes a file.
- **The disk refuses a write:** the function returns `AgentsError::Io`.

## Strict prompt rendering

The function `render_prompt(agent, executor)` returns the system prompt of one execution. It calls `render_prompt_in` with the assets folder. The function `render_str` creates a `minijinja` environment with `UndefinedBehavior::Strict` and `keep_trailing_newline`. Strict mode makes an unknown `{{token}}` a render error: `AgentsError::Template` with the path of the asset.

The next diagram shows the steps of `render_prompt_in`.

### Order of the parts of a prompt

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Render prompt.md with the 28 tokens"]
    B{"Agent has capability code?"}
    C["Prepend code-tools.md"]
    D{"Agent has capability coordinate?"}
    E["Prepend coordination.md"]
    F["Prepend output-rules.md"]
    G{"Executor kind"}
    H["Prepend Tool vocabulary"]
    I["Return the system prompt"]
    A --> B
    B -- yes --> C
    B -- no --> D
    C --> D
    D -- yes --> E
    D -- no --> F
    E --> F
    F --> G
    G -- native --> I
    G -- harness --> H
    H --> I
```

The final order of a native prompt is: output rules, coordination guide, code tools guide, agent prompt. A harness prompt starts with the `## Tool vocabulary` section, then a blank line, then the native order. Every part passes through the same strict renderer with the same tokens.

The file `assets/output-rules.md` holds the rule `Write no text outside tool calls`. Ostra reads only the submit call, so other text is lost. The test `every_prompt_forbids_text_outside_ostra_tool_calls` checks that every prompt on every executor contains this rule.

### What happens when a prompt does not render

- **A prompt uses a `{{token}}` that the code does not define:** the render fails with `AgentsError::Template` for every executor. The test `every_prompt_renders_for_every_executor_with_no_unresolved_token` finds it.
- **A prompt contains a literal `{{` or `{%`:** the renderer reads it as template syntax. Write a single brace, as in `{repo-root}` or `{name}`, when the text must stay literal.
- **`tool-mapping.toml` has no value for a key and an executor:** the token renders as the mapping key, for example `read`. No error occurs. The test does not detect it, because it looks only for `{{` and `{%`. It also checks that each prompt names its own submit tool.

## The 28 tool tokens

The constant `TOKENS` in [`crates/ostra-agents/src/mapping.rs`](crates/ostra-agents/src/mapping.rs) lists 28 tokens. The renderer also sets the token `assets_dir`. Each token resolves through a mapping key and the column of the executor in `assets/tool-mapping.toml`.

| Token | Mapping key | Native value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tool_read` | `read` | `Read` |
| `tool_write` | `write` | `Write` |
| `tool_edit` | `edit` | `Edit` |
| `tool_shell` | `shell` | `Bash` |
| `tool_search_text` | `search_text` | `Grep` |
| `tool_glob` | `glob` | `Glob` |
| `tool_skill` | `skill` | `Skill` |
| `tool_web_search` | `web_search` | `WebSearch` |
| `tool_web_fetch` | `web_fetch` | `WebFetch` |
| `tool_report` | `report` | `Report` |
| `tool_document` | `document` | `Document` |
| `tool_memory` | `memory` | `Memory` |
| `tool_memory_recall` | `memory_recall` | `MemoryRecall` |
| `tool_docs_search` | `docs_search` | `DocsSearch` |
| `tool_code_outline` | `code:outline` | `CodeOutline` |
| `tool_code_find` | `code:find` | `CodeFind` |
| `tool_code_callers` | `code:callers` | `CodeCallers` |
| `tool_code_callees` | `code:callees` | `CodeCallees` |
| `tool_code_implementations` | `code:implementations` | `CodeImplementations` |
| `tool_code_neighbors` | `code:neighbors` | `CodeNeighbors` |
| `tool_code_impact` | `code:impact` | `CodeImpact` |
| `tool_code_map` | `code:map` | `CodeMap` |
| `tool_project_list` | `manage_projects:list` | `ProjectList` |
| `tool_project_create` | `manage_projects:create` | `ProjectCreate` |
| `tool_subagent_list` | `coordinate:list` | `SubagentList` |
| `tool_subagent_ask` | `coordinate:ask` | `SubagentAsk` |
| `tool_subagent_reply` | `coordinate:reply` | `SubagentReply` |
| `tool_submit` | `submit` | `submit_<agent>` |

A key with a colon, such as `code:callers`, splits into the capability `code` and the operation `callers`. The value in the file can hold `{op}` (the operation in lowercase), `{Op}` (the operation with a capital first letter), and `{agent}` (the snake_case agent name). The method `Mapping::tool` replaces them.

| Capability key | native | claude | codex | grok | agy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `read` | `Read` | `Read` | `exec_command` | `read_file` | `view_file` |
| `write` | `Write` | `Write` | `apply_patch` | `search_replace` | `write_to_file` |
| `edit` | `Edit` | `Edit` | `apply_patch` | `search_replace` | `replace_file_content` |
| `shell` | `Bash` | `Bash` | `exec_command` | `run_terminal_command` | `run_command` |
| `search_text` | `Grep` | `Grep` | `exec_command` | `grep` | `grep_search` |
| `glob` | `Glob` | `Glob` | `exec_command` | `list_dir` | `find_by_name` |
| `skill` | `Skill` | prose: `Read` on the skill file | prose: `exec_command` on the skill file | prose: `read_file` on the skill file | prose: `view_file` on the skill file |
| `web_search` | `WebSearch` | `WebSearch` | `web_search` | `web_search` | `search_web` |
| `web_fetch` | `WebFetch` | `WebFetch` | `web_search` | `web_fetch` | `read_url_content` |
| `report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, `docs_search` | `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch` | `mcp__ostra__<key>` | `<key>` | `<key>` | `<key>` |
| `code` | `Code{Op}` | `mcp__ostra__code_{op}` | `code_{op}` | `code_{op}` | `code_{op}` |
| `manage_projects` | `Project{Op}` | `mcp__ostra__project_{op}` | `project_{op}` | `project_{op}` | `project_{op}` |
| `coordinate` | `Subagent{Op}` | `mcp__ostra__subagent_{op}` | `subagent_{op}` | `subagent_{op}` | `subagent_{op}` |
| `submit` | `submit_{agent}` | `mcp__ostra__submit_{agent}` | `submit_{agent}` | `submit_{agent}` | `submit_{agent}` |

Native names follow Claude Code, because the prompts were tuned on those names. Ostra tools (`report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, `docs_search`, the code, project, and subagent tools, and the submit tool) reach a harness from the `ostra` MCP server. Claude Code shows them with the prefix `mcp__ostra__`. The other 3 CLIs use the bare name. The file states that a value that is not a bare tool name is prose, and Ostra renders it as written.

## Tool vocabulary for harnesses

A harness CLI has its own tools, so a native prompt would name tools that the CLI lacks. The method `Mapping::vocabulary(agent, harness, capabilities)` builds a section that opens the prompt of a harness execution. The native executor gets no such section, because its tool names are the names in the prompts.

The section has these parts, in this order:

1. The heading `## Tool vocabulary` and one sentence that names the CLI, for example `You are running in Codex under Ostra.`
2. A table `Capability | Tool`. It has one row for each capability in the `capabilities` list of `agent.toml`, in list order, and a last row for `submit`. For `code`, `manage_projects`, and `coordinate`, the cell lists the tool of each operation, joined with a comma and a space. Ostra leaves out a row when the mapping has no value.
3. The strategy paragraphs of this harness, in the alphabetical order of the strategy names: `ostra_tools`, `skill`, `write`.
4. The sentence that forbids the harness subagents. Ostra schedules the work, and the only way to reach another agent is the subagent tools.
5. When the agent has a submit tool, the instruction to reply with only `Done!` after the call. Ostra reads the result from the submit call, and other text costs output tokens.

| Strategy | Included when | Harnesses with text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra_tools` | always | all 4 |
| `skill` | the agent has `skill` or `read` | all 4 |
| `write` | the agent has `write` or `edit` | `codex` only |

The `skill` text tells the agent to read `SKILL.md` completely before it acts. It gives the paths `{repo-root}/.agents/skills/{name}/SKILL.md`, the older `{repo-root}/.ostra/skills/{name}/SKILL.md`, and `{{ assets_dir }}/skills/{name}/SKILL.md` for skills that ship with Ostra. The `ostra_tools` text for Claude Code tells the agent to load a deferred tool with `ToolSearch` (`select:mcp__ostra__<tool>`). For Grok Build, it tells the agent to find a tool with `search_tool` and to call it with `use_tool`. The `write` text for Codex tells the agent to use `apply_patch` with `*** Add File:` and `*** Update File:` hunks.

This excerpt shows the start of the section for `implementer` on Codex:

```markdown
## Tool vocabulary

You are running in Codex under Ostra. This prompt names each tool by what it does. ...

| Capability | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| read | exec_command |
| edit | apply_patch |
| write | apply_patch |
| shell | exec_command |
| code | code_outline, code_find, code_callers, ... |
| submit | submit_implementer |
```

The vocabulary text also passes through `render_str`, so `{{ assets_dir }}` in a strategy gets its value. A strategy that holds another `{{x}}` token fails to render.

## Judges, references, and skills

Judges are not agents. A judge is a system prompt in `assets/judges/<name>.md`. The function `judge_prompt(name)` builds a cache of all `judges/*.md` files at the first call. The test `judges_and_references_resolve` requires that each of the 10 judge prompts names the `decide` tool, because a judge answers with one forced call to that tool. The doc comment of `judge_prompt` lists only 8 names. It does not list `feedback` and `track`, but both files exist and both load.

The factory also accepts the name `__agent:<agent>` and returns the native prompt of that agent. The page "Spawn contract and repo brief" describes that route.

## Change an asset

1. Edit the prompt in `assets/agents/<name>/prompt.md`. Use only the 28 tokens and `{{assets_dir}}`.
2. Do not write an em dash in any asset, because the test `no_em_dashes_in_any_asset` rejects it.
3. Do not write the word `ultracode` in an asset, except the allowed phrases in the initializer. The test `no_ultracode_leftovers_in_any_asset` lists them.
4. To add a token, add a pair to `TOKENS` in `mapping.rs` and add the key to all 5 columns of `tool-mapping.toml`. Then change the tests if the count changes.
5. To support a new executor, add a column to every `[capabilities.*]` table and an entry to each `[strategies.*]` table.
6. Run `cargo build --workspace`, then `cargo test --workspace`, then `cargo fmt --all`.

The `assets/` folder is the only place to change prompt text. Do not edit the copy in the data folder, because the next startup overwrites it.

code_refs.note: Embedded `Assets`, `AgentDef` loading, and `effort_for`.
Assets folder, `materialize_assets`, `instructions_path`, and `reference_path`.
Prompt order and the strict `minijinja` environment.
The 28 tool tokens, `Mapping::tool`, and `Mapping::vocabulary`.
Capability to tool name for each executor and the harness strategy texts.
The output rule that every prompt carries.
A complete `agent.toml` with effort `medium`.
Tests that guard definitions, rendering, asset text, and materialization.
Startup calls `set_assets_dir` and `materialize_assets`.

sections.title: Spawn contract and repo brief
sections.summary: How the typed SpawnParams structs render the Label: value block, how parse_block checks it, how AgentsFactory::build assembles an execution, and how augment adds the repo brief.
sections.body:
This page explains the inputs that an execution receives besides the system prompt: the spawn block and the repo brief. It covers `SpawnParams`, the block format, the required lines of each agent, `parse_block`, `AgentsFactory::build`, `augment`, and the sections and size limits of the repo brief. The page "Embedded assets and prompt rendering" covers the system prompt.

## The problem: an agent starts with no memory

An agent sees 2 texts when its execution starts: the system prompt and the first message. The first message must hold every input that the agent needs, for example the path of its report file. If one input is missing, the agent guesses or fails after it spends money.

Ostra removes this risk with a typed contract. Each agent has one Rust struct. Each required input is a field without `Option`, so a missing input does not compile. The module comment of [`crates/ostra-agents/src/spawn.rs`](crates/ostra-agents/src/spawn.rs) states this rule and says that the structs port the file `subagent-parameters.json` of Ultracode.

These terms name the 3 texts that Ostra builds:

- **Spawn block:** the `Label: value` lines that a spawn struct renders.
- **Repo brief:** the markdown sections that Ostra appends below the spawn block.
- **First message:** the spawn block, a separator, and the repo brief.

## The SpawnParams trait and the shared parts

Every spawn struct implements the trait `SpawnParams`:

```rust
pub trait SpawnParams {
    fn agent(&self) -> AgentName;
    fn mode(&self) -> Option<InitializerMode> { None }
    fn common(&self) -> &Common;
    fn render(&self) -> String;
    fn to_json(&self) -> Value;
    fn report_file(&self) -> Option<&Path> { None }
}
```

The method `render` returns the block. The method `to_json` returns the same data as JSON, and the initializer structs add a `mode` key. The method `report_file` returns the report path for the agents that write a report: `implementer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, and `prompt-generation`.

The struct `Common` holds the 4 lines that every spawn carries: `Workspace root`, `Repo root`, `Session dir`, and `Repo key`. The line `Workspace root:` replaces the line `Primary repo root:` of Ultracode, and a test rejects the old label in assets.

The struct `Extras` holds optional lines that the engine adds below the required lines. An empty or absent field renders nothing.

| Field of `Extras` | Label | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `research_docs` | `Research docs` | Research documents, oldest first (Rule D2). |
| `projects_in_scope` | `Repos in scope` | One line `key -> path` for each project. |
| `user_answers` | `User answers` | One line `id question: answer` for each answer. |
| `findings` | `Findings` | Fix instructions or findings, verbatim. |
| `required_skills` | `Required skills` | Skill names, separated by commas. |
| `ledger_file` | `Review ledger` | The ledger where the fix agent records FIXED or WONTFIX. |
| `rescue_context` | `Rescue context` | The STUCK diagnostic and the stated fact, never a plain retry. |
| `resume_instructions` | `Resume instructions` | What to do after a HANDOFF specialist finished. |
| `prior_reports` | `Prior phase reports` | Reports of earlier phases. |
| `context_files` | `Context files` | Files that the agent reads first. |
| `user_notes` | `User notes` | What the user said at an earlier gate (Rule J1). |
| `new_project` | `New project` | A project that the phase must create first (Rule O2). |
| `task_note` | none | Free text after a blank line. |

Three small enums complete the shared parts. `WorkSource` is either `PhaseFile(path)` or `NoPlan(reason)`. `TargetType` is `spec` or `plan`. `SourceCheck` is `citations` or `refetch`. Rule D3b allows `refetch` only on the first pass over a spec whose External Evidence table has rows.

## The block format

The private struct `Block` writes the lines. These rules apply to every struct:

- A single-line value renders as `Label: value`. Ostra trims the value first.
- A value with a newline renders as `Label:` and then each line, indented by 2 spaces.
- A list renders as `Label:` and then one indented line for each item. An empty list renders nothing.
- An optional value that is absent or blank renders nothing.
- The order is: required lines, the common 4 lines, then optional lines.
- The `task_note` text comes last, after a blank line.

This example shows an implementer block. The paths are examples.

```text
Report file: /ws/.ostra/sessions/s1/ostra-implementer-1.md
Phase file: /ws/.ostra/sessions/s1/ostra-plan-1-x-phase-1.md
Workspace root: /ws
Repo root: /ws/api
Session dir: /ws/.ostra/sessions/s1
Repo key: api
Research docs:
  /ws/.ostra/sessions/s1/ostra-research-1-x.md

The request: add order cancellation
```

The rule for an empty list has one consequence. A required list that is empty renders no line, and then the contract below reports a missing parameter. Two examples are `Implementer reports` and `Changed files`. The initializer avoids this case for `Scout findings`: it writes the line `Scout findings: none`, because the label is still required.

## Required lines for each agent

The table lists each struct, in the order that its `render` method writes the lines. Add the common 4 lines after the required lines. Optional lines follow them.

| Agent and struct | Required lines | Optional lines |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `explore`: `ExploreParams` | `Task` | The factory sets none. |
| `generate-spec`: `GenerateSpecParams` | `Task` | `Spec file`, `New research docs`, `Requirement changes`, then `Extras` |
| `fact-check`: `FactCheckParams` | `Target`, `Target type`, `Prior findings`, `Spec file`, `Source check` | `Research docs`, on a spec target only (Rule D5) |
| `plan`: `PlanParams` | `Spec file` | `Repos in scope`, `Findings`, `Master plan` |
| `implementer`: `ImplementerParams` | `Report file`, `Phase file` or `No plan` | `Extras` |
| `code-reviewer`: `CodeReviewerParams` | `Phase`, `Changed files`, `Change rationale`, `Phase file` or `No plan` | `Review scope`, `Review context`, `EPA report` |
| `execution-path-analyzer`: `EpaParams` | `Implementer report`, `Report file` | `Phase file`, then `Extras` |
| `write-test`: `WriteTestParams` | `Implementer report`, `EPA report`, `Report file`, `Phase file` or `No plan` | `Extras` |
| `documentation`: `DocumentationParams` | `Implementer reports` | `Existing book`, then `Extras` |
| `system-architecture`: `ArchitectureParams` | `Book parts`, `Repos in scope` | `Existing book`, then `Extras` |
| `prompt-generation`: `PromptGenParams` | `Task`, `Target files`, `Report file` | `Extras` |
| `quick-answer`: `QuickAnswerParams` | `Question` | `Repos in scope`, `Session artifacts` |
| `advisor`: `AdvisorParams` | `Failed step`, `Problem`, `Step inputs` | `Step result`, `Step context`, `Earlier guidance` |
| consult run: `ConsultParams` | `Asked by`, `Question` | none |

A consult run (Rule H3) is a question from one subagent to another. It continues the conversation of the answering subagent, so it reaches the run as a resume message and not as a first spawn.

The initializer has 6 structs, one for each mode. Each one writes `Mode` first, then its own lines, then `Advisor guidance` when the advisor gave instructions (Rule O5), then the common 4 lines.

| Mode | Struct | Lines after `Mode` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `detect` | `InitDetectParams` | `User focus` (optional) |
| `adopt` | `InitAdoptParams` | `Source harness`, `Source runtime dir`, `Source skills dir` |
| `scout` | `InitScoutParams` | `Slice`, `Slice paths`, `Stack reference`, `Scout plan` |
| `propose` | `InitProposeParams` | `Scout findings`, `Scout plan` |
| `generate-skill` | `InitGenerateSkillParams` | `Skill name`, `Skill kind`, `Disposition`, `Proposal`, `Scout findings` |
| `generate-inventory` | `InitGenerateInventoryParams` | `Generated skills`, `Reused skills`, `Proposal`, `Scout findings` |

### Phase file or No plan

Hard rule 13 says that a phase-bound agent declares either its phase file or the reason that it has none. The agents `implementer`, `code-reviewer`, and `write-test` follow this rule. The function `work_source` in the factory chooses the text of `No plan:`. It checks these cases in order:

1. The inputs hold a phase with a file: the line is `Phase file:`.
2. The request is a revision after a review: the text states a revision that the user asked for.
3. The category is `Verify`: no code change is planned.
4. The category is `Test`: the user asked for tests directly.
5. The category is `Docs`: the user asked for documentation directly.
6. The category is `Prompt`: the pipeline has no plan tier for it.
7. The category is `QuickChange`: the request names the whole edit.
8. The category is `Implement` on the light track: research found a contained change.
9. Any other case: the stakes judge rated the request low, so the plan tier was skipped.

## Runtime check with parse_block

The function `parse_block(agent, text)` validates a block as text. It returns the values by parameter id, or an error text for the model or the engine.

1. It reads the text line by line. It stops at a line that equals `---` or starts with `## `, because the brief starts there.
2. A line that starts with a space or a tab continues the label above it.
3. A line `Label: value` counts when the label is in the table `PARAMS`. The first occurrence of a label wins. Unknown labels are ignored.
4. It calls `contract(agent, mode)` to get the required ids and the one-of group. For the initializer, the `Mode:` line selects the ids. A missing mode gives `missing required parameter \`Mode:\``.
5. For each of the common 4 ids and each required id, it checks that the value exists and passes `check`.
6. For the one-of group, exactly one of `Phase file:` and `No plan:` must be present.

The function `check` applies a rule for the type of the parameter:

| Type | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Any | The value is not empty. |
| `AbsoluteDir`, `AbsolutePath` | The path is absolute, or it has a root but no drive. The second case keeps prompts portable on Windows. |
| `RepoKey` | The value is a lowercase slug (`is_project_key`). |
| `Phase` | The value is `none`, or digits with an optional `-tests` suffix. |
| `Enum` | The value is in the list: `mode`, `target_type` (`spec`, `plan`), `source_check` (`citations`, `refetch`). |
| `Path`, `Text` | No rule beyond not empty. |

The error text names the label, for example `missing required parameter \`Repo key:\``. The doc comment of the module says that `parse_block` serves the harness executors. In the code, only tests call it today. The test `every_struct_renders_a_block_its_own_contract_accepts` renders every struct and parses the result. The test `parse_block_stops_at_the_brief` shows that a line `Task: injected` below the brief does not replace the real `Task:` line.

## How AgentsFactory::build assembles an execution

The struct `AgentsFactory` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/factory.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/factory.rs) implements the trait `SpawnFactory` with 3 methods:

- `agent_meta(agent)` returns the tier, the capabilities, and the timeout from `agent.toml`.
- `judge_prompt(name)` returns the prompt of a judge. A name of the form `__agent:<agent>` returns the native prompt of that agent.
- `build(request, env)` returns a `BuiltSpawn`.

### Steps of build

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Runner
    participant Factory as AgentsFactory
    participant Params as Spawn struct
    participant Brief as brief module
    participant Prompts as ostra_agents
    Runner->>Factory: build(SpawnRequest, SpawnEnv)
    Factory->>Params: struct literal from SpawnInputs
    Params-->>Factory: render() returns the spawn block
    Factory->>Brief: augment(block, BriefInput)
    Brief-->>Factory: first message
    Factory->>Prompts: render_prompt(agent, executor)
    Prompts-->>Factory: system prompt
    Factory-->>Runner: BuiltSpawn
```

The method does these steps:

1. It builds `Common` from the session state (`workspace_root`), the environment (`repo_root`), and the request (`session_dir`, `repo_key`).
2. It picks the struct. When the purpose is `Consult`, it builds `ConsultParams` for any agent. For the initializer, the purpose `Init { mode }` selects the struct.
3. It reads each required planner input. A missing input returns `Err` with the text `missing <what>`, for example `missing task` or `missing report file`.
4. It calls `params.render()`. The result is the spawn block.
5. It reads the instructions for the agent with `settings.instructions_for(agent)`. For each text, `with_tagged_files` adds the absolute paths of tagged files or artifacts (Rule W3). A tag for a hidden or missing artifact gives nothing.
6. It reads the artifacts with `ArtifactsBrief::read` and the books with `BooksBrief::read`. The books brief gets a `search_tool` name only when the agent has the capability `docs_search`.
7. It calls `augment(block, BriefInput { ... })`. The result is the first message.
8. It calls `render_prompt(agent, env.executor)`. The result is the system prompt.
9. It resolves the effort with `resolve_effort` and falls back to `effort_for`.
10. It returns `BuiltSpawn` with `system_prompt`, `first_message`, `spawn_block`, `params` (JSON), `report_file`, and `effort`.

The runner copies these values into `ExecutionSpec`. The page "Executor contract: spec, context, result, and deltas" describes that struct.

### Planner inputs that a missing value stops

| Agent | Input that must exist | Error text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `explore`, `generate-spec`, `prompt-generation` | `task` | `missing task` |
| `fact-check` | `target`, `spec_file` | `missing target`, `missing spec file` |
| `plan` | `spec_file` | `missing spec file` |
| `implementer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, `prompt-generation` | `report_file` | `missing report file` |
| `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test` | `implementer_report` | `missing implementer report` |
| `write-test` | `epa_report` | `missing EPA report` |
| `code-reviewer` | `phase_value` | `missing phase` |
| `system-architecture` | `target` (the book parts) | `missing book parts` |
| `quick-answer` | `question` | `missing question` |
| `advisor` | `Failed step`, `Problem`, `Step inputs` | `missing <key>` |
| consult run | `task` (the asker), `question` | `missing asker`, `missing question` |
| `initializer` | the purpose `Init { mode }`, and the keys of the mode | `initializer without a mode`, `missing <key>` |

### How the factory fills Extras

The function `work_extras` copies the ledger, research documents, prior reports, context files, and user notes. Then the kind of work selects one more field:

- `Fix` and `BlockerFix` put the instructions in `Findings`.
- `Rescue` puts them in `Rescue context`.
- `Resume` puts them in `Resume instructions`.
- `Rerun` writes a task note that says an earlier run ended before it finished. The note adds the old instructions when they exist.
- `Initial` sets nothing.

When no task note exists and the inputs have a task, the note is `The request: <task>`. For the `documentation` agent, the note is `The request: ` followed by the full request of the session. For the `implementer`, the factory also sets `New project` when the phase project does not exist yet (Rule O2). The text tells the agent to create it with `ProjectCreate` before anything else.

The `code-reviewer` always gets `Review scope: unstaged`. This keeps each review on its own change. It gets `Review context: Review test code` for a test review and `Review context: Review implementation code` for all others.

## The repo brief

The repo brief gives an agent the facts about the project, so the agent does not spend its first tool calls to find them. The function `augment(first_message, input)` appends it.

### Idempotence and layout

`augment` returns the message unchanged in 2 cases: the message already holds one of 5 headings, or `build_brief` has nothing to say. The 5 headings are `## Repo brief for `, `## Project instructions`, `## Workspace artifacts`, `## Workspace documentation`, and `## Workspace instructions`. This rule makes a second render safe, because it never stacks 2 briefs. Otherwise the result is the trimmed message, then `---` between blank lines, then the brief, then a newline.

The function `build_brief` writes these sections, in this order. It leaves out a section that has no content.

1. `## Repo brief for <agent>`: facts from the project profile and the inventory. The next subsection describes it.
2. `## Project instructions`: the files `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md` at the repo root, in that order and in any letter case. The function `project_docs` skips an empty file, a file with the same real path as one already read, and a file with the same content. Many repos ship `AGENTS.md` as a link to `CLAUDE.md`, so this rule avoids a double copy.
3. `## Projects created in this session`: each project that an agent created, with its path, stack, purpose, and base requirements (Rule O3). A created project has no inventory until its init runs, so these facts come from the creating call.
4. `## Workspace artifacts`: the files that the user keeps for every task (Rule W1). The text tells the agent not to write in that folder.
5. `## Workspace documentation`: the documentation books (Rules B5 and B8). With a search tool, the text tells the agent to search the books before it reads code.
6. `## Workspace instructions`: the text of `instructions.all` and then the entry of the agent. Rule: the agent's own rules win over these instructions.

### Profile sections for each agent

The function `sections(agent)` selects which profile sections the first part contains. The code always writes the selected sections in this fixed order: Stack, Commands, Testing, Skills, Conventions, Review, Modules.

| Agent | Sections |
| --- | --- |
| `implementer` | Commands, Skills, Conventions, Modules |
| `write-test` | Commands, Testing, Skills, Conventions, Modules |
| `code-reviewer` | Commands, Review, Conventions, Skills |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | Commands, Testing, Modules |
| `explore` | Stack, Skills, Modules |
| `plan` | Stack, Commands, Skills, Modules |
| `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `system-architecture` | Stack, Modules |
| `documentation` | Stack, Commands, Modules |
| `prompt-generation` | Skills |
| `quick-answer`, `advisor` | Stack, Commands, Skills, Modules |
| `initializer` | none |

The brief never holds the routing settings. Routing means nothing to an agent and would leak tier names into its context.

The brief states a fact only once. The helper `stated_in(inventory, value)` squashes white space and tests whether the inventory text already holds the value. A value under 3 characters counts as stated. The brief leaves out a convention, a test note, or a skill purpose that the inventory states. The Review rule set is the exception: it is the whole basis of the reviewer, so a partial set would silently narrow the review.

The Modules section needs a hint. The function `scope_hints` scans the spawn block for paths with the pattern `[\w.-]+/[\w./-]+`. It keeps tokens longer than 3 characters that do not contain `ostra-`, at most 40. A module-map row matches when its glob stem has 3 or more characters and the stem and a hint contain each other. Without a hint, Ostra leaves the map out, because the map of a large repo is bigger than the rest of the brief.

This brief section is an example of the output. It comes from a documentation request:

```text
### Module map rows covering the paths in your task
- `assets/**`: assets
```

### Limits of the brief

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` | 3600 characters | The first part is cut at this length. Ostra adds `(brief truncated; see the inventory for the rest)`. The cut can remove the closing sentence that names the inventory path. |
| `MAX_PROJECT_DOC_CHARS` | 12000 characters | The limit for each instruction file. Ostra adds `(truncated; read the file for the rest)`. |
| `MAX_SKILL_ROWS` | 16 | Skill rows. `convention` skills always pass the filter. `write-test` keeps skills whose name or kind holds `test` or `spec`. `code-reviewer` keeps only `convention` skills. |
| `MAX_MODULE_ROWS` | 10 | Module-map rows. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_BOOKS` | 20 | Books that the brief lists. The text adds `and N more` and tells the agent to use Glob. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` in `ostra_core::artifacts` | 40 | Artifacts that the brief lists. The text adds `and N more`. |
| Row text | 48, 90, 150, 170, 190 characters | Cut points for skill purposes, immutability keywords and test reports (90), test matches (150), review rules (170), and naming, notes, and test notes (190). |

The limit `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` applies only to the first part. The other sections have their own limits.

### What happens when the brief has gaps

- **The project has no profile:** the first part is absent. The other sections still appear.
- **The agent is the initializer:** `sections` returns an empty list, so the first part is absent. A project instruction file still appears.
- **There is nothing to say:** `augment` returns the first message unchanged. The test `brief_is_idempotent_and_handles_a_missing_profile` checks this.
- **The first message already holds a brief heading:** `augment` returns it unchanged. The heading `## Projects created in this session` is not one of the 5 headings.
- **Instruction text is blank:** the function drops it.

## Add a line to a spawn block

1. Add the field to the struct in `spawn.rs`. Use a non-`Option` type for a required line.
2. Write the line in the `render` method of the struct, at the right position.
3. Add the label to `PARAMS` with its type. Add the id to the `contract()` arm of the agent when the line is required.
4. Set the field in the `build` arm of the agent in `factory.rs`. Add the planner input to `SpawnInputs` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs` when it does not exist.
5. Change the prompt of the agent so that it reads the new line.
6. Run `cargo test --workspace`. The round-trip test fails when `render` and `contract()` disagree.

code_refs.note: The trait, `Common`, the enums, and `Extras`.
The block format rules.
The `PARAMS` table, `contract()`, `check`, and `parse_block`.
Brief sections, limits, and `augment`.
`build`, `agent_meta`, and `judge_prompt`.
The `BuiltSpawn`, `SpawnEnv`, and `SpawnFactory` types.
Round-trip, `parse_block`, and brief tests.

sections.title: Agent catalog and submit payloads
sections.summary: The 14 agents with tier, timeout, capabilities, and write scope, the submit payload of each agent, the extra checks in validate_submit, and the steps to add an agent.
sections.body:
This page lists the 14 agents of Ostra and the result that each one returns. It gives a table of tier, timeout, capabilities, and write scope. It explains each submit payload, the extra checks in `validate_submit`, and the steps to add an agent. The page "Typed research, spec, and plan documents" covers the checks that read document files.

## The problem: the engine needs typed results

An agent that ends with free text forces the engine to scrape that text. Hard rule 4 forbids this. Each agent ends its execution with one call to its own submit tool, `submit_<agent>`. The engine reads only the payload of that call. The tool description says this: `The engine reads only this call, so any result not in it is lost.`

The payload types live in [`crates/ostra-core/src/submit.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/submit.rs). They derive `JsonSchema`, and `submit_schema(agent)` returns the JSON schema that the model sees. The function `validate_submit(agent, input)` checks the payload when the agent calls the tool.

## Catalog of the 14 agents

The enum `AgentName` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs) lists the agents. The constant `AgentName::ALL` holds all 14, in this order. The values for tier and timeout come from `agent.toml`.

| Agent | Role | Tier | Timeout | Write scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | Researches one task and writes one research document. It is the only agent that searches the web for the pipeline. | `advanced` | 1800 s | Session dir and OS temp |
| `generate-spec` | Reads every research document and writes one spec. | `advanced` | 1800 s | Session dir and OS temp |
| `fact-check` | Checks a spec or a plan and returns a verdict with findings. | `advanced` | 1800 s | Session dir and OS temp |
| `plan` | Turns an approved spec into a master plan and one file for each phase. | `advanced` | 1800 s | Session dir and OS temp |
| `implementer` | Writes the code of one plan phase or one inline change. It never writes tests. | `balanced` | 2400 s | Not confined by `is_session_only` |
| `code-reviewer` | Reviews unstaged changes against the Review Rule Set and scans for security BLOCKER findings. | `balanced` | 1200 s | Session dir and OS temp |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | Traces the execution paths of a phase and assigns a test level to each check. | `balanced` | 1200 s | Session dir and OS temp |
| `write-test` | Writes the tests that the EPA report assigns and runs them. It writes only test code. | `balanced` | 2400 s | Not confined by `is_session_only` |
| `documentation` | Writes one project's part of the documentation book. | `advanced` | 2400 s | Session dir and OS temp |
| `system-architecture` | Writes the architecture of a book that covers 2 or more projects. | `advanced` | 1800 s | Session dir and OS temp |
| `prompt-generation` | Writes or edits instruction files: prompts, `SKILL.md` files, and agent definitions. | `advanced` | 1800 s | Not confined by `is_session_only` |
| `initializer` | Bootstraps a project in one of 6 modes. | `balanced` | 2400 s | Not confined by `is_session_only` |
| `quick-answer` | Answers one question in the side panel. It never writes files. | `balanced` | 300 s | None: no `write`, `edit`, or `shell` capability |
| `advisor` | Diagnoses a failed step and tells the engine to retry or to ask the user (Rule O5). | `advanced` | 900 s | Session dir and OS temp |

The method `is_session_only` names the 9 agents that the write-scope guard confines to their session dir and the OS temp folder. The guard itself belongs to the policy engine.

The next table lists the capabilities of each agent, from `agent.toml`.

| Agent | Capabilities |
| --- | --- |
| `explore` | `read`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `memory_recall`, `memory`, `document`, `code`, `coordinate`, `docs_search` |
| `generate-spec` | `read`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `document`, `code`, `coordinate`, `docs_search` |
| `fact-check` | `read`, `write`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `code`, `coordinate`, `docs_search` |
| `plan` | `read`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `document`, `code`, `coordinate`, `docs_search` |
| `implementer` | `read`, `edit`, `write`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `skill`, `memory_recall`, `memory`, `report`, `code`, `manage_projects`, `coordinate`, `docs_search` |
| `code-reviewer` | `read`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `code`, `coordinate`, `docs_search` |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | `read`, `shell`, `write`, `search_text`, `glob`, `report`, `code`, `docs_search` |
| `write-test` | `read`, `edit`, `write`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `skill`, `memory_recall`, `memory`, `report`, `code`, `coordinate`, `docs_search` |
| `documentation` | `read`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `code`, `docs_search` |
| `system-architecture` | `read`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `code`, `docs_search` |
| `prompt-generation` | `read`, `edit`, `write`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `skill`, `report`, `code` |
| `initializer` | `read`, `write`, `edit`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `code` |
| `quick-answer` | `read`, `search_text`, `glob`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `memory_recall`, `code`, `docs_search` |
| `advisor` | `read`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `memory_recall`, `docs_search` |

These facts follow from the table and the tests:

- Only `explore`, `generate-spec`, and `plan` hold `document`. They write documents with the `Document` tool and hold no `write` or `edit` capability. The test `read_only_agents_have_no_edit_and_quick_answer_cannot_write` checks this.
- Only `implementer` holds `manage_projects`. The method `manages_projects` returns `true` for it, because only a phase of an approved plan starts a new project (Rule O2).
- Only `implementer` and `write-test` route their model tier by the complexity of the phase. The method `routes_by_complexity` returns `true` for them. The complexity comes from the `**Complexity:**` line of the phase file.
- `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, and `fact-check` hold no `edit` capability.

### Names, keys, and old names

- The enum serializes in kebab-case, which matches the folder `assets/agents/<name>/`. The method `snake()` gives `code_reviewer` for tool names. The method `label()` gives `Code reviewer`.
- `AgentName::from_str` accepts the prefixes `ostra:` and `ultracode:` and trims white space.
- The name `module-documentation` is a retired name. Log rows and saved settings from before the books feature use it. It maps to `Documentation` through a serde alias and through `from_str`. The constant `RETIRED_AGENTS` lets settings validation ignore it.
- The constant `JUDGE_ROUTE` is `judge`. The function `route_keys()` returns the 14 agent names and `judge`, which are the 15 keys that need a model route in workspace settings.

### The initializer modes

The enum `InitializerMode` has 6 values. The `Mode:` line selects one. The page "Spawn contract and repo brief" lists the lines of each mode.

| Mode | What the execution does |
| --- | --- |
| `detect` | Plans the scout and flags an Ultracode bootstrap. |
| `scout` | Runs once for each slice and captures the recurring component patterns. |
| `propose` | Merges the scout findings into a skill proposal for approval. |
| `generate-skill` | Runs once for each approved skill. |
| `generate-inventory` | Writes `INVENTORY.md` and `project.toml`. |
| `adopt` | Migrates an Ultracode bootstrap. |

## Submit tools and payloads

The method `submit_tool_name()` returns `submit_<snake>`, for example `submit_code_reviewer`. The Claude Code executor shows the tool as `mcp__ostra__submit_code_reviewer`. The function `submit_description(agent)` writes the description of the tool.

The type `SubmitStatus` has 3 values in lowercase: `ok`, `stuck`, and `handoff`. A payload with a `status` field uses it. `stuck` carries a `StuckInfo` with `diagnostic` (the exact failing output) and `need` (the fact or decision that is missing). `handoff` carries a `HandoffInfo` with `specialist` (always `prompt-generation` today), `request`, `target_files`, and `resume_instructions`. Both executors read the `status` string of the payload: `stuck` and `handoff` give those statuses, and all other values give `ok`. A payload without a `status` field always gives `ok`.

| Agent | Payload type | Fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | `ExploreSubmit` | `research_path`, `scope_covered`, `findings_summary`, `sources_retrieved`, `open_questions` (a count), `not_covered` |
| `generate-spec` | `GenerateSpecSubmit` | `spec_path`, `open_questions` (question cards), `external_evidence_rows`, `deliverables`, `requirements`, `summary` |
| `fact-check` | `FactCheckSubmit` | `verdict` (`PASS`, `FAIL`, `ERROR`), `target` (`spec` or `plan`), `findings` |
| `plan` | `PlanSubmit` | `spec_path`, `master_plan_path`, `phases`, `stakes`, `summary`, `step_count`, `requirement_coverage`, `clarifying_questions`, `new_projects` |
| `implementer` | `ImplementerSubmit` | `status`, `report_path`, `changed_files`, `summary`, `stuck`, `handoff` |
| `code-reviewer` | `CodeReviewerSubmit` | `findings`, `security_block`, `ledger_path`, `summary` |
| `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, `prompt-generation` | `ReportSubmit` | `status`, `report_path`, `changed_files`, `summary`, `stuck` |
| `documentation` | `DocumentationSubmit` | `status`, `summary`, `overview`, `sections`, `glossary`, `stuck` |
| `system-architecture` | `ArchitectureSubmit` | `status`, `summary`, `architecture`, `glossary`, `stuck` |
| `initializer` | `InitializerSubmit` | `status`, `summary`, `files`, `result`, `stuck` |
| `quick-answer` | `QuickAnswerSubmit` | `answer` (markdown), `sources` |
| `advisor` | `AdvisorSubmit` | `action` (`retry` or `escalate`), `guidance`, `reason` |

Some fields need more detail:

- **`FactCheckFinding`:** `severity` (`BLOCKER`, `HIGH`, `MEDIUM`, `LOW`), `location`, `element` (the id of the element, such as `R3`, `AC3.2`, `E2`, `D1`, `C4`, `phase 2`, or `step 2.3`), `claim`, and `issue`. The method `findings_text()` renders the findings for the `Prior findings:` line of the next pass (Rule D3a). It returns `none` when the list is empty.
- **`PlanPhaseSubmit`:** `id`, `deliverable`, `project`, `title`, `complexity` (`Low`, `Medium`, `High`), `test_policy` (`Required` or `Skip`), `test_rationale`, `depends_on`, and `file` (the absolute path of the phase file). The field `new_projects` lists the keys of projects that the plan puts phases in but that do not exist yet. The implementer of the first such phase creates each one (Rule O2).
- **`ReviewFinding`:** `severity`, `file`, `rule` (`SEC-BLOCK-*`, `PHASE-REQ-*`, or a rule id of the Review Rule Set), `description`, `fix`, and `guidance` (for BLOCKER only). The method `line()` renders `[SEVERITY] file (rule) - description Fix: fix`, and adds `Guidance:` for a BLOCKER.
- **`InitializerSubmit.result`:** a JSON object that depends on the mode. The attribute `#[schemars(extend("type" = "object"))]` forces the schema type `object`, and the test `initializer_result_is_an_object` checks it.
- **`DocumentationSubmit` and `ArchitectureSubmit`:** their types live in `crates/ostra-core/src/book.rs`. The page "Book model, submit rules, merge, and files on disk" describes them.

## Checks at the tool boundary

Both executors run the same chain of checks when an agent calls its submit tool. The native executor runs it in `Run::submit`. The harness bridge runs it in `HarnessBridge::call_tool`. The second one differs in 2 ways, which the cases below state.

### Order of the checks in the native executor

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Model calls submit_agent"]
    B{"Input marked __invalid_json?"}
    C{"Policy allows the call?"}
    D{"validate_submit passes?"}
    E{"check_submit passes?"}
    F{"Status ok and report file missing?"}
    X["Error result, run continues"]
    G["Result received, run ends"]
    A --> B
    B -- yes --> X
    B -- no --> C
    C -- no --> X
    C -- yes --> D
    D -- no --> X
    D -- yes --> E
    E -- no --> X
    E -- yes --> F
    F -- yes --> X
    F -- no --> G
```

The function `validate_submit` first parses the payload into its type with `serde`. A missing required field or a wrong type gives an error. The payload types do not set `deny_unknown_fields`, so an unknown field passes. Then 4 agents get extra checks:

| Agent | Extra check | Error text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code-reviewer` | `security_block` must equal the presence of a BLOCKER finding. | `security_block must be true exactly when a BLOCKER finding is present` |
| `documentation` | `check_documentation` returns no issue. | The issues, one on each line. |
| `system-architecture` | `check_architecture` returns no issue. | The issues, one on each line. |
| `advisor` | An action `retry` needs a guidance text that is not blank. | `give \`guidance\` for a retry: what the step's next run must do differently` |

The `code-reviewer` rule exists because a BLOCKER stops the work loop and a wrong flag would hide or invent a block. The doc comment of `FactCheckSubmit.verdict` says that `PASS` is allowed only when no finding is `HIGH` or `MEDIUM`. `validate_submit` does not enforce that sentence, so the prompt must hold the agent to it.

After `validate_submit`, `check_submit` runs. It reads files, so it runs here and never in the fold of the event log. It applies to `explore`, `generate-spec`, `plan`, and the `generate-inventory` result of the `initializer`. The page "Typed research, spec, and plan documents" describes it.

### What happens when a submit call fails or repeats

- **The streamed input is not valid JSON:** the provider layer marks it `__invalid_json`. The native executor returns an error result and the run continues.
- **A check fails in the native executor:** the tool result is an error, nothing is recorded, and the model can call the tool again. The texts are `The <name> input is invalid: <e>. Fix it and call <name> again.` for `validate_submit` and `<e> Nothing was recorded.` for `check_submit`.
- **The status is `ok`, the agent has a report file, the file does not exist, and the agent is not the `code-reviewer`:** the native executor refuses with `Write your report to <path> before you call <name>, because the engine reads the report at that path.` The harness bridge does not make this check.
- **The call succeeds in the native executor:** the result is `Result received.` Every other call in the same turn gets the error result `Not run: the run ended with the submit call.`
- **The harness bridge gets a valid payload:** `record_submit` keeps the first payload. A second call gets `A result was already recorded for this run. End your turn now.`
- **A harness agent calls another agent's submit tool:** the bridge answers `Call \`<own tool>\` instead: that is this agent's submit tool.`
- **A harness run owes a reply to another subagent:** the bridge refuses the submit call and tells the agent to reply first (Rule H3).
- **The agent ends its turn with no submit call:** the page "Native executor: turn loop, submit, and compaction" and the page "Supervising a run, usage, and the failure matrix" describe the reminders and the final status.

## Add an agent

The `match` statements on `AgentName` have no wildcard arm. The compiler stops the build for the code steps. It does not detect the asset steps.

1. Add the variant to `AgentName` in `crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`. Update `ALL` (the array length changes), `as_str`, and the flags `is_session_only`, `manages_projects`, and `routes_by_complexity`.
2. Create `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml` with all 5 effort keys. Create `assets/agents/<name>/prompt.md`. Make the prompt name its submit tool with `{{tool_submit}}`.
3. In `spawn.rs`, add the params struct, its `SpawnParams` impl, the new labels in `PARAMS`, and an arm in `contract()`.
4. In `brief.rs`, add an arm to `sections()`.
5. In `factory.rs`, add an arm to `AgentsFactory::build`.
6. In `submit.rs`, add the payload type and an arm in `submit_schema` and in `validate_submit`.
7. Make the planner in `crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs` spawn the agent at the right stage. The page "The planner, steps, and the drive loop" describes that code.
8. Run `cargo build --workspace`, `cargo test --workspace`, and `cargo fmt --all`.

A missing or invalid `agent.toml` does not fail the build. It panics at the first call to `agent_def`. The test `every_prompt_renders_for_every_executor_with_no_unresolved_token` loads every definition and every prompt, so run it before you merge.

sections.title: Typed research, spec, and plan documents
sections.summary: How research, spec, and plan documents are stored as JSON with rendered markdown, who owns each kind, how update and remove merge, which checks block a submit, and how check_submit works.
sections.body:
This page explains the typed documents that `explore`, `generate-spec`, and `plan` write. It covers the JSON source and the rendered markdown, the document kinds and owners, the merge rules for `update` and `remove`, the checks that block a submit, and `check_submit` at the tool boundary. It does not cover the documentation book. The page "Book model, submit rules, merge, and files on disk" covers that.

## The problem: free markdown breaks the pipeline

Each stage of the pipeline reads the document of the stage before. If the documents are free markdown, 4 failures occur. An id can name an item that does not exist. A count in the submit call can differ from the document. A table that the model computes by hand can be wrong. A revision can rewrite the whole document and lose text.

Ostra stores each document as typed JSON and derives the markdown from it. The module comment of [`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/mod.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/doc/mod.rs) states the goal: the browser shows each part natively, and the pipeline keeps reading markdown. The types give 4 benefits:

- The model sees a JSON schema. The doc comment of each field is its schema description, so the comments are written as instructions.
- Ostra computes the derived tables and counts, so the model does not write them.
- Ostra checks the references between ids and blocks a submit when a reference is broken.
- A revision sends only the items that changed.

## Document kinds, owners, and files

The enum `DocKind` has 3 values. The `Document` tool accepts a kind only from its owner agent. The function `DocKind::for_agent` returns `None` for every other agent.

| Kind | Owner | File name prefix | Path field in the submit call | First line of the markdown |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Research` | `explore` | `ostra-research-` | `research_path` | `# Research: <title>` |
| `Spec` | `generate-spec` | `ostra-spec-` | `spec_path` | `# Specification: <title>` |
| `Plan` | `plan` | `ostra-plan-` | `master_plan_path` | `# Plan: <title>` |
| Phase (part of a plan) | `plan` | `<plan name>-phase-<n>` | none | `# Phase <n>: <name>` |

A document `<name>` has 2 files in the session dir. The file `<name>.json` is the source. The file `<name>.md` is rendered from it, so the agents that read markdown get the text. A plan also writes `<plan name>-phase-<n>.md` and `.json` for each phase. The function `phase_path(master, id)` builds those names. The function `doc_kind_for(path)` finds the kind of a file by its prefix, and a phase file reports `Plan`.

The doc comment of `render.rs` explains why the markdown has fixed section names: the names match the templates that the downstream prompts and `fact-check` refer to.

## The types of the three documents

All types derive `JsonSchema` and `TS`, and most set `deny_unknown_fields`. An unknown field is an error, so a misspelled field cannot pass silently.

- **`ResearchDoc`:** `title`, `date`, `repo`, `scope`, and `problem` are required. The optional lists are `areas`, `asks`, `files`, `patterns`, `data_flow`, `dependencies`, `external` (facts from pages that the run retrieved), `approaches`, `recommendation`, `open_questions`, `sources`, `lessons`, `not_covered`, and `next_steps`.
- **`SpecDoc`:** `title`, `date`, `objective`, and `current_behavior` are required. The lists are `research`, `repos`, `in_scope`, `out_of_scope`, `criteria` (`C1`, `C2`, ...), `deliverables` (`D1`, ...), `requirements` (`R1`, ...), `contracts_provided`, `contracts_consumed`, `evidence` (`E1`, ...), `data_impact`, `assumptions`, `open_questions`, and `notes`. Each requirement has an EARS pattern, one statement with exactly one `SHALL`, `covers`, `rests_on`, and `acceptance` items with `given`, `when`, and `then`.
- **`PlanDoc`:** `title`, `date`, `spec`, `stakes`, `stakes_rationale`, and `summary` are required. The lists are `repos`, `success_criteria`, `clarifying_questions`, `deliverables`, `phases`, `risks`, `verification`, and `pre_checks`. Each `Phase` has `id`, `name`, `deliverable`, `repo`, `repo_root`, `complexity`, `test_policy`, `test_rationale`, `depends_on`, `context`, `skills`, `requirements`, `constraints`, `steps`, and `verification`. Each `PlanStep` has `id`, `title`, `file`, `change` (`Create`, `Modify`, `Delete`), `read_first`, `delivers`, `action`, `binding_rules`, `skills`, `verify`, and `size`.

The method `DocKind::parse` deserializes with `serde_path_to_error`. The error text names the failing field, for example `requirements[0].acceptance[0]: missing field \`then\``. For a plan, `parse` also adds the skills of each step to the `skills` of its phase, without duplicates (Rule P7). The implementer loads only the skills that the phase file lists, so this union keeps the lists in step.

## How the Document tool writes a document

The `Document` tool is in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs). The agent gives a `path` and one of 2 inputs: `document` (the whole document) or `update` with an optional `remove` list.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant Tool as Document tool
    participant Doc as ostra_core doc
    participant Disk as Session dir
    participant Exec as Executor
    Agent->>Tool: Document(path, update, remove)
    Tool->>Doc: load(md)
    Doc->>Disk: read the JSON file
    Tool->>Doc: apply_update(base, update, remove)
    Tool->>Doc: write(kind, md, value)
    Doc->>Disk: write JSON, then markdown, then phase files
    Doc-->>Tool: Written with issues
    Tool-->>Agent: summary with errors and warnings
    Agent->>Exec: submit_agent(research_path)
    Exec->>Doc: check_submit(agent, input)
    Doc-->>Exec: Ok or an error text
```

The tool checks these rules, in this order:

1. The agent must own a kind. Other agents get `Only explore, generate-spec, and plan write documents. Write your output where your prompt says.`
2. `path` must be present and not blank.
3. The file name must start with the prefix of the kind and end with `.md`. A plan name must not contain `-phase-`. The expected shape is `<prefix>{run-stamp}-{topic-slug}.md`, because later stages find the file by the prefix.
4. The file must be directly in the session dir. The tool compares both folders with `paths::fold`, so a Windows path with another prefix or letter case still matches.
5. `remove` must be a list. Each item is a string or a number.
6. The agent sends either `document`, or `update` with `remove`. Both together give an error. `document` with a non-empty `remove` is also an error.
7. For an update, the tool loads the stored JSON. A `remove` on a document that does not exist gives `There is no <kind> at <path> yet, so there is nothing to remove.`
8. `write` parses the value. A schema error gives `The <kind> does not match its schema, so nothing was written: <error>. Fix that field and call Document again.`

The function `write(kind, md, value)` then runs the checks and writes. The files go to disk one after the other: the JSON (pretty-printed, with a newline at the end), the markdown, and for a plan the pair of files of each phase. `write` does not use a temporary file, so a failed write can leave some files new and some old. A write failure returns `Could not write <path>: <error>`. After the phase files, `write` deletes each file that starts with `<plan stem>-phase-`, ends in `.md` or `.json`, and has no phase in the new plan.

The tool result lists the counts, the files, and the issues. With an error it says: `Fix the N errors below with an \`update\` before you submit, because the submit call is refused while any remain.` With only warnings it prints `Warnings to review:`. A call with only a `path` on an existing document renders and checks it again.

## Update and remove merge rules

The function `apply_update(base, update, remove)` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/merge.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/doc/merge.rs) lets a revision send only what changed. It works on the top-level fields.

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| A top-level field is not in the stored document. | The field is added. |
| The stored value and the new value are lists, and the new items all have an `id`. The stored list is empty or all its items have an `id`. | Items merge by `id`. A matching item is replaced as a whole. A new item is added. The list is sorted by natural order of the `id`. |
| Any other value: a scalar, an object, or a list without ids. | The new value replaces the stored value. |
| An `id` is a number, such as a phase id. | Ostra compares it as text. |

Natural order puts `R2` before `R10` and `AC1.2` before `AC1.10`. The test `natural_order` shows this. A new `R12` lands after `R11`, wherever the agent sent it.

The `remove` list works after the merge. It deletes each item whose `id` is in the list, from every top-level list whose items all have an `id`. An id that matches nothing returns `Nothing to remove for <ids>: no list item has that id. Check the ids and call again; nothing was written.` Then the tool writes nothing.

Three limits follow from the rules:

- **Nested items:** a merge does not reach into an item. To change one acceptance criterion, send the whole requirement with its full `acceptance` list.
- **Lists without ids:** a list such as `notes` is replaced as a whole. Send all items again.
- **Phase files:** a revision that removes a phase also removes its files, because `write` deletes stale phase files. The test `plan_writes_master_and_phase_files` checks this.

## Checks that run on every write

The function `check(document)` returns a list of `DocIssue` values. Each one has a level, an optional element id, and a message. The list is sorted with errors first. An error blocks the submit call. A warning is shown to the agent and to the reader.

The messages start with the correction, for example `Cover this criterion with a requirement, or no plan will build it (S1).` The text in parentheses is the rule id from the prompts of the agents.

### Checks for questions

Research, spec, and plan documents use the same checks for question cards:

- Error: a question id appears twice.
- Error: a question has fewer than 2 or more than 4 options.
- Error: `recommended` does not index an option.
- Warning: a `tag` has more than 12 characters, because the question card clips it.

### Checks for a research document

- Error: an `external` fact cites a `source` that is not in `sources`. Every external fact cites a page that the run retrieved.
- Error: more than one approach has `recommended` set.
- Warning: a source URL does not start with `http://` or `https://`.
- Warning: the document has approaches and no `recommendation`.

### Checks for a spec

Errors:

- A duplicate id in criteria, deliverables, requirements, acceptance criteria, or evidence rows.
- A `depends_on` that names a criterion or deliverable that does not exist.
- A cycle in the deliverables. Delivery order must be acyclic (Step 5).
- A criterion that no requirement covers (S1).
- A requirement id that does not have the form `R{n}`, a `deliverable` that does not exist, an empty `covers`, a `covers` that names a missing criterion (S8), or a `rests_on` that names a missing evidence row.
- A requirement with no acceptance criterion, an acceptance id that does not have the form `AC{n}.{m}` for its requirement, or an empty `given`, `when`, or `then`.
- A deliverable with no requirement.
- A contract `provided_by` that names a missing deliverable, or a `consumed_by` of the form `D<digits>` that names a missing one.

Warnings:

- A `provisional` that names a question that is not open.
- Requirements out of deliverable order, or not in one flat sequence `R1`, `R2`, ... (the check expects the next number).
- A statement that does not hold exactly one `SHALL` (R-a).
- A deliverable that covers more than 6 criteria, when no note in `notes` names it (S4).
- An evidence row that no requirement rests on.

### Checks for a plan and its phases

The checks of `phase_body` run for the plan and again for each phase document.

Errors:

- Phase ids that do not run 1 to N in order (P10). The check reports only the first break.
- A duplicate phase id, a `depends_on` that names a missing phase, or a cycle in the phases. Ostra schedules the phases as a graph.
- An empty `test_rationale` (P12), a phase with no step, a duplicate step id, or a step id that does not have the form `{phase}.{n}`.
- A `binding_rules` entry whose id is not in the `constraints` of the phase, whose text differs from the constraint, or whose text is empty (P13). The implementer never reads the spec, so the rule text must travel with the step.
- An empty `verify` (P5).
- Skills (P6): in a repo with installed skills, a phase with a non-delete step where no step names a skill, and a step that names a skill that is not installed. The check reads the folders `.agents/skills` and `.ostra/skills` of the `repo_root` of each phase. It does nothing for a repo with no installed skill.

Warnings:

- A `depends_on` that names the same phase or a later one.
- A phase deliverable that is not in the `deliverables` list, when that list is not empty.
- A step with an empty `delivers` (P11), or a `delivers` id that the phase does not quote in `requirements`.

## What the markdown holds

The function `render(document, md)` returns the markdown, and it removes extra blank lines at the end. A table cell has one line, and the `|` character is escaped. Ostra computes these parts, so the model does not write them:

- **Spec:** the counts for deliverables and requirements, the line `Criteria covered: <met> of <total>`, the Delivery Order table, and the Traceability table.
- **Plan:** the line `Delivers requirements`, the Deliverable Index, the Phase Index with the phase file path of each phase, the Test Policy Rationale, the Requirement Traceability table, and the step counts.
- **Phase:** a header with the plan, spec, deliverable, repo, dependencies, complexity, and test policy, then the required skills, the context, the quoted requirements, the external constraints, the steps, and the phase verification block. The implementer reads this file and nothing else, so it must be complete.

The function `load_view(md)` gives the browser a `DocumentView` with the typed document and its issues. It detects a phase file by the `-phase-<n>` suffix of the file name.

## check_submit at the tool boundary

The function `check_submit(agent, input)` runs after `validate_submit` in the native executor and in the harness bridge. It reads files, so it runs at the tool boundary and never in the fold of the event log. A read in the fold would break the replay after a restart.

1. For the `initializer`, it runs `check_inventory_submit`. If the `result` holds both `inventory_path` and `profile_path`, the inventory file must exist and `check_profile` must parse the profile. This catches the problem while the agent can still fix it, because the init fails at its last step otherwise. An example error is `Write <path> before you submit: the file does not exist.`
2. For an agent with no document kind, it returns `Ok`.
3. It reads the path field of the kind. A missing field gives `` `research_path` is missing.`` or the field that applies.
4. It loads the JSON behind the path. With no JSON it returns `Write the <kind> with the Document tool before you submit: <path> has no document behind it.`
5. It parses the document and runs `check`. Errors give `Fix these in the document with the Document tool, then submit again:` and one line for each error.
6. It compares the counts of the submit payload with the document.

| Kind | Fields that must match |
| --- | --- |
| Research | none |
| Spec | `external_evidence_rows` equals the evidence rows, `deliverables` equals the deliverables, `requirements` equals the requirements |
| Plan | `step_count` equals the total steps, `phases` has the same length as the phases of the plan. For each phase: `id`, `deliverable`, `project` (equals `repo`), `complexity`, `test_policy`, `depends_on` (in any order), and `file` (equals `phase_path`) |

The error for a count is `` `requirements` is 5, but the spec has 4.`` The error for a phase tells the agent which values to send. The check ignores other fields, for example `title`, `stakes`, and `requirement_coverage`. For a research document, it ignores `sources_retrieved` and `open_questions` of the payload.

### What happens when a document is wrong

- **The model sends a field that the schema lacks:** `write` fails, nothing is written, and the error names the field.
- **The document has errors and the agent submits:** the submit call fails and nothing is recorded. The agent fixes the document with an `update` and submits again.
- **The document has only warnings:** the submit call passes.
- **The agent edits the JSON file with another tool:** the next `Document` call or `check_submit` reads the stored JSON. The markdown can differ from the JSON until the next write, because only `write` renders it.
- **A revision runs in a later round:** the owner agent receives the same document path and sends an `update`. The merge rules above keep the unchanged items.

## Change a document type

1. Add the field to the struct in `doc/mod.rs`. Use `#[serde(default)]` for an optional field, and write a doc comment as an instruction for the model.
2. Render the field in `doc/render.rs`. Keep the section names that the downstream prompts use.
3. Add a check in `doc/check.rs` if the field holds an id that refers to another item.
4. Update the fixtures in `doc/fixtures/` and the tests in `doc/tests.rs`. The test `fixtures_parse_and_pass` requires that the 3 fixtures give no issue.
5. Run `cargo test --workspace`, then `cargo fmt --all`.

To add a new kind, add a `DocKind` variant with its owner, prefix, and label. Add the path field in `check_submit`. Give the owner the `document` capability in its `agent.toml`.
