sections.title: Book model, submit rules, merge, and files on disk
sections.summary: How a book is shaped, how the engine validates a documentation submit, how it names, merges, and writes a book, and which files it leaves on disk.
sections.body:
## Why the engine owns the book files

A documentation book has many writers and many readers, and its files must stay consistent. Without rules, an agent can write a malformed file. Two sessions that finish at the same time can overwrite each other's parts. A search tool cannot find a fact in a free-form file.

The `book` module in [`crates/ostra-core/src/book.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/book.rs) removes these problems in four steps:

- A writer agent returns its pages in one `submit_documentation` call. The agent writes no file.
- `validate_submit` runs `check_documentation` on the payload and returns each problem to the agent.
- The engine merges the payload into the book on disk with `apply`. `apply` holds a lock.
- The engine writes `book.json` and the Markdown files with `write`.

The guard `workspace-docs` in [`crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs`](crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs) denies every write, move, and delete inside the books folder. Its message tells the agent to put the documentation in the submit call. Agents can read the books. The page "Searching books: ranking and the DocsSearch tool" covers the search. The page "Closing gate, tests, documentation, and the completion report" covers the docs stage that calls `apply`.

The comments in the code label each rule with a number. Use the number to search the code.

| Rule | What it fixes | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B1 | The fixed shape and the fixed order of a section | `DocSection`, `render_body` |
| B2 | Every section lists its assumptions | `check_body` |
| B3 | The kind and the size of a diagram | `check_diagram` |
| B4 | The architecture of a book with two or more projects | `Architecture`, `check_architecture` |
| B5 | Only the engine writes book files | `write`, guard `workspace-docs` |
| B6 | The book ID and the merge | `book_id`, `merge`, `BOOK_LOCK` |
| B7 | At most 4 docs writers run at once in one session | `MAX_DOCS_WRITERS` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs` |
| B8 | Search over the books | `crates/ostra-core/src/book_search.rs` |

## The book model

A book covers a set of projects. A part is the contribution of one project to a book. A section is one unit of work in a part. A sub-section has the same fields as a section but has no children. A book of two or more projects also has one architecture.

| Type | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `Book` | `id`, `title`, `projects` (sorted), `updated_at`, `sessions` (oldest first), `architecture` (optional), `parts`, `glossary` (sorted by term) |
| `BookPart` | `project`, `overview`, `sections`, `updated_at` |
| `DocSection` | The section fields below, plus `subsections` |
| `DocSubsection` | The section fields below, without `subsections` |
| `Architecture` | `overview`, `diagram`, `components`, `links`, `failure_recovery`, `scalability` |
| `BookSummary` | `id`, `title`, `projects`, `updated_at`, `sections`, `has_architecture` |
| `BookUpdate` | `session`, `parts` (a project key and a `DocumentationSubmit` for each), `architecture`, `glossary` |

`BookSummary.sections` counts the top-level sections of all parts. It does not count sub-sections. `BookUpdate` is not serialized. The engine builds it from the event log with `SessionState::book_update`, so a replay of the log rebuilds the same update.

### Section fields

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | slug | Names the section. The file is `<project>/<id>.md`. |
| `title` | text | The heading of the section. |
| `purpose` | text | What the section does. Blank lines separate paragraphs. |
| `boundaries` | `owns`, `does_not_own` | What the code is responsible for, and what it leaves to other parts. |
| `assumptions` | list of text | What the code takes as given about inputs, callers, data, and environment. |
| `business_flow` | list of `BusinessStep` | Each step has an `actor`, an `action`, and an `outcome`. |
| `diagrams` | list of `Diagram` | Each diagram has a `title`, a `kind` (`sequence` or `flowchart`), and Mermaid `source`. |
| `tables` | list of `DocTable` | Each table has a `title`, `columns`, and `rows`. |
| `concerns` | list of `Concern` | A `component` and its `responsibility`. |
| `code_refs` | list of `CodeRef` | A `path`, an optional `symbol`, optional `lines`, and a `note`. |
| `subsections` | list of `DocSubsection` | Only `DocSection` has this field. |

The fields `boundaries`, `business_flow`, `diagrams`, `tables`, `concerns`, `code_refs`, and `subsections` have a serde default, so a payload can omit them. The fields `id`, `title`, `purpose`, and `assumptions` have no default. If a payload omits one, the JSON parse fails and `validate_submit` returns the parse error to the agent.

### The two submit payloads

- `DocumentationSubmit` holds `status`, `summary`, `overview`, `sections`, `glossary`, and `stuck`. One writer returns it for one project.
- `ArchitectureSubmit` holds `status`, `summary`, `architecture`, `glossary`, and `stuck`. The architecture agent returns it for a book of two or more projects.

Both types derive `JsonSchema`. `submit_schema` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/submit.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/submit.rs) builds the schema of the submit tool from them. The `#[ts(export)]` attribute makes ts-rs generate the TypeScript types for the console.

## Submit rules

`check_documentation` returns a list of issues. The list is empty when the payload passes. Each issue states the correction first and the reason after it, so the agent can fix the payload without a second question. `validate_submit` joins the issues with a newline and returns them as the refusal text.

The check runs only when `status` is `ok`. A payload with another status, such as `stuck`, passes with no issues, because it carries no pages to check.

### Rules for a documentation submit

- **At least one section.** `sections` must not be empty, because the book shows only what the agent submits.
- **A title for each section and sub-section.** A blank title is an issue.
- **A purpose for each section and sub-section.** A blank purpose is an issue.
- **Assumptions (Rule B2).** At least one entry must have text. The issue text says to write `None found in the code` only after checking, because readers and agents rely on the list.
- **Diagrams (Rule B3).** Each diagram passes `check_diagram`. The next heading explains it.
- **Tables.** A table must have at least one column, and every row must have one cell for each column.
- **Code references.** Each `path` must be relative to the project root. The path must not be empty. It must not start with `/`, `\`, or `~`. It must not have `:` as its second character, which blocks a drive letter. It must not have a `..` part.
- **IDs.** A section ID and a sub-section ID must be slugs. A slug starts with a lowercase letter or a digit, has at most 64 characters, and holds only lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. All IDs of one submit share one namespace, so a sub-section cannot reuse a section ID.
- **Glossary.** Each entry needs a term and a definition. A term must appear once. The check ignores case and surrounding spaces.

The unit tests in `book.rs` show the effect. A test changes one valid submit in three ways: a repeated ID, an empty assumptions list, and an absolute path. The check returns exactly 3 issues.

### Rules for an architecture submit

`check_architecture` returns one issue and stops when `architecture` is missing. Otherwise it checks the following:

- The overview is not blank.
- The diagram has the kind `flowchart`, and it passes `check_diagram`.
- The list holds at least two components, and each name is unique. Links name the components, so a repeated name makes a link unclear.
- Each link names a listed component at both ends.
- `links`, `failure_recovery`, and `scalability` are not empty.
- The glossary follows the same rules as a documentation submit.

## Diagram limits

`check_diagram` keeps a diagram small. The reason is in the issue text: a reader follows a small diagram and loses a large one. The check reads the first line of the Mermaid source that is not blank and does not start with `%%`.

| Declared kind | The first line must be | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sequence` | exactly `sequenceDiagram` | At most 8 participants (`MAX_SEQUENCE_PARTICIPANTS`) and at most 20 messages (`MAX_SEQUENCE_MESSAGES`) |
| `flowchart` | a line that starts with `flowchart` or `graph` | At most 15 nodes (`MAX_FLOWCHART_NODES`) |

If the first line does not match the declared kind, the check reports a kind issue and does not count the size. The check is a text count. It is not a Mermaid parser.

### How the count works

- **Sequence participants.** The count holds each name in a `participant` or `actor` line (the text before ` as `). It also holds each name at the two ends of a message arrow.
- **Sequence messages.** A message is a line that has a colon and has one of these arrows before the colon: `-->>`, `->>`, `<<->>`, `<<-->>`, `-->`, `->`, `--x`, `-x`, `--)`, `-)`. The count strips a leading `+` or `-` from the target name.
- **Flowchart nodes.** The count removes node shapes (`[...]`, `(...)`, `{...}`), quoted text, and `|edge labels|`. It splits each line on edges and on `&`. Each piece gives a node ID of letters, digits, and underscores. Lines that start with `subgraph`, `end`, `style`, `classDef`, `class`, `linkStyle`, `click`, or `direction` add no node.

The tests `sequence_counts_declared_and_aliased` and `flowchart_counts_nodes` fix these counts. For example, the flowchart test source has 8 nodes.

## The book ID

A book ID names the folder of the book. `book_id` makes the ID from the set of project keys, so a later session on the same projects updates the same book. This is Rule B6.

### Flowchart: how `book_id` builds an ID

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Project keys] --> B[Sort and remove duplicates]
    B --> C[Join with underscore]
    C --> D{"80 bytes or fewer?"}
    D -->|yes| E[Use the joined text]
    D -->|no| F["Hash the full text with FNV-1a 64"]
    F --> G["Cut the text to at most 63 bytes"]
    G --> H["Append underscore and 16 hex digits"]
```

The join character is `_`. Project keys hold only lowercase letters, digits, and dashes, so `_` never appears inside a key. The sets `a-b` plus `c` and `a` plus `b-c` give different IDs for this reason. A test checks this case.

A long set gives a long ID. Ostra limits an ID to `MAX_BOOK_ID` = 80 bytes, so a folder name stays short on every file system. For a longer ID, `book_id` computes the FNV-1a 64-bit hash of the full joined text. It cuts the text at the last character start at or before byte 63. Then it appends `_` and the hash as 16 lowercase hex digits. The result has at most 80 bytes. Two long sets that share a prefix still get different hashes.

`is_book_id` accepts an ID when all of these are true:

- The first character is a lowercase ASCII letter or a digit.
- The ID has at most 80 bytes.
- Every other character is a lowercase ASCII letter, a digit, `-`, or `_`.

The check blocks `..`, `/`, and `\`, so an ID cannot leave the books folder. Four places use it: `list` and `load_books` skip folders whose names fail it, the REST routes return status 400 for a bad ID, and `create_session` refuses a bad `docs_book`.

### Which ID a session uses

The user can pick an existing book on the New task form. The session stores the pick as `docs_book`. `SessionState::book_id` and the planner use the pick when `is_book_id` accepts it. Otherwise they call `book_id` with the projects whose parts the session wrote. An abandoned part names no book, because the planner reads the parts that finished.

A changed project set gives a new book. A session that documents `api` writes the book `api`. A later session that documents `api` and `web` writes the book `api_web`. The first book stays. Pick the old book on the New task form to add the new part to it.

## The locked merge

`merge` is a pure function. It takes the existing book (or none), the ID, a `BookUpdate`, and the time. It returns the new book. `apply` wraps it with a read, a write, and a lock.

### Sequence diagram: how the engine writes a book

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Runner as Engine runner
    participant Apply as book apply
    participant Lock as BOOK_LOCK
    participant Merge as book merge
    participant Disk as Book folder
    Runner->>Apply: Step WriteBook with the BookUpdate
    Apply->>Lock: lock
    Apply->>Disk: read book.json
    Disk-->>Apply: existing Book or none
    Apply->>Merge: merge existing and update
    Merge-->>Apply: merged Book
    Apply->>Disk: write book.json and Markdown
    Apply-->>Runner: Book or io error
```

The lock is released when the guard goes out of scope, after the write.

### What `merge` does

1. It starts from the existing book, or from an empty book with the given ID.
2. For each project in the update, it removes the old part of that project and adds a new `BookPart` with the new overview and sections. The new part replaces the old part completely, so a section that the new submit omits disappears.
3. It sorts the parts by project key.
4. If the update has an architecture, it replaces the old one. If not, the old one stays.
5. It merges the glossary. The incoming entries are the glossaries of the parts, then the glossary of the update. For each entry, `merge` removes the old entry with the same term (trimmed and lowercase) and adds the new one. The newer definition wins. Then it sorts the list by lowercase term.
6. It sets `projects` to the sorted set of the part projects. It sets `title` to `Documentation for` and the project keys joined with a comma.
7. It adds the session ID to `sessions` when the list does not hold it, and sets `updated_at`.

Parts of projects that the update does not name stay as they are. Glossary entries also stay. If a new part no longer uses a term, the old entry remains in the book.

### The book lock

`BOOK_LOCK` is one static `std::sync::Mutex` for the whole process. `apply` and `remove` hold it for the full read-merge-write. Without it, two sessions that finish at the same time can both read the old book. The session that writes last then removes the part of the other. The test `concurrent_updates_keep_every_part` runs 8 threads that update one book. After it, the book has 8 parts and 8 sessions.

Three facts limit the lock:

- The lock covers all books of all workspaces, not one book. Two books wait for each other. This is acceptable because a write is short.
- The lock lives in process memory. It does not coordinate two Ostra processes.
- `read` and `list` take no lock. A reader that runs during a write can see a `book.json` that does not parse. `read` then returns `None`, and that book is missing from that one call.

A poisoned lock does not stop the engine, because `apply` takes the inner guard with `into_inner`.

## Files on disk

The books folder is `<workspace>/.ostra/docs/`. `dir` builds it from `paths::workspace_runtime`. Each book has its own folder named with its ID.

```
<workspace>/.ostra/docs/<book id>/
  book.json            the whole Book, as pretty JSON
  index.md             the table of contents
  glossary.md          the glossary table
  architecture.md      only when the book has an architecture
  <project>/<section id>.md   one file for each section
```

`write` creates the folder, writes each file, and records each relative path in a keep set. `book.json` is first. After the last file, `remove_stale` walks the book folder. It deletes every file that is not in the keep set. It also deletes every folder that is empty after that. Sub-sections have no file of their own, because their text is inside the file of their section.

> Caution: Do not put your own files in a book folder. The next write deletes every file that the engine did not write.

The write is not atomic. Each file is written in turn with `std::fs::write`. If a write fails, `apply` returns the I/O error. The engine records the error text in the `BookWritten` event, and the session goes on without the files. The text is: `The book could not be written to <folder>: <error>`.

### What the Markdown files hold

The renderer writes the same fields in the same order for each section (Rule B1). `render_section` writes the title as the only level-1 heading and a `Project:` line. Then `render_body` writes the body at level 2.

| Part of the file | When it appears |
| --- | --- |
| The `purpose` text | Always |
| `## Boundaries` with `Owns:` and `Does not own:` lists | When either list has items |
| `## Assumptions` | Always |
| `## Business flow` as a table with the columns Step, Actor, Action, Outcome | When the list has steps |
| One heading for each diagram, then a `mermaid` code block | For each diagram |
| One heading for each table, then the table | For each table |
| `## Separation of concerns` as a table | When the list has items |
| `## Code references` as a table with the columns Path, Symbol, Lines, What it holds | When the list has items |

Each sub-section follows its section. It starts with a `##` heading, and its own headings are at level 3. A table cell has each `|` escaped as `\|` and each newline replaced with a space.

The other files follow the same method:

- `architecture.md` starts with `# System architecture` and the overview. Then it has the diagram and the sections Components, Communication, Failure and recovery, and Scalability. Each of the four sections is a table.
- `glossary.md` starts with `# Glossary` and one table with the columns Term, Definition, and Code.
- `index.md` starts with the book title and the line `Written by Ostra's docs stage. Updated <date> UTC.` It links the glossary, and the architecture when one exists. For each part it writes the project key, the overview, and one link for each section with the first sentence of its purpose. The first sentence ends at the first `. ` in the text. The index does not list sub-sections.

## How the engine and the API use a book

The engine starts the write with `Step::WriteBook { book }` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs). The runner takes a snapshot of the session, builds the `BookUpdate`, calls `apply`, and appends `SessionEvent::BookWritten { book, projects, error }`.

When the file `book.json` of the session's book exists, `existing_book` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/factory.rs` gives its path to the writer at spawn time. The writer then updates the pages that it knows. The path is read outside the fold.

The server has three routes, all in `crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`:

| Route | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/docs` | A list of `BookSummary`, newest first. Equal times sort by ID. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/docs/{book}` | The full `Book`. Status 404 with `No such book in this workspace.` when the book is missing. |
| `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/docs/{book}` | Removes the book folder and returns the new list. |

A bad book ID gives status 400. `DELETE` first checks that `book.json` exists, and gives status 404 if not. Then it tries to take the workspace work lock for writing. If work is starting in the workspace, it gives status 409 with `Try again in a moment, because work is starting in this workspace.` This is Rule W4: no session starts between the check and the removal. A failed removal gives status 500. The console reader of books is covered in the web console topic.

### What happens when

- **Two sessions update one book at the same time.** `BOOK_LOCK` makes the second wait. Both parts stay.
- **A session documents a project again.** The new part replaces the old part of that project. Other parts stay.
- **A new submit omits a section.** The section is gone from `book.json`, and `remove_stale` deletes its Markdown file.
- **The disk write fails.** The session records the error in `BookWritten` and continues. The old book files can be partly changed, because the write is not atomic.
- **The picked `docs_book` is not a valid ID.** `create_session` returns the error `Pick a documentation book from the list instead of ...`. If a stored value is invalid anyway, `SessionState::book_id` ignores it and uses the ID from the project set.
- **`book.json` does not parse.** `read` returns `None`. `list`, `load_books`, and the routes treat the book as missing.
- **The status of a submit is not `ok`.** `check_documentation` reports no issues, and the engine does not treat the submit as a part with pages.
- **A log was written before books existed.** The aliases `module_docs`, `module-documentation`, and `module-docs` still read as the current purpose, agent, and stage. The test `logs_from_before_books_still_read` checks this.

## Change the shape of a section

A new section field must change several places, because the same eight fields appear in more than one struct. Follow these steps:

1. Add the field to `DocSection` and to `DocSubsection` in `book.rs`. Give it a serde default so old `book.json` files still parse.
2. Add the field to the private `Body` struct and to both `From` impls in `book.rs`.
3. Render the field in `render_body`, and keep its place in the fixed order.
4. Add a check to `check_body` when the field has a rule.
5. Add the field to the `Body` struct and to `Builder::body` in `crates/ostra-core/src/book_search.rs`, so the search finds it. Also add the field to the two `Body` literals in `Builder::book`.
6. Run `cargo test --workspace`.

The search keeps its own copy of `Body` and has its own passage kinds. A field that is missing there is written to the files but is invisible to `DocsSearch`.

## Limits

| Name | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_SEQUENCE_PARTICIPANTS` | 8 | Participants in a sequence diagram |
| `MAX_SEQUENCE_MESSAGES` | 20 | Messages in a sequence diagram |
| `MAX_FLOWCHART_NODES` | 15 | Nodes in a flowchart |
| `MAX_BOOK_ID` | 80 bytes | Length of a book ID |
| Slug length (`is_slug`) | 64 characters | Length of a section or sub-section ID |
| `MAX_DOCS_WRITERS` | 4 | Docs writers that run at once in one session |
| Hash width | 16 hex digits | Suffix of a long book ID |

sections.title: Searching books: ranking and the DocsSearch tool
sections.summary: How DocsSearch cuts books into passages, makes tokens, ranks with BM25 and three weighted fields, and returns only the passages that matched.
sections.body:
## The problem that book search solves

An agent that must learn an area has two bad choices. It can read the code again, which costs many tool calls. It can read a whole book section, which holds many facts that the agent does not need. The search in [`crates/ostra-core/src/book_search.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/book_search.rs) gives a third choice. It returns the best sections for a question and shows only the passages that matched. This is Rule B8.

The agent calls the tool `DocsSearch`. The function `docs_search` in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/misc.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/misc.rs) runs it. This page covers the tool input and output, the passages, the tokens, the ranking, and the limits. The page "Book model, submit rules, merge, and files on disk" covers the book files that the search reads.

## The DocsSearch tool

The tool takes three arguments. The schema is in `docs_search_def` in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/defs.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/defs.rs).

| Argument | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `query` | yes | The question, with any names that the agent knows: types, functions, file paths, or domain terms. |
| `project` | no | A project key. The search then covers only the part of that project. |
| `limit` | no | The number of sections to return. The default is `DEFAULT_LIMIT` = 5. The value is clamped to the range 1 to `MAX_LIMIT` = 15. |

The tool always searches all books of the workspace. The `book` field of `Filter` exists, but `docs_search` sets it to `None`.

### Sequence diagram: one DocsSearch call

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant Tool as docs_search
    participant Load as load_books
    participant Index
    Agent->>Tool: DocsSearch with query project limit
    Tool->>Load: read every book.json
    Load-->>Tool: books sorted by ID
    Tool->>Index: build the index
    Tool->>Index: search with query filter limit
    Index-->>Tool: hits
    Tool->>Index: render the hits
    Tool-->>Agent: numbered sections with passages
```

The tool builds the index again for each call. It reads every `book.json` of the workspace, builds the passages, and discards the index at the end. It does the work inside `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, so the async runtime does not wait for the disk. The index has no cache, so the next call always sees the newest books. The cost is that each call reads all books.

### The output

The output starts with a count line, for example `2 sections matched, most relevant first:`. A numbered entry follows for each hit. The entry shows the title, the book, the project, the path of the Markdown file, and the matching passages. This is the format for a hit:

```
1. Execution slots (app, project `app`)
   File: `<workspace>/.ostra/docs/app/app/slots.md`
   Purpose:
   Caps concurrent executions.
```

A passage label ends with a colon, and the passage text follows with three spaces of indent. The score does not appear in the output. The agent reads the file when it needs the whole section. For a sub-section hit, the file is the file of the parent section, because sub-sections have no file of their own. The title of a sub-section hit has the form `Section > Sub-section`.

A book describes the code when it was written. The tool description tells the agent to check a passage against the code before it relies on the passage.

### Where agents learn about the tool

The spawn brief of an agent lists the books of the workspace. It shows at most `MAX_BRIEF_BOOKS` = 20 books, each with its `index.md` path, projects, and section count. If the agent has the capability `Capability::DocsSearch`, the brief names the tool and tells the agent to search before it reads code. The native executor calls the tool `DocsSearch`. A harness executor sees it as `mcp__ostra__docs_search`, and the adapter maps the name back to `DocsSearch`. A permission rule can name `DocsSearch`, because it is in the known tool list of `crates/ostra-policy/src/perms.rs`.

## How a book is cut into passages

The search treats the book as a set of units. A unit is one part of a book that a hit can point at. Each unit holds passages. A passage is a short text with a label. The ranking scores passages and then groups them by unit.

| Unit kind | `Unit.id` | Title | File |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Overview | `project/overview` | `<project> overview` | `index.md` |
| Section | `project/section` | The section title | `<project>/<section>.md` |
| Sub-section | `project/section/sub` | `Section > Sub-section` | The file of the parent section |
| Glossary term | `glossary/<term in lowercase>` | `Glossary: Term` | `glossary.md` |
| Architecture aspect | `architecture/overview`, `components`, `communication`, `failure`, `scalability` | `System architecture > Overview`, and so on | `architecture.md` |

Glossary and architecture units have an empty `project`. The `Unit` also keeps the paths of its code references in `code_paths`.

The builder cuts each unit into passages with these rules:

| Passage kind | Label | How it is cut |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overview | `Overview` | One passage for each paragraph. A blank line ends a paragraph. |
| Purpose | `Purpose` | One passage for each paragraph of the purpose. |
| Boundaries | `Boundaries` | Lines `- Owns: ...`, then lines `- Does not own: ...`, in windows of 5 lines. |
| Assumptions | `Assumptions` | Windows of 5 lines. |
| Business flow | `Business flow` | Windows of 5 lines. A line reads `N. actor: action Then: outcome`. |
| Diagram | `Diagram: <title>` | One passage for each diagram. The text is the Mermaid code block. |
| Table | `Table: <title> (<columns>)` | Windows of 5 rows. A row reads `- cell \| cell`. |
| Concerns | `Separation of concerns` | Windows of 5 lines. |
| Code references | `Code references` | Windows of 5 references. |
| Glossary | `Definition` | One passage with the definition and the code reference. |
| Architecture | `Overview`, `Component: <name>`, `Links`, `Failure case`, `Scaling` | One passage for each paragraph, component, and failure case. Windows of 5 for links and scaling cases. The diagram is also a passage. |

The constant `WINDOW` = 5 sets the window size. A long list becomes many small passages. This keeps a hit short, because a hit shows only the passages that matched. A table of 40 rows gives 8 passages. A passage with blank text is not stored.

## How the text becomes tokens

The function `tokens` turns text into the words that the index counts. The same function runs on the query and on the book text, so both sides agree.

1. Split the text at every character that is not a letter, a digit, or `_`. Each piece is a run.
2. Split each run into identifier parts. The function `split_ident` splits at `_`, at a change from a lowercase letter or a digit to an uppercase letter, and at the end of a capital run before a lowercase letter.
3. If the run has more than one part, add the whole run in lowercase as one token.
4. For each part, convert it to lowercase. Drop it when it has 1 byte or is in the stop list.
5. Stem each remaining token with `stem`.

The stop list `STOP` has common English words such as `the`, `how`, `what`, `does`, `can`, `should`, `each`, `get`, and `use`. The stem rules are simple:

- A word with more than 4 bytes that ends in `ies` becomes a word that ends in `y`.
- A word with more than 4 bytes that ends in `sses` loses the last 2 bytes.
- A word with more than 3 bytes that ends in `s` loses the `s`, unless it ends in `ss`, `us`, or `is`.

The unit tests show the result. `SessionState::fold` gives `sessionstate`, `session`, `state`, `fold`. `max_parallel_executions` gives `max_parallel_execution`, `max`, `parallel`, `execution`. `HTTPServer` gives `httpserver`, `http`, `server`. The query `auth.rs` gives `auth` and `rs`, so it finds a section whose code reference path is `src/auth.rs`.

The split of identifiers has a reason. An agent that searches for a type name and an agent that searches for the words of that name must find the same passage.

### Diagram words

A diagram passage does not count its raw Mermaid source. The function `diagram_words` keeps only the labels and the messages. It removes words with 2 bytes or less, which covers most node IDs. It also removes the Mermaid keywords in `MERMAID_WORDS`, for example `sequenceDiagram`, `flowchart`, `participant`, `actor`, `subgraph`, `loop`, and `TD`. The reason is that these words appear in every diagram and say nothing about the content. The test `diagram_syntax_does_not_match` shows it: the query `participant` returns nothing, and the query `cart submit` finds the diagram.

## The three fields and the BM25 score

BM25 is a ranking formula that scores a text for a set of query words. It rewards rare words, and it limits the reward for a word that repeats. It also compares the length of the text with the average length. Ostra applies it to each passage with three weighted fields.

| Field | Weight | What it holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Title (`W_TITLE`) | 2.0 | The label of the passage, for example `Assumptions` or `Diagram: Slot hand-off`. |
| Code (`W_CODE`) | 1.5 | The paths and symbols of a code reference passage, the code reference of a glossary term, or the project of an architecture component. |
| Body (`W_BODY`) | 1.0 | The text of the passage. For a code reference passage it holds only the notes. For a diagram it holds the diagram words. |

The code field exists so that a query with a file name or a symbol ranks a passage that names it, even when the notes do not repeat the name. The comment in the code says: notes rank as body text, and paths and symbols rank in the code field.

### The formula

The code uses these values: `K1` = 1.2 and `B` = 0.75. A term is a token of the query. `N` is the number of passages plus the number of units. `df` is the number of passages that hold the token in any field, plus the number of unit titles that hold it.

```
idf(t)   = ln(1 + (N - df(t) + 0.5) / (df(t) + 0.5))
tf       = 2.0 * title(t) + 1.5 * code(t) + 1.0 * body(t)
len(p)   = 2.0 * title tokens + 1.5 * code tokens + 1.0 * body tokens
norm(p)  = K1 * (1 - B + B * len(p) / avg_len)
score(p) = sum over the terms of idf(t) * tf * (K1 + 1) / (tf + norm(p))
```

`avg_len` is the mean of `len(p)` over all passages, with a minimum of 1.0. A term that is not in the index has no `df`, so the search drops it. This means that a query with one unknown word still finds results for its other words. The search is an OR of the terms, not an AND.

## From passage scores to hits

The search scores the passages that pass the filter. Then it groups the scores by unit and builds one hit for each unit.

### Flowchart: the ranking steps

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[Query text] --> T[Make tokens and remove duplicates]
    T --> I[Compute idf for each known token]
    I --> P[Score each passage that passes the filter]
    P --> U[Group passage scores by unit]
    U --> W[Add the title score and 0.35 of the second passage]
    W --> S[Sort the units by score]
    S --> L[Keep the first limit units]
    L --> R[Keep at most 2 passages at 50 percent of the best]
```

The rules for a unit are:

- **Unit title score.** The title of the unit scores once for the unit: `2.0 * idf * c * (K1 + 1) / (c + K1)` for each term, where `c` is the count of the term in the title. It has no length term.
- **Unit score.** `score = title + best + SECOND_SHARE * second`. `best` is the best passage score. `second` is the second best. `SECOND_SHARE` = 0.35. A section with two good passages ranks above a section with one equal passage.
- **Shown passages.** The hit keeps passages whose score is at least `SHOW_SHARE` = 0.5 times `best`. It keeps at most `PASSAGES_PER_HIT` = 2 of them.
- **Title only.** If a term appears in the unit title but in no passage, the unit still gets a hit. Its score is the title score, and the hit shows the first passage of the unit with score 0.
- **Order.** Hits sort by score, highest first. Equal scores sort by the order in which the index built the units. A passage list sorts by score, then by passage order.

The code for the last steps is short:

```rust
let score = title + best + SECOND_SHARE * ps.get(1).map_or(0.0, |p| p.1);
ps.retain(|p| p.1 >= best * SHOW_SHARE);
ps.truncate(PASSAGES_PER_HIT);
```

The title counts once and never picks the shown passages. Without this rule, a unit whose title matches would show passages that have no relation to the query. The test `ranks_the_section_that_matches_and_shows_only_its_matching_passage` shows the result. A query about concurrent executions ranks the section `slots` first and shows only its `Purpose` passage. The `Assumptions` passage does not match, so it does not appear.

### The project filter

`Filter { book, project }` keeps a unit when each set field equals the unit field. With a `project` set, the search covers only units of that project. Glossary and architecture units have an empty project, so the filter removes them. The test `project_filter_applies` checks that an unknown project returns no hits. The filter also changes the ranking only through `df` and `avg_len`, because both come from all passages, not from the filtered ones.

## What happens when

- **The `query` argument is missing.** The tool returns an error: `Pass query: the question you want the documentation books to answer.`
- **The query has only stop words or one-letter words.** The token list is empty, so the search returns no hits. The agent gets the no-match message.
- **The run has no workspace.** The tool answers that there are no books and tells the agent to read the code. This case is a workspace root that is an empty path.
- **The workspace has no books.** The tool answers `This workspace has no documentation books yet. Read the code instead.` The first test of `docs_search_returns_matching_passages` checks this case.
- **No passage matches.** The tool answers `No section of the documentation books matches this query. Try other names or terms, or read the code.`
- **A `book.json` is damaged.** `load_books` skips that book without an error. The book is missing from the results.
- **A book changes between two calls.** The second call sees the change, because each call builds a new index.
- **The `limit` is 0 or more than 15.** The tool clamps it to 1 or to 15.
- **The blocking task fails.** The tool returns the error `The documentation search failed: <error>`.

## Change the ranking

A change of the ranking has effects that no compile error shows. Use the unit tests in `book_search.rs` to check each change. Follow these rules:

- To add a passage kind, add a variant to `PassageKind` and a case in `Builder::body` or `Builder::book`. Choose the label with care, because it is the title field.
- To change a weight, change `W_TITLE`, `W_CODE`, or `W_BODY`. The weights also change `len(p)`, so the average length changes too.
- To change the number of passages in a hit, change `PASSAGES_PER_HIT` and `SHOW_SHARE` together. Then update the tool text in `DOCS_SEARCH` in `defs.rs` if the behavior that it describes changes.
- Keep `tokens` the same for the query and for the book text. If the two differ, a word that is in the book cannot match the query.

## Limits

| Name | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_LIMIT` | 5 | Sections returned when `limit` is absent |
| `MAX_LIMIT` | 15 | Largest `limit` |
| `WINDOW` | 5 | List items or table rows in one passage |
| `PASSAGES_PER_HIT` | 2 | Passages shown in one hit |
| `SHOW_SHARE` | 0.5 | A shown passage must score at least this share of the best |
| `SECOND_SHARE` | 0.35 | Share of the second passage that adds to the unit score |
| `K1` | 1.2 | BM25 term saturation |
| `B` | 0.75 | BM25 length normalization |
| `W_TITLE`, `W_CODE`, `W_BODY` | 2.0, 1.5, 1.0 | Field weights |
| `MAX_BRIEF_BOOKS` | 20 | Books that the spawn brief lists |

sections.title: Executor contract: spec, context, result, and deltas
sections.summary: Explains the types that the engine gives to an executor and reads back, the Executor and ExecutionHost traits, and the steps to add an executor.
sections.body:
## Why the engine uses one executor contract

The engine must start an agent without knowing how the agent runs. Ostra has two kinds of executor. The native executor calls a model API with an API key. A harness executor drives an installed CLI in a terminal.

Without one contract, the engine needs a separate code path for each kind. The contract in `crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs` removes that need. The engine builds one `ExecutionSpec`, calls `Executor::run`, and reads one `ExecutionResult`. During the execution, the executor reports progress through the `ExecutionHost` trait.

An execution is one run of one leaf agent. This page covers the types of the contract, the two traits, and the steps to add an executor. The native loop is on the page Native executor: turn loop, submit, and compaction. The harness executors are on the page Launching a harness CLI: plans, terminal, and sandbox wrap. The cost formula is on the page Shared types: ids, paths, usage, pricing, and wire shapes.

## How the engine calls an executor

The runner in `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` is the only caller in the normal pipeline. The diagram shows the calls for one execution.

### Call sequence of one execution

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Runner as Engine runner
    participant Services as ServerServices
    participant Factory as AgentsFactory
    participant Exec as Executor
    participant Host as EngineHost
    Runner->>Services: executor(route.executor)
    Services-->>Runner: Some(executor) or None
    Runner->>Factory: build(request)
    Factory-->>Runner: system_prompt, first_message, effort
    Runner->>Exec: run(spec, host, cancel)
    Exec->>Host: emit(ExecutionDelta)
    Exec->>Host: ask_permission(call, reason, rule)
    Host-->>Exec: PermissionAnswer
    Exec->>Host: record_message(role, content)
    Exec-->>Runner: ExecutionResult
    Runner->>Runner: add usage_base, map Cancelled to Interrupted
    Runner->>Runner: finish_execution(result)
```

The runner does these steps in order:

1. Read the route of the agent. The route holds an `ExecutorKind` and a model.
2. Call `Services::executor(kind)`. If the answer is `None`, record a `Denied` execution with the text `The <kind> executor is not available.` and stop.
3. Call `AgentsFactory::build`. It returns the system prompt, the first message, and the effort.
4. Build the `ExecutionSpec`, a `CancellationToken`, and an `EngineHost`.
5. Call `executor.run(spec, host, token)` and wait for the result.
6. Add the usage of earlier runs of the same execution (`usage_base`) to `result.usage`.
7. If the status is `Cancelled` and the engine interrupted the execution, set the status to `Interrupted` and put the reason in `error`.
8. Store the result with `finish_execution`, send `EngineNotice::ExecutionStatus`, and append `SessionEvent::ExecutionFinished`.

Two other paths build a spec outside the pipeline. `Engine::ask` runs a side-panel quick answer on the native executor. It has no session, uses the permission mode `Plan`, and uses the effort `Medium`. `Engine::inspect_execution` reopens an ended harness execution so that the user can read it.

## ExecutionSpec: what the engine hands over

`ExecutionSpec` holds everything that one execution needs.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `ExecutionId` | Identity of this execution. |
| `agent` | `AgentName` | One of the 14 leaf agents. |
| `route` | `ResolvedRoute` | Fields `executor`, `model`, and `tier`. A native model is `provider:model`. A harness model is the slug of the CLI. |
| `effort` | `Effort` | Reasoning level: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`. |
| `system_prompt` | `String` | The agent prompt, rendered with the tool names of this executor. |
| `first_message` | `String` | The spawn block, the repo brief, and the custom instructions. |
| `capabilities` | `Vec<Capability>` | The capabilities of the agent from its `agent.toml`. |
| `submit_schema` | JSON | Input schema of `submit_<agent>`. The value is `null` for a reopened read-only session. |
| `timeout_secs` | `u64` | The time budget. The runner copies it from `timeout_seconds` of `agent.toml`. |
| `ctx` | `ExecContext` | The facts that the policy layer needs. |
| `resume` | `Option<ResumeInfo>` | Present when the execution continues an earlier one. |
| `harness_session_id` | `Option<String>` | A session id that the engine chooses before launch. |

The runner sets `harness_session_id` only for Claude Code and Grok, because only these two CLIs accept an id at launch. The id is `resume.native_session_id` when the execution resumes. Otherwise it is a new UUID v4. For every other executor the field is `None`.

The system prompt depends on the executor, because each executor has its own tool names. For this reason the engine renders the prompt after it knows the route.

## ExecContext: what the policy layer needs

The engine builds one `ExecContext` for each execution. The native loop passes it to `ExecutionPolicy::new`.

| Group | Fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity | `execution_id`, `session_id`, `agent`, `initializer_mode`, `executor` | Who runs. `session_id` is `None` for a quick answer and for a reopened session. |
| Paths | `workspace_root`, `repo_root`, `project_key`, `session_dir`, `session_root`, `report_file`, `memory_db`, `protected_paths` | Where the agent works. `repo_root` is the `Repo root:` of the spawn and the working directory. `report_file` is the `Report file:` of the spawn, when the agent has one. |
| Permission | `yolo`, `permission_mode`, `permissions`, `enforce_tool_calls` | How to judge a tool call. `permissions` merges the global, workspace, and session rules. `enforce_tool_calls` is Rule G1: layer 1 checks where tool calls read and write. |
| Sandbox | `sandbox_mode`, `sandbox_network`, `sandbox_allowed_hosts`, `sandbox_decoys`, `sandbox_loopback`, `sandbox_blocked_ports` | The workspace choices. Each one replaces or extends the global `[sandbox]` choice. `ExecContext::sandbox()` returns them as a `WorkspaceSandbox`. |
| Run shape | `phase`, `creates_project`, `answer_only`, `owes_reply` | `phase` is `N`, `N-tests`, or `none` in review loops. The three flags are explained below. |

`protected_paths` lists the paths that no agent can write, delete, or execute from. The list holds the Ostra binary, its config, its databases, and every engine state directory.

The three run-shape flags change how an executor ends the execution:

- `creates_project` (Rule O2): the phase is in a project that does not exist yet. The execution starts outside the project and must create the project first.
- `answer_only` (Rule H3): the execution is a consult run. It answers one question and writes no file.
- `owes_reply` (Rule H3): the execution starts with a question from another subagent. It must answer with `SubagentReply` and submit nothing before that.

`ExecContext.yolo` is only the value at the start. The user can switch YOLO on or off during an execution. Therefore the executor must read `host.yolo()` before each policy check.

## ResumeInfo: continue an execution

`ResumeInfo` has four fields: `from`, `native_session_id`, `note`, and `inspect`. `from` is the execution that the new execution continues. `note` is the first message of the resumed execution. It replaces the default interruption notice. `native_session_id` is the CLI session id that a harness resume command needs.

The contract has three kinds of resume:

- **Resume in place:** `from` equals `spec.id`. The engine continues a paused, waiting, or interrupted execution under the same id.
- **Resume from another execution:** `from` is a different id. The new execution starts from the stored conversation of the old one.
- **Inspect:** `inspect` is `true`. The session reopens for the user to read and ask about. It has no first prompt, no tools, and no submit. It ends when the user leaves or stops it.

Only a harness execution can be inspected. `Engine::inspect_execution` refuses a native execution with the text `Only a harness execution has a session to reopen. Read a native run in its Activity tab.` It also refuses these cases:

- The execution is still running.
- The execution recorded no harness session.
- The execution is itself an inspect session.
- A paused agent will resume the same conversation.

The engine gives an inspect session `INSPECT_TIMEOUT_SECS`, which is `4 * 60 * 60` seconds. A harness inspect session that exits or times out returns status `Ok` with the final text `The read-only session ended.`

## ExecutionResult and ExecutionStatus

`Executor::run` returns an `ExecutionResult`, not a `Result`. Every failure becomes a result with a status and an `error` text. The fields are:

- `status`: an `ExecutionStatus`.
- `submit`: the payload of the `submit_<agent>` call, when the agent called it.
- `final_text`: the last assistant text, kept for display and for the transcript.
- `usage`: the `Usage` of this run.
- `native_session_id`: the CLI session id, for harness resume.
- `error`: the error text.

Two helpers build results. `ExecutionResult::error(message)` sets the status `Error`. `ExecutionResult::with_status(status)` sets a status and no error text.

| Status | Who sets it | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `running` | The engine | The only status that is not terminal. `is_terminal()` is true for every other status. |
| `ok` | The executor | The agent submitted with a status other than `stuck` or `handoff`. The native loop also returns `ok` with `submit` set to `None` when the agent ends twice without a submit. A consult reply returns `ok` with a coordination payload. |
| `stuck` | The executor | The `status` field of the submit payload is `stuck`. |
| `handoff` | The executor | The `status` field of the submit payload is `handoff`. |
| `waiting` | The executor | Rule H2: the agent asked another subagent and waits for the answer. |
| `error` | The executor | The execution failed, timed out, or hit a limit. `error` holds the text. |
| `denied` | The engine | The executor was not available, so the engine records the denial itself. |
| `interrupted` | The engine | The engine cancelled the execution, and it rewrites `cancelled` to this status. |
| `cancelled` | The executor | The cancel token fired. |

The engine, not the executor, decides what each status means for the session. The page How a session runs from request to completion explains that part.

## Usage: the cost record of one run

Every executor reports usage in the `Usage` struct. All fields default to zero.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `input_tokens` | Input tokens that are not cache reads or cache writes. |
| `output_tokens` | Output tokens. |
| `cache_read_tokens` | Tokens read from the prompt cache. |
| `cache_write_tokens` | Tokens written to the prompt cache, with the 5-minute and the 1-hour TTL together. |
| `cache_write_1h_tokens` | The part of `cache_write_tokens` that has the 1-hour TTL, which costs more. |
| `cost_usd` | Cost in US dollars. |
| `tool_calls` | Count of tool calls. |
| `build_ms` | Wall time in build and test commands, for the build-loop metric. |
| `context_tokens` | Size of the latest request: its prompt plus its output. |

`Usage::add` sums every field except `context_tokens`. For `context_tokens`, it takes the new value when the new value is above zero. The reason is that the context size describes the latest request. A sum of the sizes has no meaning.

```rust
pub fn add(&mut self, other: &Usage) {
    self.input_tokens += other.input_tokens;
    ...
    self.build_ms += other.build_ms;
    if other.context_tokens > 0 {
        self.context_tokens = other.context_tokens;
    }
}
```

An executor counts from zero. It must report only the usage of its own run. The engine adds the earlier spend of a resumed execution, which is `usage_base` in `EngineHost`. `EngineHost::emit` adds `usage_base` to every `Usage` delta, and the runner adds it to the final result. Without this rule, a resume would lose the earlier cost.

## ExecutionDelta: the live stream

An executor sends `ExecutionDelta` values to `host.emit`. The engine stores each delta as an activity row and publishes it to the console. The serialized form has a `kind` field in snake case.

| Kind | Fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | `text` | Assistant text. |
| `thinking` | `text` | Reasoning text. |
| `tool_call` | `call_id`, `call` | A tool call before it runs. |
| `policy` | `call_id`, `decision` | The policy decision for the call. |
| `tool_output` | `call_id`, `chunk` | Live output of a running shell command. |
| `tool_result` | `call_id`, `output`, `is_error`, `duration_ms` | The result of a call. |
| `usage` | `usage` | The running total of the run. |
| `turn` | `usage`, `call_ids` | The own usage and cost of one model response, and the ids of its tool calls. |
| `status` | `message` | A line of progress text. |
| `native_session_id` | `id` | The CLI session id. |
| `egress` | `host`, `port`, `allowed`, `reason`, `local` | The first answer of the egress proxy for a host and port. |
| `decoy` | `path` | A sandbox process opened a decoy credential file (Rule P3). |

The `turn` delta comes after the thinking and text of its response and before its tool calls. A native execution shows these deltas in the Activity view. A harness execution shows a terminal instead. `ExecutorKind::stream()` returns `ExecStream::Activity` for native and `ExecStream::Terminal` for every harness.

## ExecutionHost: callbacks into the engine

`ExecutionHost` is the set of callbacks that an executor uses during a run. The engine implements it as `EngineHost`. Four methods have default bodies, so a simple host, such as a test host, can skip them.

| Method | Default | What `EngineHost` does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `emit(delta)` | None | Stores the delta, updates the execution summary line, and adds `usage_base` to `usage` deltas. It writes the cost of the execution and of the session. It also records a containment signal when the delta is one. |
| `ask_permission(call, reason, rule)` | None | Opens a permission gate and waits for the answer. Under YOLO it answers `AllowOnce` at once. With no session, it answers `Deny`. |
| `record_message(role, content)` | No operation | Stores one transcript message, so that a resume can continue from it. |
| `transcript(execution)` | Empty list | Returns the stored `(role, content)` pairs of an execution, oldest first. |
| `yolo()` | `false` | Returns the live YOLO state of the session. |
| `wait_for_wake()` | `None` | Rule H2: waits until a message arrives for the execution. Then it returns a `Wake`. |

`wait_for_wake` frees the execution slot while it waits and takes a slot again before it returns. Without this rule, a waiting run would hold the only slot, and the run that it waits for could not start. The result is `None` when the engine drops the sender, which means that no message will come. Only the harness executor calls this method. The native loop returns the status `Waiting` instead.

A `Wake` has a `note` and an `owes_reply` flag. The note is the text that goes into the run. `owes_reply` is true when the note is a question that the run must answer with `SubagentReply`.

`ask_permission` answers `Deny` when the host has no session, cannot read the session state, cannot append the gate event, or loses the waiter. A side-panel run is read-only and never asks the user.

## The Executor trait and the rules of an executor

```rust
#[async_trait::async_trait]
pub trait Executor: Send + Sync {
    async fn run(
        &self,
        spec: ExecutionSpec,
        host: Arc<dyn ExecutionHost>,
        cancel: CancellationToken,
    ) -> ExecutionResult;
}
```

The code does not enforce these rules with types. An executor must keep them:

- Return a result for every end. Do not leave `run` with a panic or an unreported failure.
- Put the submit payload in `ExecutionResult.submit`. The engine reads only that field and never the assistant text.
- Report only the usage of this run.
- Stop when `cancel` fires, and return the status `Cancelled`.
- Respect `spec.timeout_secs`. The native executor uses `max(1)` seconds. The harness executor uses `max(30)` seconds.
- Send progress through `host.emit`, because the console shows only what the host receives.
- Report `native_session_id` when the executor can resume a session.

The reason for the first rule is that the engine has no error path for an executor. It reads the status of the result and decides the next step from it.

## Choose the executor in the server

`ServerServices::executor` in `crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs` maps an `ExecutorKind` to an instance:

- `ExecutorKind::Native` returns the shared `NativeExecutor` that `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` builds at startup.
- `ExecutorKind::Harness(h)` returns `shared.harness.executor(h, &global)`. This call currently returns `Some` for every harness kind. The harness argument is not used.

`ExecutorKind` is written as the string `native` or `harness:<name>` in JSON, settings, and the database. The names are `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. `HarnessKind` also accepts `antigravity` as an alias for `agy`. `ExecutorKind::tier_table()` returns the key for the `[tiers.<table>]` section of the global config and for the effort table of `agent.toml`.

## Add an executor

Follow these steps to add an executor that is not one of the four harness CLIs:

1. Add a variant to `ExecutorKind` in `crates/ostra-core/src/executor.rs`.
2. Update `Display`, `FromStr`, `tier_table`, `all`, and `stream`. The compiler shows each `match` that needs a change.
3. Write a type that implements `Executor`. Keep the rules in the previous section.
4. Build the instance at startup in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` and store it in `Shared`.
5. Add a match arm in `ServerServices::executor` that returns the instance.
6. Add the executor key to `[tiers.<table>]` of the global config. Add an `[effort]` key to each `agent.toml`, or accept the fallback to the `native` value.
7. Write tests with a fake host. `FakeHost` in `crates/ostra-exec-native/src/tests.rs` is a model.
8. Run `cargo test --workspace`.

To add a fifth harness CLI, follow the steps on the page Launching a harness CLI: plans, terminal, and sandbox wrap. That change touches the adapters, the launch plan, and the sandbox wrap.

### What happens when

- **The executor is not available.** The runner records `Denied` with the text `The <kind> executor is not available.` and does not call `run`.
- **The cancel token fires.** The executor returns `Cancelled`. If the engine caused the cancel, for example with a pause or a stop, the runner changes the status to `Interrupted`.
- **The time budget ends.** The executor returns `Error`. The native text is `timed out after N s`. The harness text is `The execution passed its N s budget and was stopped.`
- **The agent asks another subagent.** The native executor returns `Waiting` with a coordination payload. The harness executor waits in `wait_for_wake` and does not return.
- **A resumed execution reports usage.** The executor counts from zero. The engine adds `usage_base`.
- **The user turns on YOLO during a run.** The next policy check reads `host.yolo()`, and the engine allows the ask.
- **A side-panel run asks permission.** `EngineHost` answers `Deny` because the run has no session.
- **The executor sends a `Usage` delta.** The engine writes the cost of the execution and of the session at once, so the session list stays current during the run.
