sections.title: Native executor: turn loop, submit, and compaction
sections.summary: Explains how NativeExecutor runs one agent on an API key: setup, the turn loop, stop-reason branches, tool routing, the submit checks, compaction, resume, limits, and the result of a timeout or a cancel.
sections.body:
## Why an agent needs a loop

One model request returns one answer. An agent must call tools many times, finish with typed data, and survive a full context window. It must also stop on a timeout or a cancel. `NativeExecutor` in `crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs` provides this loop for an execution on an API key. Every tool call passes the policy engine before it runs. The `submit_<agent>` call ends the execution with data that the engine can read.

This page covers the setup of an execution, the turn loop, the stop-reason branches, the routing of tool calls, the checks of the submit tool, compaction, resume, the limits, and the result of a timeout or a cancel. The types of the contract are on the page Executor contract: spec, context, result, and deltas. The wire details of each model API are on the page Model providers: keys, retry, streams, and cost.

A model turn is one request to the model and the handling of the tool calls in its answer. A tool call is a request from the model to run one tool.

## Build the executor and share it

`NativeExecutor::new(providers, skill_resolver, code)` creates the executor. Three builder methods add optional connectors: `with_mcp`, `with_manage`, and `with_coord`. A connector that is not set leaves the matching tools without a backend. The server builds one instance at startup in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` and uses it for every execution. The instance holds the `Arc<Providers>` registry. When the registry reloads after a key change, the next model call uses the new keys.

## Wrap the run with a timeout and a cancel

`Executor::run` does not run the loop directly. It races the loop against the cancel token and a timer.

1. Create a shared `Usage` in an `Arc<Mutex<...>>`.
2. Create a child token `inner` of the cancel token.
3. Set the budget to `spec.timeout_secs.max(1)` seconds.
4. Build a `Run` and pin the future of `Run::execute`.
5. Wait in `tokio::select!` for the first of three events: the future ends, the caller cancels, or the budget ends.

```rust
let outcome = tokio::select! {
    r = &mut fut => return r,
    _ = cancel.cancelled() => ExecutionStatus::Cancelled,
    _ = tokio::time::sleep(budget) => ExecutionStatus::Error,
};
inner.cancel();
let _ = tokio::time::timeout(CLEANUP_GRACE, &mut fut).await;
let mut result = ExecutionResult::with_status(outcome);
result.usage = *usage.lock();
```

When the future ends first, its result is the result of the execution. In the other two cases, the executor cancels `inner` and gives the future `CLEANUP_GRACE`, which is 3 seconds, to stop its tools. The result of the future is then discarded. The executor builds the result from the outcome and the shared `Usage`. The shared usage is the reason that a timed-out run still reports the cost that it spent.

| Outcome | Status | `error` | Status line in the Activity view |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Caller cancels | `Cancelled` | none | `Cancelled.` |
| Budget ends | `Error` | `timed out after N s` | `Timed out after N s.` |

The budget is wall time for the whole execution. It does not pause when the execution waits for a user answer to a permission ask. A long ask uses budget. When the execution ends with the status `Waiting`, the future ends and the timer stops.

## Set up the execution before the first turn

`Run::execute` does these steps in order. Each failure returns an `Error` result and emits the same text as a `Status` delta.

1. **Resolve the provider.** `providers.for_model(spec.route.model)` splits `provider:model`. For `NoKey`, the text is `The <provider> provider has no API key. Set its key in the environment or the OS keychain.` Other errors give `Cannot run model <model>: <error>`.
2. **Open MCP tools.** If an `McpConnector` exists, the executor opens the workspace MCP tools. It emits each note as a `Status` delta.
3. **Build the policy.** `ExecutionPolicy::new` receives the `ExecContext` and the commands from the project profile. `policy_inputs` reads `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `lint`, and `typecheck` from the profile of the repo. It drops blank values and the placeholder dash. It also passes the read-only MCP tools.
4. **Build the tool environment.** `ToolEnv` receives the repo, workspace, and session paths, the report file, the memory database, the skill resolver, and the connectors. It also receives the hosts that `WebFetch` can use for private addresses. It receives the names of secret environment variables that shell commands must not inherit.
5. **Decide the sandbox.** `sandbox_for` reads the `[sandbox]` table of the global config on every execution, so a change applies to the next execution. The workspace choice replaces the global mode. A sandboxed execution gets a scratch directory, one egress proxy, and decoy files. An unsandboxed execution with a warning emits `Bash runs without a sandbox. <warning>`. If `ostra_sandbox::decide` returns an error, the execution fails with that text.
6. **Choose the server tools.** The provider says which server tools it offers for the model. Web search is on when the provider offers it and `ostra_tools::wants_web_search` accepts the capabilities. Web fetch runs on the server when the provider offers it and the agent has the `WebFetch` capability. In that case the local `WebFetch` tool leaves the list.
7. **Build the tool list.** The list holds the tool definitions of the capabilities, the `Document` tool when the agent has that capability, the MCP tools, and last the submit tool. The submit tool uses `spec.submit_schema`. If the schema is `null`, it uses the default schema of `submit_tool_definition`.
8. **Build the messages.** A fresh execution starts with one user message that holds `spec.first_message`, and records it. The section Resume a native execution explains the other case.

The Anthropic provider puts a cache breakpoint on the last client tool. The submit tool is always last. Therefore the cache breakpoint covers the whole tool list.

## Run one model turn

The loop runs at most `MAX_TURNS` times, which is 400. The diagram shows one pass.

### Decisions in one turn

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start turn] --> B{Cancelled}
    B -->|yes| C[Return Cancelled]
    B -->|no| D{Context near full}
    D -->|yes| E[Compact]
    D -->|no| F[Call provider chat]
    E --> F
    F --> G[Add usage and record reply]
    G --> H{Stop reason}
    H -->|PauseTurn| A
    H -->|Refusal| I[Return Error]
    H -->|MaxTokens no tool calls| J[Ask to continue]
    H -->|no tool calls| K[Remind then return Ok]
    H -->|tool calls| L[Run the tool calls]
    L --> M{Submit accepted}
    M -->|yes| N[Return result]
    M -->|no| A
```

Each turn builds a `ChatRequest` with these values:

- `system`: one block with the system prompt, marked for caching.
- `tools` and `server_tools`: the lists from the setup.
- `effort`: `spec.effort`.
- `max_tokens`: the output limit of the model from the models.dev catalog (`pricing::max_output`). If the catalog has no entry, the value is `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT`, which is 32000.
- `tool_choice`: `ToolChoice::Auto`.

The loop asks for the whole output limit, so that no effort level is cut short. The user chose the effort and agreed to its cost.

The loop calls `provider.chat`. The stream goes through a `Coalescer`. It sends a `Text` or `Thinking` delta when the buffer holds 160 bytes, when the text ends with a newline, or when the kind changes between text and thinking. A server tool use flushes the buffer and emits a `Status` delta with `name: summary`.

After the answer arrives, the loop does these steps:

1. Set `usage.context_tokens` to input plus cache read plus cache write plus output.
2. Emit a `Turn` delta and then a `Usage` delta with the running total.
3. Keep the last text that is not empty as `final_text`.
4. Record the assistant message in the transcript and append it to the messages.
5. Branch on the stop reason.

## Branch on the stop reason

| Stop reason | Tool calls | What the loop does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PauseTurn` | Any | Continue. The next request sends the assistant turn again without a change. |
| `Refusal` | Any | Return `Error` with `The model refused to continue (category X): <text>`. The category part is absent when the provider names none. |
| `MaxTokens` | None | Add the user message `You reached the output limit. Continue from exactly where you stopped.` and continue. After `MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` (3) such messages, return `Error` with `The model kept hitting its output limit without finishing.` |
| Any other | None | The first time, add a reminder to call `submit_<agent>` and continue. The second time, return `Ok` with `submit` set to `None` and the last text. |
| Any other, or `MaxTokens` | One or more | Run the tool calls. |

Two counters have the scope of the whole execution. `continues` and `reminded` are never reset. A second text-only turn at any time in the execution returns `Ok`, even when it comes many turns after the first reminder.

The reminder text is `Call submit_<agent> now with your result. The engine reads only that call, so a result given in text is lost.` When `ctx.owes_reply` is true, the reminder is the reply instruction for `SubagentReply`. The reason for the reminder is that the engine ignores assistant text.

An output limit that cuts a tool call has a special case. The stop reason is `MaxTokens`, but the answer has tool calls. The loop runs them. A cut tool input does not parse, so the provider marks it with `__invalid_json`. The loop then returns an error result for that call, and the model can try again.

## Route the tool calls of a turn

`run_tools` handles the calls of one answer in order. Before it starts, it converts fields of the submit input that hold JSON in a string into real JSON values. It uses the submit schema for this (`coerce_json_strings`).

The loop sorts each call into one of four classes:

| Class | Members | How the loop runs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Submit | `submit_<agent>` | Checks the call with `Run::submit`. A valid call ends the execution. |
| Concurrent | `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebFetch`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, `Skill`, and the eight code tools | Runs a group of consecutive calls at the same time with `join_all`. These tools do not change files, so their order does not matter. |
| Coordination | `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply` | Runs alone. The call can end the execution. |
| Serial | Every other tool, such as `Bash`, `Write`, and `Edit` | Runs one call at a time, in order. |

A concurrent group ends at the first call that is not concurrent. The results keep the order of the calls.

### Run one ordinary call

`tool_end` does these steps for each call that is not a submit call:

1. Make the call canonical. Relative paths and the working directory of `Bash` become absolute, so that the policy, the user approval, and the tool all see the same target.
2. Emit a `ToolCall` delta and add 1 to `usage.tool_calls`.
3. If the input has the `__invalid_json` key, return the error `The tool input was not valid JSON, so the call did not run: <first 500 characters>`.
4. Call `policy.set_yolo(host.yolo())`, then `policy.check`. Emit a `Policy` delta.
5. Handle the decision. A deny returns an error with the layer, the rule, and the reason. An ask calls `host.ask_permission`. `AllowOnce` continues. `AlwaysInWorkspace` adds a session allow rule to the policy and continues. `Deny` returns `The user denied this call (<reason>). Continue without it, or explain in your report why it is needed.`
6. Run `ostra_tools::execute` with a live-output callback that emits `ToolOutput` deltas, and with the cancel token.
7. For `Bash`, repair planted git metadata. Add the call time to `usage.build_ms` if the command is a build or test command.
8. Let `policy.observe` add notes. After repeated failures it can ask for a lesson recall. Then the loop reads up to 5 lessons from the memory database and appends them to the result.
9. Emit a `ToolResult` delta. The delta text is cut to `EMIT_LIMIT`, which is 8 KiB. The model gets the full text.

A tool error never ends the execution. The model gets an error result and can choose another step. For a repaired git directory, the loop appends a note to the result. It also emits a `Policy` delta with a deny for the `git-metadata` guard. The engine counts this delta as a containment signal. The page Containment signals, build streak, and lesson gate explains the signals and the lesson recall.

### End the turn after a coordination call

A coordination call returns a `RunEnd` value. The value `Continue` keeps the loop going. The value `Wait` ends the execution with the status `Waiting`. The value `Finish` ends it with the status `Ok`. This is Rule H2 and Rule H3. In both end cases, `submit` is `{ coordination: <tool>, message: <text> }`. Each call of the turn that did not run gets the error result `Not run: the run stopped to wait for another subagent.` The engine wakes a waiting execution later with a resume.

## Check the submit call

`Run::submit` checks the call in this order. The first failure returns an error result, and the loop continues. The model can call the tool again.

1. **Valid JSON.** If the input has the `__invalid_json` key, the text is `The <name> input was not valid JSON. Call <name> again with a valid object.`
2. **Policy.** The policy checks the call. Only a deny stops it. The submit call never asks the user. A deny gives an error with the layer, the rule, and the reason. For example, the rule `reply-first` denies the call while `ctx.owes_reply` is true.
3. **Schema.** `ostra_core::submit::validate_submit` gives `The <name> input is invalid: <e>. Fix it and call <name> again.`
4. **Document completeness.** `ostra_core::doc::check_submit` gives `<e> Nothing was recorded.`
5. **Status.** The `status` field of the payload decides the result status. The value `stuck` gives `Stuck`, `handoff` gives `Handoff`, and every other value gives `Ok`.
6. **Report file.** The check applies when the status is `Ok`, `ctx.report_file` is set, and the agent is not the code reviewer. If the file does not exist, the text is `Write your report to <path> before you call <name>, because the engine reads the report at that path.`

When all checks pass, the tool result is `Result received.` Each other call of the turn that has not run gets the error result `Not run: the run ended with the submit call.` The error result keeps the transcript well formed, because every tool use needs a result. The loop returns `ExecutionResult` with the status, `submit` set to the input, `final_text`, and the usage.

The design has one reason. The engine reads only the submit call. The data is typed and checked at the moment that the model gives it, so the model can fix a mistake in the same execution. A failed submit call records nothing.

## Compact the conversation

A long execution fills the context window of the model. Compaction replaces the conversation with a summary, so that the execution can continue.

### When the loop compacts

Before each request, the loop estimates the size of the next request:

`next = measured + estimate_tokens(messages not yet measured)`

`measured` is the `context_tokens` of the last response. `estimate_tokens` counts 4 characters as 1 token. The window is `pricing::context_window(model)`, or `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` (200000) when the catalog has no entry. The loop compacts when all three conditions are true:

- `next` is at least `COMPACT_AT` times the window. `COMPACT_AT` is 0.95.
- `retry_ok` is true.
- The last message is a user message. This means that no tool call is open, and a compaction cannot split a tool use from its result.

```rust
let next = measured + estimate_tokens(&messages[measured_len.min(messages.len())..]);
let retry_ok = failed_compaction_at.is_none_or(|at| {
    next as f64 >= at as f64 + COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH * window as f64
});
if next as f64 >= COMPACT_AT * window as f64
    && retry_ok
    && messages.last().is_some_and(|m| m.role == Role::User)
{ ... }
```

### What the loop does

1. Emit the status `Compacting the conversation: about N of W context tokens used.`
2. Call `provider.compact(request, COMPACT_INSTRUCTIONS, cancel)`. The page Model providers: keys, retry, streams, and cost explains the three forms of this call.
3. Add the usage of the call to the run with `add_usage`. A `Turn` delta with no call ids reports it.
4. If the provider returns a summary, replace the messages with the compacted window. Append the user message `AFTER_COMPACTION`. Store a transcript record with the role `compaction` that holds the new window.

`COMPACT_INSTRUCTIONS` tells the model to keep the task and every requirement, the files that it read and the facts from them, the files that it changed, the decisions, the failed commands, what is left, and the next step. It tells the model to keep paths and error text exact, to call no tools, and to answer with the summary only.

### What happens when compaction fails

- **No summary returns.** The status line is `Compaction returned no summary, so the run continues without it.` The loop stores `failed_compaction_at` and continues with the full conversation.
- **The call is cancelled.** The execution ends with `Cancelled`.
- **Another error occurs.** The status line is `Compaction failed, so the run continues without it: <e>`. The loop stores `failed_compaction_at`.

After a failure, `retry_ok` stays false until `next` grows by `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` times the window. The value is 0.02, which is 4000 tokens for a window of 200000. The reason is that each try sends the whole conversation, and a try on every turn would spend money without gain.

## Resume a native execution

The host stores every message of a native execution as a `(role, content)` record. A resume rebuilds the conversation from these records.

1. `stored_messages` reads the records. It merges adjacent messages of the same role. At each `compaction` record, it resets the list to the stored window, so that a resume after a compaction starts from the summary.
2. If the stored list is empty, the loop starts with a fresh first message.
3. `resume_turn` builds one user message. It first holds an error result for each tool call that the interruption left open, with the text `Interrupted: this call did not finish.` Then it holds the note. The note is `resume.note` or the default `The previous run was interrupted. Continue from where it stopped.`
4. `append_turn` joins this message to a last user message when one exists, because two user messages in a row are not valid.

Two cases differ in what the loop records:

- **Resume in place** (`resume.from` equals `spec.id`, and the list is not empty). The loop records only the new turn. The reason is Rule P2: the stored transcript already belongs to this execution, and the replayed prefix then hits the prompt cache.
- **Resume from another execution.** The loop records every message of the rebuilt conversation for the new execution.

The engine never gives the native executor an inspect resume. `Engine::inspect_execution` refuses native executions.

## Limits and constants

| Name | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_TURNS` | 400 | Model turns in one execution. Then the error is `The run passed 400 model turns without calling submit_<agent>.` |
| `MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` | 3 | Continue messages after an output limit, for the whole execution. |
| `COMPACT_AT` | 0.95 | Share of the context window at which the loop compacts. |
| `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` | 0.02 | Window share of growth that the loop waits for after a failed compaction. |
| `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` | 200000 tokens | Window for a model that models.dev does not list. |
| `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT` | 32000 tokens | Output limit for a model that models.dev does not list. |
| `EMIT_LIMIT` | 8 KiB | Size of tool output in an Activity row. The model gets the full output. |
| `CLEANUP_GRACE` | 3 seconds | Time that a cancelled or timed-out execution has to stop its tools. |
| `Coalescer::FLUSH_AT` | 160 bytes | Size at which streamed text goes to the Activity view. |
| `spec.timeout_secs` | 300 to 2400 seconds | Time budget. The value comes from `timeout_seconds` of `agent.toml`: 300 for `quick-answer`, 900 for `advisor`, 2400 for `implementer`. |

### What happens when

- **The provider has no key.** The execution returns `Error` before the first model call.
- **The model call fails.** After the retries of the provider, the execution returns `Error` with `The model call failed: <error>` and the usage so far.
- **The model returns an invalid tool input.** The call gets an error result, and the loop continues.
- **The policy denies a call.** The model gets an error result with the layer and the rule. The loop continues.
- **The user denies a permission ask.** The model gets an error result and can continue without the tool.
- **The budget ends while an ask waits.** The executor cancels the run and drops the unfinished future after the 3-second grace period.
- **The model submits an invalid payload.** The model gets an error result. The loop continues until a valid call or `MAX_TURNS`.
- **The model calls submit and another tool in one turn.** Calls before the submit call run in order. Calls after it do not run.
- **The model ends its turn without a tool call.** The first time, it gets a reminder. The second time, the result is `Ok` with `submit` set to `None`. The engine decides what that means.
- **The user cancels.** The status is `Cancelled`. The engine can rewrite it to `Interrupted`.
- **YOLO changes during the run.** The next policy check reads the new state.
- **The key changes during the run.** The call in progress keeps the old key. The next call uses the new key, because the registry reloads in place.

sections.title: Model providers: keys, retry, streams, and cost
sections.summary: Explains how the native loop reaches Anthropic and OpenAI: key and base URL lookup, the registry, the retry policy, error mapping, request and stream details, usage normalization, the structured judge call, and the steps to add a provider.
sections.body:
## Why one provider interface exists

The native loop needs one chat interface for two vendor APIs. The two APIs differ in the request body, the authentication, the stream events, the error shapes, and the usage fields. Without one interface, the loop would hold vendor code. The crate `ostra-providers` hides these differences behind the `Provider` trait and a set of neutral types.

This page covers the neutral types, the key and base URL lookup, the registry, the retry policy, the mapping of errors, the request and stream details of Anthropic and OpenAI, the normalization of usage, the structured judge call, and the steps to add a provider. The loop that calls a provider is on the page Native executor: turn loop, submit, and compaction. The cost formula is on the page Shared types: ids, paths, usage, pricing, and wire shapes.

## Neutral types and the Provider trait

`ChatRequest::new(model)` sets these defaults: `max_tokens` is 32000, `effort` is `High`, `tool_choice` is `Auto`, and `refusal_fallback` is `true`. The model id has no provider prefix.

A `Message` has a `Role` and a list of `Block` values. The block types are:

| Block | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Text` | Plain text. |
| `Thinking` | Reasoning text with a signature. |
| `RedactedThinking` | Reasoning that the vendor hides. |
| `ToolUse` | A tool call with an id, a name, and an input. |
| `ToolResult` | The result of a tool call. |
| `Opaque` | A block that belongs to one provider, such as a server tool block or a reasoning item. The same provider gets it back unchanged. Any other provider drops it. |
| `Compaction` | Earlier turns as one block. It holds the summary and the provider form `value`. The same provider gets `value` back unchanged. Any other provider gets the summary as text. |

`StreamEvent` has five kinds: `TextDelta`, `ThinkingDelta`, `ToolUseStarted`, `ToolInputDelta`, and `ServerToolUsed`. `StopReason` has `EndTurn`, `ToolUse`, `MaxTokens`, `PauseTurn`, `Refusal`, and `Other(String)`. `ChatResponse` holds the content, the stop reason, the usage, the model that answered, and an optional refusal category.

The `Provider` trait has four methods:

- `name()` returns the provider name.
- `server_tools(model)` returns the tools that the vendor runs. The default is none.
- `chat(req, on_event, cancel)` returns a `ChatResponse`.
- `compact(req, instructions, cancel)` returns a `Compacted` value. The default is `compact_on_client`.

A `Compacted` value holds `messages` and `usage`. When `messages` is `None`, no summary came back, and the conversation can continue as it is.

## Find the key and the base URL

`lookup_key` tries five places and returns the first hit. The `source` text of the hit is `env:NAME`, `saved`, or `keychain`.

1. The environment variable that `api_key_env` names.
2. The environment variable that `auth_token_env` names. Ostra sends this value as `Authorization: Bearer`.
3. The saved `api_key`, which the user stored from the browser.
4. The saved `auth_token`.
5. The OS keychain entry. The service is `keychain_service` and the user is the provider name.

Environment and saved values are trimmed. An empty value counts as absent. The default config sets no `keychain_service`, so step 5 runs only when the user sets one.

`resolve_base_url` has its own order: the `base_url` of `config.toml`, then the environment variable that `base_url_env` names, then the saved URL, then the default of the provider. The `config.toml` value wins because it is the explicit choice of the user.

The default config has these entries:

| Provider | `api_key_env` | `auth_token_env` | `base_url_env` | Default base URL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `https://api.anthropic.com` |
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | none | `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `https://api.openai.com` |

Two rules protect the key. `ApiKey` prints `ApiKey(***)` for `Debug` and `***` for `Display`, so a log line cannot leak it. `display_url` removes the user, password, query, and fragment from a base URL before the browser shows it, because any of them can carry a credential.

## The Providers registry

`Providers` maps a provider name to an instance. These methods build and read it:

- `from_config(cfg, saved)` builds the registry at startup.
- `reload(cfg, saved)` rebuilds it in place after a key or config change. Executors hold the same registry, so the next model call uses the new keys. A call in progress keeps its old instance.
- `register(name, provider)` adds a ready instance with the source `registered`. A reload keeps it. Tests use this for `ScriptedProvider` under the name `mock`.
- `status()` returns one `ProviderStatus` for each configured provider. It shows `has_key`, the source of the key, and the base URL with its source. A provider with no key appears in the status but not in the registry.
- `for_model(provider_model)` returns the instance and the bare model id.

`rebuild` creates only the providers named `anthropic` and `openai`. A config entry with another name logs a warning and is ignored.

`for_model` splits the text at the first colon. These cases give errors:

| Input | Error |
| --- | --- |
| No colon, or an empty part | `BadModel` |
| `anthropic` or `openai` without a key | `NoKey` |
| Any other name that is not registered | `UnknownProvider` |

Each provider builds its own `reqwest::Client`. The connect timeout is 20 seconds. Redirects are off, because the key header would follow a redirect to another host. The client has no overall request timeout. The execution budget of the native executor bounds a call instead.

## Retry policy

`retry::run` wraps every request. It takes a `RetryPolicy`, the cancel token, a `started` flag, and a function that makes one attempt.

The default policy has `max_retries` 4, `base_delay` 1000 ms, and `max_delay` 60 seconds. A call makes at most 5 requests. The delay before retry number `n` (counted from 0) is:

`min(base_delay * 2^min(n, 16), max_delay) * jitter`

The jitter is a factor from 0.5 up to but not including 1.0. It comes from the sub-second part of the clock. If the server sent a `Retry-After` header, the wait is the larger of the jittered delay and that many seconds.

| Retry number | Delay before jitter | Wait after jitter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 1 s | 0.5 s to 1 s |
| 1 | 2 s | 1 s to 2 s |
| 2 | 4 s | 2 s to 4 s |
| 3 | 8 s | 4 s to 8 s |

With 4 retries, the total wait is at most 15 seconds, and the 60-second cap never applies. The cap matters only when a caller sets a higher `max_retries` with `with_retry`. The cap does not limit a `Retry-After` value from the server. `RetryPolicy::fast(n)` gives 1 ms delays for tests.

```rust
match result {
    Err(e) if e.is_retryable() && !started.load(Ordering::SeqCst)
            && n < policy.max_retries => {
        let wait = policy.delay(n, e.retry_after());
        ...
        n += 1;
    }
    Err(e) if e.is_retryable() && started.load(Ordering::SeqCst) => {
        return Err(ProviderError::Stream(e.to_string()));
    }
    other => return other,
}
```

### The started flag

The flag `started` becomes true when output begins. Anthropic sets it at `content_block_start`. OpenAI sets it at `response.output_item.added`, at the first text delta, and at the first reasoning delta. After that point, a retryable error is not retried. It becomes `ProviderError::Stream`, with the text `stream failed: ...`. The reason is that a new request would send the same deltas again, and the loop already shows and uses the first ones.

### Which errors the policy retries

| Error | Retried | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RateLimited` | Yes | Status 429, or a rate limit event |
| `Overloaded` | Yes | Status 529, or an overloaded error |
| `Server` | Yes | Status 408, 409, or 500 to 599, or a server error event |
| `Network` | Yes | Transport error, or a stream that ends early |
| `Auth` | No | Status 401 or 403 |
| `InvalidRequest` | No | Any other status |
| `Decode` | No | A body or event that does not parse |
| `Stream` | No | A retryable error after output started |
| `BadModel`, `NoKey`, `UnknownProvider` | No | Registry errors |
| `Cancelled` | No | The cancel token fired |

The policy checks the cancel token during an attempt and during the wait between attempts. A cancel drops the attempt, which closes the connection, and returns `Cancelled`. The native loop turns any other final error into the text `The model call failed: <error>` and ends the execution with `Error`.

## Map errors to ProviderError

`status_error` maps an HTTP status and body to an error in this order:

1. Status 401 or 403 gives `Auth`.
2. Status 429 gives `RateLimited`.
3. Status 529 gives `Overloaded`.
4. Any status with `error.type` equal to `overloaded_error` in the body gives `Overloaded`.
5. Status 408, 409, or 500 to 599 gives `Server`.
6. Every other status gives `InvalidRequest`.

The message is `error.message` from the body. If the body has none, the message is the first 300 characters of the body. The `Retry-After` header is read as a number of seconds and rounded up. A date value does not parse, so the wait then uses only the jittered delay. A transport error becomes `Network` with the URL removed from the text.

The stream can also carry an error event. The mapping differs by vendor:

| Vendor | Event | Error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anthropic | `error` with `overloaded_error` | `Overloaded` |
| Anthropic | `error` with `rate_limit_error` | `RateLimited` |
| Anthropic | `error` with `api_error` | `Server` with status 500 |
| Anthropic | `error` with any other type | `InvalidRequest` with status 400 |
| OpenAI | `error` with code `rate_limit_exceeded` | `RateLimited` |
| OpenAI | `error` with code `server_error`, `server_is_overloaded`, or `slow_down` | `Server` with status 500 |
| OpenAI | `error` with any other code | `InvalidRequest` with status 400 |
| OpenAI | `response.failed` | `Server` with status 500 |

A stream that ends before `message_stop` (Anthropic) or before `response.completed` or `response.incomplete` (OpenAI) gives `Network` with the text `stream ended before ...`. Such an error is retryable until output starts. `sse::json_events` parses the stream. It skips empty data and `[DONE]`. A transport error becomes `Network`. An event that is not JSON becomes `Decode`.

## Anthropic request details

The provider posts to `{base}/v1/messages`. The body always has `stream: true`. The headers are:

- `x-api-key` with the key, or `Authorization: Bearer` when the key is a bearer token.
- `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01`.
- `accept: text/event-stream`.
- `anthropic-beta` with a comma list, when at least one beta applies.

`max_tokens` is the smaller of the request value and the output limit of models.dev. If the catalog has no entry, the request value stays.

### Betas

| Beta | When the provider sends it |
| --- | --- |
| `compact-2026-09-04` | A signed compaction block is in the messages, and every compaction request. |
| `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01` | `refusal_fallback` is true and the model supports fallbacks. The body then has `fallbacks: default`. |
| `interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14` | A budget model has a thinking budget, the model supports interleaving, and the request has client tools. |
| `model-context-window-exceeded-2025-08-26` | Models before Claude 4.5. Without it, a request with input plus `max_tokens` past the window fails validation. |

### Capabilities of each model

The function `caps(model)` decides the request shape from the model id. A dated snapshot such as `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` counts as the same model as its base id.

| Models | Thinking | Effort sent | Forced tool choice | Fallbacks | Server compaction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude-fable-5-1`, `claude-mythos-5-1`, `claude-opus-5-5` | Adaptive | All values | No | Yes | Yes |
| `claude-opus-5` | Adaptive | All values | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `claude-sonnet-5-5` | Adaptive | All values | No | No | Yes |
| `claude-fable-5`, `claude-mythos-5`, `claude-opus-4-8`, `claude-opus-4-7`, `claude-sonnet-5` | Adaptive | All values | Yes | No | Yes |
| `claude-opus-4-6`, `claude-sonnet-4-6` | Adaptive | `xhigh` is sent as `high` | Yes | No | Yes |
| `claude-opus-4-5` | Budget | `low`, `medium`, `high` | Yes | No | No |
| Ids that start with `claude-haiku-4-5`, `claude-sonnet-4-5`, `claude-opus-4-1`, `claude-opus-4`, `claude-sonnet-4`, or `claude-3` | Budget | None | Yes | No | No |
| Any other id | Adaptive | All values | No | No | Yes |

The last row is for unknown and newer models. It uses the surface that every current model accepts. For `claude-opus-4-5`, the efforts `xhigh` and `max` are sent as `high`.

Among the budget models, `claude-opus-4-5`, `claude-sonnet-4-5`, `claude-opus-4-1`, `claude-opus-4`, and `claude-sonnet-4` support the interleaved beta. The beta for the context window applies to `claude-opus-4-1`, `claude-opus-4`, `claude-sonnet-4`, and `claude-3`.

### Thinking, effort, and forced calls

An adaptive model gets `thinking: {type: adaptive, display: summarized}` and `output_config.effort`. A budget model gets `thinking: {type: enabled, budget_tokens}`. The budget is a share of the output limit of the model:

| Effort | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| `low` | No thinking |
| `medium` | Output limit divided by 8 |
| `high` | Output limit divided by 4 |
| `xhigh` | Output limit divided by 2 |
| `max` | Output limit minus `ANSWER_RESERVE` (16000) |

The request lowers the budget to `max_tokens - 16000`, unless thinking interleaves with tool calls. The API needs a budget below `max_tokens`, and the answer can be a whole file in a tool call. A budget under `MIN_BUDGET` (1024) means no thinking.

A forced tool choice (`any` or a named tool) is sent only when the model allows it. Otherwise the provider sends `auto`. A forced call drops the explicit thinking config for both thinking modes.

### Prompt cache and tools

Every cache breakpoint uses `{type: ephemeral, ttl: 1h}`. The reason is that the turns of an execution can sit more than 5 minutes apart, for example during a long build or a permission ask. Mixed TTLs need the longer entries first. The provider sets at most 4 breakpoints:

- Up to two system blocks that carry `cache`. If none carries it, the last system block.
- The last client tool.
- The last block of the most recent user message, when it is text or a tool result.

Server tools come first in the tool list: `web_search_20250305` and `web_fetch_20250910`. The newer `20260209` versions are not used, because they run inside code execution, and each of their failures costs a turn. Every client tool has `eager_input_streaming: true`.

### Stream events and stop reasons

The `Accumulator` folds the events into a `ChatResponse`:

| Event | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `message_start` | Stores the model and the first usage. |
| `content_block_start` | Sets `started` and opens a block. |
| `content_block_delta` | Appends text, thinking, a signature, or tool input JSON. Emits the matching `StreamEvent`. |
| `content_block_stop` | Finishes the block. A tool input that does not parse becomes `{ __invalid_json: <raw text> }`. |
| `message_delta` | Stores the stop reason, the refusal category, and the final usage. |
| `message_stop` | Ends the stream. |

A `server_tool_use` block becomes an `Opaque` block and emits `ServerToolUsed` with the query or URL. The stop reasons map as follows:

- `end_turn` and `stop_sequence` give `EndTurn`.
- `tool_use` gives `ToolUse`.
- `max_tokens` and `model_context_window_exceeded` give `MaxTokens`.
- `pause_turn` gives `PauseTurn`, and `refusal` gives `Refusal`.
- Every other text gives `Other`.

The vendor can fall back to another model in the middle of an answer. Then the stream carries a `fallback` marker. The provider drops thinking, tool use, and unpaired server tool use before the last marker. The declined part is then neither run nor sent back. The `model` field of the response is the model from `message_start`, which differs from the request after a fallback.

## OpenAI request details

The provider posts to `{base}/v1/responses` with `Authorization: Bearer` and `accept: text/event-stream`. The body has `stream: true`, `store: false`, and `max_output_tokens` equal to `req.max_tokens`. The provider does not lower this value to a ceiling. The native loop already asks for the output limit of the model. `store: false` makes the API stateless, so each request sends the whole conversation.

The system blocks join with a blank line into `instructions`. The provider ignores the `cache` flags, because this API has no cache marker per block.

A model id that starts with `gpt-5`, `gpt-6`, or `o` is a reasoning model. It gets `reasoning: {effort, summary: auto}` and `include: [reasoning.encrypted_content]`. The encrypted content lets a reasoning item return to the API in the next request.

### Conversion of blocks to input items

| Block | Input item |
| --- | --- |
| User `Text` | `message` with role `user` and an `input_text` part |
| Assistant `Text` | `message` with role `assistant` and the text |
| `ToolUse` | `function_call` with `call_id`, `name`, and `arguments` as a JSON string |
| `ToolResult` | `function_call_output`. An error result gets the prefix `Error: ` unless it starts with `Error`. |
| `Opaque` reasoning from OpenAI | `reasoning` item with `id`, `summary`, and `encrypted_content` |
| `Compaction` from OpenAI | The stored item, unchanged |
| `Compaction` from another source | A user message with the summary text |
| Other `Opaque` | Dropped |

Tools go out as `{type: function, name, description, parameters}`. When server web search is on, the list also has `{type: web_search}`. The body sets `parallel_tool_calls: true`. `tool_choice` maps `Auto` to `auto`, `Any` to `required`, `None` to `none`, and a named tool to a function choice. OpenAI has no server-side fetch, so `server_tools` returns web search only, and the native loop keeps the local `WebFetch` tool.

### Stream events and stop reasons

| Event | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `response.created`, `response.in_progress` | Stores the model. |
| `response.output_item.added` | Sets `started`. A `function_call` item emits `ToolUseStarted`. |
| `response.output_text.delta` | Sets `started` and emits `TextDelta`. |
| `response.reasoning_summary_text.delta` | Sets `started` and emits `ThinkingDelta`. |
| `response.function_call_arguments.delta` | Emits `ToolInputDelta`. |
| `response.output_item.done` | Stores a message, a function call, or a reasoning item. A web search call adds 1 to the search count and emits `ServerToolUsed`. |
| `response.completed`, `response.incomplete` | Stores the usage and the stop reason. |

A function call input that does not parse gets the same `__invalid_json` marker as in the Anthropic provider. The stop reason for an incomplete answer depends on the reason: `max_output_tokens` gives `MaxTokens`, `content_filter` gives `Refusal`, and any other reason gives `Other`. A completed answer with a refusal part gives `Refusal`. A completed answer with a function call gives `ToolUse`. Every other completed answer gives `EndTurn`. OpenAI gives no refusal category.

## Compaction forms

The native loop calls `provider.compact`. Three forms exist:

- **Anthropic server form.** For a model with `compaction` support, the provider sends the normal request body with the field `compaction: {type: summarize, instructions}` and the compact beta. It accepts the answer only when the answer holds a signed compaction block and the stop reason is `compaction`. The block returns as one assistant message. The provider reads the cost of the summary from the `iterations` entries with type `compaction` in the usage, because the top-level counts are zero.
- **OpenAI server form.** The provider posts `{model, input, instructions}` to `{base}/v1/responses/compact`. Here `instructions` are the system blocks of the request. The compaction instructions of the loop are not sent. The provider accepts the answer only when it holds a compaction item, and passes the encrypted item back unchanged. The request does not stream, so `started` stays false and every retryable error is retried.
- **Client form** (`compact_on_client`). The provider sends the same request with the instructions as the last user message and `tool_choice` set to `None`. The cached prefix stays the same. The text answer is the summary only when the stop reason is `EndTurn` and the text is not empty. A cut-off summary is never used.

Both server forms fall back to the client form on an `InvalidRequest` error. The reason is that a model that this build treats as newer, or a gateway without the endpoint, can reject the server form.

## Usage normalization and cost

Every provider must report `Usage` with one rule: `input_tokens` excludes cache reads and cache writes. `pricing::cost` assumes this rule for every provider and every harness transcript.

| Field | Anthropic | OpenAI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `input_tokens` | `input_tokens` as reported | `input_tokens` minus cached tokens minus cache write tokens |
| `output_tokens` | `output_tokens` | `output_tokens` |
| `cache_read_tokens` | `cache_read_input_tokens` | `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` |
| `cache_write_tokens` | `cache_creation_input_tokens` | `input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens` |
| `cache_write_1h_tokens` | `cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens` | Not reported, so 0 |
| Web searches | `server_tool_use.web_search_requests` | Count of `web_search_call` items |

The Anthropic reader overwrites the counts. It does not add them. Both `message_start` and `message_delta` carry counts, and the later `message_delta` carries the final ones. At the end, each provider sets `usage.cost_usd` to `pricing::cost(model, usage, web_searches)`. The model is the one that answered. The cost is 0 when no price catalog is installed or when the catalog does not list the model.

## The structured judge call

A judge is one structured model call, not an agent execution. `ostra_providers::structured` builds it:

1. Build a request with the judge prompt as one cached system block and the input as one user message.
2. Add one tool named `decide` (`DECIDE_TOOL`). Its input schema is the schema of the judge, and it is marked for caching.
3. Set `tool_choice` to the forced tool `decide`, `max_tokens` to 16000, and `effort` to the value of the caller.
4. Call `chat`. If the answer has a `decide` call, return its input and the summed usage.
5. If the stop reason is `Refusal`, return `Decode` with the text `the model refused the decision`.
6. If the first answer has no `decide` call, add the assistant turn and a user message that tells the model to call `decide` now and not to answer in text. Then call `chat` once more.
7. If the second answer also has no call, return `Decode` with the text `the model did not call the decide tool`.

The second attempt exists because some models reject a forced tool choice. The Anthropic provider then sends `auto`, and the model can answer in text.

`ServerServices::judge` in `crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs` calls `providers.for_model(route.model)` and then `structured`. A judge therefore needs an Anthropic or OpenAI key, even when the agents run on a harness executor. The engine resolves the route with the key `judge` (`JUDGE_ROUTE`). Its `call_judge` function uses the effort `Low`. It tries up to 3 times, with a pause of 500 ms times the attempt number after each attempt. A worst case is 30 HTTP requests: 3 engine attempts, 2 chat calls each, and 5 requests for each chat call. The page Judges: what each one decides and how a call runs explains the decisions.

## Test with ScriptedProvider

`ScriptedProvider` in `crates/ostra-providers/src/mock.rs` implements `Provider` without a network. The default name is `mock`, so the model string is `mock:<any id>`. Tests queue answers with `push`, `push_text`, `push_tool_use`, `push_tool_uses`, and `push_error`. `with_responder` answers every request after the queue is empty. `requests()` returns the requests that the provider received. The SSE fixtures for the real providers are in `crates/ostra-providers/tests/fixtures/`. The tests `tests/anthropic.rs` and `tests/openai.rs` use them.

## Add a provider

Follow these steps:

1. Create `crates/ostra-providers/src/<name>.rs` and add `pub mod <name>;` in `lib.rs`.
2. Implement `Provider`: `name`, `server_tools`, `chat`, and optionally `compact`.
3. Build the request body. Send it inside `retry::run` with a shared `started` flag.
4. Use `error_from_response` and `network_error` for failures, and `sse::json_events` to read the stream.
5. Set `started` when the first output arrives.
6. Fold the events into a `ChatResponse`. Map the stop reasons to `StopReason`.
7. Normalize the usage so that `input_tokens` excludes cache reads and writes.
8. Set `usage.cost_usd` with `pricing::cost(model, usage, web_searches)`.
9. Add a match arm for the name in `Providers::rebuild`.
10. Add the name to the `matches!` call in `for_model`, so that a missing key gives `NoKey`.
11. Add a default `[providers.<name>]` entry in `GlobalConfig`, with `api_key_env`, `base_url_env`, and the other fields.
12. Add the vendor id from models.dev to `FIRST_PARTY` in `crates/ostra-core/src/pricing.rs`, if its own listing must win over resellers.
13. Add SSE fixtures and tests like `tests/anthropic.rs`.
14. Run `cargo test --workspace`.

The key variable names of the new entry reach `credential_env_names` automatically, because that function reads every entry of `providers`. Agent processes then do not inherit the key.

### What happens when

- **The API returns 429 with `Retry-After: 30`.** Before output starts, the provider waits at least 30 seconds and retries, up to 4 times.
- **The API returns 401.** The provider returns `Auth` at once. The native loop ends the execution with `The model call failed: authentication failed (401): ...`.
- **The stream breaks after the first text delta.** The provider returns `Stream` and does not retry.
- **The stream breaks before any output.** The provider retries as `Network`.
- **The user cancels during a retry wait.** The provider returns `Cancelled` at once.
- **The model refuses.** The loop ends the execution with an error. On a model that supports fallbacks, Anthropic can first run the request again on its fallback model.
- **The output limit cuts a tool input.** The provider marks the input with `__invalid_json`, and the loop answers with an error result.
- **The user changes the key in the browser.** `Providers::reload` rebuilds the registry. The next call uses the new key.
- **The model has no models.dev entry.** Cost is 0. The loop uses 200000 for the window and 32000 for the output limit.

sections.title: Launching a harness CLI: plans, terminal, and sandbox wrap
sections.summary: Explains how Ostra starts Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Antigravity: the launch sequence, the per-harness plans, the environment, the first message, the terminal mirror, the sandbox wrap, and the machine setup.
sections.body:
## What a launch must achieve

A harness is an installed command-line program that runs a model. Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, and Antigravity are the four harnesses. This page calls the program the CLI. Ostra does not own the CLI. But Ostra must run one leaf agent in it and check every tool call.

An uncontrolled launch causes four problems:

- The CLI loads hooks, settings, and MCP servers from the repository. These run outside the guards of Ostra.
- The CLI runs its own tools, and Ostra sees no call.
- The CLI inherits provider credentials from the environment of the Ostra server.
- The CLI writes hooks or instructions in the home folder. These run in later sessions of the user.

The launch code closes each gap. It builds a launch plan for the harness, wraps the plan in the sandbox of the execution, and starts the plan in a pseudo-terminal (PTY). An execution is one run of one leaf agent. The page "Hook bridge, MCP shim, and adapters" explains the callbacks from the CLI. The page "Supervising a run, usage, and the failure matrix" explains what happens after the start.

## Objects that start a run

The engine asks `ServerServices::executor` for an executor. For a harness route, the server returns `HarnessRuntime::executor` ([services.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs)). That method returns a `Wrapped` executor. The `Wrapped` executor holds the one shared `HarnessExecutor`.

`HarnessRuntime::inner` creates the `HarnessExecutor` at the first call. Every call then runs `set_global` with the current global config. Thus each execution reads the current `[harness.*]` and `[sandbox]` settings, and a change needs no restart. A change does not reach an execution that already runs.

`Wrapped::run` ([bridge.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs)) does these steps before the CLI starts:

1. It opens the MCP tools of the workspace with `McpConnector::open` and emits the notes as status rows. It opens them first because the CLI lists the Ostra MCP tools one time at startup.
2. It builds an `ExecutionPolicy` from the `ExecContext` and the build and test commands of the project profile.
3. It builds a `ToolEnv` with the repository, the session folder, the memory database, and the handles for code navigation, MCP, project management, and coordination.
4. It stores the policy, the tool environment, and the host in a `Running` record under the execution id.

After the inner run returns, `Wrapped::run` removes the `Running` record. `BridgeServices::authorize` returns true only while the record exists. Thus a hook call that arrives after the run is denied.

`HarnessExecutor::run` ([executor.rs](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/executor.rs)) does these steps:

1. It returns the error `the harness executor was given a native route` when the route is native.
2. It registers the execution in `LiveRegistry`. The registry mints the per-execution token.
3. It copies the `owes_reply` flag and the inspect flag from the spec.
4. It finds the git repositories of the repo root and the workspace root, for the `commondir` check.
5. It calls `launch`, then starts the usage follower and the supervise loop.

## Launch sequence

The diagram shows the calls from the engine to the running CLI.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Engine
    participant Wrap as Wrapped executor
    participant Exec as HarnessExecutor
    participant Plan as launch plan
    participant Box as sandbox wrap
    participant Pty as PtySession
    participant CLI
    Engine->>Wrap: run spec host cancel
    Wrap->>Wrap: open MCP tools and store Running
    Wrap->>Exec: run spec host cancel
    Exec->>Exec: register LiveExecution and mint token
    Exec->>Plan: plan LaunchInput
    Plan-->>Exec: LaunchPlan
    Exec->>Exec: materialize files and links
    Exec->>Box: wrap plan with sandbox config
    Box-->>Exec: wrapped plan and members
    Exec->>Pty: spawn plan 120 by 40
    Pty->>CLI: start process in the PTY
    Exec->>Exec: start usage follower and supervise
```

The `launch` method of `HarnessExecutor` does these steps in this order:

1. It reads the sandbox settings for the workspace and the command from `harness_command`. The command is `[harness.<name>].command`, or the harness name when that field is empty.
2. It calls `which::which` on the command. A missing command returns the error `harness-launch: <command> (<Display name>) is not installed`.
3. For Antigravity, it calls `ensure_agy_integration`.
4. It creates the config dir `harness_execution_dir(session_root, execution id)`. This is the folder `harness/<execution id>` in the state folder of the session.
5. It builds a `LaunchInput` and calls `launch::plan`.
6. It calls `launch::materialize` to write the files and create the links.
7. It calls `sandbox::wrap`.
8. It stores the session id that the plan chose, when the plan has one.
9. It creates the `TermLog`, spawns the `PtySession`, and gives the sandbox members to the session.
10. It emits the status row `<Name> is running in the terminal on <model>. Every tool call it makes goes through Ostra's guards.`

After `launch` returns, `run` inserts the session in `PtyRegistry`. Viewers that wait for a PTY wake at that point.

## The launch plan

`LaunchInput` holds the inputs of one plan: the spec, the harness, the command, the extra arguments, the path of the `ostra` binary, the server URL, the bridge socket, the token, the config dir, the session id to resume, the home folder, the credential names, and the `sandboxed` flag. `launch::plan` returns a `LaunchPlan`. The plan holds the program, the arguments, the environment, the working folder, the files to write, the links to create, the session id, the variables to remove, and the `tty_param` that Seatbelt needs.

All four plans share these rules:

- The working folder is `ctx.repo_root`.
- Each hook runs `<ostra binary> hook --execution <id> --harness <name> --event <event>`. `shell_quote` quotes each word.
- The MCP server `ostra` runs `<ostra binary> mcp-stdio --execution <id>`.
- `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS` is 86,400 seconds for each hook and each MCP tool, because a permission ask waits for the user.
- The arguments of `[harness.<name>].args` go into every launch.
- The effort word is the effort of the spec, capped at the maximum that the CLI accepts.
- The git settings for agents (`ostra_core::git::agent_env`) join the environment.

`materialize` writes each file with owner-only rights and creates the parent folders. It then creates each link and skips a link that exists. The owner-only rule exists because the Grok config holds the token of the execution.

The code comment in [launch.rs](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/launch.rs) names the CLI versions that the flags were checked against: claude 2.1.280, codex 0.153.4, grok 1.0.30, and agy 1.2.6.

### How the four plans differ

| Item | Claude Code | Codex | Grok Build | Antigravity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hook and MCP config | Files `claude-settings.json` (`--settings`) and `claude-mcp.json` (`--mcp-config`, `--strict-mcp-config`) | Flags `-c hooks.<Event>=...` and `-c mcp_servers.ostra.*=...` | Folder `grok-home` with links to the real Grok home and a new `config.toml` | One global plugin and `agy mcp add`, plus one agent file |
| Hook events | PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SessionStart | PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionStart | PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionStart | PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PreInvocation, PostInvocation |
| System prompt | `--append-system-prompt-file system-prompt.md` | `-c developer_instructions=<prompt>` | `--rules <prompt>` | Body of the agent file |
| Session id | Ostra chooses it: `--session-id`. Resume: `--resume <id>` | The CLI reports it in hook payloads. Resume: `resume <id>` as the first arguments | Ostra chooses it: `--session-id`. Resume: `--resume <id>` | The CLI reports it in hooks or on screen. Resume: `--conversation <id>` |
| Model and effort | `--model`, `--effort` (cap `Max`) | `-m`, `-c model_reasoning_effort` (cap `Xhigh`) | `-m`, `--reasoning-effort` (cap `High`) | `--model`, `--effort` (cap `High`) |
| Tool limits | `--tools` from the capabilities plus `ToolSearch`. `--disallowed-tools Agent,Task,AskUserQuestion,EnterPlanMode,ExitPlanMode`. `--permission-mode default` | `--disable multi_agent`, `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` | `--no-subagents`, `GROK_SUBAGENTS=0`, `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` | `tools:` list in the agent file, `subagent: false`, `--dangerously-skip-permissions` |
| Repository config | `--setting-sources user` | Profile `ostra-restricted-<id>` marks the repository untrusted | Trust list copy with only the session folder added | None in the plan |
| Extra folders | `--add-dir` for the session folder, and for the artifacts and books folders when they exist | `-C <repo root>` | `--cwd <repo root>` | `--add-dir`, same folders as Claude Code |
| Other | `sandbox.enabled=false` in the settings when Ostra sandboxes the CLI | `check_for_update_on_startup=false` | `--leader-socket <farm>/leader-ostra.sock` | The first prompt goes with `-i` |

The next list gives the reason for each isolation rule. Each rule keeps repository-owned configuration out of the run.

- **Claude Code:** `--setting-sources user` loads only the settings of the user. The project and local settings are files of the repository. Their hooks, environment, and permissions would run outside the guards. `--strict-mcp-config` loads only the MCP config of Ostra.
- **Codex:** Codex reads folder trust only from config files, not from `-c`. The plan writes the profile file `<codex home>/ostra-restricted-<id>.config.toml`. The file marks the repository and each parent folder up to the git root as `untrusted`, for at most 32 folders. An untrusted folder keeps its `.codex/` config, hooks, and exec policies off. The profile name uses the execution id, so removing it at the end never affects another run. The plan skips the profile when `[harness.codex].args` already holds `-p`, `--profile`, or `--profile=`.
- **Grok Build:** Grok runs the hooks and MCP servers of a trusted folder. The plan therefore copies the trust list and adds only the session folder. The repository stays trusted only if the user trusted it in Grok. The new Grok home links every entry of the real home except `config.toml`, `trusted_folders.toml`, `leader.sock`, names that start with `leader-`, and names that end with `.lock`. The plan also removes any `[mcp_servers.ostra]` table of the user config, so Ostra holds the only definition.
- **Antigravity:** The CLI reads hooks and MCP servers only from global config. Ostra installs one integration that does nothing unless `OSTRA_EXECUTION` is set. A later section explains it.

`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`, and `--dangerously-skip-permissions` turn off the approval prompts of the CLI. The hook bridge decides each call instead.

Codex has a second reason for `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`. The hooks of Ostra change with every execution, so they can never hold saved hook trust.

## Environment of the CLI process

`PtySession::spawn` ([pty.rs](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/pty.rs)) builds the environment in this order:

1. It copies every variable of the Ostra server.
2. It removes the 16 names of `PARENT_SESSION_ENV`, such as `CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, `GROK_SESSION_ID`, and `ANTIGRAVITY_AGENT`. A CLI that inherits them runs as a nested child of the session that started Ostra. Claude Code does not save such a session, so the run could never resume.
3. It removes the names in `plan.env_remove`.
4. It sets `TERM=xterm-256color` and `COLORTERM=truecolor`.
5. It sets the variables of the plan: `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_HARNESS`, and the git settings. Grok adds `GROK_HOME` and `GROK_SUBAGENTS=0`.

`plan.env_remove` is the list of credential names minus the names that the CLI needs to sign in. `credential_env_names` builds the list. It holds the five default provider names (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_BASE_URL`), the four `OSTRA_*` names, the environment names of each `providers.*` entry, and the `client_secret_env` of each MCP server of the workspace.

The CLI keeps these names because it needs them to sign in:

| Harness | Kept variables |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` |
| Codex | `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_BASE_URL` |
| Antigravity | `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY` |
| Grok Build | None |

Caution: treat the kept variables as readable by the agent. The shell commands that the CLI runs inherit them.

## The first message

The first message is the spawn block plus the repository brief. The engine builds it, and `ExecutionSpec.first_message` holds it. The plan passes it as the prompt argument. Claude Code, Codex, and Grok Build take it as the last positional argument. Antigravity takes it after `-i`.

A long message does not fit on a command line. `first_prompt` solves this:

```rust
fn first_prompt(inp: &LaunchInput<'_>, files: &mut Vec<(PathBuf, String)>) -> String {
    let msg = &inp.spec.first_message;
    if msg.len() <= MAX_ARG_PROMPT {
        return msg.clone();
    }
    let path = inp.config_dir.join("first-message.md");
    files.push((path.clone(), msg.clone()));
    format!("Your full task is in `{}`. Read that whole file ...", path.display())
}
```

`MAX_ARG_PROMPT` is 96 KiB. A longer message goes to `first-message.md` in the config dir. The prompt then tells the agent to read that file before its first other tool call.

The prompt differs for a resumed session:

- **Resume with a note:** the prompt is `resume.note`.
- **Resume without a note:** the prompt is `Ostra resumed this session after an interruption. Continue the task from where it stopped: check what is already done before redoing it, finish the rest, then call` the submit tool.
- **Inspection:** the prompt does not exist. An inspection is a read-only reopening of an ended session, and the user types in the terminal.

## Terminal mirror

A browser can attach to the terminal of a run at any time. The PTY session keeps a screen model for that purpose. `PtySession` ([pty.rs](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/pty.rs)) runs on `portable-pty`. It keeps a `vt100` screen with 2,000 lines of scrollback.

The session starts three threads:

- **Writer:** it takes byte chunks from a queue of `WRITE_QUEUE` (256) entries and writes them to the PTY.
- **Reader:** it reads 16 KiB chunks. For each chunk it updates `last_output`, feeds the screen, broadcasts the chunk, passes it to the log sink, and answers terminal queries.
- **Waiter:** it waits for the CLI to exit and publishes the exit code.

Ostra alone answers the terminal queries of the CLI. Browsers mute their own replies. Thus any number of viewers, or none, gives the CLI exactly one answer. `answer_queries` handles these queries: cursor position, status, primary and secondary device attributes, foreground and background color, kitty keyboard state, the terminal version, and DEC mode queries of the form `?<1 to 5 digits>$`. The mode form is strict, so program output cannot type text into the input of the CLI.

The terminal size and input have these limits:

| Item | Value | Constant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default size | 120 columns by 40 rows | `DEFAULT_COLS`, `DEFAULT_ROWS` |
| Smallest size | 20 by 5 | `MIN_COLS`, `MIN_ROWS` |
| Largest size | 1,000 by 500 | `MAX_COLS`, `MAX_ROWS` |
| Scrollback | 2,000 lines | `SCROLLBACK` |
| Pending writes | 256, then `write` fails with `WouldBlock` | `WRITE_QUEUE` |
| Viewer lag | 256 chunks, then the viewer gets a fresh snapshot | `STREAM_BUFFER` |
| Browser input per message | 64 KiB | `MAX_TERM_INPUT` in [ws.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs) |

The smallest size exists because `vt100` 0.16 panics the reader thread on a one-row screen that wraps a line. It also panics on a one-column screen that draws a wide character. `resize` clamps each request to the table range. The write queue refuses input when full because a CLI that stops reading must not block the callers.

`type_line` types a line as a person does. It sends the text inside bracketed-paste marks (`ESC[200~` and `ESC[201~`), waits 150 ms, then sends `\r`. The marks keep the CLI from treating a newline in the text as a submit. The supervise loop uses `type_line` for nudges and wake notes.

`PtySession::stream` returns the current screen and a receiver for all later chunks. It takes both under one lock, so a viewer neither misses nor repeats output. A viewer that lags more than 256 chunks gets a fresh screen. The WebSocket channel `term:<execution id>` carries the stream. The messages `TermInput` and `TermResize` go back to `PtyRegistry`.

### Terminal transcript on disk

`TermLog` ([term_log.rs](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/term_log.rs)) appends the raw bytes of the terminal to `terminal.log` in the config dir. The Terminal tab replays this file for an ended run. These rules apply:

- `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` is 2 MiB. When the file passes 4 MiB, `TermLog` rewrites it with its last 2 MiB. Writes stay appends and memory stays flat.
- The folder has mode 0700 and the file has mode 0600, because harness output can carry secrets.
- A new run replaces the old file. A run that resumes under the same execution id appends to it.
- A failed write stops the transcript. The run goes on.
- `read_transcript` returns at most the last 2 MiB.

## Sandbox wrap

The CLI and everything it starts must run in the sandbox of the execution. `sandbox::wrap` ([sandbox.rs](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/sandbox.rs)) changes the plan to do this. The page "Profile and backends: bubblewrap and Seatbelt" explains the backends. This section explains what the harness side adds.

`wrap` does these steps:

1. It calls `sandbox::decide`. The result is a backend, an unsandboxed warning, or an error. An error means the config requires a sandbox that this machine cannot give. The launch then fails.
2. For an unsandboxed result, it returns the plan unchanged with the warning. `launch` emits the status row `<Name> runs without a sandbox. <warning>`.
3. It builds the profile with `Profile::for_execution`. It allows the model hosts of the harness (`ostra_sandbox::egress::model_hosts`) and the hosts of the base URLs that the user chose.
4. It starts the egress proxy and plants the decoy files.
5. It forwards the hook bridge into the sandbox. With a bridge socket, it uses `forward_socket`. Without one, it uses `forward`.
6. It makes the config dir writable and mounts a scratch folder `tmp` of the config dir as `/tmp`.
7. With a mount namespace (bubblewrap), it overlays the home folder, so the CLI can write its state folders but cannot leave files that later shells would run.
8. It makes the state folders of the CLI writable and protects their settings files as read-only.
9. For Claude Code with a mount namespace, it copies `~/.claude.json` into the config dir and links the copy. Claude Code rewrites that file through a rename, and a read-only home would refuse it.
10. It builds the sandbox command and returns the new plan, the members, and no warning.

The base URL hosts come from `*_BASE_URL` variables, from the `env` block of the Claude Code `settings.json`, and from `model_providers.*.base_url` in the Codex `config.toml`. These endpoints are often a gateway on this machine or on the LAN, so the egress proxy allows them even if they resolve to a private address.

The forwarded bridge has its own address inside the sandbox. `wrap` replaces `OSTRA_URL` with `http://127.0.0.1:<forwarded port>`. It also rewrites the old URL in every plan file that holds it, for example the Grok config. `replace_url` replaces a URL only where the port number ends, so `:4100` never matches inside `:41000`. `bridge_addr` needs the callback URL in the form `http://<ip>:<port>`. Another form fails the launch with the text `The hook bridge URL ... is not http://<ip>:<port>.`

The settings files stay read-only because a hook or instruction written there would run in later sessions of the user. These are the protected entries:

| Harness | State folder | Read-only entries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `~/.claude` | `settings.json`, `settings.local.json`, `CLAUDE.md`, `commands/`, `agents/`, `skills/`, `plugins/`, `hooks/`, `output-styles/` |
| Codex | `CODEX_HOME` or `~/.codex` | `config.toml`, `AGENTS.md`, `hooks.json`, `rules/` |
| Grok Build | `GROK_HOME` or `~/.grok` | `config.toml`, `trusted_folders.toml`, `hooks/` |
| Antigravity | `~/.gemini` | `settings.json`, `GEMINI.md`, `config/plugins/` |

Seatbelt has no overlay. Under Seatbelt the rest of the home folder stays read-only, and the writes of a CLI at the top of the home fail. Claude Code writes `~/.claude.json` there. The CLIs survive these failures. Seatbelt also denies `/tmp` and the keychain, so `wrap` adds `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR` (the scratch folder) and, when unset, `SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/cert.pem`. Codex needs the certificate bundle because it reads trusted roots from the keychain otherwise.

After the run, `sandbox::cleanup` removes three items from the config dir: the copy `claude.json`, the file `grok-home/config.toml` that holds the token, and the `tmp` folder. The other files stay, including `terminal.log`.

## Windows command resolution

`command::resolve` ([command.rs](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/command.rs)) turns the harness command into a program that Windows can start. On Unix it uses the name as given. On Windows it searches `PATH` with the `PATHEXT` extensions. An npm install makes three files: a `sh` script, a `.cmd`, and a `.ps1`. `CreateProcessW` cannot start the first, and `cmd.exe` cannot pass the multi-line arguments of a harness. Thus `resolve` reads the `.cmd` shim and starts its script with `node`. A plain `.bat` file fails with the text `Set the harness command to an .exe`.

## Machine setup: detect, install, and sign in

The server must know which CLIs exist before a user routes work to one. [env.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/env.rs) does this check.

`EnvStatus::detect` runs for each of the four harnesses. It calls `which`, then runs `<command> --version` with an 8-second timeout, and keeps the first non-empty line. It then reads the login state:

| Harness | Logged in when | Unknown when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set, or `~/.claude/.credentials.json` exists, or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` is set, or `~/.claude.json` has `oauthAccount` | None of these exist, because the credentials can live in the OS keychain |
| Codex | `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set, or `auth.json` exists in `CODEX_HOME` or `~/.codex` | Never. A missing file means not logged in |
| Grok Build | Not checked | Always |
| Antigravity | Not checked | Always |

An uninstalled CLI has the login state `false`. `EnvStatus::stale` returns true after 60 seconds, and `refresh_env` then detects again. The server does not call `all_harness_status` of the harness crate. It uses `EnvStatus::detect`.

At startup, `extend_path` adds the install folders of the official installers to `PATH`. On Unix these are `~/.local/bin` and `~/.grok/bin`. On Windows they also include `AppData/Roaming/npm`. The call happens before any other thread starts, because it writes the process environment. A CLI that a user installs while the server runs then resolves by name without a restart.

[harness_setup.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/harness_setup.rs) runs the install and login commands in a PTY on the server machine. The route `POST /api/harnesses/{harness}/setup` starts them. These rules apply:

- The terminal id is `setup_<harness>_<action>`. A second click reattaches to the terminal that still runs.
- The PTY is 100 columns by 30 rows and starts in the home folder with no extra environment.
- The install command is the official installer: `curl -fsSL <vendor URL> | bash` (or `| sh` for Codex) on Unix. On Windows it is `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` for Claude Code and `npm install -g @openai/codex` for Codex. Grok Build and Antigravity print a message on Windows and exit with code 1.
- A prefix checks for `curl` (or `npm` on Windows). A missing tool prints a message and exits with code 127.
- The login commands are `claude auth login`, `codex login`, `grok login`, and `agy`.
- A login action fails at once with `Install <Name> first` when the program is not on `PATH`.
- When the terminal exits, the server detects again and pushes `ServerMsg::HarnessStatus` on the channel `home`.

### Antigravity global integration

Antigravity reads hooks and MCP servers only from global config. `ensure_agy_integration` ([setup.rs](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/setup.rs)) runs before each Antigravity launch. It is idempotent. It does this:

1. It writes `plugin.json` and `hooks.json` in `~/.gemini/config/plugins/ostra/`.
2. It sets `plugins.ostra.enabled` to `true` in `~/.gemini/config/config.json`.
3. It runs `agy mcp list`. If no line starts with `ostra` and holds the path of the binary, it runs `agy mcp add ostra <binary> mcp-stdio`.

The hook commands of the plugin have no `--execution` argument. They read `OSTRA_EXECUTION` from the environment. Without that variable, `ostra hook` exits with code 0 and prints nothing, so the plugin is inert in the own sessions of the user.

Each launch also writes the agent file `~/.gemini/config/plugins/ostra/agents/ostra-<agent>.md`. The file holds the model, the effort (`xhigh` and `max` become `high`), the `tools:` list, the timeout, `subagent: false`, `hidden: true`, `inheritMcp: true`, and the system prompt as the body. The name of the file depends on the agent, not on the execution. A later launch of the same agent overwrites the file.

The `tools:` list comes from `agy_tools`: `view_file`, `write_to_file`, `replace_file_content`, `run_command`, `grep_search`, `find_by_name`, `search_web`, and `read_url_content`. An agent file without a `tools:` list gets no native tools. One unknown name makes the whole session fail to start. Thus only verified names are listed.

## What happens when

- **The CLI is not installed:** `launch` returns `harness-launch: ... is not installed`. No PTY starts. The result has status `Error`.
- **The Antigravity integration fails:** the error is `harness-launch: installing the Antigravity integration failed: <reason>`.
- **The config dir or a plan file cannot be written:** the error starts with `harness-launch: creating ...` or `harness-launch: writing the harness config: ...`.
- **The config requires a sandbox and none exists:** `wrap` returns the error of `sandbox::decide`, and the launch fails.
- **The config allows no sandbox:** the run goes on. `launch` emits a status row with the warning and logs one line for the process.
- **The PTY cannot start:** the error is `harness-launch: starting <program>: <reason>`.
- **The terminal log cannot be created:** the run goes on without a transcript.
- **No browser watches:** the run goes on. Ostra answers the terminal queries itself.
- **The user changes `[harness.*]` or `[sandbox]` during a run:** the run keeps its settings. The next execution uses the new values.
- **The run resumes under the same execution id:** `terminal.log` keeps its old bytes and gets the new ones.

## Settings and limits

| Name | Value | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[harness.<name>].command` | Program name. Default: the harness name (`claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy`) | Global config, read on each execution |
| `[harness.<name>].args` | Extra arguments for each launch. Default: none | Global config, read on each execution |
| `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS` | 86,400 seconds | `launch.rs` |
| `MAX_ARG_PROMPT` | 96 KiB | `launch.rs` |
| `DEFAULT_COLS`, `DEFAULT_ROWS` | 120 by 40 | `pty.rs`, `HarnessExecutorConfig.cols` and `rows` |
| `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` | 2 MiB | `term_log.rs` |
| Version check timeout | 8 seconds | `env.rs` |
| Detection refresh | 60 seconds | `EnvStatus::stale` |
| Token length | 64 hex characters | `LiveRegistry::register` |
