sections.title: Egress proxy and decoy files
sections.summary: Explains how the egress proxy is the only way out of a sandbox, the four network choices, host rules, address classes, request handling, and the decoy credential files.
sections.body:
## The problem that the proxy solves

A sandbox with the host network reaches every service on the host and on the local network. A sandbox with an empty network namespace cannot download a crate or an npm package. The egress proxy gives a controlled way out. It sees the destination host and port of every connection and lets through only what the policy allows. It connects to the address that it checked and never looks up a name a second time. The proxy also reports refusals of local addresses, because such a refusal can show an attempt to reach a service on the machine.

The decoy files solve a second problem. A command can read a credential file, and the policy cannot see this when a shell hides the path. A decoy is a fake credential file. The kernel reports the open of a decoy, so Ostra sees the read.

This page covers the proxy topology, the four network choices, the host rules, the address classes, the request steps, and the decoys. The page "Profile and backends: bubblewrap and Seatbelt" explains how each backend renders the network rules.

## Proxy topology

The topology depends on the OS, because only bubblewrap gives each sandbox its own loopback.

- **Linux.** Each execution gets one Unix socket under `<data dir>/egress`. Bubblewrap binds the socket into that sandbox only. The helper `ostra sandbox-init` listens on `127.0.0.1:<free port>` inside the network namespace and splices each connection to the socket. The socket path is limited to 107 bytes. The error text says "Keep the data dir path short".
- **macOS.** Every sandbox shares the loopback of the host. Each proxy gets its own port on `127.0.0.1` (IPv4 only) and one credential. Clients get `http://ostra:<secret>@127.0.0.1:<port>`. The secret is a random UUID. Every request must carry the matching `Proxy-Authorization: Basic` header. Ostra compares it in constant time. Without it, the proxy answers `407 Proxy Authentication Required`. The credential exists because a sandbox that can reach the loopback also reaches the proxy ports of other executions.

Both topologies share these rules:

- One Tokio runtime with 2 worker threads, named `ostra-egress`, serves every listener.
- One proxy serves every command of a profile. A command that Ostra wraps without a profile proxy starts its own proxy. That proxy reports decisions to the log only (`log_decision`).
- The command gets `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `ALL_PROXY`, each also in lowercase. It gets `NO_PROXY` and `no_proxy` set to `localhost,127.0.0.1,::1`. It gets `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`.
- Loopback traffic skips the proxy because of `NO_PROXY`. A loopback entry in `allowed_hosts` therefore works only as a forwarded port.
- When Ostra drops a `Listener`, it stops the listener, ends its open connections, and removes the socket.

### One CONNECT request on Linux

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Cmd as Command
    participant Help as sandbox-init
    participant Prox as Egress proxy
    participant Site as Remote host
    Cmd->>Help: connect 127.0.0.1:port
    Help->>Prox: splice to the egress socket
    Cmd->>Prox: CONNECT host:443
    Prox->>Prox: route, resolve, check address
    Prox->>Site: connect to the checked address
    Prox-->>Cmd: 200 Connection established
    Cmd->>Prox: TLS ClientHello
    Prox->>Prox: compare server name with host
    Prox->>Site: forward the hello and copy both ways
```

## The four network choices

`[sandbox] network` and the workspace setting `sandbox_network` choose one of four values. The default is `allowlist`.

| Choice | Network namespace | What leaves | Proxy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `none` | Yes | Nothing. A harness CLI still reaches its own model hosts. | Only when a rule exists |
| `allowlist` | Yes | The built-in hosts, the model hosts of every harness, and `allowed_hosts` | Yes |
| `public` | Yes | Any public address. User hosts keep full access. | Yes |
| `host` | No | Everything, unfiltered | No |

Under `none`, `Policy::new` creates no rules from `allowed_hosts`. The sandbox then needs a proxy only when a harness adds its model hosts (`needs_proxy`). The refusal text under `none` tells the user to set `network` to `allowlist`. Under `host`, Seatbelt allows outbound IP, a listener on localhost, and the `mDNSResponder` socket. Other Unix sockets stay denied, for example the SSH agent and Docker.

## Host rules

`HostRule::parse` reads one `allowed_hosts` entry. An entry has one of four forms, each with an optional `:port`:

- `host`: one name.
- `*.domain`: every name below the domain, but not the domain itself.
- An IPv4 address.
- `[v6]`: an IPv6 address in brackets.

Without a port, a rule allows ports 443 and 80. Ostra converts names to lowercase and removes a trailing dot. The parser rejects an empty entry, whitespace, and the characters `/`, `@`, `?`, and `#`. It rejects port 0 and a port that is not a number. A name can have 253 characters. A label can have 63 characters. A label can hold letters, digits, `-`, and `_`, and cannot start or end with `-`. Ostra turns an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address into the IPv4 address that it carries.

Two kinds of rule exist:

- A *trusted* rule comes from the user: `allowed_hosts` entries and the base-URL hosts of a harness launch.
- A *builtin* rule comes from Ostra: the built-in host list and the model hosts of the harnesses.

### Built-in hosts

`DEFAULT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` holds 26 hosts. They are the registries and source hosts that builds use:

- Rust: `index.crates.io`, `static.crates.io`, `static.rust-lang.org`, `crates.io`.
- npm and yarn: `registry.npmjs.org`, `registry.yarnpkg.com`, `repo.yarnpkg.com`.
- Python: `pypi.org`, `files.pythonhosted.org`.
- Go: `proxy.golang.org`, `sum.golang.org`.
- GitHub: `github.com`, `codeload.github.com`, `objects.githubusercontent.com`, `raw.githubusercontent.com`, `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`.
- JVM: `repo.maven.apache.org`, `repo1.maven.org`, `services.gradle.org`, `plugins.gradle.org`, `plugins-artifacts.gradle.org`, `dl.google.com`, `maven.google.com`.
- Ruby: `rubygems.org`, `index.rubygems.org`.
- .NET: `api.nuget.org`.

`model_hosts` returns the hosts of each harness. Ostra measured them with one run for each harness. A harness gets its own hosts under every network choice. Under `allowlist`, every command reaches the hosts of all harnesses, so a build or a test can call a model API.

| Harness | Model hosts |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `api.anthropic.com`, `console.anthropic.com`, `platform.claude.com`, `claude.ai` |
| Codex | `api.openai.com`, `chatgpt.com`, `auth.openai.com` |
| Grok | `api.x.ai`, `auth.x.ai`, `accounts.x.ai`, `grok.com`, `cli-chat-proxy.grok.com` |
| Antigravity | `cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`, `daily-cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`, `generativelanguage.googleapis.com`, `oauth2.googleapis.com`, `www.googleapis.com`, `lh3.googleusercontent.com` |

A workspace can add hosts with `sandbox_allowed_hosts`. It cannot remove a global host or a built-in host. The harness launch also reads base URLs from `*_BASE_URL` variables, from Claude Code `settings.json` (`env`), and from the Codex `model_providers`. It treats these hosts as trusted, because the user chose them and they often point to a gateway on the local network.

## Address classes

`Policy::access` gives each destination one of three classes:

| Class | When | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AnyAddress` | A trusted rule matches | The name can resolve to any address, a private address included. |
| `PublicOnly` | The network is `public`, or a builtin rule matches | The name must resolve to at least one public address. |
| `Refused` | No rule matches | The proxy answers `403` with the setting to change. |

For `PublicOnly`, the proxy applies two more checks:

1. A local-only name is refused without a lookup. Local-only names are `localhost`, a name with one label, and names that end in `.localhost`, `.local`, `.internal`, `.lan`, or `.home.arpa`. A `.local` lookup goes out on the LAN and takes seconds to fail on macOS.
2. The proxy resolves the name and removes private addresses. When none remain, it refuses the destination.

The function `is_private` defines a private address:

- IPv4: loopback, private ranges, link-local (the cloud metadata address is included), unspecified, broadcast, multicast, `0.0.0.0/8`, CGNAT `100.64.0.0/10`, benchmarking `198.18.0.0/15`, and `240.0.0.0/4` and above.
- IPv6: loopback, unspecified, multicast, unique-local, link-local, and site-local. It also covers IPv4-mapped and IPv4-compatible addresses, and NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96`, where it checks the IPv4 address that the address carries. Local-use NAT64 `64:ff9b:1::/48` is always private.

Each refusal message starts with the correction and names the setting. For a public destination, it names `[sandbox] allowed_hosts` or `network = "public"`. For a local destination, it says to add the host to `allowed_hosts` when the user runs the service.

## Request handling

### Decisions for one connection

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Read the request head"] --> B{"Head valid and under 8 KiB?"}
    B -- no --> R400["400 Bad Request"]
    B -- yes --> C{"macOS credential correct?"}
    C -- no --> R407["407 Proxy Authentication Required"]
    C -- yes --> D{"Policy allows host and port?"}
    D -- no --> R403["403 Forbidden and report the refusal"]
    D -- yes --> E{"Connect within 10 s?"}
    E -- no --> R502["502 Bad Gateway"]
    E -- yes --> F["200 Connection established"]
    F --> G{"TLS server name equals CONNECT host?"}
    G -- no --> H["Close the tunnel and report the refusal"]
    G -- yes --> I["Copy both ways"]
```

The function `handle` runs these steps:

1. It reads the request head. The head can have 8 KiB (`MAX_HEAD`). The read times out after 30 seconds (`HEAD_TIMEOUT`). A bad head gets `400 Bad Request`.
2. On macOS, it checks the `Proxy-Authorization` header.
3. It parses the request. It accepts `CONNECT host:port`, or an absolute-form `http://` URL for plain HTTP. It accepts HTTP/1.x only. It rejects folded header lines.
4. It routes the destination (see "Address classes"). A refusal gets `403 Forbidden` with the reason. The proxy reports the refusal.
5. It reports the allowed connection.
6. It connects to each checked address in order. Each try times out after 10 seconds (`CONNECT_TIMEOUT`). When all fail, the proxy answers `502 Bad Gateway`.
7. For `CONNECT`, it answers `200 Connection established`. For plain HTTP, it sends the rewritten head upstream. The rewrite uses origin form, adds `Connection: close`, and drops the `Proxy-*`, `Host`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` headers. It then adds `Host` again from the URL.
8. For a `CONNECT` to a name, it reads the TLS ClientHello and compares the server name with the `CONNECT` host.
9. It copies data both ways.

The server name check exists because a CDN that routes by SNI would carry the tunnel to any site that it serves. These rules apply to the check:

- The hello can have 32 KiB (`MAX_HELLO`). Ostra reassembles it across TLS records.
- When the server name differs from the `CONNECT` host, the proxy closes the tunnel and reports a refusal.
- When the hello cannot be read or is too large, the proxy does the same.
- A first byte that is not TLS, or a hello without a server name, passes.
- When the destination speaks first, for example an SSH banner, the proxy does not treat the stream as TLS.
- A `CONNECT` to an IP address skips the check.

## Upstream proxy

A machine can reach the internet only through a proxy. Set `[sandbox] upstream_proxy` to `http://host:port`, without a path and without credentials. The proxy then routes in this way:

- It resolves the name first. When any address is private, it connects directly, because an internal mirror is rarely behind the corporate proxy.
- When all addresses are public, it connects through the upstream proxy with `CONNECT`.
- When the name does not resolve here, it uses the upstream proxy. This applies to trusted names and to names that are not local-only. A local-only name that the user did not list is refused, because it would reach the network of the upstream proxy unchecked.
- When the upstream proxy answers with a status other than 200, the client gets `502`. The text names the status.

## Loopback and the macOS policy

Under bubblewrap, the loopback belongs to the sandbox. Ostra forwards each loopback port that a trusted rule lists, for example `127.0.0.1:8317`, to the loopback of the host. A blocked port is not forwarded.

Under Seatbelt, every sandbox shares the loopback of the host. The policy allows a listener on localhost. For outbound connections, these rules apply, in this order:

1. Allow every port when `sandbox_loopback` is `open` and the network is `allowlist` or `public`. Never under `none`.
2. Allow each loopback port in `allowed_hosts`.
3. Deny each port in `sandbox_blocked_ports`, and deny the port of the Ostra server (`set_server_port`), because it serves the console API.
4. Allow the own proxy and forward ports of the sandbox last, so they win.

Under Seatbelt with a private network, the policy has no DNS resolver socket. The proxy resolves names, and a lookup from the command could carry data out in the name. `localhost` still resolves from `/etc/hosts`.

## What the proxy reports

The proxy reports the first allowed connection and the first refusal for each `(host, port, allowed)` key. A retry loop therefore reports once. `report::egress` sends each decision to the engine as `ExecutionDelta::Egress` from a thread named `ostra-egress-report`, because the proxy runtime must not block.

The field `local` is true when the destination is loopback, private, or link-local. An egress refusal with `local` set is a containment signal. A refusal of a public host is not a signal, because builds call telemetry hosts. It shows in the Activity view only. The page "Containment signals, build streak, and lesson gate" explains the pause after the third signal.

## Decoy files

A decoy is a credential path that an agent has no reason to read. The kernel reports each open, so a Bash `cat` is seen like a tool call. The first open of a decoy becomes `ExecutionDelta::Decoy`, and this is a containment signal.

### Which decoys exist

`HOME_DECOYS` holds four built-in decoys: `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `~/.git-credentials`, and `~/.vault-token`. Ostra leaves out `~/.netrc`, because Python `requests` and Go module downloads read it on every fetch.

The profile plants the two SSH keys only when no SSH port is reachable (`reaches_port(22)` is false). The `ssh` program reads its keys when it authenticates, so a reachable SSH port would trigger the decoy by accident.

A workspace adds decoys with `sandbox_decoys`. It cannot remove a built-in decoy. These rules apply to an added entry:

- It must start with `~/` and name a file.
- It must have no empty component, no `.` or `..` component, and no NUL character.
- It must not be the sign-in file of a harness CLI, because a decoy there signs that CLI out.
- A workspace can add at most 32 entries (`MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS`).
- An entry `.ssh/id_*` that does not end in `.pub` is an SSH key. Other entries are generic.

The fake contents authenticate nowhere. An SSH key is an OpenSSH private key block of random text. A git credential is `https://git:<40 hex>@github.com`. A vault token is `hvs.` and 24 random characters. A generic decoy is 40 hex characters.

### How each backend watches a decoy

| Topic | Bubblewrap (Linux) | Seatbelt (macOS) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decoy path must be | An existing file, or a missing file inside a hidden dir or the overlaid home | An existing file |
| Mechanism | A fake file bound read-only over the path | A `file-read-data` deny with a message tag `dev.ostra.decoy.<16 hex>` |
| Where the fake lives | `<data dir>/decoys/<16 hex>` | No fake file |
| Watch | `inotify` with `IN_OPEN` on each fake file | `log stream` with a kernel predicate |
| Needs | Nothing | An admin account (group 80) |
| `stat` or a listing | Not an open | Silent, because only `file-read-data` carries the message |

On Linux, the host file is never written, because the fake is a bind mount over a path inside the sandbox. A decoy reports its first open only. The watcher removes the watch after the first report. The path in the report is the path that the sandbox saw. When Ostra drops the `Decoys` value, the watch ends and the directory is deleted.

On macOS, Seatbelt cannot bind a file in, and it reports no refusal for a missing file. A decoy is therefore an existing file that the policy refuses to read. One `log stream` reader per process reads the refusals. The server starts it at start with `watch_reports`, and the start waits up to 10 seconds for the reader to attach.

### What happens when

- **A command opens a decoy.** The proxy-independent watcher reports the first open once. The engine gets `ExecutionDelta::Decoy`, and the signal counts toward the pause.
- **A command only runs `stat` or lists the directory.** No report appears.
- **The user on macOS is not an admin.** `decoys_supported` is false. The profile plants no decoys, and no error appears.
- **`log stream` cannot attach.** Ostra logs the warning "decoy files are not watched". The execution runs without decoys.
- **The inotify watch fails on Linux.** The execution fails with "Cannot plant the sandbox's decoy files".
- **No decoy path fits.** The profile plants nothing. This is not an error.
- **The server stopped without cleanup.** At the next start, the server removes old sockets and decoy dirs. It does this only when no other server runs for the data dir.
- **The OS is Windows.** The code returns `Unsupported` for every watch, so Ostra watches no decoy.

## Limits

| Limit | Value | Name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request head | 8 KiB | `MAX_HEAD` |
| Read of the request head | 30 s | `HEAD_TIMEOUT` |
| One connect try | 10 s | `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` |
| TLS ClientHello | 32 KiB | `MAX_HELLO` |
| Connections for each listener | 256 | `MAX_CONNECTIONS` |
| Runtime worker threads | 2 | in `runtime()` |
| Socket path | 107 bytes | OS limit |
| Workspace decoys | 32 | `MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS` |
| Built-in hosts | 26 | `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` |

When a listener has 256 open connections, it drops the next connection.

The `IN_OPEN` watch for decoys on Linux.
The `log stream` reader for Seatbelt decoy refusals.
Which egress and decoy deltas count as containment signals.

sections.title: Sandbox settings, modes, and failure cases
sections.summary: Lists the sandbox settings with defaults, the result of `decide`, what a missing sandbox does for each caller, backend failures, save-time validation, and when a change takes effect.
sections.body:
## The problem that the modes solve

A machine can lack a sandbox backend. Bubblewrap can be missing, or a container can block user namespaces. Ostra must then choose between two bad results. It can refuse to run agent commands, or it can run them with the full rights of the user. The sandbox mode lets the user choose. The default is safe on Linux and macOS: the mode is `required`, so a missing sandbox stops the execution.

This page lists the settings, the decision function, the effect on each caller, the failure cases, the validation, and the time when a change takes effect. The other pages of this topic explain the profile and the proxy.

## The sandbox settings

The global settings live in the `[sandbox]` table of `config.toml`. The workspace settings live in the registry, never in `workspace.toml` (Rule A2). The pages "Settings files and every setting" and "Trust approvals and registry-only settings" explain both stores.

| Setting | Stored in | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `[sandbox] mode` | Global. The workspace `sandbox_mode` replaces it. | `required` on Linux and macOS, `auto` on Windows | `auto`, `required`, or `off` |
| `[sandbox] network` | Global. The workspace `sandbox_network` replaces it. | `allowlist` | `none`, `allowlist`, `public`, or `host` |
| `[sandbox] allowed_hosts` | Global. The workspace `sandbox_allowed_hosts` adds to it. | Empty | Hosts that the proxy lets through |
| `[sandbox] upstream_proxy` | Global only | None | `http://host:port` for the proxy to route through |
| `[sandbox] extra_writable` | Global only | Empty | More writable paths, absolute or `~/...` |
| `[sandbox] extra_hidden` | Global only | Empty | More hidden paths, absolute or `~/...` |
| `sandbox_decoys` | Workspace only | Empty. Four built-in decoys always exist. | More decoy files, `~/...`, at most 32 |
| `sandbox_loopback` | Workspace only, macOS | `open` | `open` or `listed` |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` | Workspace only, macOS | Empty | Loopback ports, 1 to 65535, at most 64 |
| `OSTRA_SANDBOX_CACHE` | Environment | `~/.cache/ostra/sandbox` | Location of the sandbox caches |
| `OSTRA_CONFIG`, `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` | Environment | Not set | The sandbox hides these paths |

The three modes mean:

- `auto`: use a sandbox when the machine has one. Otherwise run without a sandbox and warn.
- `required`: refuse to start an execution that cannot be sandboxed.
- `off`: run without a sandbox and do not warn.

`SandboxConfig::for_workspace` merges the workspace over the global config. The workspace `mode` and `network` replace the global values when they are set. The workspace hosts are added to the global hosts, and a workspace never removes a host. The fields `loopback` and `blocked_ports` are `#[serde(skip)]`, so Ostra never reads them from `config.toml`.

## The decision of `decide`

`decide(cfg)` in `crates/ostra-sandbox/src/backend.rs` combines the mode with the result of the backend probe.

### Decision for one config

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M{"Mode?"}
    M -- off --> U0["Unsandboxed, no warning"]
    M -- "auto or required" --> B{"Backend works?"}
    B -- yes --> S["Sandboxed with the backend"]
    B -- no --> C{"Mode?"}
    C -- auto --> U1["Unsandboxed with a warning"]
    C -- required --> E["Err: the sandbox is required but not available"]
```

The warning text is the reason of the probe followed by the fix text of the OS. The `Err` text starts with "The sandbox is required by the workspace settings or by `[sandbox] mode` in config.toml, but it is not available." and then adds the same reason and fix.

Each fix text ends with an instruction to choose sandbox mode `off` in the workspace settings, or to set `[sandbox] mode = "off"` in `config.toml`, to run without a sandbox on purpose.

| OS | Probe error | Fix text starts with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux | "The `bwrap` command is not installed." and other probe errors | "Install bubblewrap (the `bwrap` command) on the Linux machine that runs Ostra, or allow unprivileged user namespaces" |
| macOS | "`/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` is missing." and other probe errors | "Run Ostra outside any other sandbox, because macOS cannot nest them" |
| Windows | "The Windows sandbox is not built yet." | "Run Ostra inside WSL 2 or in Docker to sandbox agent commands" |
| Other | "The sandbox needs Linux or macOS." | "Run Ostra on Linux or macOS to sandbox agent commands" |

## The effect of a missing sandbox on each caller

The result of `decide` reaches six callers. Each caller handles `Unsandboxed` and `Err` in its own way.

| Caller | `Unsandboxed` with a warning | `Err` (mode `required`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native executor (`sandbox_for`) | The Bash tool runs without a sandbox. Ostra logs the warning once for each process and emits a `Status` delta "Bash runs without a sandbox." for each execution. | The execution fails with the error text. |
| Harness executor (`wrap`) | `wrap` returns the plan unchanged with the warning. The executor logs once and emits "`<harness>` runs without a sandbox." | `wrap` returns `Err`. The executor reports a launch error. |
| `host_command` | The program starts directly. Ostra still removes credential variables and `OSTRA_*`, and sets the safe git variables. | `host_command` returns `Err`. |
| Server start (`build`) | The server writes the warning to the log and to stderr, and it starts. | The server logs the message, writes it to stderr, and starts. Each execution then fails. |
| Setup check (`status`) | `active` is false and `message` holds the warning. | `active` is false and `message` holds the error. |
| Mode `off` | No warning and no `Status` delta. The server logs that the sandbox is off. | Not possible. |

The function `first_warning` returns true only on the first call. This keeps the log free of one warning for each execution. The `Status` delta still appears in the Activity view of each execution, so the user sees it.

The setup check reads `SandboxStatus`. It has these fields: `mode`, `default_mode`, `available`, `backend`, `active`, `message`, `gaps`, `decoys`, `builtin_decoys`, and `builtin_hosts`. The field `default_mode` shows `required` on Linux and macOS and `auto` on Windows, so the console does not assume `required`. The field `gaps` holds a value only when the sandbox is active.

## Backend failure cases

### Probe failures

The probe runs once for each process and Ostra caches the result in a `OnceLock`.

- **Linux.** `probe_bwrap` finds `bwrap` on `PATH` and finds the helper binary. It then runs a real test sandbox: `bwrap --ro-bind / / --dev /dev --proc /proc --unshare-pid --unshare-net -- <helper> sandbox-init --proxy /dev/null -- true`. A failure gives one of these messages: the command is not installed, the `ostra` binary was not found, the command does not start, or the command "is installed but cannot create a sandbox here". The last message tells the user that a container profile can block user namespaces. It names `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0` as one fix on the host.
- **macOS.** `probe_seatbelt` requires `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` to exist, to be owned by root, and not to be writable by group or others. The check exists because the Homebrew prefix on `PATH` is writable by the user. It then runs `sandbox-exec -p '(version 1)(allow default)' /usr/bin/true`. When stderr holds `sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`, the message says that Ostra runs inside another sandbox, and macOS cannot nest sandboxes.
- **Other OS.** The probe always returns an error.

Because the probe result stays for the life of the process, a user who installs bubblewrap after the server started must restart the server.

### Failures when an execution or a call starts

The backend can fail after the probe succeeded. Ostra never falls back to an unsandboxed run in these cases.

- **Native executor, at the start of an execution.** `sandbox_for` returns an error that fails the execution. The messages are "Cannot create the sandbox's /tmp", "Cannot start the sandbox's egress proxy", and "Cannot plant the sandbox's decoy files".
- **Native Bash call.** The Bash tool returns the tool error "Cannot prepare the sandbox: `<error>`". The command does not run. The error can come from the pwd file, from a missing helper ("The sandbox helper (the `ostra` binary) is missing."), from a proxy that cannot start, from a loopback port that cannot be forwarded, or from a Seatbelt path that is not UTF-8.
- **Harness executor.** `wrap` prefixes each error with the action: "starting the sandbox's egress proxy", "planting the sandbox's decoy files", "forwarding the hook bridge into the sandbox", "creating the sandbox's /tmp", or "writing the harness config". The executor reports a launch error.
- **The helper cannot start the command.** The helper prints "ostra sandbox-init: `<error>`" and exits with status 125.
- **A program for a project is missing.** `host_command` checks the program before it starts the sandbox. It returns "Cannot start `<program>`: no such program in the folder or on PATH."
- **The seccomp filter is missing.** On an architecture other than `x86_64` and `aarch64`, the sandbox runs without the filter. The setup check shows the gap in `gaps`, and the server logs it at start.

## Validation at save time

The module `crates/ostra-sandbox/src/validate.rs` states one rule. A value that the sandbox cannot enforce is an issue at save time, never a silent fallback at spawn time. Each issue has a `path` and a `message`, and the message starts with the correction.

| Setting | Issue | Path example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allowed_hosts` entry | Not a host name, `*.domain`, or IP address with an optional port | `sandbox.allowed_hosts[0]` |
| `allowed_hosts` loopback entry | A loopback entry without a port | `sandbox_allowed_hosts[2]` |
| `extra_writable`, `extra_hidden` | Not an absolute path and not a `~/` path, or the path holds a NUL character | `sandbox.extra_writable[0]` |
| `upstream_proxy` | Not `http://host:port`, or it has a path or credentials | `sandbox.upstream_proxy` |
| `sandbox_decoys` entry | Not a `~/` file path, or it is a harness sign-in file | `sandbox_decoys[1]` |
| `sandbox_decoys` list | More than 32 entries | `sandbox_decoys` |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` entry | Port 0 | `sandbox_blocked_ports[0]` |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` list | More than 64 entries | `sandbox_blocked_ports` |

Two functions run the checks. `validate::workspace` covers the workspace entries, and `ostra_workspace::settings` calls it when the user saves workspace settings. `validate::global` covers the `[sandbox]` table. The server calls it at start, and a failure stops the start with the path and the message.

The server also reads `config.toml` again each time that code needs the global config (`Shared::global`). When the file has a sandbox issue, or fails to parse, the server logs a warning and keeps the last good copy. An edit with an error therefore does not change the running behavior.

## When a change takes effect

- **The `[sandbox]` table.** Ostra reads it again at the start of each execution. The native executor (`sandbox_for`), the harness executor, and `host_command` each read it fresh. A change applies to the next execution, without a restart.
- **The workspace sandbox settings.** The engine copies them into `ExecContext` when it spawns the execution. A change applies to executions that start later.
- **A running execution.** It keeps the profile that it started with. The proxy, the decoys, and the mounts exist once for each execution. A lowered network choice does not cut a running Bash call.
- **The backend probe.** It is cached for the life of the process. A change of the machine, for example a new `bwrap`, needs a server restart.
- **The server port.** `set_server_port` runs at server start. Seatbelt policies name that port as blocked.

## Work that the server does at start

| Call | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `scrub_startup_env` | On macOS, moves the startup environment off the stack and zeroes the original strings, because an unsandboxed program of the same user can read it with `sysctl(KERN_PROCARGS2)`. On Linux it does nothing. |
| `set_helper` | Names the server binary as the `sandbox-init` helper. |
| `set_server_port` | Names the port that Seatbelt sandboxes never reach. |
| `kill_leftovers` | Stops processes that sandboxes of an earlier server left on macOS. |
| `egress::remove_stale_sockets` | Removes egress sockets of an earlier server. |
| `decoy::remove_stale` | Removes decoy dirs of an earlier server. |
| `decoy::watch_reports` | Starts the `log stream` reader on macOS for admin users. |

The last three cleanups run only when no other server runs for the same data dir (`!server_running()`). Call `scrub_startup_env` first in `main`, before any thread starts. The function moves the environment, and a running thread that reads it can see a broken value.

## Related behavior in other topics

The sandbox is the second line of defense. The guards and permission rules run first. The page "Containment signals, build streak, and lesson gate" explains how egress refusals and decoy opens pause a session after the third signal for one execution. The page "Spawn contract and repo brief" explains how the engine builds `ExecContext`.

Save-time checks for hosts, decoys, ports, paths, and the upstream proxy.
Builds `SandboxStatus` for the setup check.

sections.title: Windows support and the probe results
sections.summary: Explains that Windows has no sandbox, which hardening and shell and process tree handling exist, and what the 54 rows of the Windows probe show.
sections.body:
## The problem on Windows

Ostra builds and runs on Windows, but it has no Windows sandbox. Agent commands there run with the full rights of the user. Bubblewrap and Seatbelt do not exist on Windows, and no code in the repo replaces them. This page states what Windows has instead, and what a standalone probe measured for a future sandbox.

The repo cites a design document, `WINDOWS_HANDOVER.md`, in source comments. The file is not in the repo. This page therefore describes only the shipped code and the measured probe results. It does not describe a planned design.

## The status of the Windows sandbox

The module `crates/ostra-sandbox/src/sys/other.rs` implements `Os` for Windows and for every OS without a sandbox. Its probe returns the error "The Windows sandbox is not built yet." Every other operation refuses or does nothing:

- `watch_opens` and `watch_refusals` return `Unsupported`, so Ostra watches no decoy.
- Unix sockets do not exist, so the egress proxy cannot bind its socket.
- `scrub_startup_env`, `marked`, and `kill` do nothing.

The fix text for Windows says: "Run Ostra inside WSL 2 or in Docker to sandbox agent commands, because Ostra has no Windows sandbox yet and agent commands otherwise run with the full rights of your user." The text ends with the instruction to choose mode `off`.

### The default mode on Windows

`SandboxMode::default()` returns `auto` on Windows and `required` on Linux and macOS. The reason is stated in the code. A default of `required` would refuse every execution on Windows, because no backend exists. With `auto`, Ostra runs agent commands without a sandbox and shows a warning. The setup check reports `default_mode`, so the console shows `auto` and does not assume `required`.

A user on Windows can set the mode to one of these values:

- `auto`: run without a sandbox and warn. This is the default.
- `off`: run without a sandbox and do not warn.
- `required`: every execution fails with the "not available" error.

The page "Sandbox settings, modes, and failure cases" lists the effect of each mode on each caller. The warning appears as a log line, as text on stderr at server start, and as a `Status` delta for each execution.

## What exists on Windows instead of a sandbox

Three groups of code give some protection on Windows: the guards of the policy layer, the shell handling, and the process tree.

### Policy hardening

The policy layer has Windows-specific rules. The pages of the Policy engine topic explain them. In short:

- The guard `windows-path` refuses path forms that the guards do not compare: alternate data streams, reserved device names such as `CON` and `NUL`, UNC and device paths, drive-relative paths, and `..` right after a junction or symlink.
- The guards read Windows path forms and MSYS paths from Git Bash, for example `/c/Users/me`.
- Text of `PowerShell` and `Cmd` tool calls is scanned for protected paths. The permission layer never auto-allows these tools, because Ostra cannot parse them.

These rules reduce risk. They are not a kernel boundary, because a command can still read and write anything that the user can.

### Shells

`crates/ostra-core/src/shells.rs` chooses the shell for each tool.

| Tool | Windows program | Unix program |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bash | `bin\\bash.exe` of Git for Windows | `bash` from `PATH` |
| PowerShell | Windows PowerShell 5.1 at `System32\\WindowsPowerShell\\v1.0\\powershell.exe` | Not used |
| Cmd | `System32\\cmd.exe` under `%SystemRoot%`, default `C:\\Windows` | Not used |

Ostra finds Git Bash with `git --exec-path`, or in `%ProgramFiles%\\Git` or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\\Programs\\Git`. It does not use the first `bash` on `PATH`. That program is often `C:\\Windows\\System32\\bash.exe`, the WSL launcher, which runs the command in a Linux VM with a different view of the files. When Git Bash is missing, the Bash tool returns an error that starts with "Git Bash was not found." and tells the user to install Git for Windows and restart Ostra. The setup check shows the same text in `ShellStatus`.

### Process trees

`crates/ostra-core/src/proctree.rs` stops a child and everything that it starts as one unit. The type `Tree` holds the handle.

| Aspect | Unix | Windows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container | A process group. The child leads it (`process_group(0)`). | A Job Object with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` and no breakaway |
| `terminate` | `SIGTERM` to the group | Does nothing, because console programs have no such request outside their own console |
| `kill` | `SIGKILL` to the group | `TerminateJobObject` |
| `end` | Nothing to close | Closes the job handle, which kills what remains in it |

On Windows, a child must be in its job before it starts anything. Otherwise its first children escape the job. `prepare_tokio` and `prepare_std` set `CREATE_SUSPENDED | CREATE_NO_WINDOW`. `Tree::of_tokio` assigns the process to a new job and then resumes it with `NtResumeProcess`. `NtResumeProcess` resumes all threads that the kernel holds, and a thread snapshot taken right after creation can miss the new thread. When the assignment or the resume fails, Ostra resumes the process first and then terminates it. A process that never ran cannot finish terminating.

`Tree::adopt_running` serves a PTY child that Ostra did not create suspended. On Windows, processes that the child started before this call are not in the job.

The callers are the native Bash tool, the PowerShell and Cmd tools, the stdio MCP client, and the PTY of a harness CLI. A Bash call that times out or is cancelled calls `kill` on the tree. It also calls `kill` again when background processes keep the output pipe open, so nothing outlives the call.

### What happens when

- **The job cannot be created or assigned on Windows.** `of_tokio` returns an error, and the Bash tool returns "Cannot start bash".
- **A grandchild starts through WMI or out-of-process COM.** The job does not hold it. The probe rows for verify 11 show this case.
- **The server exits on Windows.** The job handle closes, and the OS kills the tree.

## The probe program

The folder `tests/windows-probes` holds a standalone crate named `winprobe`. It contains no Ostra code. The workspace excludes it (`exclude = ["tests/windows-probes"]` in the root `Cargo.toml`), so `cargo build --workspace` and `cargo test --workspace` never build it. The crate has its own `Cargo.lock`. It uses only `windows-sys` 0.61. The file `.cargo/config.toml` sets `-C target-feature=+crt-static`, so the one executable runs on a bare VM without the Visual C++ runtime.

Caution: run the probe only on a throwaway VM. The `setup` role creates local users, ACLs, and firewall rules, and changes the state of the machine.

The executable has these roles, chosen by the first argument:

| Role | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `setup` | Creates the local users `OstraProbeA` and `OstraProbeB`, a password file, and the ACL test tree under `C:\\ostra-probe`. |
| `run` | Spawns the confined probes, runs the host checks, and writes `results.md`. |
| `cleanup` | Removes the users, the profile folders, the firewall rules that start with `OstraProbe`, and the test tree. |
| `asuser <group> <out>` | Runs one group of checks as a probe user. The `run` role spawns it. |
| Helpers | `markself`, `medspawn`, `sleeper`, `openone`, `spinjob`, and `netfilter` serve the roles. |

An unknown role prints the role list and exits with status 2. The host role runs elevated, for example over SSH as the admin account.

The ACL test tree copies the layout that a Windows renderer would build. The repo root has an inheritable Modify grant for `OstraProbeA`. The `.git` folder has an inheritable deny of write and delete. `.git\\hooks` has its own deny. The repo root has a deny of `FILE_DELETE_CHILD`, so `.git` cannot be removed through its parent. A `secret` folder has a deny of read. Each finding has a verify number, a name, a status, an expected value, and an observed value.

## What the 54 probe rows show

The file `tests/windows-probes/results-full.md` records one run on Microsoft Windows Server 2025 Datacenter Evaluation, build 26100. The VM was headless and reached over SSH. The file has 54 rows:

| Status | Count | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PASS` | 43 | The assumption of the design held. |
| `FAIL` | 3 | A gap that a later phase must handle. |
| `INCONCLUSIVE` | 4 | The VM cannot decide the question. |
| `NEEDS_CLIENT` | 4 | The check needs a Windows 11 client or the antivirus machine. |

The rows group into 17 numbered checks. Each group answers one question of the design.

| Verify | Question | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Can Ostra start a program as another local user with `CreateProcessWithLogonW`, also from a medium-integrity caller? | `PASS`. The confined user holds only `SeChangeNotifyPrivilege` and `SeIncreaseWorkingSetPrivilege`. |
| 2 | Can Ostra start a child under a restricted primary token without `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege`? | `PASS` |
| 3 | Does a Job Object kill the child and a nested-job grandchild? | `PASS` |
| 4 | Can the sandbox user list the profile of the host user? Can it list `Program Files` and `Windows`? | `PASS`. The profile is denied and the system trees are readable. Per-user toolchains are `INCONCLUSIVE`, because none exist on the VM. |
| 5 | Do ACLs reproduce the rules for `.git` and secrets? | All 14 rows `PASS`. See the list below. |
| 6 | Do hard links bypass the ACLs? | All `PASS`. The ACL travels with the file. |
| 7 | Can a firewall rule limit the network of the sandbox user? | One `FAIL`, two `INCONCLUSIVE`, two `PASS`. See below. |
| 8 | Do processes of one sandbox user isolate each other? | Two `FAIL`. See below. |
| 9 | Does the sandbox user need a window station and a desktop? | `PASS` for the grant. Input isolation is `NEEDS_CLIENT`. |
| 10 | Can the sandbox user write its own `HKCU`? Can it write the `HKLM` Run key? | `PASS`. `HKCU` is writable and the Run key is denied. |
| 11 | Can the sandbox user escape through Task Scheduler, WMI, COM, or BITS? | `PASS` for each tested mechanism, with one caveat. See below. |
| 12 | Does the sandbox user hold credentials, and can it read the credentials of the host user? | `PASS`. Its own list is empty and the host profile is unreadable. |
| 13 | Does ConPTY work for each harness CLI? | `NEEDS_CLIENT`, because no harness CLI is installed. |
| 14 | Does Git Bash work as the sandbox user? | `NEEDS_CLIENT`, because Git for Windows is not installed. |
| 15 | Do process mitigation policies break `node`, `cargo`, `rustc`, `python`, `java`, or a harness? | `NEEDS_CLIENT` |
| 16 | How much time does a recursive ACE cost? | `PASS`. `icacls /t` granted a Modify ACE over 8,000 files in 40 dirs in 1,273 ms. |
| 17 | Does Defender or SmartScreen block the unsigned executable? | `PASS`. Neither blocked it. The antivirus of the user still needs a test. |

### ACL rows (verify 5)

The probe user writes a file inside the granted repo. It cannot write `.git\\hooks` through any of six spellings: the canonical path, a case-folded path, a trailing dot, a trailing space, an alternate data stream, and an 8.3 short name. It cannot write the protected `.git\\config`, but it can read it (26 bytes). It cannot read the hidden secret through the canonical or case-folded path. An alternate data stream of the secret does not exist, so it gives no bypass. It cannot rename `.git`, and `rmdir /s .git` fails. ACLs therefore reproduce the read-only, hidden, and rename-pin rules of the Unix backends.

### Network rows (verify 7)

- `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` stay reachable under a block-all rule. Windows Firewall does not filter loopback traffic. Both rows are `PASS` as observations.
- The check "restrict loopback to only the proxy port" is `FAIL`. Windows Firewall cannot do this, because it exempts loopback and own-IP traffic. The probe notes that a raw WFP filter is needed.
- A connection to the own LAN IP of the VM is `INCONCLUSIVE`. Windows treats its own addresses like loopback. A test against a remote host needs a second machine.
- DNS through the `Dnscache` service is `INCONCLUSIVE`. The service runs under another account, so a per-user filter does not see it. The VM has no resolver, so the probe did not run it live.

### Isolation rows (verify 8)

- A process of the sandbox user cannot open a process of the host user (`PASS`).
- Two processes of the same sandbox user can open each other (`FAIL`). The gap is confirmed.
- A per-execution restricting SID does not isolate same-user processes (`FAIL`). A restricting set that is open enough to start a process includes a SID that the DACL of the sibling also grants.
- A restricting set that would isolate the process cannot start it. The child dies at load with exit code `0xc0000142` (`PASS`, as a confirmation).

The probe concludes that isolation needs one user for each execution slot and distinct accounts across slots.

### Escape rows (verify 11)

A Task Scheduler task as the same user, a task as `SYSTEM`, and a BITS notify command did not escape. WMI `Win32_Process.Create` and out-of-process COM `Shell.Application` ran as the sandbox user through a service, outside the job. The ACLs and the network filter contain such a process, but a job kill misses it. The probe notes that the policy denylist must block these mechanisms. The row for `runas` is `INCONCLUSIVE`, because it needs a password prompt.

## What the results imply

The results file states the plan that the probe supports. It is not code in the repo:

- Local sandbox users and ACLs reproduce the read-only, hidden, and write-protected paths.
- A Job Object ends the process tree.
- A per-user network filter needs a raw WFP filter, because Windows Firewall cannot limit loopback.
- One user for each execution slot gives isolation between executions.
- The policy layer must deny WMI and COM process creation, because the job does not hold the new process.

The repo has no Windows backend, no ACL renderer, no user pool, and no WFP code.

### What happens when

- **A user runs Ostra on Windows with the default mode.** Agent commands run without a sandbox and the server shows a warning.
- **A user needs a sandbox on Windows.** Run Ostra inside WSL 2 or Docker, where the Linux backend applies. The check passes only when `bwrap` can create namespaces there.
- **A developer wants to extend the probe.** Add a check to `confined.rs` or `host.rs`, and give it a verify number and a `Status`. Build and run it on a throwaway VM, because the workspace commands skip it.

sections.title: Native tool catalog and shared behavior
sections.summary: Explains how `execute` dispatches a tool call, how canonical calls make the policy and the tool see one target, the rules of Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob, and WebFetch, why the names follow Claude Code, and the steps to add a tool.
sections.body:
## What the `ostra-tools` crate does and where it stops

A tool is a named function. A model calls it with a JSON input, and it returns text. The `ostra-tools` crate holds the code of every tool that the native executor gives to a model. The harness bridge reuses the Ostra-only part of the crate. Harness executors such as Claude Code use their own tools for Read, Write, and Bash.

Each executor must run the same actions: read a file, run a command, fetch a URL. One crate gives all executors the same behavior, and the policy engine can predict what a call does. The crate has one entry point, `execute`. It also has `canonical_call`, which makes the policy and the tool see the same target.

The crate checks no permission. The header of [`crates/ostra-tools/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/lib.rs) says that the policy layer runs before `execute`. A call that reaches `execute` already passed the guards, and the user already answered any approval. The page "Two layers and the guard catalog" lists the checks.

## Tool catalog

The enum `Capability` has 17 values. An agent definition lists the capabilities that the agent has. The function `definitions(capabilities)` turns that list into tool definitions in declaration order and removes duplicates. The page "Skill, Report, Document, Memory, project, coordination, and MCP tools" covers the Ostra-only tools. The page "The eight code tools for agents" covers the `Code*` tools.

| Tool | Capability | Handler | Input (a trailing `?` marks an optional field) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Read` | `Read` | `fs::read` | `file_path`, `offset?`, `limit?` |
| `Write` | `Write` | `fs::write` | `file_path`, `content` |
| `Edit` | `Edit` | `fs::edit` | `file_path`, `old_string`, `new_string`, `replace_all?` |
| `Bash` | `Shell` | `bash::run` | `command`, `timeout?`, `description?` |
| `PowerShell`, `Cmd` | `Shell` on Windows only | `winshell::run` | same as `Bash` |
| `Grep` | `SearchText` | `search::grep` | `pattern`, `path?`, `glob?`, `type?`, `output_mode?`, `-i?`, `-n?`, `-A?`, `-B?`, `-C?`, `head_limit?`, `multiline?` |
| `Glob` | `Glob` | `search::glob` | `pattern`, `path?` |
| `Skill` | `Skill` | `misc::skill` | `name?`, `path?` |
| `WebSearch` | `WebSearch` | none | none |
| `WebFetch` | `WebFetch` | `web::fetch` | `url`, `prompt?` |
| `Report` | `Report` | `misc::report` | `content`, `reason?` |
| `Document` | `Document` | `doc::document` | `path`, `document?`, `update?`, `remove?` |
| `Memory` | `Memory` | `misc::memory` | `area`, `lesson`, `source?` |
| `MemoryRecall` | `MemoryRecall` | `misc::memory_recall` | `query`, `area?`, `limit?` |
| `DocsSearch` | `DocsSearch` | `misc::docs_search` | `query`, `project?`, `limit?` |
| `CodeOutline`, `CodeFind`, `CodeCallers`, `CodeCallees`, `CodeImplementations`, `CodeNeighbors`, `CodeImpact`, `CodeMap` | `Code` | `code::run` | see the code tools page |
| `ProjectList`, `ProjectCreate` | `ManageProjects` | `manage::run` | see the Ostra-only tools page |
| `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply` | `Coordinate` | `coord::run` | see the Ostra-only tools page |
| `mcp__<server>__<tool>` | none, set by workspace settings | `mcp::run` | set by the external server |

These facts about the catalog help when you read the code:

- `WebSearch` has no local handler. The function `wants_web_search` tells the loop to enable the search tool of the model provider. If a `WebSearch` call arrives, `execute` returns the error `WebSearch runs on the model provider's side and has no local implementation.`
- `Document` has no entry in `definitions`, because its schema depends on the agent. Use `document_tool_definition(agent)`. It returns a definition only for the explore, generate-spec, and plan agents.
- On Windows the `Shell` capability grants `Bash`, `PowerShell`, and `Cmd`. On Linux and macOS it grants `Bash`.
- The native loop lists `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebFetch`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, `Skill`, and the `Code*` tools in `is_concurrent`. Calls to these read-only tools can run at the same time in one turn.

## How `execute` runs one call

The function `execute(env, call_id, call, live, cancel)` is the only way to run a tool. The native loop calls it. The harness bridge calls it for the Ostra-only tools.

### Dispatch of one call

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[execute starts a timer] --> B[input_schema for the tool and agent]
    B --> C[coerce_json_strings on the input]
    C --> D{shell tool?}
    D -- yes --> E[handler runs and watches the cancel token]
    D -- no --> F[race the handler against cancel]
    F -- cancel first --> G[error Cancelled]
    F -- handler first --> H[handler output]
    E --> I[set duration_ms]
    G --> I
    H --> I
```

The steps run in this order:

1. `execute` starts a timer.
2. It gets the input schema with `input_schema(tool, agent)`. For `Document`, the schema depends on the agent. For other tools, `input_schema` searches `definitions(&EVERY)`.
3. It calls `coerce_json_strings` from `ostra_core::args`. This function parses an argument that the schema does not type as a string but that arrived as a string of JSON object or array text. A handler that expects an array, such as `requirements` or `paths`, would otherwise see a string.
4. It matches the tool name. Exact names come first. Then the predicates `is_code_tool`, `is_manage_tool`, `is_coord_tool`, and `is_gateway_tool` run in that order. Then `WebSearch` matches. Any other name gives the error `Unknown tool` with the name.
5. It races the handler against the cancel token. If the cancel token wins, the result is the error `Cancelled.` The shell tools are the exception. They drain their own output and handle cancellation inside, so the partial output stays in the result.
6. It writes `duration_ms` into the result.

### What happens when

- **A required field is missing:** the helper `required` returns ``Missing required parameter `key`.`` with the field name.
- **A number arrives as a float:** `u64_arg` accepts integers and floating point numbers. A negative float becomes 0.
- **A server-backed handle is missing:** the tool returns its own error text. The table in the next section lists the texts.
- **A tool name contains `__` and starts with `mcp__`:** `is_gateway_tool` is true, and `mcp::run` handles it. Ostra's own tools never contain `__`.
- **The native loop cancels a non-shell tool:** the result is `Cancelled.` and `is_error` is true.

## The environment of one execution

One `ToolEnv` serves one execution. It holds state that must live between calls. The type `ToolEnvConfig` holds the fixed inputs.

| Field | Holds | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `config` | `agent`, `repo_root`, `workspace_root`, `session_dir`, `report_file`, `memory_db`, `memory_source`, `skill_resolver`, and four handles | all tools |
| `cwd` | the working directory of the shell, which starts at `repo_root` | `Bash`, path resolution |
| `read_files` | the folded paths that this execution read | `Write`, `Edit` |
| `http` | the HTTP client | `WebFetch` |
| `private_hosts` | hosts that `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` allow rules name exactly | `WebFetch` |
| `scrub_env` | variable names that Ostra removes from every child process | `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Cmd` |
| `sandbox` | the sandbox backend and profile, or `None` for no sandbox | `Bash` |

`ToolEnv::new` reads the credential variable names from `config.toml` when it starts. The builder methods `with_scrub_env`, `with_sandbox`, and `with_private_hosts` add the rest. The executor uses `with_scrub_env` to add the MCP secrets of the workspace.

The index, the engine, the workspace, and the MCP connections live in the server. The tools crate cannot depend on the server. A tool that needs server state takes an optional trait object in `ToolEnvConfig`. The server implements the trait and binds the app after it builds the app, because executors exist before the app (see `code_tools.bind(&app)` in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`).

| Handle | Trait | Error text when the handle is `None` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | `CodeNav` | `Code navigation is not available in this run. Use Grep, Glob, and Read instead.` |
| `manage` | `Manage` | `<tool> is not available to this run, because its agent does not manage projects.` |
| `coord` | `Coordinate` | `<tool> is not available to this run, because its agent does not coordinate with other subagents.` |
| `mcp` | `McpTools` | `Unknown tool` with the name |

## Canonical calls

A model sends `file_path: x.toml`. The policy must decide if the write is allowed. The tool resolves the path against the working directory of the shell. If the policy resolved the path against another directory, the policy would check one file and the tool would write another file.

The method `ToolEnv::canonical_call` removes this gap. Callers check the policy on the canonical call and then run the same canonical call. Both see one target.

| Tool | Field that changes | New value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Read`, `Write`, `Edit` | `file_path` | absolute path from `resolve` |
| `Grep`, `Glob`, `Skill`, `Document` | `path`, when not empty | absolute path from `resolve` |
| `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Cmd` | `cwd` | the current shell directory, even if the model sent another `cwd` |
| `WebFetch` | `url` | the parsed form of the URL |
| every other tool | none | the call is unchanged |

The method `resolve` expands a leading `~/` to the home folder and joins a relative path to the shell directory. Under bubblewrap, `/tmp` inside the sandbox is the scratch directory of the execution, so `sandbox_to_host` maps it to the host path.

The `WebFetch` rule has a test. The URL `https://evil.example\@docs.rs/x` parses with the host `evil.example`. The policy then sees the host that the HTTP client will contact. A missing `path` for `Grep` stays missing, and the tool uses the shell directory.

## Output rules shared by all tools

Every handler returns a `ToolOutput`.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `text` | the text that the model reads |
| `is_error` | true when the call failed. The text then says how to fix the call. |
| `exit_code` | set by `Bash` and the Windows shells |
| `duration_ms` | set by `execute` |
| `diff` | the unified diff of a `Write` or `Edit`, for the Activity view |
| `end` | a `RunEnd` from a coordination call: `Continue`, `Wait`, or `Finish` |

Error texts name the fix. The test `descriptions_follow_writing_rules` in `defs.rs` rejects an em dash in a tool description.

Three helpers in `crates/ostra-tools/src/text.rs` cut text. All three cut on a character boundary.

| Helper | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `truncate_middle(s, max)` | keeps the first and last `max / 2` bytes and writes `... [N characters truncated] ...` between them |
| `truncate_end(s, max)` | keeps the first `max` bytes and writes `... [truncated: N more characters]` |
| `unified_diff(path, old, new)` | returns `None` when the text is equal, else a diff with 3 lines of context cut at 50,000 bytes |

The limits of all tools count bytes, although some messages say characters.

## Read, Write, and Edit

These tools live in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/fs.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/fs.rs). They share one rule: the execution must read an existing file before it changes the file. The reason is that the model must not overwrite content that it has not seen. The set `read_files` holds the proof. The tools `Read`, `Write`, `Edit` (on create), `Skill`, `Report`, and `Document` add a path to the set.

### Read

`Read` takes `file_path` (required), `offset`, and `limit`. A relative path resolves against the shell directory. Each output line has a line number padded to 6 characters, a tab, and the text. The handler removes a trailing carriage return.

| Input or limit | Value | Constant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `offset` | default 1, minimum 1 | none |
| `limit` | default 2000 lines, minimum 1 | `DEFAULT_LINES` |
| line length | 2000 bytes, then `... [line truncated]` | `MAX_LINE_CHARS` |
| file size | 50 MiB | `MAX_READ_BYTES` |

What happens when:

- **The path does not exist:** the error is `File does not exist: <path>`.
- **The path is a directory:** the error tells the model to use `Glob` or `ls`.
- **The file is larger than 50 MiB:** the error tells the model to use `head`, `tail`, or `sed -n`.
- **The first 8192 bytes hold a NUL byte or invalid UTF-8:** the result says that the file is binary. The file still counts as read.
- **The file is empty:** the result says that the file exists and is empty.
- **`offset` is past the last line:** the result says how many lines the file has.
- **The view is partial:** the result ends with the note `(Showing lines A to B of N. Use offset and limit to read other lines.)`. The note also appears when `offset` is greater than 1.

### Write

`Write` takes `file_path` and `content`. It replaces the whole file and creates the parent folders.

- **The file exists and the execution did not read it:** the call fails with an error that tells the model to read the file first.
- **The path is a directory:** the call fails.
- **The write succeeds:** the file counts as read. The text is `File created successfully at: <path>` or `The file <path> has been updated.` The result carries the diff.

### Edit

`Edit` takes `file_path`, `old_string`, `new_string`, and `replace_all` (default false).

- **The strings are equal:** the call fails.
- **The file does not exist and `old_string` is empty:** the tool creates the file with `new_string`.
- **The file does not exist and `old_string` is not empty:** the error is `File does not exist`.
- **The file exists and the execution did not read it:** the call fails.
- **The file exists and `old_string` is empty:** the call fails.
- **No match:** the error tells the model to read the file again and copy the current text.
- **More than one match and `replace_all` is false:** the error gives the count.
- **`replace_all` is true and the count is greater than 1:** the tool replaces every match and says `All N matches were replaced.`
- **One replacement:** the result shows a numbered snippet with 4 lines of context on each side of the change.

## Bash

`Bash` takes `command` (required), `timeout` in milliseconds, and `description`. An empty command returns `The command is empty.` The timeout defaults to `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS` (120,000) and is clamped to the range 1 to `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS` (600,000).

The shell directory must persist between calls, and a `cd` must carry over. The tool uses a fixed script:

```rust
const SCRIPT: &str = r#"exec 2>&1
__ostra_cmd=$OSTRA_CMD
__ostra_pwd=$OSTRA_PWD_FILE
cd -- "$OSTRA_CWD" || exit 1
unset OSTRA_CMD OSTRA_PWD_FILE OSTRA_CWD
trap 'pwd -P > "$__ostra_pwd" 2>/dev/null' EXIT
eval "$__ostra_cmd"
"#;
```

The command travels in the variable `OSTRA_CMD`, so no extra layer of quoting changes it. The script runs the command with `eval` in the same shell. The `EXIT` trap writes the final directory to a temporary file `ostra-pwd-<uuid>`. After the call, that directory becomes the shell directory if it exists. On Windows the trap uses `pwd -W`.

The tool runs these steps:

1. Reset the shell directory to `repo_root` if the saved directory no longer exists.
2. Build the process. With a sandbox, the profile makes the pwd file writable and wraps `bash`. If that fails, the error is `Cannot prepare the sandbox: <reason>`.
3. Remove the credential variables from `scrub_env`, every `OSTRA_*` variable, and `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF`. Apply `ostra_core::git::agent_env()`. Set `GIT_PAGER=cat` and `PAGER=cat`. Set stdin to null.
4. Read the output while it waits for exit, the timeout, or cancellation. Each chunk goes to the `live` callback. The callback holds back an incomplete UTF-8 sequence.
5. If the process did not exit, kill the whole process tree and wait at most `KILL_WAIT` (5 seconds).
6. Drain the pipes. If no chunk arrives within `DRAIN_GRACE` (300 ms) and the pipes stay open, a background process holds them. The tool then kills the tree.

The tool kills the tree because a server or a watcher that the command started must not outlive the call.

| Result | Text |
| --- | --- |
| exit code 0 | the output, `exit_code` 0 |
| exit code N | the output, then `Exit code: N`, with `is_error` true |
| killed by a signal | the output, then `The command was terminated by a signal.` |
| timeout | `The command timed out after N ms and was stopped. Output so far:` and the output |
| cancellation | `The command was cancelled. Output so far:` and the output |
| no output | `(no output)` |

The tool keeps the first 128 KiB and the last 128 KiB of output (`CAPTURE_HALF`) and writes `... [N bytes dropped] ...` between them. It then cuts the text to `MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS` (30,000 bytes) with `truncate_middle`.

### PowerShell and Cmd on Windows

`PowerShell` and `Cmd` exist only on Windows. They have the same input, timeout range, 30,000-byte output cut, 300 ms drain, variable scrubbing, and process-tree kill. The policy parser reads Bash commands with tree-sitter-bash. It cannot read these shells. The policy therefore never allows them without asking, always applies the permission of the mode, and refuses them when the raw text names Ostra's own state or a credential path.

## Grep and Glob

Both tools live in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/search.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/search.rs) and use the `ignore` walker. The walker searches hidden files. It honors `.gitignore`, `.git/info/exclude`, the global gitignore, and parent ignore files, even if the folder is not a git repository. It skips the `.git` folder. A `SecretFilter` hides the credential stores from `ostra_core::paths::secret_paths` and the Ostra data folder, except its `assets` folder. A search from a parent folder therefore cannot read them.

### Grep

`Grep` requires `pattern`, a Rust regular expression. The anchors `^` and `$` match at each line. The flag `multiline` also lets `.` match a newline and lets a match span lines. The input `path` defaults to the shell directory and can name a file.

| Input | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `glob` | split at commas or spaces outside braces, so `{a,b}` stays one glob |
| `type` | a ripgrep type. Aliases include `rs`, `python`, `golang`, `javascript`, `typescript`, `kt`, `rb`, `md`, `yml`, `c++`, and `sh`. |
| `output_mode` | `files_with_matches` (default, newest file first, header `Found N file(s)`), `content`, or `count` |
| `-n` | line numbers in `content` mode, default true |
| `-A`, `-B`, `-C` | context lines in `content` mode only. `-C` fills `-A` and `-B` when they are absent. |
| `head_limit` | cuts files, rows, or lines. The value 0 means no limit. |

In `content` mode a match line is `path:line:text` and a context line is `path-line-text`. A `--` line separates groups that are not adjacent. A line longer than 500 bytes ends with `...`. The whole output is cut with `truncate_end` at `MAX_GREP_OUTPUT` (30,000 bytes). When `head_limit` cuts `content` output, the result ends with a note that names the limit.

What happens when:

- **Nothing matches:** the result is `No files found` or `No matches found`.
- **The regex is invalid:** the error is `Invalid regex` with the reason.
- **`output_mode` is unknown:** the error lists the three valid values.
- **A file holds a NUL byte:** the search of that file stops at the NUL byte.
- **The path does not exist:** the error is `Path does not exist`.

### Glob

`Glob` requires `pattern`. The symbol `*` does not cross `/`, and `**` does. The tool matches the path relative to the search folder, with forward slashes. The input `path` must be a folder, or the error is `Not a directory`. Results come newest first and the list has at most `MAX_GLOB_RESULTS` (100) paths. If more files match, the last line says `(Results are truncated: showing 100 of N. Use a more specific path or pattern.)`.

## WebFetch

`WebFetch` takes `url` (required) and `prompt`. It accepts only `http` and `https` URLs. The HTTP client sends the header `Accept: text/html, text/markdown, text/plain, application/json;q=0.9, */*;q=0.5` and the user agent `ostra/<version>`. The client timeout is 20 seconds. The client uses no proxy, because a proxy resolves names itself and skips the address check.

The tool refuses private targets for these reasons:

- The `PublicResolver` returns only public addresses. A name cannot reach this machine or the local network, even if its DNS answer changes between the check and the connection.
- A URL with a private IP literal is refused before the connection.
- Both refusals tell the user to add the allow rule `WebFetch(domain:<host>)`. A host that such a rule names exactly can resolve to a private address.

A redirect is followed only when the host, the port, and the scheme (`http` or `https`) stay the same, up to `MAX_REDIRECTS` (10). The policy checked only the first URL. A redirect to another host therefore returns the new URL to the model, and the model must fetch it with a new call.

The tool reads at most `MAX_BODY_BYTES` (5 MiB) of the body. HTML is converted to markdown with `htmd`. A body counts as HTML when the content type contains `html`, or when the type is empty and the first 512 characters contain `<html` or `<!doctype html`. Other types return as text when the content type is empty, starts with `text/`, or contains `json`, `xml`, `javascript`, `yaml`, or `markdown`, and the first 8192 bytes hold no NUL byte. Other types return the error `The response is <type>, which is not text, so it cannot be shown.` The text is cut at `MAX_TEXT_CHARS` (100,000 bytes).

The output has an optional line `Prompt: <prompt>`, a line `Redirected to: <url>` when the final URL differs, and then `Content of <url> (HTTP <status>):` with the text. A status outside 200 to 299 returns the same content with `is_error` true.

## Why the names follow Claude Code

The header of `lib.rs` states the reason: names and input shapes follow Claude Code's tools, because the agent prompts are tuned to them. The comments in `crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs` and `assets/tool-mapping.toml` repeat the rule. A prompt that names `Read` and `file_path` works on the native executor without change.

The rule has these visible effects:

- The native tools `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Skill`, `WebSearch`, and `WebFetch` use the Claude Code argument names, such as `file_path`, `old_string`, `replace_all`, `output_mode`, `-i`, `head_limit`, and `multiline`.
- Ostra-only tools use PascalCase native names (`Report`, `MemoryRecall`, `CodeCallers`, `ProjectCreate`, `SubagentAsk`) and snake_case MCP names (`report`, `memory_recall`, `code_callers`, `project_create`, `subagent_ask`).
- External MCP tools use the Claude Code spelling `mcp__<server>__<tool>` inside Ostra.
- `assets/tool-mapping.toml` maps each capability to one tool name for each executor table: `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. The `native` and `claude` tables use Claude Code names. The `codex`, `grok`, and `agy` tables use their own names, such as `exec_command`, `read_file`, and `view_file`.
- The placeholders `{op}`, `{Op}`, and `{agent}` fill in the operation or the agent name. The key `code` with `Code{Op}` gives `CodeCallers` for the operation `callers`.
- A value that is not a bare tool name is prose, and the prompt renders it as written.
- `crates/ostra-agents/src/mapping.rs` loads the file once. An invalid file makes the program panic at start.

The page "Embedded assets and prompt rendering" explains how prompts use these names.

## Steps to add a tool

Follow these steps in order. A tool name appears in many places, and a missing place causes a compile error or a silent gap.

1. Add a `Capability` variant and a `native_tool()` arm in `crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`.
2. For a family of tools, add a const table of `(op, NativeName)` pairs and an `is_*_tool` predicate. Copy `CODE_TOOLS`, `PROJECT_TOOLS`, or `COORD_TOOLS`.
3. In `crates/ostra-tools/src/defs.rs`, add the description constant, a `*_def()` function, and an arm in `definitions()`.
4. Add the capability to `EVERY` and change the array length. `input_schema` reads `EVERY` to coerce arguments.
5. Write the handler in its own module and add an arm in `execute()` in `crates/ostra-tools/src/lib.rs`.
6. If the tool needs server state, add an optional trait handle to `ToolEnvConfig`. Return a tool error when the handle is `None`.
7. Implement the trait in `ostra-server` and bind it in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`.
8. For harness executors, add the MCP name to `MCP_TOOLS` in `crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`.
9. Add the key to `capability_key` and `TOKENS` in `crates/ostra-agents/src/mapping.rs`. Add a `[capabilities.<key>]` table in `assets/tool-mapping.toml` with one value for each executor table.
10. List the variant in the exhaustive `match` of `agy_tools` in `crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/setup.rs`. The crate does not compile without it.
11. Add the capability to the agent definitions that use the tool.
12. Check how the policy engine classifies the new tool name, because the policy runs before `execute`.
13. Extend the tests at the end of `defs.rs`.

Do not give a tool a name that contains `__`. The function `is_gateway_bare` treats such a name as an external MCP tool, and `execute` sends it to `mcp::run`.
