sections.title: Skill, Report, Document, Memory, project, coordination, and MCP tools
sections.summary: Explains the inputs, limits, and error cases of the Ostra-only tools, the ProjectCreate flow with its approval and engine gate, the coordination tool inputs, and the naming and validation of external MCP tools.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra has its own tools

A model that only reads and writes files cannot do several jobs that Ostra needs. It cannot hand a report to the next stage, record a lesson, search the documentation books, ask another agent, add a project, or call an external service. The Ostra-only tools do these jobs. Their code is in [`crates/ostra-tools/src`](crates/ostra-tools/src). The page "Native tool catalog and shared behavior" explains the dispatcher that runs them.

A native execution reaches these tools through `execute`. A harness execution reaches them through Ostra's own MCP server, named `ostra`. The table `MCP_TOOLS` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs) lists the tools that this server offers. The bridge checks the policy, makes the call canonical, and then calls the same `execute`.

| Native name | Name on the `ostra` MCP server | Name that Claude Code sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Report` | `report` | `mcp__ostra__report` |
| `Document` | `document` | `mcp__ostra__document` |
| `Memory` | `memory` | `mcp__ostra__memory` |
| `MemoryRecall` | `memory_recall` | `mcp__ostra__memory_recall` |
| `DocsSearch` | `docs_search` | `mcp__ostra__docs_search` |
| `CodeOutline`, `CodeFind`, `CodeCallers`, `CodeCallees`, `CodeImplementations`, `CodeNeighbors`, `CodeImpact`, `CodeMap` | `code_outline`, `code_find`, `code_callers`, `code_callees`, `code_implementations`, `code_neighbors`, `code_impact`, `code_map` | `mcp__ostra__code_<op>` |
| `ProjectList`, `ProjectCreate` | `project_list`, `project_create` | `mcp__ostra__project_list`, `mcp__ostra__project_create` |
| `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply` | `subagent_list`, `subagent_ask`, `subagent_reply` | `mcp__ostra__subagent_<op>` |

`Skill` has no MCP tool. A harness reads the `SKILL.md` file with its own read tool. The method `mcp_tools` in `bridge.rs` offers the management tools only to an execution that has a `manage` handle. It offers the coordination tools only to an execution that has a `coord` handle. It offers `Document` only to the agents that have a document schema.

## Skill

`Skill` loads a `SKILL.md` file, a set of instructions for a kind of task. It takes `name` or `path`.

- **`path` is given:** the tool reads that file. If it cannot, the error is `No skill file at <path>.`
- **`name` is given:** the tool removes a leading `ostra:`. A name that contains `/` or `..` is refused, and the error tells the model to pass a `path`.
- **Lookup order for a name:** first the project skill folders (`.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, then the older `.ostra/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`), then a custom skill among the workspace artifacts, then a skill that Ostra ships (`skill_resolver`).
- **No skill is found:** the error lists the project paths that the tool tried and tells the model not to guess a path.
- **Neither field is given:** the error asks for the skill `name` or the `path`.

A loaded project skill or artifact skill counts as read. The result starts with `Skill loaded from <path>. Follow its instructions for this task.`

## Report

`Report` takes `content` (required) and `reason`. It writes the complete report to the `Report file:` path that Ostra fixed for the run (`ToolEnvConfig::report_file`). The model does not choose the path, because later stages must find the report.

- **The run has no `Report file:`:** the error says that there is nothing for `Report` to write.
- **The write succeeds:** the reply is `Report written to <path> (N bytes).`
- **`reason`:** the handler ignores it. The lesson gate in the policy engine reads it. The gate refuses a report when a failure-to-recovery lesson is not recorded yet, unless the model gives `reason`. The page "Containment signals, build streak, and lesson gate" explains the gate.

## Document

`Document` writes a typed research document, spec, or plan. Ostra renders the markdown that the next stage reads from the typed JSON. The tool takes `path` (required), `document`, `update`, and `remove`.

Only three agents can use it. The function `DocKind::for_agent` maps `explore` to a research document, `generate-spec` to a spec, and `plan` to a plan. Any other agent gets the error `Only explore, generate-spec, and plan write documents.`

The tool checks the file name before it writes:

| Kind | Required file name prefix |
| --- | --- |
| research document | `ostra-research-` |
| spec | `ostra-spec-` |
| plan | `ostra-plan-` |

The name must end in `.md`. A plan file name cannot contain `-phase-`, because Ostra writes the phase files itself. The file must sit directly in the session folder. The tool compares both folders with `fold`, because a resolved path and a stored path can differ on Windows in prefix, case, and separators.

| Input | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `document` | replaces the whole stored document |
| `update` | merges into the stored JSON. Each named top-level field replaces the stored field, except a list whose items have an `id`. The tool merges such a list by `id`. |
| `remove` | drops list items by id. With nothing stored, the error says that there is nothing to remove. |
| `document` with `update` or `remove` | error: send either `document` or `update` with `remove` |

If the document does not match its schema, the tool writes nothing and the error names the field. After a write, the reply lists the counts, the files that the tool wrote (the markdown and a `.json` beside it), and the check issues. The model must fix every error with an `update`, because the submit call is refused while an error remains. The model must not write these files with `Write`, `Edit`, or the shell. The policy refuses that, because the markdown comes from the document.

## Memory and MemoryRecall

`Memory` records a durable lesson in the memory store of the project (`ToolEnvConfig::memory_db`). It takes `area`, `lesson`, and `source`. The tool trims all three. An empty `area` or `lesson` is an error. The `source` defaults to `ToolEnvConfig::memory_source`, for example `implementer x_123`. The same `area` and `lesson` update the stored entry in place. The reply is `Recorded the lesson under <area>. The store now holds N lessons.`

`MemoryRecall` takes `query` (required), `area`, and `limit`. The `limit` defaults to `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT` (8) and is clamped to the range 1 to `MAX_RECALL_LIMIT` (50). Each result line has the form `N. [area] lesson (source: ..., date)`. With no match the reply is `No lessons recorded for this query.` Both tools run the SQLite work in `spawn_blocking`. A store error returns `Recording the lesson failed` or `Recall failed` with the reason.

## DocsSearch

`DocsSearch` searches the documentation books of the workspace. It takes `query` (required), `project`, and `limit`. The `limit` defaults to 5 and is clamped to the range 1 to 15 (`book_search::DEFAULT_LIMIT` and `MAX_LIMIT`).

- **The run has no workspace:** the reply tells the model to read the code.
- **The workspace has no books:** the reply is `This workspace has no documentation books yet.`
- **No section matches:** the reply tells the model to try other names or to read the code.
- **Sections match:** the reply is a numbered list with the matching passages and the path of each section file.

The page "Searching books: ranking and the DocsSearch tool" explains the ranking.

## ProjectList and ProjectCreate

`ProjectList` takes no input. It returns the workspace root and one line for each project: the key, the folder, the stack, the init status (`initialized`, `not initialized`, `initializing`, or `folder missing`), and `in this session's scope` when it applies. With no projects it returns `No projects yet.`

`ProjectCreate` makes a new empty project when a request needs a codebase that no project holds.

| Input | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `key` | required. Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes, starting with a letter or digit. |
| `stack` | required. A stack name as the Add project dialog accepts it. |
| `purpose` | required. At most `MAX_PURPOSE_CHARS` (800) characters. The user approves the project from it. |
| `requirements` | required. 1 to `MAX_REQUIREMENTS` (20) entries of at most `MAX_REQUIREMENT_CHARS` (400) characters. Ostra trims entries and drops empty ones. |
| `folder` | optional. Relative to the workspace root, with no `..`. Defaults to the key. |
| `git_init` | optional. Defaults to true. |

The function `ProjectCreateInput::parse` checks the input that needs no workspace state. A malformed call fails before Ostra asks the user. Each error names the fix.

### Flow of one ProjectCreate call

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant Policy
    participant User
    participant ExecManage
    participant Engine
    participant Workspace
    participant Git
    Agent->>Policy: ProjectCreate call
    Policy->>Policy: check_manage guard
    Policy->>User: approval card with ask_reason
    User-->>Policy: allow
    Policy->>ExecManage: call ProjectCreate
    ExecManage->>Engine: project_creation_refusal
    ExecManage->>Workspace: create_target
    ExecManage->>Git: claim folder, git init
    ExecManage->>Workspace: import_project
    ExecManage->>Engine: add_created_project
    Engine-->>Agent: interrupt ProjectCreated
```

1. **The guard `check_manage`** (Rule O2, in `crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs`) denies the call unless the agent manages projects, the run is the implementer of a phase that the approved plan puts in a new project, and the session exists. It parses the input. It denies a call whose `key` differs from the key of the phase project.
2. **The approval** (Rule O1, in `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs`): the user answers every call that changes Ostra. This holds in every permission mode and whatever the allow rules say. A deny rule still refuses the call. In plan mode the policy uses the default of the mode. YOLO answers the ask. The card shows `ask_reason`, which is cut to 250 characters.
3. **The engine gate** `project_creation_refusal` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` returns the first failing reason from this list:
    - the session is not a pipeline session
    - the session ended
    - the run that asked has ended
    - the project key is already in the session
    - the approved plan does not name the key as a new project
    - the phase of the run is not in that project
4. **The folder check** `create_target` in `crates/ostra-workspace/src/projects.rs` applies the key and stack rules of the Add project dialog. The folder must lie inside the workspace root and cannot be the root. A symlinked parent that leaves the root is refused. The folder must be new or empty. It cannot be inside the `.ostra` folder, and it cannot be inside or around another project.
5. **The folder claim** `git::claim` locks the folder. If another git operation holds it, the error is `Another git operation holds this folder. Try again.`
6. **The create step** makes the folder. If `git_init` is true, it runs `git init --quiet` with the timeout `QUICK_TIMEOUT` (30 seconds). If git fails, Ostra clears the folder and the error is `git init failed, so nothing was created`.
7. **The import step** `import_project` adds the project entry to the workspace settings. If it fails, Ostra clears the folder.
8. **The session step** `add_created_project` checks the gate again, makes the session folder of the project, and appends the event `ProjectCreated`. It then interrupts the run with `Interrupt::ProjectCreated` (Rule O4). The phase starts again after Ostra initializes the new project, and no phase runs in it before that.

The reply says that the project is in the scope of the session and that its folder is empty. It tells the agent to tag the deliverables with the project key and to write a first deliverable that creates the skeleton: manifest, entry point, and build command.

### What happens when

- **The user denies the call:** the tool description tells the agent to put the work in a project that is already in scope and to say so in its document.
- **The tool runs without a `manage` handle:** the error is `ProjectCreate is not available to this run, because its agent does not manage projects.`
- **The workspace is not open:** the error is `This run's workspace is not open in Ostra.`
- **The server shuts down:** the error is `The Ostra server is shutting down.`
- **The session cannot take the project after the folder exists:** the error says that Ostra created the project but it could not join the session.

## Coordination tools

The coordination tools let one subagent ask another. The page "Agent coordination: ask, reply, and pair loops" explains the loops. This section lists the inputs and the checks.

| Tool | Input | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SubagentList` | none | lists the own subagent ID and each subagent with ID, agent, label, status, what it waits on, and its report |
| `SubagentAsk` | `message` (required), `agent`, `subagent_id`, `project` | exactly one of `agent` and `subagent_id` |
| `SubagentReply` | `message` (required) | answers the question that woke this run |

`AskInput::parse` and `ReplyInput::parse` in `crates/ostra-core/src/coord.rs` trim the fields. The `message` must not be empty and has at most `MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS` (8000) characters. The error tells the model to put longer text in a file and name the path. The `agent` value must be in `HELPER_AGENTS`, which holds only `explore`.

The engine in `crates/ostra-engine/src/coord.rs` refuses a `SubagentAsk` in these cases:

- The run is a consult run. The error tells the model to use `SubagentReply`.
- The run owes an answer. It must call `SubagentReply` first.
- The session already has `MAX_SESSION_ASKS` (24) asks.
- A helper tries to start a helper.
- The run already started `MAX_HELPERS_PER_RUN` (3) helpers.
- The `project` key is not in the scope of the session.
- The `subagent_id` is unknown, or it is the ID of the asking subagent.

The constant `MAX_CONVERSATION_RUNS` (6) limits the runs of one conversation before a pair loop starts fresh. The handle returns a `CoordReply` with `text` and `end`. The `end` value makes the run continue, wait, or finish.

## External MCP tools

A workspace can list external MCP servers in its settings. Their tools reach the agent as external MCP tools. The page "External MCP client, OAuth, and Web Push" covers the connection and the sign-in. This section covers the names and the save-time checks.

### Names

A tool `create_issue` of the server `github` has the bare name `github__create_issue`. Three forms exist:

| Form | Example | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bare name | `github__create_issue` | the `ostra` MCP server |
| canonical name | `mcp__github__create_issue` | the native loop, the policy, and permission rules |
| harness name | `mcp__ostra__github__create_issue` | a harness CLI |

The function `is_gateway_tool` is true for a name that starts with `mcp__` and has a `__` after that prefix. A harness-native MCP call arrives as `Other:mcp__...` and does not count. Ostra's own tool names never contain `__`.

The bare name follows `bare_name(server, tool)`:

```rust
let plain = format!("{server}{SEPARATOR}{tool}");
let clean = tool.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || c == '_' || c == '-');
if clean && plain.len() <= MAX_BARE_NAME {
    return plain;
}
let hash = format!("{:08x}", fnv1a(tool.as_bytes()) as u32);
```

If the tool name has other characters, or the plain name is longer than `MAX_BARE_NAME` (52), the name becomes `server__<sanitized>_<hash>`. Other characters turn into `_`. The readable part is cut to fit. The hash is 8 hexadecimal digits of the FNV-1a hash of the original tool name. The hash keeps two tools from sharing one name. The limit 52 exists because harnesses add the prefix `mcp__ostra__` (12 characters) and providers cap tool names at 64 characters.

### Save-time checks

The function `mcp::validate` checks `mcp_servers` when the user saves settings. Each failure gives an issue with a path such as `mcp_servers[1].name`.

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | lowercase letters, digits, and single dashes, starting with a letter, at most `MAX_SERVER_NAME` (24) characters. The name is unique. The name `ostra` is reserved. |
| `command` and `url` | exactly one. A `url` must start with `http://` or `https://`. The first item of `command` must not be empty. |
| `headers` | remote servers only. A local server gets secrets in `env`. |
| `oauth` | remote servers only |
| `agents` | each item is a known agent name. An empty list serves every agent. |
| `timeout_secs` | 1 to `MAX_TIMEOUT_SECS` (600) |

The name rule has a reason. A server name cannot contain `__`, so `__` always separates the server from the tool. The function `serves` also needs `enabled` to be true.

Header and `env` values can use `${VAR}`. Ostra fills it from the environment of the server process. The function `expand_env` returns `ExpandError::Refused` for a variable that holds a credential that Ostra keeps from MCP servers, such as a provider key. It returns `ExpandError::Unset` for a variable that is not set. A literal secret is stored encrypted in the registry. The file `workspace.toml` holds `${ostra_secret}` in its place (`SAVED_SECRET`).

### Execution

`execute` sends a gateway name to `mcp::run`. That function calls the `McpTools` handle of the execution. The handle lists definitions under canonical names, lists the tools that their server marks with `readOnlyHint` (`read_only`), and runs a call. An execution fixes its tools when it starts. A server that cannot be reached at that time adds one line to `McpOpened.notes` for the Activity view, and its tools are absent. Without a handle the error is `Unknown tool`. For a harness execution, the hook path passes a gateway tool without a check (Rule M2). The MCP server checks and logs the call when it runs the call.

sections.title: Code index: tokenizer, outline, imports, and usages
sections.summary: Explains the language table, the tokenizer and its coordinates, the outline pass, import resolution, the incremental per-project index, and the name-level and position-level usage search.
sections.body:
## The problem that the code index solves

The Files view and the agent code tools must answer four questions. Where is a name defined? Where is it used? Which files does a file import? Which files import it? Ostra must answer for 16 languages. It cannot start one language server for each language, and a project can hold thousands of files.

The crate `crates/ostra-code` answers from a table-driven tokenizer and an incremental index for each project. The index stores names, definitions, and imports. It never stores file text. This page covers the tokenizer, the outline pass, imports, the index, and the usage search. The page "Code providers, language servers, and the Files view" covers who calls the index and what happens when a provider fails. The page "The eight code tools for agents" covers the graph that the index feeds.

## Language table

The file [`crates/ostra-code/src/lang.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/lang.rs) holds 22 `Lang` statics in `ALL`. One entry covers a language for display, outline, usages, and imports. A `Lang` holds these facts: the id, the family, line comment markers, block comment markers and whether they nest, string quote bytes, the flags `multiline_strings` and `triple_quotes`, keywords with the flag `case_insensitive`, builtin types, constants, extra identifier bytes, the flag `at_attributes`, and `defs`. The list `defs` maps a definition keyword (`fn`, `struct`, `class`, `def`) to a `Def` kind.

The `Family` of a language selects its definition and import rules.

| Family | Languages |
| --- | --- |
| `Rust` | rust |
| `Js` | typescript, javascript |
| `Python` | python |
| `Go` | go |
| `Jvm` | java, kotlin, scala, csharp, swift, php |
| `C` | c, cpp |
| `Ruby` | ruby |
| `Lua` | lua |
| `Shell` | shell |
| `Data` | sql, toml, yaml, json, css, html |

The method `Lang::indexed()` is true for every family except `Data`. Files in the six `Data` languages show colors in the Files view, but they never enter the index. The other 16 ids are `NAV_LANGUAGES` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/code.rs). A `language_servers` entry can name only these ids.

The function `for_path(path)` picks the language. It checks the file name first and then the lowercase extension.

| File name or extension | Language |
| --- | --- |
| `Makefile`, `Dockerfile` | none |
| `Gemfile`, `Rakefile`, `rb`, `rake`, `gemspec` | ruby |
| `.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, `.profile`, `sh`, `bash`, `zsh` | shell |
| `rs` | rust |
| `ts`, `tsx`, `mts`, `cts` | typescript |
| `js`, `jsx`, `mjs`, `cjs` | javascript |
| `py`, `pyi` | python |
| `go`, `java`, `swift`, `php`, `lua`, `cs` | go, java, swift, php, lua, csharp |
| `kt`, `kts` | kotlin |
| `scala`, `sc` | scala |
| `c`, `h` | c |
| `cc`, `cpp`, `cxx`, `hpp`, `hh`, `hxx`, `ipp`, `m`, `mm` | cpp |
| `sql`, `toml` | sql, toml |
| `yaml`, `yml` | yaml |
| `json`, `jsonc` | json |
| `css`, `scss`, `less` | css |
| `html`, `htm`, `xml`, `svg`, `vue`, `svelte` | html |

An unknown extension gives no language. The file then has no colors and stays out of the index.

## Tokenizer rules

The function `lex(src, lang)` in [`crates/ostra-code/src/lex.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/lex.rs) never fails. Text that it does not understand is skipped. At each position it tries these forms in order:

1. a block comment
2. a line comment
3. a family-specific form
4. a string
5. a number
6. an identifier
7. one ASCII punctuation byte
8. a skip of one UTF-8 sequence

Whitespace (space, tab, carriage return, form feed) is skipped. A newline resets the line start.

The token kinds are `Ident`, `Keyword`, `Type`, `Constant`, `Str`, `Num`, `Comment`, `Attr`, `Macro`, `Lifetime`, and `Punct(byte)`. An identifier starts with an ASCII letter, `_`, or any byte of 0x80 or more. The `$` byte counts when `ident_extra` holds it. A word is a `Keyword` if the language lists it. Otherwise it is a `Constant` or a `Type` if the language lists it as one. Otherwise it is an `Ident`.

These language rules matter when a name is not found:

- **Rust:** `name!` that is not followed by `=` is one `Macro` token with the `!`. The text `#[...]` and `#![...]` is one `Attr` token up to the matching `]`. A quote `'a` that has no closing quote is a `Lifetime`. Raw strings `r#"..."#` and byte strings are one string token.
- **Python:** a prefix of 1 or 2 letters from `r`, `b`, `f`, and `u` before a quote makes one string. Triple quotes work where `triple_quotes` is true, except for backticks.
- **Strings in general:** a backtick string always spans lines. Another string spans lines only if `multiline_strings` is true. Otherwise an unterminated string ends at the newline. A backslash skips two bytes, except in Go backtick strings and shell single-quoted strings.
- **C family:** `#directive` at the start of a line is a keyword, and `<...>` after `include` or `import` is one string.
- **Ruby:** `:symbol` is a constant, and `@x`, `@@x`, and `$x` are identifiers.
- **Shell:** `$VAR` and `${VAR}` give the name as an identifier. A `#` starts a comment only at the start of a word, so `$#` and `a#b` are not comments.
- **PHP and Java style:** `@name` is an attribute where `at_attributes` is true. In PHP, `#[` starts an attribute and not a comment.
- **Numbers:** a number takes letters, digits, `_`, a `.` before a digit, and a sign after `e` or `E` (not in `0x` numbers).
- **Unterminated block comments and strings:** they run to the end of the file.

### Token coordinates

The browser indexes JavaScript strings, which count UTF-16 code units. A `Tok` therefore carries two coordinate sets: the byte range (`start`, `end`) for the analysis, and a 1-based `line`, a 0-based UTF-16 `col`, and a UTF-16 `len` for the browser. A character of 4 UTF-8 bytes counts as 2 units.

A comment or string that spans lines becomes one token for each line. Each later token has `cont` set to true, and a trailing carriage return is cut off. The wire form in `CodeFile.tokens` is a flat list of runs of four numbers: line, column, length, and an index into `classes`. The list `classes` always holds the 11 `CLASSES` in this order: keyword, type, function, name, constant, macro, attribute, string, number, comment, operator. Tokens that have no class (punctuation and plain words of `Data` files) are left out.

The function `render(path, src, resolver)` in [`crates/ostra-code/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/lib.rs) returns a `CodeFile` with `path`, `provider`, `language`, `classes`, `tokens`, `symbols`, `imports`, and `warning`. An unknown language returns an empty answer with `language: None` and no warning. Import targets are filled only when the caller passes a resolver.

## Outline pass

The function `analyze(src, lang, toks)` in [`crates/ostra-code/src/outline.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/outline.rs) makes one pass over the tokens that are not comments and not string continuations. For `Data` files it only assigns display classes. It matches names by text. It has no type information.

The result `Analysis` has four lists: `classes` (one entry for each token), `symbols`, `imports`, and `supers`.

Definitions come from three sources:

- **Keyword rules:** the `defs` table of the language, for example `fn`, `struct`, `class`, and `def`.
- **Member rules inside class bodies:** the pass skips modifiers and the words in `NOT_BEFORE_MEMBER` (`new`, `return`, `await`, `throw`, `typeof`, `case`, `yield`, `else`, `in`, `of`, `is`, `as`, `extends`, `implements`, `delete`, `void`).
- **Family forms:** C function bodies, Go receivers, Go `const (`, `var (`, and `type (` blocks, and Python indentation scopes.

A Rust `impl` block and a Swift `extension` are containers. They give no new name (`Def::Impl`).

A `Symbol` has these fields: `name`, `kind`, `line`, `col`, `len`, `end_line`, `container`, `via`, and `byte`. The `container` is the enclosing type, module, or impl. The `via` is the trait or interface that the enclosing impl implements, for example `Display` for `fmt` in `impl Display for Point`. The kinds are function, method, class (struct, class, record, union), enum, interface (trait, interface, protocol), type, module, constant, variable, field, and macro.

A `Super { sub, sup, line }` records `class A extends B`, `impl B for A`, and `trait A: B`. These records feed the implementations tool, supertype jumps, and member lookup.

The index stores one line of text with each definition, the signature. The function `signature(src, at)` starts at the line start and runs through the parameter list. It joins wrapped lines. It stops at a `{` or `;` or a newline at parenthesis depth 0. It cuts the text at 300 bytes and adds an ellipsis. The function `preview(src, at)` returns the trimmed source line of a usage, cut at 240 bytes with an ellipsis.

## Imports and resolution

The outline pass records each import as a `RawImport` with `spec`, `line`, `style`, `alts`, `star`, and `names`.

| Style | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Use` | a path of names: Rust `use`, Python modules, Java and C# imports, PHP `use` |
| `Mod` | Rust `mod name;` |
| `Module` | a string module spec: JavaScript, Go, Lua |
| `Include { quoted }` | a C include |
| `Require { relative }` | a Ruby or PHP require |

The field `alts` holds more specific specs that the resolver tries first. For `from a import b` it tries `a.b` before `a`. The flag `star` marks `export * from`. The list `names` holds the names that a JavaScript import or re-export brings in.

The `Resolver` in [`crates/ostra-code/src/resolve.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/resolve.rs) turns a spec into a `Target { path, folder }`, or into nothing. Nothing shows as `external`. `Resolver::new(paths, read)` indexes the file list and reads these manifests: `Cargo.toml` (the `[package]` name, with `-` changed to `_`), `package.json` (the name and the entry points from `exports`, else `types`, `module`, or `main`, skipped under `node_modules`), and `go.mod` (the `module` line). A folder that holds any manifest is a package unit. The manifests are `Cargo.toml`, `package.json`, `go.mod`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts`, `composer.json`, `Gemfile`, `Package.swift`, `mix.exs`, and files that end in `.csproj`, `.gemspec`, or `.rockspec`. The unit of a folder is its nearest ancestor with a manifest, or the empty string.

| Family | Resolution rule |
| --- | --- |
| Rust | `mod x;` is `x.rs` or `x/mod.rs` in the module folder. `crate::` starts at the `src` root of the crate. `self::` and `super::` start at the module folder. Another workspace crate resolves by its Cargo name. Otherwise the first segment is a child module. The walk follows later segments while child files exist and stops at the first missing one. |
| JavaScript and TypeScript | relative specs, `@/` and `~/` through the nearest `package.json` or `tsconfig.json`, workspace package names (longest match, subpath through `exports`), and a leading `/`. Candidates: the base path, `.js` swapped for `.ts`, then the extensions `.ts .tsx .d.ts .js .jsx .mjs .cjs .mts .cts .vue .svelte` and `/index<ext>`. |
| Python | leading dots are relative. Otherwise each ancestor folder, then `src`. It tries `.py`, `.pyi`, `__init__.py`, then the folder. |
| Go | the import path must start with a `go.mod` module path on a `/` boundary. The target is that folder. |
| Java, Kotlin, Scala, C#, Swift, PHP | a dotted or backslash spec becomes a path suffix, longest prefix first. The file that shares the most leading path segments with the importer wins. Ties go to the shorter path. `pkg.*` resolves to a folder. |
| C and C++ | a quoted include tries the folder of the file, the root, `include/`, and `src/`. Then it tries a path-suffix match. |
| Ruby, Lua, Shell | Ruby adds `.rb` and tries the file folder, `lib/`, the root, and a suffix match. Lua turns dots into slashes and tries `.lua` and `/init.lua`. Shell tries the file folder and the root. |
| Data | never resolves |

A path that would leave the project, with `..` past the root, resolves to nothing.

## The incremental index

The type `ProjectIndex` in [`crates/ostra-code/src/index.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/index.rs) holds one project. It keeps names, definitions, and imports, and it never keeps file text. Only the files that mention a name are read again when a query needs their lines.

Each file has an `Entry`:

| Field | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `path`, `lang`, `stamp`, `bytes` | the file, its language, its size and modification time, and its size in bytes |
| `names` | the sorted distinct ids of every `Ident`, `Type`, and `Macro` token, with a trailing `!` cut off |
| `mentions` | the sorted distinct mentions: a bare name, a name qualified by a `self`-like word or by a name, or a member after `.` or `->` |
| `defs` | each definition with name id, kind, line, column, length, end line, container, `via`, and the signature |
| `imports`, `supers` | the raw imports and the supertype records |
| `targets` | the resolved imports, filled by `link` |
| `alive` | false after removal |

The project holds shared maps. Names are interned into ids (`names` and `name_list`). The map `postings` sends a name id to the sorted ids of the files that mention it. The map `defs_by_name` sends a name id to its (file, definition) pairs. The maps `importers` and `folder_importers` (for Go packages) come from `link`. Removal sets `alive` to false and clears the lists. Entries are never compacted, so ids stay stable.

### How `sync` brings the index up to date

`sync(paths, only)` takes the file list. The argument `only` is `None` for a full check or a set of changed paths for a partial check.

1. Keep only the paths whose language is indexed.
2. With `only = None`, remove every indexed file that left the list. With a set, remove each touched path that is missing from the list, because the file was deleted or is now ignored.
3. Read the size and modification time of each file in parallel. A failed read, or a size over `MAX_FILE_BYTES` (1 MiB), removes an existing entry and skips the file. An equal stamp skips the file.
4. Read and analyze the changed files in parallel. The number of workers is the smaller of the core count (4 if unknown), 8, and the item count. The order of the input stays. A file with a NUL byte in its first 8000 bytes is skipped. Other bytes decode with replacement characters. A file is skipped as minified when it is over 50,000 bytes and its average line is over 1000 bytes.
5. Apply the results one at a time. Remove the old entry first. Insert the new entry unless it was skipped. If the total bytes plus the file size is over `MAX_INDEX_BYTES` (256 MiB), skip the file and set `truncated`. The order of the file list decides which files stay out. Only a new index clears `truncated`.

The method `link()` runs on demand for `deps` and for graph queries. It resolves every import with the `Resolver`, builds the file-to-file importer edges, and ignores self-imports. Any insert, remove, or resolver change sets `linked` to false and drops the cached graph.

### How `Indexes` keeps one index for each project

The type `Indexes<K>` holds one slot for each project key. It builds a slot on first use. The first call to `with` reads every source file, so the server calls it from `spawn_blocking`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Query arrives] --> B[Indexes with takes the slot lock]
    B --> C{root changed?}
    C -- yes --> D[Replace the index]
    C -- no --> E[Take the dirty set]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Rebuild resolver if the file list changed]
    F --> G{list changed or 30 s passed?}
    G -- yes --> H[Full sync]
    G -- no --> I{dirty set empty?}
    I -- no --> J[Partial sync of dirty paths]
    I -- yes --> K[Run the query]
    H --> K
    J --> K
```

```rust
let list_changed = st.list.as_ref().is_none_or(|l| !Arc::ptr_eq(l, list));
let stale = st.last_full.is_none_or(|t| t.elapsed() > FULL_SYNC);
if list_changed || stale {
    st.index.sync(&list.paths, None);
} else if !dirty.is_empty() {
    st.index.sync(&list.paths, Some(&dirty));
}
```

- `touch(key, rel)` puts a path in the dirty set. The set has its own mutex, so a write never waits for a build. A project with no slot ignores the touch.
- The resolver is rebuilt only when the file list `Arc` changed, because it reads only manifests.
- A full sync runs when the file list changed or when `FULL_SYNC` (30 seconds) passed since the last full sync. The 30-second check catches edits that Ostra did not see.
- A full sync makes the dirty set unnecessary, so the code drops it.
- `forget(key)` drops the slot. The reindex route uses it.

## Usage search

A usage answer is a `CodeUsages` with `definitions`, `references`, `truncated`, and `warning`. Two searches exist.

### Name level

`ProjectIndex::usages(symbol, from, limit)` matches the name only. It cuts a trailing `!`. An unknown name returns an empty answer. The definitions come from `defs_by_name`.

The search reads the files in the posting list of the name. It ranks them in three tiers: tier 0 is the requesting file, tier 1 is the files in its folder, and tier 2 is the rest, then by path. It cuts the list at `MAX_SCAN_FILES` (4000) and sets `truncated`. It reads and lexes each file in parallel. A mention is an `Ident`, `Type`, or `Macro` token with that text, at a position that is not a definition, that passes the `keep` filter. Collection stops at `limit` references and sets `truncated`. The index stores names and not text, so only the files that mention the name need a read.

### Position level

`usages_at(symbol, path, line, col, limit)` in [`crates/ostra-code/src/usage.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/usage.rs) runs when the request has `path` and `line`. It makes `a.name` and `b.name` of two unrelated classes stay apart.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[usages_at called] --> B{file indexed and name on the line?}
    B -- no --> N[Name level answer]
    B -- yes --> C{token is a definition?}
    C -- yes --> D[Target is that definition]
    C -- no --> E[meaning resolves the use]
    E --> F{meaning resolved?}
    F -- no --> N
    F -- yes --> D
    D --> G[Widen to interface methods]
    G --> H[Read the files of the posting list]
    H --> I[Keep mentions that can mean a target]
```

The function falls back to the name-level answer in these cases: the file is not indexed, the name is unknown, the file cannot be read, no token with that name is on the line (the nearest column wins), or the meaning cannot be resolved.

The function `meaning` looks at the qualifier of the token:

- `self.`, `this.`, or `Self::` gives the members of the enclosing owner type.
- `super.` gives the members of the supertypes.
- `Q.x`, or `x` after `.` or `->`, resolves through the declared type of the receiver. The declared type comes from forms such as `Repo repo`, `repo: Repo`, `repo = new Repo()`, `T::new(`, and `T{`. It can also come from the return type of the last call of a chain, up to `MAX_CHAIN` (6) calls.
- A type in `WRAPPERS` (`Box`, `Rc`, `Arc`, `Option`, `Result`, `Optional`, `Readonly`, `Promise`) stands for its first type argument.
- A call in `PASSTHROUGH` (`unwrap`, `expect`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_default`, `unwrap_or_else`, `get`, `orElse`, `orElseThrow`, `orElseGet`, `clone`, `as_ref`, `as_mut`, `borrow`, `borrow_mut`) returns the wrapped value.
- A call in `FIRST_ARG` (`verify`, `spy`, `requireNonNull`) returns its first argument.
- Member lookup follows supertypes up to `MAX_SUPER_DEPTH` (8) steps.
- In the Jvm and C families, a bare name inside a class body can be an implicit-`this` member, unless a local declaration hides it.

A target that implements an interface method widens by up to 8 implementation steps, because a call through the interface can reach it. Then each candidate mention is filtered. An exact meaning counts when it is one of the targets. A guess counts only when the name means nothing else in the same language family, or when the file can name the type that holds the target. A file can name that type when it mentions the container type and, for nested types, the outer type.

The graph limits a guess. A name that is defined in more than `MAX_DEF_FILES` (3) files links none of them, unless the mentioning file imports the defining file directly. A receiver whose type the tokens do not tell falls back to the guess of the graph.

## Symbol search

`symbols(query, limit)` trims and lowercases the query. An empty query returns nothing. Each defined name gets a score:

| Score | Match |
| --- | --- |
| 110 | the name equals the lowercase query |
| 100 | the name equals the query when case is ignored |
| 80 | the name starts with the query |
| 60 | the name contains the query |
| 40 | the query starts the initials of the name. Initials are the first letter and each uppercase letter or letter after `_`. The name needs at least 2 initials. |

For example, `pn` finds `parse_name` and `ParseName`. The result is sorted by score, then by shorter name, then by name. Each name expands to all its definitions. The search stops at `limit` and sets `truncated`.

## Limits of the index

| Limit | Value | Constant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| file size that Ostra tokenizes and indexes | 1 MiB | `MAX_FILE_BYTES` |
| total bytes of indexed files | 256 MiB | `MAX_INDEX_BYTES` |
| files that one name-level search reads | 4000 | `MAX_SCAN_FILES` |
| importers that `deps` returns | 2000 | `MAX_IMPORTERS` |
| time between full syncs | 30 seconds | `FULL_SYNC` |
| signature length | 300 bytes | `signature` |
| preview length | 240 bytes | `preview` |
| supertype steps | 8 | `MAX_SUPER_DEPTH` |
| call chain length | 6 | `MAX_CHAIN` |

## The Markdown outline is a different module

The file [`crates/ostra-core/src/outline.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/outline.rs) is not the source-code outline. It lists the headings of a markdown file, for the artifact view and the search index. The function `headings(markdown)` returns each heading as a `Heading { id, level, title }` in document order.

- It reads ATX headings (`#` to `######`, up to 3 spaces of indent, with a closing `#` run removed) and setext headings (`===` for level 1 and `---` for level 2 under an open paragraph).
- It skips fenced code with backticks or tildes, indented code, a leading YAML front matter block, and headings with no text. An unclosed fence hides the rest of the file.
- The title keeps only the text that a reader sees. Code spans, emphasis, links, and images reduce to their text.
- The `Slugger` makes GitHub-style anchor ids. It lowercases the title, keeps letters, digits, `-`, and `_`, turns spaces into `-`, and drops other characters. A repeat gets the suffix `-1`, `-2`, and so on.

sections.title: Code providers, language servers, and the Files view
sections.summary: Explains the provider chain and its fall-through, the program protocol, the language server pool and its limits, the REST and WebSocket routes for code, and the outside-change watcher.
sections.body:
## The problem that the provider chain solves

The built-in index gives fast answers for 16 languages, but it matches names by text. A project can have a better source: its own program, or a language server such as `rust-analyzer`. A better source can also fail. The program can be missing, the server can crash, or an answer can be invalid. The Files view must still show something, and the user must see why the preferred source did not answer.

Ostra solves this with a chain of providers. A provider is a source of answers to four requests: `file`, `usages`, `deps`, and `symbols`. Each request goes through the chain in order. The first answer wins. A failure becomes a warning on the answer of a later provider. The built-in provider is always last and always answers.

## Chain order and fall-through rules

The method `Code::ask` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs) builds the chain for each request:

1. A `CommandProvider`, if the project has a `code_provider`.
2. One `LspProvider` for each `language_servers` entry, in the order of the settings.
3. The `NativeProvider`.

The server reads the settings on every request, so a saved change applies to the next request. It reads `effective_settings()`. While the file `.ostra/workspace.toml` waits for the approval of the user after a change outside Ostra, the effective settings hold no code provider and no language server. The chain then holds only the native provider.

The function `provider::ask` runs the chain. Each provider returns `Ok(Some(answer))`, `Ok(None)`, or `Err(text)`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Request] --> B[Next provider]
    B --> C{Result}
    C -- Ok Some --> D[Stamp name and warnings, return answer]
    C -- Ok None --> E{More providers?}
    C -- Err --> F[Log warning, store the problem text]
    F --> E
    E -- yes --> B
    E -- no --> G{Problems stored?}
    G -- yes --> H[Return Err with the problems]
    G -- no --> I[Return Err No code provider answered]
```

```rust
match p.answer(req).await {
    Ok(Some(mut a)) => {
        let warning = (!problems.is_empty()).then(|| problems.join(" "));
        a.stamp(&p.name(), warning);
        return Ok(a);
    }
    Ok(None) => {}
    Err(e) => { /* log with tracing::warn, push a problem text */ }
}
```

| Result | Meaning | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Ok(None)` | the provider leaves the request to the next provider | silent. No warning. |
| `Err(text)` | the provider failed | `tracing::warn!` logs it. The chain stores `The code provider <name> failed, so the built-in index answered: <text>`. |
| `Ok(Some(answer))` | the provider answered | `Answer::stamp` sets `provider` to the provider name and prefixes the stored problems to the own warning of the answer. |

The provider name is `native` (the constant `NATIVE_PROVIDER`), the base name of the program for a command provider, or the base name of the server program for a language server.

### What happens when

- **A program or server fails and a later provider answers:** the answer carries the failure text as its `warning`. The text names the built-in index even when another language server answers.
- **No provider answers and nothing failed:** the error is `No code provider answered this request.`
- **No provider answers and some failed:** the error is the failure texts joined with spaces.
- **Any error leaves the chain:** the REST handler returns HTTP 400 with that text.
- **The native provider cannot read the file:** it returns `Cannot read <path>: <reason>` as an `Err`. This is the one case where the built-in provider fails.
- **A language server answers `Deps`:** it never does. `LspProvider` returns `Ok(None)` for `Deps`, so dependencies come only from a `code_provider` or the built-in index.

## The native provider

The `NativeProvider` in [`crates/ostra-code/src/provider.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/provider.rs) runs every call in `spawn_blocking`. It answers all four requests.

| Request | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `file` | Uses the cached `Resolver` and needs no index. A file over `MAX_FILE_BYTES` (1 MiB) returns an uncolored file with the warning `The file is larger than the size Ostra tokenizes, so it shows without color.` |
| `usages` | Calls `usages_at` when `path` and `line` are given. Otherwise it calls `usages`. |
| `deps` | Calls `ix.deps(path)`. |
| `symbols` | Calls `ix.symbols(query, limit)`. |

If the index hit its byte cap (`ix.truncated`), `usages` and `symbols` add the warning `The project is larger than the size Ostra indexes, so some files are not searched.`

## The program protocol of `code_provider`

A project can name one program in `[projects.code_provider]`. It is the first provider in the chain.

| Setting | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `command` | the program and its arguments. The first item must not be empty. |
| `timeout_secs` | default 10, from 1 to `MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT` (120). Ostra checks it when the user saves settings. |

Ostra runs the program once for each request, in the project folder. It wraps the process with `ostra_sandbox::host_command` and the workspace sandbox settings. The environment variable `OSTRA_CODE_PROTOCOL` holds `1` (`PROTOCOL_VERSION`). The process gets one JSON object and a newline on stdin. It must write one JSON value on stdout.

Every request has `op`, `version`, and `root`. The field `op` is `file`, `usages`, `deps`, or `symbols`.

| `op` | Extra fields | Response shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `file` | `path` | `CodeFile` |
| `usages` | `symbol`, `path?`, `line?`, `col?`, `limit` | `CodeUsages` |
| `deps` | `path` | `CodeDeps` |
| `symbols` | `query`, `limit` | `CodeSymbols` |

A request for usages looks like this:

```json
{"op":"usages","version":1,"root":"/work/app","symbol":"parse_config","path":"src/a.rs","line":12,"col":8,"limit":500}
```

The program answers `null` or empty output for a request that it leaves to the built-in provider. A write error on stdin is ignored, because a program can answer without reading its input.

Each failure becomes a warning on the answer of the next provider:

| Case | Text |
| --- | --- |
| empty `command` | `The command is empty.` |
| the program cannot start | `Cannot start <program>: <reason>.` |
| longer than `timeout_secs` | `It took longer than N seconds.` Ostra kills the process when it drops the handle. |
| exit status not 0 | `It exited with <status>: <last line of stderr>`. Ostra keeps at most `MAX_STDERR` (1 MiB) of stderr. |
| stdout over `MAX_OUTPUT` (64 MiB) | `Its answer is larger than 64 MB.` |
| stdout is not UTF-8 | `Its answer is not UTF-8.` |
| JSON does not match the shape | `Its answer to <op> does not match the protocol: <reason>.` |

`parse_answer` checks each response before Ostra uses it:

- **`file`:** the request `path` replaces the path in the answer. The `tokens` list must have a multiple of 4 numbers and at most `MAX_TOKENS` (16 Mi numbers). Each token needs a line of 1 or more and a class index below the length of `classes`. At most `MAX_ITEMS` (20,000) symbols and 20,000 imports are allowed. Import targets must be project-relative.
- **`usages` and `symbols`:** at most 20,000 locations in each list. Each `path` must be project-relative and each `line` must be 1 or more. Ostra clears `uri`, because it reads back outside files only for language server URIs. An empty `name` becomes the symbol.
- **`deps`:** at most 20,000 imports and 20,000 importers, with project-relative paths.
- **A bad path** is empty, starts with `/`, contains a backslash or a NUL byte, or has a `.` or `..` segment.

## The language server pool

The settings `[[projects.language_servers]]` add one `LspProvider` for each entry. The native provider is the `base` of each entry.

| Setting | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `command` | the program and arguments. The first item must not be empty. |
| `languages` | at least one id from `NAV_LANGUAGES`. A language can belong to only one server in a project, because each file asks one server. |
| `timeout_secs` | default 10, from 1 to 120 |
| `initialization_options` | optional JSON that Ostra sends in the `initialize` request |

The `LspPool` keys a server by the project key and the command. The first request for a language that the server answers calls `LspPool::get`. That call starts the server with `spawn_process`, under the workspace sandbox, because a server runs the build scripts and macros of the project.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[LspPool get] --> B{entry exists and fresh?}
    B -- no --> C[Replace entry, stop the least recently used if 8 run]
    B -- yes --> D[Use the entry]
    C --> D
    D --> E[Start task behind a OnceCell]
    E --> F{Started within timeout_secs?}
    F -- yes --> G[Return the server]
    F -- no --> H[Err is still starting]
```

The start runs in a spawned task behind a `OnceCell`. A caller that stops waiting leaves the server in its start for the next request. A caller waits at most `timeout_secs`. A hint request waits at most 3 seconds. On a timeout the error is `<name> is still starting. Ask again in a moment.` The `initialize` request has its own timeout `INIT_TIMEOUT` (60 seconds), because some servers read the project first. Java servers get `extendedClientCapabilities.classFileContentsSupport = true` unless the user set it, because `jdtls` answers `jdt://` URIs only with it.

Ostra sends these capabilities: UTF-16 position encoding only, work-done progress, workspace folders, definition and implementation with link support, references, completion with snippets, signature help, hierarchical document symbols, full semantic tokens in relative format without multiline or overlapping tokens, type hierarchy, and `experimental.serverStatusNotification`. If the server answers with another `positionEncoding`, Ostra closes the connection with the error `<name> counts columns in <encoding>. Ostra needs a server that counts them in utf-16.`

| Limit | Value | Constant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| running servers across all projects | 8. A new start stops the least recently used server. | `MAX_SERVERS` |
| open documents for each server | 32. A new open sends `didClose` for the least recently used. | `MAX_OPEN` |
| idle time before a server stops | 10 minutes | `IDLE` |
| time between sweeps of idle entries | 60 seconds | `SWEEP` |
| time before a failed or dead server starts again | 30 seconds | `RETRY` |
| outside URIs that the pool remembers | 20,000 | `MAX_EXTERNALS` |
| definitions from `workspace/symbol` | 50 | `MAX_DEFINITIONS` |
| size of one server message | 256 MiB | `MAX_MESSAGE` |
| lines of stderr that Ostra keeps | 20 | `STDERR_LINES` |

Ostra hashes the text of a document. The first use sends `didOpen` with version 1. A changed hash sends a full-text `didChange` with the next version. A file must be UTF-8 text of at most 1 MiB, or the error is `Cannot read <path> as UTF-8 text under 1 MB.` The method `touch(key, rel)` sends `workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles` (type 2 for changed, type 3 for deleted) to the running servers of the project.

### What happens when

- **The program is missing or does not start:** the error is `Cannot start <name>: <reason>.` The provider returns `Err` and the chain falls through. The pool caches the failed start. After `RETRY` (30 seconds) the entry is stale, and the next request starts the server again. A dead server restarts the same way.
- **The sandbox settings change:** the pool replaces a server that started under other settings on the next request.
- **The server exits or sends a broken message:** every pending request fails with the reason, such as `The language server exited.`, `The language server exited with <status>.`, `The language server closed its input.`, or `The language server sent a broken message: <reason>.` The text adds `Its last output: <last stderr line>`.
- **A request takes longer than `timeout_secs`:** the error is `<name> did not answer <method> within N seconds.` Ostra sends `$/cancelRequest`. It also sends it when the caller drops the future.
- **The server answers with error code -32801 or -32802:** the error is `<name> is still loading the project and dropped the request.` Other error codes give `<name> answered with an error: <message>`.
- **The server is still loading:** `busy()` is true while a progress token is open, or while `rust-analyzer` reports `quiescent` as false. The answer then carries the warning `<name> is still loading the project, so this answer may be incomplete.`
- **The server sends a request to Ostra:** `workspace/configuration` gets nulls. `workspace/workspaceFolders` gets the root folder. The register, unregister, progress create, show message, and refresh requests get null. `workspace/applyEdit` gets `applied: false`. Any other request gets error -32601.
- **A server stops:** Ostra sends `shutdown` (waits 3 seconds), then `exit`, waits 2 seconds, and then kills the process. It drops the sandbox member set, so leftover processes die.

## What a language server answers

- **`file`:** only for a path whose language is in `languages`. Otherwise the result is `Ok(None)`. The provider first takes the native answer, and imports always stay native. If the native answer has a warning, such as the size warning, the provider returns it unchanged, because a server would get the same cut. Otherwise the provider opens the document and sends `textDocument/semanticTokens/full` (if the server returned a legend) and `textDocument/documentSymbol` (if the server can) in parallel. Each uses `timeout_secs`. Semantic tokens overlay the native tokens. A server outline that is not empty replaces the native symbols. A failed part adds `Colors come from the built-in tokenizer: <reason>` or `The outline comes from the built-in tokenizer: <reason>` to the warning. If the provider used neither part, the result is `Ok(None)` when nothing failed and `Err` with the problems when something failed.
- **`usages`:** with `path` and `line`, and the name on that line, it sends `textDocument/definition` at that position. Otherwise it uses `workspace/symbol` and keeps exact name matches. It then sends `textDocument/references` with `includeDeclaration: false`. It drops references outside the project, because the own uses of a library would crowd out the project. It removes definitions from the references, sorts with the file of the request first, removes duplicates, and cuts to `limit`. With no definitions and no references the result is `Ok(None)`, so the native index answers.
- **`symbols`:** it sends `workspace/symbol`. With no capability or no items the result is `Ok(None)`.
- **`deps`:** `Ok(None)`.

## Editor hints over WebSocket

The editor sends three client messages: `CodeComplete`, `CodeSignature`, and `CodeNavigate`. The replies are `CodeCompletion`, `CodeSignatureHelp`, and `CodeNavigation`, each with `id`, `result`, and `error`. The server keeps one task for each kind. A new request of a kind aborts the old task of that kind (`streams.replace`).

The function `hint_rig` rejects a request in these cases:

- The text is over 1 MiB.
- The cursor line is 0 or outside the text.
- The `trigger` is not exactly one character.
- The path is empty, is a directory, or is outside the project.

| Hint | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| completion | Asks each language server in order, waiting at most `HINT_WAIT` (3 seconds). The server keeps starting. The trigger kinds are 1 invoked, 2 trigger character, and 3 incomplete-list retrigger. A typed character that the server does not list as a trigger returns an empty list. If no server answers, the index gives names that start like the word at the cursor, at most `MAX_INDEX_COMPLETIONS` (50). The list is incomplete, so the editor asks again. After a trigger character the index list is empty, because the index does not know members. A failed server adds `<name> did not complete, so the code index did: <reason>`. |
| signature help | Asks the servers only. The index has none to give. A server error gives HTTP 502. No answer gives `null`. |
| navigate (supertypes or implementations) | Asks the index first, because it is fast and holds every language it parses. It asks the language servers only when the index does not hold the file or does not know the name. Locations are capped at `MAX_NAVIGATION` (50). When the name is not defined in its own file, the index asks about at most 8 definitions (`NAVIGATION_GROUPS`). |

## REST routes for code

All routes are under `/api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/code/`. The handlers are in `crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`.

| Route | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET file` | `path` | `CodeFile`. The text comes from the `file` route of the files API. |
| `GET usages` | `symbol`, `path?`, `line?`, `col?`, `limit?`, or `uri` with `line` | `CodeUsages` |
| `GET deps` | `path` | `CodeDeps` |
| `GET symbols` | `q`, `limit?` | `CodeSymbols` |
| `GET external` | `uri` | `CodeExternalFile`, read-only |
| `GET graph` | `package?`, `path?`, `symbol?`, `line?`, `depth?` | `CodeGraph` |
| `POST reindex` | none | `CodeReindex { indexed_files, millis, truncated }` |

The function `Code::ask` checks each request before it builds the chain:

- The path goes through `files::contain`, so it stays inside the project. An empty path or a folder gives HTTP 400 `Name a file with path.`
- A usages `symbol` must not be empty, at most `MAX_SYMBOL_LEN` (256) bytes, and without whitespace or control characters. Otherwise HTTP 400 says to name one symbol.
- The usages `limit` defaults to `DEFAULT_USAGES` (500) and is clamped to the range 1 to `MAX_USAGES` (2000).
- The symbols `limit` defaults to `DEFAULT_SYMBOLS` (50) and is clamped to the range 1 to `MAX_SYMBOLS` (200). The query is cut to 256 characters.
- A provider that answers a different request gives HTTP 500 `The code provider answered a different request.`

The `graph` route uses the built-in index only. These rules apply:

- `path` together with `package` gives HTTP 400 `Give either package or path, not both.`
- `path` with `symbol` gives the symbol view. `path` alone gives the file view. `package` gives the package view, where `.` means the top package. No parameter lists all packages.
- `depth` defaults to 1 and is clamped to the range 1 to `MAX_GRAPH_DEPTH` (3).
- A missing package, file, or symbol gives HTTP 404 `That package, file, or symbol is not in the code index.` with the reasons: the index leaves out ignored files, files over 1 MB, and languages it does not parse.

The `reindex` route invalidates the file list, builds it again, drops the index slot, and builds the index again. It returns the file count and the time in milliseconds.

## Files outside the project

A language server can point at a file outside the project, such as a library source file or a class in a jar. The location keeps a `uri` and a display path. The path starts with `~/` under the home folder, or it has the form `<jar> > <class path>` for `jdt://` URIs. The pool remembers the URI with the command of the server.

The routes `external` and `usages` with `uri` accept only URIs that a language server of this process answered with. The browser cannot name an arbitrary file. The limit for a URI is `MAX_URI_LEN` (4096) bytes.

- **The URI is unknown:** HTTP 404 says that no language server of this project pointed at it since the Ostra server started.
- **The server left the settings:** HTTP 404 says that the server is no longer in the project settings.
- **A `file://` URI:** the tool reads UTF-8 text of at most 1 MiB. Over that size, the error is `<name> is larger than 1 MB, the size Ostra reads.`
- **A jar class:** the tool asks the server with `java/classFileContents`. An empty answer gives `<server> has no source or decompiled text for <class>.`
- **Any other URI scheme:** the error is `Ostra cannot read this kind of location.`
- **A server error:** HTTP 502.

## Freshness and the outside-change watcher

The index must stay current when files change. Five paths keep it current:

1. **Writes by an agent.** A write touch from a tool call reaches `app.code.touch` through `run_touches` in `crates/ostra-server/src/files/mod.rs`.
2. **A save by the user.** `announce_save` calls `app.code.touch`.
3. **The watcher.** It reports edits that Ostra did not make, such as a shell command, an editor, or a checkout.
4. **The 30-second full sync** in `Indexes::with`.
5. **The `reindex` route.**

The method `Code::touch` marks the path in the index and sends `didChangeWatchedFiles` to the running servers. The method `ensure_watch` starts the watcher. The routes `file`, `usages`, `deps`, `symbols`, and `graph`, the hint requests, `reindex`, and the agent tool adapter call it. It replaces a watch on an old root. If the platform refuses even the root, the server logs `cannot watch <root>; outside edits reach the code index within 30 s`. The next call tries again.

The watcher in [`crates/ostra-server/src/code_watch.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/code_watch.rs) works like this:

- It watches the project root and every folder that holds a listed file, each without recursion. Ignored build output therefore adds no watches. A folder that the OS refuses, for example at the watch limit, is counted and logged. The 30-second check covers it.
- `Create`, `Remove`, and rename events are structural. `Modify` data events are content changes. Other event kinds are ignored.
- It drops paths under `.git` and paths that `<root>/.gitignore` or `<root>/.git/info/exclude` match. It reads no nested or global ignore file. A new or renamed folder is added to the watch.
- After the first event, it absorbs more events until `QUIET` (250 ms) passes without one, or until `MAX_WAIT` (2 seconds) pass since the batch began. A batch with no changed path is not delivered.

The callback `on_outside_change` runs for each batch. A structural batch invalidates the file list of the project. Each changed path calls `Code::touch`. Then the server pushes `ServerMsg::ProjectFsChanged { workspace, key, paths }` on the channel `workspace:{id}`. A batch of more than `MAX_PUSHED_PATHS` (200) paths sends an empty `paths` list. The browser then reloads the whole listing.

## Settings that control code navigation

| Setting | Default | Where | When a change applies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `projects[].code_provider.command` | none | workspace settings | the next request |
| `projects[].code_provider.timeout_secs` | 10 | workspace settings | the next request |
| `projects[].language_servers[].command` | none | workspace settings | the next request. A new command starts a new server. |
| `projects[].language_servers[].languages` | none | workspace settings | the next request |
| `projects[].language_servers[].timeout_secs` | 10 | workspace settings | the next request |
| `projects[].language_servers[].initialization_options` | none | workspace settings | the next start of the server |

The workspace file can arrive with a repository or a `git pull`. Ostra starts the programs that it names only after the user approved that content. The page "Trust approvals and registry-only settings" explains the approval. The page "Settings files and every setting" lists the other settings.
