sections.title: The eight code tools for agents
sections.summary: Explains the routing, input, output, and limits of CodeOutline, CodeFind, CodeCallers, CodeCallees, CodeImplementations, CodeNeighbors, CodeImpact, and CodeMap, and the graph rules and limits behind them.
sections.body:
## The problem that the code tools solve

An agent that explores code with `Grep` and `Read` finds text, not meaning. A search for a name returns comments, strings, and uses of unrelated definitions with the same name. The agent then reads whole files to find the few lines that matter. The eight code tools answer structural questions from the code index: what a file defines, where a name is defined, who uses it, what it uses, what implements it, how files connect, what a change can break, and how the project is laid out.

The tools return compact text and not JSON. They read the index, so they cost far less than a read of the files. The tool descriptions tell the model to call `CodeOutline` before `Read` on a file that it has not seen, and to call `CodeMap` once at the start of work in an unfamiliar project. The page "Code index: tokenizer, outline, imports, and usages" explains how the index gets its facts.

## How a code tool call reaches the index

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Model
    participant Execute
    participant CodeRun as code run
    participant CodeTools
    participant Index as ProjectIndex
    Model->>Execute: CodeCallers call
    Execute->>CodeRun: is_code_tool match
    CodeRun->>CodeTools: CodeNav call with repo_root
    CodeTools->>CodeTools: project_holding and file list
    CodeTools->>Index: Indexes with, tools run
    Index-->>Model: compact text answer
```

The steps are:

1. `execute` sends a name from `CODE_TOOLS` to `code::run` in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/code.rs). That function calls the `CodeNav` handle with the repository root of the execution. Without a handle the error is `Code navigation is not available in this run. Use Grep, Glob, and Read instead.`
2. `CodeTools::call` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs) makes the root canonical. It picks the innermost project of any open workspace that holds the root. The innermost project is the one with the longest root (`project_holding`). If none holds it, the error is `<dir> is not inside a project of an open workspace, so it has no code index.`
3. It loads the file list, makes sure that the watcher runs, and calls `ostra_code::tools::run` on the index of the project in `spawn_blocking`.
4. If the server is shutting down, the error is `The Ostra server is shutting down.`

Over MCP the tools are `code_outline`, `code_find`, `code_callers`, `code_callees`, `code_implementations`, `code_neighbors`, `code_impact`, and `code_map`. The native loop treats all eight as read-only tools that can run at the same time in one turn.

## Input rules shared by the eight tools

- Every input struct uses `deny_unknown_fields`, and the JSON schema has `additionalProperties: false`. A bad input returns `Invalid input: <reason>.`
- The field `limit` is an integer from 1 to 300. The default is `DEFAULT_LIMIT` (40). The code clamps a value outside the range. `CodeOutline` and `CodeImpact` use other defaults.
- A path is relative to the project root. The tool also accepts an absolute path inside the project, a path that starts with `./`, and a path that starts with the project folder name when the file exists only without that prefix. The last form helps an agent that works across the workspace and names files from the workspace root.
- A symbol is a bare name such as `next_steps` or `Button`, without its type or module.
- A path that is not in the index gives the error ``<path> is not in the code index. Give a project-relative path of a source file; the index leaves out ignored files, files over 1 MB, and languages it does not parse.``

The index leaves out these files: files that the file list ignores, files over 1 MiB, minified files, files with a NUL byte, and files in languages that the tokenizer does not parse (the `Data` languages and unknown extensions).

## CodeOutline

`CodeOutline { path, limit? }` lists the imports and definitions of one file without a read of its text.

```text
crates/ostra-tools/src/defs.rs (rust, 744 lines)
imports:
  L1 ostra_core::AgentName -> crates/ostra-core/src/lib.rs
  L2 serde::Deserialize -> external
symbols:
  L6-10 class ToolDefinition
    L7 field name in ToolDefinition
```

The first line has the path, the language, and the line count. Each import line has the line number, the spec, and the project file that it resolves to, or `external`. Each symbol line has a line or line range, the kind word, the name, and `in <container>`. Members of a container have 4 spaces of indent. Other symbols have 2.

This tool reads the file itself and renders it with the resolver of the index. The symbol cap defaults to 300 and not 40. When more symbols exist, the last line says `(N more symbols)`. The tool makes no size check.

## CodeFind

`CodeFind { query, limit? }` finds definitions by name across the project. It uses the symbol search of the index, with the scores 110, 100, 80, 60, and 40 (see the index page).

Each line is `path:line kind name in container (impl via)  <signature>`. The signature is the first line of the definition. With no match the answer is `No definition matches <query>.` If more matches exist, the last line says `(more matches; narrow the query or raise limit)`.

## CodeCallers

`CodeCallers { symbol, path?, limit? }` lists every place that uses a symbol, grouped by the enclosing definition.

- With no `path`, if exactly one file defines the symbol, the tool uses that file. If several files define it, the answer holds the hint to pass `path`, so that mentions of the other definitions drop out.
- The answer starts with `defined at:` and the definition locations.
- Then `used by (N places in M files):` lists each group: the file, the kind and name of the enclosing definition with `in <container>`, and the line numbers. A group with no enclosing definition shows `import` when every line is an import line, and `top level` otherwise.
- With no caller the answer says `no callers found`. With no definition it says that the symbol has no definition in the index.
- If the tool cuts the list, the last line says `(more callers; raise limit)`.

The tool reads up to `MAX_CALLER_REFS` (5000) references. When the caller passes `path`, a mention in another file counts only if it resolves to the definition in that file. The tool drops mentions that mean another definition of the same name. This is the difference between `CodeCallers` and `Grep`.

## CodeCallees

`CodeCallees { path, symbol, line?, limit? }` lists the project definitions that the body of one function or type uses. The inputs `path` and `symbol` are required. The input `line` picks one definition when the file defines the name more than once. The tool picks the definition whose line is nearest to `line`.

The tool reads the body of the definition, from its first line to its end line. It resolves each distinct mention. The definition's own name is not a use. Inside one body, a member counts only when the body names the owner type.

- If the file does not define the symbol, the error tells the model to use `CodeOutline` on the file.
- If the index has no end line, the answer says `(the body's end is unknown; only its first line was read)`.
- If the body uses nothing from the project, the answer says `nothing defined in this project`.
- If the tool cuts the list, the last line says `(more; raise limit)`.

## CodeImplementations

`CodeImplementations { symbol, path?, line?, limit? }` shows what a type or method implements or extends, and what implements or extends it. For a method it shows the interface method that it implements and the methods that implement it.

Links come from declarations: `extends`, `implements`, `:`, Python base classes, and Rust `impl Trait for Type`. For Go they come from matching method sets. Methods that code generation adds are not seen. The tool shows at most `MAX_IMPL_GROUPS` (8) definitions of the name.

- With `path` and `line`, the tool picks the one definition that is nearest to the line.
- Without `path`, the tool asks every type or method of that name. It lists the ones with links first, most linked first. If none has links, it lists the first one with empty lists.
- A name with several definitions adds the line `<symbol> has N definitions; showing the ones with implementation links. Pass path for one.`
- Each definition has two sections: `implements or extends` and `implemented or extended by`. An empty section says `none`.
- If no definition exists, the error suggests `CodeOutline` (with `path`) or `CodeFind` (without `path`).
- If the tool cuts a list, the last line says `(more; pass path or raise limit)`.

## CodeNeighbors

`CodeNeighbors { path, limit? }` shows how one file connects to the rest of the project. The header has the path, the package, and `test` if the file is a test file.

- The list `uses (N)` holds the files that this file depends on. The list `used by (N)` holds the files that depend on it. The strongest links come first. Each line has the path, `[import L..]` with the import lines or `[child module]` for a Rust `mod` declaration, and the names that link the pair. The tool shows at most `MAX_NAMES` (12) names and then `, +N more`.
- If a list is cut at `limit`, the answer says `(lists cut at N; raise limit)`.
- The section `also related (through a shared neighbor)` shows at most 5 files at distance 2, from 8 candidates. Each file has `via <neighbor>`.
- A file that is not indexed gives the not-indexed error.

## CodeImpact

`CodeImpact { symbol?, path?, paths?, direction?, depth?, limit? }` shows what a change can break. Give either `symbol` or `paths`.

| Mode | Input | What the tool walks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| symbol | `symbol` and optionally `path` | the definitions that use the symbol, then the definitions that use those, hop by hop |
| files | `paths` and optionally `direction` | the files that depend on the seed files (`dependents`, the default) or that the seed files use (`dependencies`) |

The `depth` defaults to 3 and is clamped to the range 1 to 10. The `limit` defaults to 100 and is clamped to the range 1 to 300.

Errors:

- `symbol` together with `paths`: `Give either symbol or paths, not both.`
- Neither `symbol` nor `paths`: the error asks for one of them.
- `symbol` with `direction: dependencies`: the error tells the model to call `CodeCallees`.
- A symbol that several files define, without `path`: the error lists the files.
- A symbol that the given file does not define: the error suggests `CodeFind`.

The symbol walk follows names. A file that uses something else from the same file is left out. This differs from the file walk. The answer starts with `changing <definitions> affects:` and then lists `hop 1 (uses it directly):`, `hop 2 (uses something in hop 1):`, and so on. Each line has the file, the kind and name of the user, the lines, and `via <name>` after hop 1. An import line is not a use, so the walk skips it. The last line is `files to change or recheck (N): <files>`. If no definition uses the symbol, the answer says `nothing: no other definition uses it`.

The file walk lists the files by hop, with `via <file>` after hop 1 and the linking names. A seed that is not indexed is named in the answer as not indexed. The walk visits at most `MAX_REACH` (5000) files. If the tool cuts the answer, the last line says `(cut short; lower depth or raise limit)`.

## CodeMap

`CodeMap { prefix? }` summarizes the project. The input `prefix` limits the answer to one folder.

The answer has these parts:

- The first line `N files indexed`.
- The list `packages (files; depends on, with link counts)`. Each package has its file count, its test file count, and the packages that it depends on with link counts. The top package shows as `.`.
- The list `package cycles`, when packages depend on each other in a loop.
- The list `most depended-on files (dependents)`: the 15 files with the most dependents, taken from the top 200.
- The list `import cycles`: at most 10 cycles, taken from the first 50. Only imports count. A `mod` declaration and an import of an index module do not count.

A package is a folder with a manifest, or the top folder. A test file is a file in a folder named `test`, `tests`, `__tests__`, `spec`, `specs`, `testdata`, or `fixtures`, or a file with a name such as `.test.`, `.spec.`, `test_`, `_test.go`, `_test.py`, `_test.rs`, `_spec.rb`, `_test.rb`, `Test.java`, `Tests.java`, `Test.kt`, `Tests.cs`, or `Test.php`.

## How the graph decides who uses what

The graph in [`crates/ostra-code/src/graph.rs`](crates/ostra-code/src/graph.rs) comes from the index without a read of files. The index builds it on the first graph query after a link, and the next link drops it. Two kinds of edges exist:

- **Import edges** come from the resolver. An import that names a file links the importer to that file.
- **Reference edges** link a file to the files that define the names it mentions. The graph skips names with one character.

A reference resolves the way a reader looks for the definition. The method `tier` gives each candidate file a distance:

| Tier | Candidate file |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | the file that the mentioning file imports, or a file in a folder that it imports |
| 1 | a file in the same folder |
| 2 | a file in the same package |
| 3 | a file in a package that the package of the mentioning file imports |

The nearest tier wins. A file in none of the tiers cannot see the definition. A name that is defined in more than `MAX_DEF_FILES` (3) files links none of them unless the mentioning file imports a defining file directly. The graph resolves a candidate only in the same language family. It skips test files unless the mentioning file is a test file.

The qualifier of a mention narrows the match. A `self`-like qualifier means the own definitions of the file. A qualifier that is a name restricts the match to definitions inside that name. A member after `.` or `->` can match only member kinds.

Each edge has a weight: 2 for each linking name (at most `MAX_LINK_NAMES` (8) names) and 1 if any import exists. The tools sort by this weight. A transitive walk follows an edge when it has linking names, or when it is a real import that does not go into an index module. An index module is a `lib`, `main`, `mod`, `index`, or `__init__` file, or a file with an `export * from`. The reason is that an import of an index module only re-exports names that already link to their own files.

The method `related` adds files that are one step further, with 25% of the weaker link. It skips a stepping stone that is an index module or that links to more than `MAX_BRIDGE_DEGREE` (200) files.

## Limits of the graph and the tools

| Limit | Value | Constant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| default and maximum `limit` | 40 and 300 | `DEFAULT_LIMIT`, `MAX_LIMIT` |
| default symbol cap of `CodeOutline` | 300 | `MAX_LIMIT` |
| default `limit` of `CodeImpact` | 100 | none |
| `depth` of `CodeImpact` | default 3, range 1 to 10 | none |
| linking names shown for a file | 12 | `MAX_NAMES` |
| definitions listed by `CodeImplementations` | 8 | `MAX_IMPL_GROUPS` |
| files that share a definition name before links stop | 3 | `MAX_DEF_FILES` |
| names that weigh an edge | 8 | `MAX_LINK_NAMES` |
| files in a transitive walk | 5000 | `MAX_REACH` |
| references that `CodeCallers` reads | 5000 | `MAX_CALLER_REFS` |
| links of a stepping stone for `related` | 200 | `MAX_BRIDGE_DEGREE` |

The Files view uses the same graph through the REST route `graph`. Its views have their own caps: `MAX_VIEW_FILES` (150) files in a package view, `MAX_VIEW_NEIGHBORS` (80) neighbors in a file view, `MAX_VIEW_CALLEES` (200) callees, `MAX_MEMBERS` (40) members for each type node, `MAX_FILE_DEFS` (30) definitions for each file node, and `MAX_VIEW_EDGES` (300) edges. When a view has too many edges, it keeps implementation edges first and then the heaviest reference edges. A view sets `truncated` when it leaves nodes out. The request `depth` is clamped to the range 1 to 3.

### What the tools cannot see

- **Type information.** The index matches names by text. A receiver whose type the tokens do not tell falls back to a guess.
- **Generated code.** The tools do not see methods that code generation adds.
- **Files outside the index.** Ignored files, files over 1 MiB, minified files, and languages with no parser are not there. Use `Grep`, `Glob`, and `Read` for them.
- **A stale file.** The index reads a changed file at the next query after a write, a save, a watcher event, or a 30-second full check. A change that happened in the last moments can be missing.
- **A very large project.** Past `MAX_INDEX_BYTES` (256 MiB) the index leaves files out, and the list order decides which files stay out.

sections.title: Startup sequence, request guard, and sign-in
sections.summary: Explains the order in which the server starts, how it picks a port, how the guard checks every request, how a browser signs in with a one-time token, and how the master key is chosen.
sections.body:
## The problem this part solves

The `ostra` binary is one process. It serves a web app, a REST API, a WebSocket, and local `/internal` endpoints for harness hooks. The same process starts agents that run commands with the rights of the user. Without a fixed startup order and a strict request check, a web page or a machine on the network can reach that power. This page explains how the process starts, how the guard checks each request, how a browser signs in, and how the master key protects saved credentials.

The page covers:

- The entry point and the subcommands (`main`, `serve`).
- The port and bind choice (`bind_addr`, `bind`).
- The bootstrap order (`app::build`) and one engine for each workspace (`App::attach`).
- The request guard (`guard`, `refusal`, `secure_headers`).
- The sign-in flow, the cookie, and revocation (`auth.rs`).
- The master key (`master_key.rs`).

The page "REST routes, errors, and the WebSocket protocol" lists the routes. The page "Run, install, and extend the server" lists the flags and the environment variables.

In this book, a session is an engine session of the pipeline. A browser that signed in has a sign-in. The names `ostra sessions` and `/api/auth/sessions` list sign-ins, not engine sessions.

## Entry point and subcommands

`main` in [crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs) runs before a tokio runtime exists. It does these steps in order:

1. If the first argument is `sandbox-init`, run `ostra_sandbox::init::main` and exit. This command is hidden from `--help` and runs inside a sandbox.
2. Call `ostra_sandbox::scrub_startup_env()` and `ostra_sandbox::set_helper` with the path of the executable.
3. Parse the command line with clap.
4. Call `ostra_server::env::extend_path()`. It adds the install folders of the official harness CLIs to `PATH`. It runs now because a change to the environment is safe only while no other thread exists. A harness that the user installs while the server runs then resolves by name without a restart.
5. Build a multi-thread tokio runtime and run the subcommand.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ostra` or `ostra serve` | Starts the server. |
| `ostra config` | Prints the path of `config.toml`. It writes the default file when none exists. |
| `ostra url` | Prints a fresh sign-in URL for the running server. |
| `ostra sessions` | Lists the signed-in browsers. |
| `ostra sessions revoke <id>` or `--all` | Revokes one sign-in or every sign-in. |
| `ostra signout` | Revokes every sign-in. It equals `sessions revoke --all`. |
| `ostra stop <session>` | Stops an engine session while the server is off. It refuses when the server runs. |
| `ostra hook`, `ostra mcp-stdio` | Harness entry points. Harnesses call them. The topic "Harness executors" explains them. |

The `serve` function sets up logging before it calls `app::run`. The log filter comes from the `OSTRA_LOG` variable and defaults to `info`. Logs go to stdout and to `<data dir>/server.log` in append mode, without color codes. If the log file cannot open, the server logs to stdout only.

## Port and bind choice

`app::run` loads the global config only to find the bind address and the port. If the file is missing or unreadable, it uses the default config. The bind address comes from `bind_addr` and follows this order: the `--bind` flag, then `server.bind`, then `127.0.0.1`.

`bind_addr` accepts these values:

- `localhost`, which means `127.0.0.1`.
- `all` or `*`, which means `0.0.0.0`.
- An IP address. Brackets around an IPv6 address are removed.

Any other value stops startup with a message that names the bad value.

The port comes from `--port`, then `server.port`. If one of them is set, `bind` makes one attempt and a failure stops startup. If neither is set, `bind` tries the ports 7878 to 7897 (20 ports) in order. If all 20 are busy, it asks the OS for a free port with port 0.

```rust
async fn bind(ip: std::net::IpAddr, port: Option<u16>) -> anyhow::Result<tokio::net::TcpListener> {
    let start = port.unwrap_or(DEFAULT_PORT);
    if port.is_some() {
        return Ok(tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(SocketAddr::new(ip, start)).await?);
    }
    for p in start..start + 20 {
        if let Ok(l) = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(SocketAddr::new(ip, p)).await {
            return Ok(l);
        }
    }
    Ok(tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(SocketAddr::new(ip, 0)).await?)
}
```

The doc comment of `ServerConfig.port` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs` says that an absent port means a free port. The code is right: it tries 7878 first. The server binds the listener before `build` runs, because the host allowlist, the sandbox, and the hook callback address all need the final port.

## Bootstrap order in build

`app::run` does these steps before `build`. It stops sandbox processes that an earlier server left running, but only if no live server pid is in `server.json`. It removes stale egress sockets and decoy files. It starts the decoy report watcher on a blocking thread. It does this first because `engine.recover()` can start executions again.

`app::build` in [crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs) then does these steps in order:

1. Tell the sandbox the port (`set_server_port`).
2. Write a default `config.toml` if none exists, then load it. A sandbox section that fails validation stops startup.
3. Log the sandbox status. If the sandbox is not active, print a WARNING to stderr and to the log. The warning says that agent commands run with the full rights of the user.
4. Create the data dir with mode 0700 on Unix (`ensure_data_dir`).
5. Start the model price refresh (`prices::start`).
6. Open the registry, set its file and its `-wal` and `-shm` files to mode 0600, and call `master_key::unlock`.
7. Write the embedded agent assets to `<data dir>/assets` and register that folder with `ostra_agents`.
8. Build the providers from the config and the saved credentials.
9. Create `CodeTools`, `McpGateway`, `Management`, `Coordination`, and the `NativeExecutor`.
10. Create the `Notifier` with the VAPID keys from the registry.
11. Detect the installed harness CLIs (`EnvStatus::detect`).
12. Build `Access` from the flags and the config.
13. Build `HarnessRuntime` with a callback address: `127.0.0.1:<port>` when the bind is loopback or unspecified, else `<bind>:<port>`.
14. Build `Shared`, then `App`, with the `hub` channel (capacity 8192), the `push` channel (capacity 1024), and `Auth::new`.
15. Call `bind` on `CodeTools`, `Management`, and `Coordination`.
16. On Unix, create the hook bridge socket. An error stops startup.
17. Spawn `files::run_touches` and `nav::run`.
18. Attach every registered workspace.
19. Remove the tool caches of sessions that are Completed or Failed (`sweep_session_caches`).

The order has reasons that the code comments give. The registry opens after the data dir gets its owner-only mode, because the registry holds provider keys, git credentials, and the push signing key. The executors exist before the `App` exists, so step 15 gives them a weak reference to the app afterward. The workspaces attach last, because recovery can start executions that call the hook bridge.

After `build`, `app::run` writes `server.json` (port, `url_host`, pid) in the data dir, prints the sign-in URL, and opens the browser unless `--no-open` is set. If the browser cannot open, it prints "Could not open a browser; copy the URL above." Then it serves the router with `axum::serve` and connect info. Ctrl-C (SIGINT) starts a graceful shutdown. After the shutdown, the server removes the bridge socket and `server.json`.

If the bind address is not loopback, the server prints a warning. The warning says that the server uses plain HTTP, that anyone with a sign-in link can run commands as the user, and that push notifications need HTTPS or localhost. If the machine has more than one LAN address, the server also lists the other addresses.

## One engine for each workspace

`App::attach` opens one runtime for each registered workspace. If a runtime already exists, it returns that runtime. Otherwise it opens `WorkspaceRt`, calls `engine.recover()`, and subscribes to the engine notices. A task forwards each notice to `files.observe`, to `nav.observe`, and to the `hub` channel as a `HubMsg`. If the task lags, it logs `hub lagged by N notices` and calls `nav.lagged`. The runtime goes into `App.workspaces`.

These rules apply at startup:

- A workspace whose `.ostra/workspace.toml` is missing is skipped with a warning.
- If `attach` fails for one workspace, the server logs the error and starts. That workspace stays unavailable.
- A failure in `engine.recover()` fails the attach of that workspace.

`App::delete_workspace` holds the write lock of the workspace map while it calls `rt.retire()` and removes the entry. A busy workspace refuses retirement. Then the server unregisters the workspace, forgets its nav state and MCP connections, and pushes `workspace_updated` on `workspace:<id>` and `home`.

`Shared::global()` reads `config.toml` on each call. If the file does not parse or the sandbox section fails validation, it logs a warning and returns the last good copy. Edits to the config therefore apply without a restart. The listen address, the port, and the host allowlist are the exception: the server fixes them at startup.

## The request guard

`router` in [crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) applies the `guard` middleware as its only layer. The layer covers every route: the REST routes, the `/ws` upgrade, the merged `/internal/*` routes, and the static fallback. A request is an API request when its path starts with `/api/` or equals `/ws`.

### Decisions of the guard

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Request] --> B{Host on allowlist}
  B -- no --> R1[421]
  B -- yes --> C{"IP alias of the private name and path not internal"}
  C -- yes --> R2["307 for pages, 421 for API"]
  C -- no --> D{Path under internal}
  D -- yes --> E{"Local peer and no Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site"}
  E -- no --> R3[403]
  E -- yes --> H["Handler checks bearer token"]
  D -- no --> F{"Path is api or ws"}
  F -- no --> S["Static page or OAuth callback"]
  F -- yes --> G{"Origin and Sec-Fetch headers ok"}
  G -- no --> R3
  G -- yes --> I{"Cookie valid or path is exchange"}
  I -- no --> R4[401]
  I -- yes --> J[Route handler]
```

The guard checks in this order:

1. **Host allowlist.** `Auth::allowed_host` compares the `Host` header with the allowed list, without case. A missing or unknown host gets status 421 with the text "This host is not allowed." This check blocks DNS rebinding.
2. **Private-name redirect.** A loopback server serves a private name `ostra-<16 hex>.localhost` unless `server.use_ip_host` is `true`. If a request arrives on `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>`, or `[::1]:<port>`, an API request gets 421 with the private URL. A page request gets 307 to the same path and query on the private name. The `#token=` fragment survives the redirect. `/internal/*` is exempt. The reason: a cookie that the browser gets on 127.0.0.1 goes to every other local port, because cookies do not have a port scope.
3. **`refusal`.** This function returns a refusal or nothing. Its rules are in the list below.

The `refusal` function applies these rules:

- **Local peers only for `/internal/*`.** The peer IP must be loopback or an address of one of the interfaces of this machine. Otherwise the status is 403 with "This endpoint accepts local connections only." Harnesses always run on this machine, even when the server listens on every interface.
- **No browser pages for `/internal/*`.** A request with an `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` header gets 403. A browser page on this machine is a local peer too, but a browser always sends one of these headers.
- **Origin rules for API paths.** `Origin` must be absent or equal `http://` or `https://` plus an allowed host. A `Sec-Fetch-Site` of `cross-site` or `same-site` is refused, because a page on another localhost port is same-site and its `SameSite` cookie would ride along. `Sec-Fetch-Dest` must be absent or one of `empty`, `websocket`, or `document`, so an image, script, or frame request is refused. A Markdown image that an agent wrote is an example. The status is 403 with "This origin is not allowed."
- **Cookie for API paths.** Every API path except `/api/auth/exchange` needs the `ostra_session` cookie, and `Auth::check_cookie` must accept it. Otherwise the status is 401 with "Sign in with the URL the ostra command printed." The server writes an info log line with the request facts. The line never holds a cookie value.

### Paths that need no cookie

- The static fallback, because the app shell must load before the user signs in.
- `POST /api/auth/exchange`, because it is the sign-in step.
- `/internal/*`, which uses a per-execution bearer token. The handler checks it. A missing `Authorization: Bearer` header gives 401.
- `GET /mcp/oauth/callback`. It is outside `/api` because the redirect from the authorization server is a cross-site navigation, and the browser does not send a `SameSite=Strict` cookie. The single-use `state` value authenticates it.

### Allowed host list

`Access::hosts` builds the list once at startup:

- Always `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>`, and `[::1]:<port>`.
- For a bind to `0.0.0.0` or `::`: every interface address (bridge interfaces too), `<hostname>:<port>`, and `<hostname>.local:<port>`.
- For a bind to one non-loopback address: that address with the port.
- For each extra host from `--allow-host` or `server.allowed_hosts`: `name:<port>` and the bare `name`, unless the value already ends in `:<digits>`. A reverse proxy on its default port sends the bare name.
- With `--dev`: `localhost:5173` and `127.0.0.1:5173`.

The list is lower-cased, sorted, and free of duplicates. An origin matches when its text after `http://` or `https://` equals a list entry. `https` is accepted because a TLS reverse proxy can sit in front of Ostra.

### Response headers

`secure_headers` runs on every response, including refusals:

| Header | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `default-src 'self'`, scripts, workers, and manifest from `'self'`, styles `'self' 'unsafe-inline'`, images and fonts `'self' data:`, `connect-src 'self' ws://<host> wss://<host>`, `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'none'`, `form-action 'self'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`, `frame-src 'none'` |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `no-referrer` |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `DENY` |
| `Cache-Control` | `no-store`, on API paths only |

The policy names the host only after the host passed the allowlist. It allows no remote images, because an injected agent could otherwise send data out through the URL of a Markdown image.

## Sign-in with a one-time token

A browser has no password. The server prints a sign-in link that contains a one-time token in the URL fragment. The fragment is not sent to the server in a request and does not appear in the request log. The web app reads the fragment and posts the token to `/api/auth/exchange`.

### Sign-in exchange

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as ostra process
  participant R as registry
  participant B as Browser
  participant G as guard
  participant X as exchange handler
  participant A as Auth
  P->>R: kv_set auth:token:HASH with expiry
  P->>B: prints link with fragment token
  B->>G: GET page without cookie
  G-->>B: embedded index.html
  B->>G: POST /api/auth/exchange with token
  G->>X: Host and Origin checks pass
  X->>A: exchange_wait for the peer IP
  X->>A: exchange with token and metadata
  A->>R: kv_replace marks the token used
  A->>R: kv_set auth:cookie:HASH with record
  X-->>B: 204 with Set-Cookie ostra_session
  B->>G: API request with cookie
  G->>A: check_cookie
```

### Mint a token

`mint_token` makes 32 random bytes as 64 hex characters. It stores `auth:token:<sha256 of the token>` in the registry `kv` table. The value is the expiry time in Unix seconds: now plus `TOKEN_TTL_SECS` (900 seconds). The server never stores a token in plain text. `app::run` mints the first token and prints `http://<url_host>/#token=<token>`. `ostra url` reads `server.json`, opens the registry, mints another token, and prints the link. This works for a running server because the server reads the same registry.

### Exchange a token for a cookie

`POST /api/auth/exchange` takes the body `{"token": "..."}`. The handler reads at most 64 KiB. If the body does not parse, the status is 400 with `Send {"token": "..."}.` The handler then does these steps:

1. **Rate limit.** `exchange_wait` allows 5 failures for each client IP in 60 seconds (`MAX_FAILURES`, `FAILURE_WINDOW`). After that, the status is 429 with the number of seconds to wait. Loopback peers have no limit. A token has 256 bits and cannot be guessed. If local failures counted, any local process could lock the user out. The limit only stops a guessing loop from filling the log and the registry.
2. **Claim the token.** `Auth::exchange` reads the hash. An unknown token gives `Unknown`. A value that starts with `used:` gives `Used` with the seconds since use. Otherwise `kv_replace` changes the stored value to `used:<now>` in one atomic step. If another request wins that race, the result is `Used` with 0 seconds. The server keeps a used token as used, so a second try says so and does not say unknown.
3. **Check the expiry.** If the stored expiry is in the past, the result is `Expired`. The token is already marked used.
4. **Make the cookie.** On success, the server makes 32 random bytes as hex. It stores a record under `auth:cookie:<sha256 of the cookie>`. The record holds an id (`si_` and 16 hex characters), `created`, `last_seen`, the first 300 characters of the user agent, and the IP. The raw cookie is never stored.
5. **Answer.** The status is 204 with `Set-Cookie: ostra_session=<cookie>; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/; Max-Age=2592000`. The handler adds `; Secure` only when the request `Origin` starts with `https://`. The code does not read `X-Forwarded-Proto`, because any client can send that header.

A failed exchange gives 401 with a message for the failure kind: not issued by this server, already used, or expired (links last 15 minutes). `note_exchange` records each failure, and a success clears the failures of that address.

### Check a cookie

`check_cookie` hashes the cookie and looks in an in-memory cache. If the cache entry is younger than `RECHECK` (5 seconds), the server trusts it and compares the stored expiry with the clock. Otherwise it reads the registry row. The cookie is valid while the row exists and `created` plus `COOKIE_TTL_SECS` (30 days, 2,592,000 seconds) is in the future. A missing or expired row is deleted and the cache entry is dropped.

The server rewrites `last_seen` at most once in `SEEN_EVERY_SECS` (60 seconds), so an active tab does not write on each request. The write uses `kv_replace` over the row that the server just read. A revoke that lands in between is therefore not undone. `Auth::new` calls `load_records` at start. It deletes rows that do not parse and rows that expired. It also rewrites old rows that hold only a creation time.

### Revoke a sign-in

- **Browser routes.** `GET /api/auth/sessions` lists the sign-ins and marks the current one. `DELETE /api/auth/sessions/{id}` revokes one and answers 404 if none has that id. `POST /api/auth/sessions/revoke-others` revokes all but the caller and returns `{revoked: n}`. `POST /api/auth/signout` revokes the caller, sends `Max-Age=0`, and answers 204 even without a cookie.
- **Effect on this server.** A revoke deletes the row, removes the cache entry, and broadcasts the cookie hash on a channel with capacity 64. Open WebSockets with that cookie close at once with code 4401 and the reason "Signed out".
- **CLI.** `ostra sessions`, `ostra sessions revoke <id>`, `ostra sessions revoke --all`, and `ostra signout` edit the registry directly. They work when the server is off. A running server refuses the revoked cookie within `RECHECK` (5 seconds), and open sockets check again at the same interval.

`server.json` holds `{port, url_host, pid}`. `server_running()` checks the pid: on Unix with `kill(pid, 0)` where EPERM counts as alive, on Windows with `OpenProcess`.

With a loopback bind and `use_ip_host` set to `false`, `private_name` creates `ostra-<16 hex>.localhost` once and stores it in the `server:private_host` row of the registry. Later starts reuse it, so the sign-in URL stays stable.

## Master key for saved credentials

The registry holds credentials that the user types in the browser. The master key seals them. The rows that the server seals are the rows whose key starts with one of the entries of `SECRET_KEYS` in [crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs](crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs): `vapid_private`, `provider_credentials:`, `git_credential:`, `mcp_oauth:`, and `mcp_secret:`. Each value is `enc:v1:` plus base64 of a 12-byte random nonce and the AES-256-GCM ciphertext. The row key is the associated data, so a sealed value cannot move to another row. A registry without a sealer refuses to read or write credentials (`StoreError::Locked`).

`master_key::unlock` picks the 32-byte key. The first rule that matches wins.

### Key selection

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[unlock] --> B{"OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE set"}
  B -- yes --> K1["Use that file, create it if missing"]
  B -- no --> C{"Recorded backend is file"}
  C -- yes --> F["Use master.key in the data dir"]
  C -- no --> D{"Keychain read"}
  D -- key found --> K2["Record keychain and use the key"]
  D -- no entry --> E["Generate a key, store it, read it back"]
  E -- matches --> K3["Record keychain"]
  E -- not kept --> F
  D -- unreachable --> G{"Recorded backend is keychain"}
  G -- yes --> X["Startup fails"]
  G -- no --> F
```

1. **`OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE`.** The server uses this file and creates it with owner-only mode if it is missing. It records no backend. The sandbox also hides this file from agents. The variable is meant for a mounted Docker secret.
2. **The OS keychain.** This step runs unless the registry row `secrets:backend` says `file`. The service name is `ostra` and the account is `master-key <canonical data dir>`, so each data dir has its own key. Each keychain call runs on a thread that the server abandons after `KEYCHAIN_TIMEOUT` (10 seconds), because a keychain can block on an unlock prompt or a dead D-Bus.
3. **The file `<data dir>/master.key`.** It holds 64 hex characters. The server creates it with `create_new`, mode 0600 on Unix, and `sync_all`. It records the backend `file`.

### What happens when

- **The keychain has no entry and the recorded backend was `keychain`.** The server logs a warning that it creates a new key and that the user must enter saved credentials again. Then it generates, stores, and reads back a key. If the keychain returns the same key, the backend stays `keychain`. If not, the server falls back to the file.
- **The keychain is unreachable and the recorded backend was `keychain`.** Startup fails with "Unlock the system keychain and start Ostra again ..." The server does not make a new key, because that would lose the old key and every saved credential. To move to a key file, set `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE`.
- **The keychain is unreachable and no backend was recorded.** The server logs the reason and uses `master.key`.
- **`master.key` has group or other permission bits.** The server sets the mode to 0600. If the file system is read-only, the server logs a warning and goes on. A secret mount that cannot change is the choice of the operator.
- **`master.key` does not hold 64 hex characters.** Startup fails. The message says to restore the file, or to delete it and enter credentials again. On Windows the file keeps the ACL that it inherits from the data dir.
- **The key does not open the `secrets:check` row.** The row holds the sealed word `ostra`. If it exists but does not open, the server logs a warning that saved credentials were sealed with another key. It seals the check row again with the new key. Old credentials read as not set. On the first run the server only writes the check row.
- **Plain-text rows exist from an older version.** `seal_plaintext_secrets` seals them with `kv_replace`, so a write at the same time is not lost. Then it rewrites the database file and empties the WAL once, so no plain text stays on disk. It logs how many rows it sealed.

### Provider credentials

`PATCH /api/providers/{name}` saves a provider key in a `provider_credentials:<name>` row. Only `anthropic` and `openai` are allowed, and only if the global config has that provider. Otherwise the status is 404. Each of `base_url`, `api_key`, and `auth_token` follows one rule: absent keeps the value, empty or white space clears it, and any other text replaces it after trimming. `base_url` must parse as an http or https URL with a host, and must have no user, password, or query, because the settings screen shows it. The keys must have no white space or control characters, because the server sends them in HTTP headers. A failure is 422 with one issue for each field. After a save, `Providers::reload` applies the change without a restart. Environment variables that `ProviderConfig` names override saved values, and `ProviderConfig.base_url` wins over both. Credentials never reach `config.toml` or a response body. The response shows only `has_key`.

## Limits and defaults

| Name | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_PORT` | 7878 | `app.rs` |
| Port scan without a set port | 20 ports, then port 0 | `app::bind` |
| `TOKEN_TTL_SECS` | 900 seconds | `auth.rs` |
| `COOKIE_TTL_SECS` | 2,592,000 seconds (30 days) | `auth.rs` |
| `RECHECK` | 5 seconds | `auth.rs` |
| `SEEN_EVERY_SECS` | 60 seconds | `auth.rs` |
| `MAX_FAILURES` in `FAILURE_WINDOW` | 5 failures in 60 seconds, for non-loopback IPs | `auth.rs` |
| Exchange body | 64 KiB | `api.rs` `exchange` |
| User agent kept in a record | 300 characters | `auth.rs` |
| Revoke channel capacity | 64 | `Auth::new` |
| `hub` capacity | 8192 notices | `app::build` |
| `push` capacity | 1024 messages | `app::build` |
| `KEYCHAIN_TIMEOUT` | 10 seconds | `master_key.rs` |
| Master key | 32 bytes, 64 hex characters in a file | `master_key.rs` |
| Seal nonce | 12 bytes, random for each seal | `secrets.rs` |

The tests in `crates/ostra-server/src/auth.rs` and `crates/ostra-server/src/master_key.rs` cover the exchange, the cookie checks, and the fallback to a key file. Read them before you change a rule on this page.

sections.title: REST routes, errors, and the WebSocket protocol
sections.summary: Lists the route groups of the REST API, how handlers resolve ids and map errors, the body limits, and the WebSocket channels, messages, binary terminal frames, and limits.
sections.body:
## The problem this part solves

The web console must read and change the state of many workspaces, and it must also see changes that other tabs, agents, and git commands make. REST routes answer a request and close. They cannot tell a tab that an agent wrote a file. The WebSocket carries those live changes. This page lists the route groups, explains the helpers that every handler uses, maps errors to status codes, and defines the WebSocket protocol.

The page "Startup sequence, request guard, and sign-in" explains the checks that run before a handler. The page "Files, git, artifacts, skills, and commands routes" explains the rules of those routes. The topic "Web console and design system" explains the browser side.

## Route groups

[crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) builds the whole router in `router`. The `guard` layer requires the session cookie for every `/api/*` path except `/api/auth/exchange`. A handler never checks sign-in itself.

| Group | Routes |
| --- | --- |
| Meta and sign-in | `GET /api/info`, `POST /api/auth/exchange`, `GET /api/auth/sessions`, `DELETE /api/auth/sessions/{id}`, `POST /api/auth/sessions/revoke-others`, `POST /api/auth/signout` |
| Setup and providers | `GET /api/environment`, `PATCH /api/providers/{name}`, `GET /api/onboarding`, `POST /api/onboarding/complete`, `POST /api/harnesses/{harness}/setup`, `GET /api/fs/list`, `GET /api/fs`, `POST /api/fs/mkdir`, `POST /api/push/subscribe` |
| Workspaces | `GET` and `POST /api/workspaces`, `POST /api/workspaces/validate`, `GET`, `PATCH`, and `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}`, `POST` on `.../validate`, `.../settings/fix`, and `.../approve`, `GET` and `PATCH` on `.../ui`, `GET` on `.../cost`, `.../tree`, `.../search`, and `.../activity` |
| Projects | `POST .../projects`, `POST .../clone`, `DELETE .../projects/{key}`, `POST .../projects/{key}/init`, `POST .../projects/{key}/pull` |
| Project git | `GET .../projects/{key}/git`, `GET .../git/branches`, `POST .../git/stage`, `unstage`, `commit`, `fetch`, `push`, `checkout`, and `GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` on `/api/git/credentials` |
| Project files | `GET .../tree`, `.../file`, `.../files`, `.../diff`, `.../changes`, `PUT .../file`, `POST .../mkdir` |
| Code navigation | `GET .../code/file`, `usages`, `deps`, `external`, `symbols`, `graph`, and `POST .../code/reindex` |
| Skills, commands, memory | `GET .../workspaces/{ws}/skills`, `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE .../skills/{name}`, `POST .../skills/{name}/adopt`, `GET .../harness-skill`, `PUT .../commands`, `GET`, `PATCH`, `DELETE .../memory` |
| Sessions and engine | `GET` and `POST .../sessions`, `POST .../ask`, `GET /api/sessions/{id}`, `/events`, `/diff`, `POST /api/sessions/{id}/yolo`, `amend`, `pause`, `resume`, `stop`, `POST /api/gates/{id}/answer`, `POST /api/decisions/{id}/override`, `GET /api/executions/{id}`, `/activity`, `POST /api/executions/{id}/cancel`, `resume`, `inspect` |
| Artifacts and uploads | `GET /api/artifacts`, `GET /api/artifacts/download`, `GET`, `POST`, `DELETE .../workspaces/{ws}/artifacts`, `GET .../artifacts/download`, `POST .../artifacts/hidden`, `POST .../artifacts/move`, `POST .../workspaces/{ws}/uploads`, `GET .../docs`, `GET` and `DELETE .../docs/{book}` |
| MCP | `GET .../workspaces/{ws}/mcp`, `POST .../mcp/{name}/refresh`, `login`, `logout`, `GET /mcp/oauth/callback` |
| Other | `GET /ws`, `POST /internal/policy`, `POST /internal/mcp`, and the static fallback |

The prefix `...` stands for `/api/workspaces/{ws}`. The `/internal` routes come from `bridge::internal_routes`, and the fallback is `assets::static_handler`. The static handler serves the embedded React build. For an unknown path that does not look like a file, it returns `index.html`, so client routes such as `/w/{ws}/settings` load directly. A missing `api/`, `internal/`, or `assets/` path returns 404.

## How a handler resolves its target

A handler turns ids from the URL into runtime objects before it acts.

- **Workspace.** `ws(app, id)` finds the open `WorkspaceRt` in `App.workspaces`. A missing workspace gives 404 "No workspace {id}."
- **Session, gate, execution, decision.** `ws_of_session`, `ws_of_gate`, `ws_of_execution`, and `ws_of_decision` scan the database of every open workspace. If none holds the id, the status is 404. The ids carry no workspace, so the scan is the only way to find the owner.
- **Start work.** `create_session`, `init_project`, `ask`, and `inspect_execution` hold `w.work.read()` through `start_work`. A workspace that is being deleted refuses with 404. The read lock stops a delete between the busy check and the start.
- **Destructive work.** Artifact delete, artifact move, and book delete use `w.work.try_write()`. If a session is starting, the status is 409 with "Try again in a moment, because work is starting in this workspace."
- **Work that must finish.** Git commands and clones run in a task from `tokio::spawn`. If the tab closes, git does not stop halfway.

## Error mapping

Every handler returns `Result<Json<T>, ApiErr>`. `ApiErr` holds a status and an `ApiError` body `{error, issues}`. `issues` is a list of `{path, message}`.

| Source | Status |
| --- | --- |
| `EngineError::NotFound` | 404 |
| `EngineError::Invalid`, `EngineError::Ended` | 409 |
| `EngineError::Store`, `StoreError` | 500 |
| Settings that fail validation (`ApiErr::invalid`) | 422 with "The settings have problems. Fix them and save again." and one issue for each field |
| A request with several problems (`invalid_request`) | 422. One issue: its message. Many issues: "Fix these problems and ... again:" plus the messages |
| A custom message with issues (`invalid_with`) | 422 |
| A stale field (`conflict_on(field, message)`) | 409 with one issue that names the field |
| `GitError::Busy` | 409 |
| `GitError::Git` | 502 |
| `GitError::Invalid` | 400 |
| `GitError::Import` with issues, or a failure | 422, or 500 |
| A path that leaves its root (containment) | 403 |
| Guard refusals | 421, 307, 403, 401, and 429 (exchange) |

The clients that show only `error` still see the issues, because `invalid_request` copies the issue text into the message.

## Body limits and downloads

| Route | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Default for every route | 2 MB (the default of axum) |
| `PUT .../projects/{key}/file` | 8 times `TEXT_CAP`, which is 8 MiB. JSON escaping can double a text at the 1 MiB cap. |
| `POST .../workspaces/{ws}/uploads` | `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` plus 1,024 bytes. The upload limit is 25 MiB and at most 20 uploads for each request. |
| `.../workspaces/{ws}/artifacts` | `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` (25 MiB) plus 1,024 bytes |
| `POST /api/auth/exchange` | 64 KiB, read by the handler |

Download routes answer with `attachment`. It sets `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` and `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*=UTF-8''<name>`. The name is percent-encoded (RFC 5987). Only letters, digits, and `-._~` stay as they are.

`GET /api/artifacts` and `GET /api/artifacts/download` read files of sessions. The path must resolve, after symlinks, to a place inside the `.ostra/sessions` folder of an open workspace. Otherwise the status is 403 "Only files inside a session directory can be opened here." A missing file gives 404 and a folder gives 400. `/api/artifacts` returns text up to `ARTIFACT_LIMIT` (4 MiB). A larger file or a file that is not UTF-8 comes back with `binary: true`, empty content, and its size.

## The WebSocket

The web console opens one socket for each tab at `/ws`. The handler in [crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs) sets `max_message_size` and `max_frame_size` to `MAX_MESSAGE` (1 MiB). The upgrade passes the guard like any `/api` path, so the Origin rules and the cookie rule apply.

After the upgrade, the socket checks its cookie once. A revoke between the upgrade and the subscription to the revoke channel would otherwise be missed. Then it checks every `RECHECK` (5 seconds) and when its cookie hash arrives on the revoke channel. A cookie that fails closes the socket with code 4401 and the reason "Signed out".

### Channels

A client subscribes to channels. The server sends a message only to a socket that subscribed to one of the target channels of the message.

| Channel | Carries |
| --- | --- |
| `session:<id>` | `session_event` and `session_updated` for one engine session |
| `execution:<id>` | `execution_delta` and `execution_status` for one execution |
| `term:<execution id>` | Binary terminal frames of a harness execution |
| `workspace:<id>` | `workspace_updated`, `session_updated`, `project_fs_changed`, `git_progress`, `tree_patch`, `activity` |
| `home` | `session_updated`, `workspace_updated` after workspace changes, and `harness_status` |

One socket can hold at most `MAX_CHANNELS` (256) channels. The 257th distinct subscribe gets an `error` message: "Too many subscriptions on one connection. Unsubscribe from channels you no longer show." The server keeps no history. When the socket falls behind, it sends `error` with the message `lagged`, and the page fetches its REST snapshots again.

### Messages from the client

The type `ClientMsg` in [crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs](crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs) has 7 variants. Each is a JSON text frame with a `type` field in snake case.

| Message | Fields | Server action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `subscribe` | `channel` | Adds the channel and answers `subscribed`. For `term:<id>` it starts the terminal stream. A repeated subscribe restarts the stream and sends the screen again. For `home` it first sends `harness_status`. |
| `unsubscribe` | `channel` | Stops the stream and removes the channel. |
| `term_input` | `execution`, `data` | Writes `data` to the PTY. Above `MAX_TERM_INPUT` (64 KiB) it sends `error`: "Terminal input is limited to 64 KiB per message. Paste in smaller parts." If the write fails, it sends "The harness is not reading terminal input right now, so the input was dropped." An unknown execution is ignored. |
| `term_resize` | `execution`, `cols`, `rows` | Resizes the PTY. A value of 0, or above `MAX_COLS` (1000) or `MAX_ROWS` (500), gives "Terminal size is out of range." |
| `code_complete` | `id`, `workspace`, `key`, `path`, `text`, `line`, `col`, `trigger`, `retrigger` | Asks for completions in unsaved text. |
| `code_signature` | same fields as `code_complete` | Asks for signature help. |
| `code_navigate` | `id`, `workspace`, `key`, `path`, `text`, `line`, `col`, `target` | Asks for supertypes or implementations. |

The three `code_*` messages use 1-based lines and 0-based columns in UTF-16 units. Each runs in its own task and answers with `code_completion`, `code_signature_help`, or `code_navigation` and the same `id`. `result` is null when nothing answered. `error` says why the server could not ask. A newer request of the same kind from the same socket aborts the older one, and the older one never answers. Answers queue up to `HINT_QUEUE` (8). The topic "Native tools and code navigation" explains the providers behind them.

If a text frame does not parse as a `ClientMsg`, the server sends `error` "Unreadable message." The server ignores binary and ping frames from the client. A close frame ends the loop.

### Messages from the server

The type `ServerMsg` has 15 variants.

| Message | Channels | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session_event {session, seq, at, event}` | `session:<id>` | `EngineNotice::Event` |
| `execution_delta {execution, seq, at, delta}` | `execution:<id>` | `EngineNotice::Delta` |
| `execution_status {execution, status}` | `execution:<id>` | `EngineNotice::ExecutionStatus` |
| `session_updated {summary}` | `session:<id>`, `workspace:<ws>`, `home` | `EngineNotice::SessionUpdated` |
| `workspace_updated {workspace}` | `workspace:<ws>` | `EngineNotice::ProjectsChanged`, and server pushes after clone, pull, commands save, settings change, and workspace delete (also on `home`) |
| `harness_status {statuses}` | direct reply | Sent when a socket subscribes to `home`, and when a setup terminal ends |
| `subscribed {channel}` | direct reply | Answer to `subscribe` |
| `error {message}` | direct reply | Limit errors, parse errors, and `lagged` |
| `project_fs_changed {workspace, key, paths}` | `workspace:<id>` | File writes. An empty list means: reload every listing. |
| `git_progress {workspace, key, line}` | `workspace:<id>` | Clone progress, at most one in 250 ms for each clone |
| `tree_patch {workspace, session}` | `workspace:<id>` | Changed Sessions tree node, at most four each second for each session |
| `activity {workspace, activity}` | `workspace:<id>` | Running executions, open gates, or spend changed. At most two each second. |
| `code_completion`, `code_signature_help`, `code_navigation` | direct reply | Answers to the `code_*` messages |

`project_fs_changed` groups the write touches of executions for 150 ms (`DEBOUNCE`) and sends at most 500 paths (`MAX_PUSHED_PATHS`) in one message. The code watcher sends an empty path list when more than 200 files changed. The page "Files, git, artifacts, skills, and commands routes" explains who sends these messages.

### Binary terminal frames

The server sends terminal output as binary frames. A frame holds one byte `n`, then `n` bytes of the execution id, then the raw terminal bytes. `n` is the smaller of the id length and 255.

```rust
fn frame(execution: &str, bytes: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let id = execution.as_bytes();
    let n = id.len().min(255);
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(1 + n + bytes.len());
    out.push(n as u8);
    out.extend_from_slice(&id[..n]);
    out.extend_from_slice(bytes);
    out
}
```

The frame names its execution, so one socket can carry many terminals. `stream_terminal` does these steps for a `term:<id>` channel:

1. If no live PTY exists, read the saved transcript once and send it as the first frame.
2. Wait until a PTY for that execution appears.
3. Send the current screen, then each output chunk.
4. If the stream lags, send a fresh screen. If the PTY closes, wait for another one.

Each socket has a queue of `TERM_QUEUE` (64) frames. A slow socket makes its PTY stream lag, and the stream then resynchronizes from a fresh screen.

### How a notice reaches a tab

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant E as Engine
  participant F as attach forwarder
  participant H as hub channel
  participant W as ws run loop
  participant T as Browser tab
  T->>W: subscribe session channel
  W-->>T: subscribed
  E->>F: EngineNotice
  F->>H: HubMsg with workspace
  H->>W: recv
  W->>W: route builds channels and ServerMsg
  W-->>T: session_event when the channel is subscribed
```

The `run` function of `ws.rs` has one `tokio::select!` loop for each socket. It waits on these sources: the recheck timer, the revoke channel, terminal frames, hint answers, `app.push`, client messages, and `app.hub`. The two broadcast channels have different roles. `app.hub` (capacity 8192) carries engine notices from every workspace. `app.push` (capacity 1024) carries messages that the server itself starts, as `Pushed {channels, msg}`. The loop sends a pushed message only if one of its channels is in the set of the socket.

### What happens when

- **The socket falls behind `hub` or `push`.** The server sends `error` with `lagged`. The page fetches its REST snapshots again.
- **A revoke arrives for the cookie.** The socket sends the close frame 4401 and ends. Its terminal streams stop, because `Streams` aborts its tasks when it drops.
- **The revoke channel lags.** The socket asks the registry with `check_cookie` instead.
- **Two `code_complete` messages arrive close together.** The server aborts the first task. Only the second answers.
- **A tab subscribes to `term:<id>` twice.** The second subscribe stops the first stream and starts a new one.
- **A client sends a frame larger than 1 MiB.** The socket layer refuses it.

## Limits

| Name | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `MAX_MESSAGE` | 1 MiB |
| `MAX_TERM_INPUT` | 64 KiB |
| `MAX_CHANNELS` | 256 |
| `TERM_QUEUE` | 64 frames |
| `HINT_QUEUE` | 8 answers |
| `RECHECK` | 5 seconds |
| `hub` and `push` capacity | 8192 and 1024 |
| `TREE_TICK` | 250 ms |
| `ACTIVITY_GAP` | 500 ms |
| `PROGRESS_EVERY` (clone) | 250 ms |

Code 4401 is the only custom close code.
