sections.title: External MCP client, OAuth, and Web Push
sections.summary: Explains how Ostra connects to external MCP servers over stdio and HTTP, how the OAuth sign-in works, and how Web Push keys, subscriptions, and delivery work.
sections.body:
## The problem this part solves

Agents need tools that Ostra does not ship, such as a database tool or a browser tool. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) defines how a client lists and calls such tools. Ostra must also tell the user when a gate waits, even when the console tab is closed. Web Push does that. This page explains the MCP client, the OAuth sign-in for remote MCP servers, and the Web Push sender.

The page covers:

- The connection lifecycle in `McpGateway`.
- The protocol, the stdio transport, and the HTTP transport in `ostra-mcp`.
- The OAuth sign-in steps.
- The VAPID keys, push subscriptions, and delivery rules in `ostra-notify`.

The topic "Skill, Report, Document, Memory, project, coordination, and MCP tools" explains how a native run calls the tools. The topic "Hook bridge, MCP shim, and adapters" explains how a harness reaches them. The topic "Trust approvals and registry-only settings" explains Rule A1.

## The MCP client

Ostra is the only MCP client. It keeps one connection for each pair of workspace root and server name. Native runs call tools directly. Harness runs reach the same tools through the MCP server of Ostra (`/internal/mcp`, `ostra mcp-stdio`). One policy and one allow list therefore cover every executor.

### Server settings

The workspace setting `mcp_servers` is a list. Each entry (`McpServerConfig`) has these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | The server name. |
| `enabled` | Defaults to `true`. |
| `command` | A local program and its arguments. The server runs it in the workspace root. |
| `url` | A remote server. An entry has `command` or `url`. |
| `env`, `headers` | Values. `${VAR}` expands from the environment of the Ostra server. |
| `oauth` | `client_id`, `client_secret_env`, `scopes`. |
| `disabled_tools` | Tool names that agents cannot use. |
| `agents` | Agents that can use the server. Empty means all agents. |
| `timeout_secs` | Time limit of one tool call. The default is 120 seconds. |

The special value `${ostra_secret}` (`SAVED_SECRET`) means a value that the user saved in the browser. It lives sealed in a `mcp_secret:` registry row. If a `${VAR}` variable is not set, the error says: set the variable in the environment of the Ostra server, then restart the server. Provider keys, bridge tokens, and OAuth client secrets cannot be named. The server refuses them and removes them from the environment of a stdio child. The reason: an MCP server is third-party code and must not get the keys of the user.

### Connection lifecycle

`McpGateway::ready` returns a live client and its tool list. It works in this order:

1. Find the connection for the key. A connection has a fingerprint of `command`, `env`, `url`, `headers`, `oauth`, and the sandbox mode, network, allowed hosts, loopback setting, and blocked ports. If the fingerprint changes, the gateway makes a new connection.
2. Lock the connection. Under the lock, a live client is reused. If its tool list is older than `RELIST_AFTER` (30 seconds) or the server sent `notifications/tools/list_changed`, the gateway lists the tools again. If listing fails, the gateway reconnects.
3. If an earlier connect failed less than `RETRY_AFTER` (20 seconds) ago, return the cached error. Parallel executions then do not each restart a server that fails.
4. Check Rule A1. A server starts only from the approved copy of the workspace file. If the file waits for approval, the error is `PENDING_MESSAGE`.
5. Build the endpoint, call `Client::connect` with `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` (30 seconds), then `list_tools` with the same timeout.

The status route `GET .../workspaces/{ws}/mcp` connects to every enabled server in parallel. `POST .../mcp/{name}/refresh` resets the connection and connects again. An unknown name gives 404 "This workspace has no MCP server `name`." Each server has one of these states:

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Disabled` | `enabled` is `false`. |
| `Connected` | The tools are listed with `name`, `canonical`, `description`, `enabled`, and `read_only`. |
| `NeedsAuth` | The server refused the request. `signed_in` is `false`. |
| `Error` | The connection failed. The message says why. |

When an execution opens (`Connector::open`), the gateway skips read-only inspections and filters the servers with `mcp::serves(server, agent)`. It connects in parallel. An unreachable server becomes a note and does not stop the execution. It skips disabled tools. It makes tool names canonical and removes duplicates, and the first name wins. A tool call uses the `timeout_secs` of its server.

### The protocol

`Client::connect` in [crates/ostra-mcp/src/lib.rs](crates/ostra-mcp/src/lib.rs) sends `initialize` with `protocolVersion` `2025-11-25` (`PROTOCOL_VERSION`), empty capabilities, and the client info `ostra`. The reply must name a version in `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS`: `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, or `2024-11-05`. Otherwise the error says that the server speaks a version that Ostra does not support. Then the client sends `notifications/initialized`.

- `list_tools` follows `nextCursor` for at most 50 pages. A description falls back to the `title`. A missing schema becomes an empty object schema. `annotations.readOnlyHint` sets `read_only`.
- `call_tool` sends `{}` when the arguments are not an object.
- Every request has a timeout and a cancellation token. After a timeout or a cancel, the client stops waiting and sends `notifications/cancelled`. The `initialize` request is the exception.
- The errors are `Timeout(secs)`, `Cancelled`, `Rpc{code, message}`, `Transport`, `Closed`, and `NeedsAuth`.
- Ostra declares no client capabilities. It answers only `ping` from a server. Other requests get the JSON-RPC error -32601 "Ostra does not support <method>".
- `content::result_text` converts a result to text. Text parts join with newlines. An image or audio part becomes a bracketed note with its size. A resource shows its text or a note. `structuredContent` is used when no text exists. `isError: true` makes the call an error. The text is cut at `MAX_RESULT` (100 KiB) and ends with "... (N more bytes cut)".

### Stdio transport

The stdio transport starts the program with piped stdin, stdout, and stderr. It sets `kill_on_drop` and puts the program in its own process group or job. It reads newline-delimited JSON-RPC. It skips lines that are not JSON, and logs them at debug level. It handles JSON arrays as batches. It keeps the last `STDERR_TAIL` (4,096) bytes of stderr.

If the pipe closes, the client is no longer alive and each pending request fails with "the server exited:" and the last 5 lines of stderr. The client waits up to 500 ms for stderr to finish. When the client drops, it ends the whole process tree, because servers that start with `npx` or `uvx` run in grandchildren. The gateway builds the command with `ostra_sandbox::host_command`, so a workspace server runs under the agent sandbox. The topic "Sandbox" explains the sandbox.

### HTTP transport

The HTTP transport (streamable HTTP) sends each message as a POST to `url`. The headers are `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`, the configured headers, `Authorization: Bearer <token>` from the `TokenSource`, and, after `initialize`, `mcp-session-id` and `mcp-protocol-version`. The reply is JSON or an event stream. The client reads until the response with the matching id and routes other messages as side messages. The connect timeout is 15 seconds, and the user agent is `ostra/<version>`.

The transport handles these answers:

- **403 without an `insufficient_scope` challenge.** A plain refusal. The error holds at most 300 characters of the body.
- **401, or 403 with `insufficient_scope`.** The client tries one token refresh (`refused`). If that does not help, the error is `NeedsAuth` with the `WWW-Authenticate` text.
- **404 when a session id exists.** The client is no longer alive: "the server ended the session".
- **Other statuses that are not 2xx.** "the server answered N:" and a snippet.

`same_origin_redirects` follows at most 5 redirects, and only within the scheme, host, and port of the first request. The reason: secrets in headers must never reach another host or drop to plain http.

## OAuth sign-in for remote servers

A remote MCP server can require OAuth 2.1. The sign-in follows the MCP authorization specification with discovery (RFC 9728 and RFC 8414 or OpenID), dynamic registration (RFC 7591), PKCE with S256, and the `resource` parameter (RFC 8707).

### Sign-in steps

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as Browser
  participant S as Ostra server
  participant G as McpGateway
  participant A as Authorization server
  participant R as registry
  U->>S: POST mcp login with cookie
  S->>G: login with root, name, origin
  G->>A: discover and register
  G-->>U: authorization_url
  U->>A: user approves
  A->>U: redirect to callback with code and state
  U->>S: GET /mcp/oauth/callback
  S->>G: callback with state and code
  G->>A: exchange code with verifier
  G->>R: secret_set mcp_oauth row
  S-->>U: Signed in page
```

1. **Start.** `POST .../mcp/{name}/login` passes the guard with the cookie. The gateway uses the approved workspace file (Rule A1), because sign-in sends `oauth.client_secret_env` to the endpoints of the server. Only a server with a `url` can sign in: "Sign-in applies to remote servers only ..." The redirect base is the `Origin` header, else `http://<Host>`. The redirect URI is that base plus `/mcp/oauth/callback` (`CALLBACK_PATH`). A failure gives 502.
2. **Discover.** `discover` starts from the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge of the last 401 (`resource_metadata`, `scope`). Then it reads `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` and takes `authorization_servers[0]`, `resource`, and `scopes_supported`. If there is no resource metadata, the server hosts its own authorization server. The metadata comes from `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` or the OpenID variants. Metadata that names another issuer is refused (RFC 8414 section 3.3). If no metadata exists at all, `discover` guesses the default endpoints `/authorize`, `/token`, and `/register`, and sets `guessed`. Every OAuth URL must be `https`, or `http` on a loopback host or on the origin of the MCP server. Anything else, such as `javascript:`, is refused: "OAuth endpoints must use https ..."
3. **Pick a client.** If `oauth.client_id` is set, use it with the secret from the variable that `client_secret_env` names. That variable must not be a provider or bridge variable. Otherwise use a client that the registry holds for the same url, redirect URI, and issuer. Otherwise register a public client (`token_endpoint_auth_method: none`, grant types `authorization_code` and `refresh_token`). If registration is impossible and the endpoints were guessed, the error says: give the server a token in a header, such as `Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN_VAR}`.
4. **Build the URL.** The gateway makes a PKCE verifier and a `state`, each 32 random bytes in base64url. The URL has `response_type=code`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `state`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method=S256`, `resource`, and `scope`. The scope is the configured scopes, else the scopes of the challenge or the metadata. The gateway keeps the pending login in memory under `state` for `LOGIN_TTL` (600 seconds) and removes older ones at each login. It returns `{authorization_url}`.
5. **Callback.** `GET /mcp/oauth/callback?code=&state=` needs no cookie. An `error` parameter gives a 400 page: "The authorization server refused the sign-in: ..." A missing code or state gives a 400 page. An unknown, expired, or used `state` gives "This sign-in link has expired or was already used ..." Otherwise the gateway exchanges the code with `grant_type=authorization_code`, `code_verifier`, `redirect_uri`, and `resource`. The client secret goes by HTTP Basic only when the server lists `client_secret_basic` and not `client_secret_post`, and otherwise goes in the form.
6. **Save.** The tokens `{access_token, refresh_token, expires_at}` are saved sealed in `mcp_oauth:<root>:<name>`. The gateway resets the connection. The server answers a small HTML page "Signed in" with escaped text.

### Token use and sign-out

`Stored` is the `TokenSource` of a connection. It returns the access token. If the token expires within 60 seconds (`Tokens::expired`), it refreshes the token with the refresh token. One mutex lets only one refresh run at a time, because a refresh token can work only once. If the server refuses a token, `refused` reuses a token that another call already refreshed, and otherwise refreshes. A refresh that fails clears the tokens, and the user must sign in again. A refresh response without a new refresh token keeps the old one. `POST .../mcp/{name}/logout` deletes the record and resets the connection. The HTTP client of the gateway has a 30-second timeout and the same redirect policy.

### What happens when

- **The callback arrives after 10 minutes.** The pending login is gone, and the page says that the link expired.
- **The user opens the callback in another browser.** The `state` still matches and the sign-in completes, because the state authenticates the callback, not the cookie.
- **The workspace file changes and waits for approval.** The server does not start from it. The status shows `PENDING_MESSAGE` until the user approves.
- **A stdio server exits.** Pending calls fail with the last lines of stderr. The next call reconnects, but not sooner than 20 seconds after a failed connect.
- **The server uses plain http on a public host for OAuth.** The endpoint check refuses it.

## Web Push

Web Push lets the server show a notification in the browser when the console is closed. `ostra-notify` in [crates/ostra-notify/src/lib.rs](crates/ostra-notify/src/lib.rs) implements it without OpenSSL: RFC 8291 encryption in the RFC 8188 `aes128gcm` coding, and RFC 8292 VAPID authentication with an ES256 token. The crates `p256`, `hkdf`, and `aes-gcm` provide the cryptography.

### VAPID keys

`app::vapid_keys` reads the registry secret `vapid_private` at startup. The value is the raw P-256 private key, sealed with the master key. If it is missing or does not parse, the server generates a new pair and stores it. `GET /api/info` returns `{version, vapid_public_key}`. The public key is the uncompressed point in URL-safe base64 without padding. The browser uses it as `applicationServerKey`. The contact subject is the constant `mailto:ostra@localhost`. A new key pair cannot decrypt for an old subscription, because a browser subscription is tied to the key that created it. The code does not state this, so treat it as an inference from the Web Push standard.

### Subscriptions

`POST /api/push/subscribe` takes `{endpoint, keys: {p256dh, auth}}`. An endpoint that does not start with `https://` gives 400 "Push endpoints must use https." The registry table `push_subscriptions` stores the subscription with the endpoint as the key. A repeated subscribe updates `p256dh`, `auth`, and the workspace. The route stores the workspace as `None`, which means all workspaces. Service workers need HTTPS or localhost, so the startup banner for a non-loopback bind says that push notifications need HTTPS.

### What triggers a push

The engine builds a `Notice` and calls `Services::notify`. These events produce one:

| Event | Title | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A gate or a step waits for the user | gate waiting | `gate-<session>` |
| A session completes | Session complete | `done-<session>` |
| A session fails | Session stopped | `done-<session>` |
| A phase is blocked | Phase N is blocked | `blocked-<session>-<phase>` |
| A containment signal pauses a session | Session paused | `contained-<session>` |

A notification with the same tag replaces the earlier one on the device. `ServerServices::notify` in [crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs](crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs) returns at once if the workspace setting `notifications.push` is off. Otherwise it spawns a task. The task loads all subscriptions and keeps those with no workspace or with this workspace. It builds the payload `Notification {title, body, url, tag}` with `url = /w/<workspace id><notice.url>`, a deep link to the screen that needs the user.

### Delivery

`Notifier::send` does these steps for each subscription:

1. Decode `p256dh` and `auth` from URL-safe base64, with or without padding.
2. Serialize the payload to JSON. If it has more than `MAX_PLAINTEXT` (3,993 bytes), return `TooLarge`. Push services accept a body of 4,096 bytes, and the header and the tag use the rest.
3. Encrypt (RFC 8291). The server makes an ephemeral P-256 key, computes ECDH with the key of the subscription, and derives keys with HKDF-SHA256. It derives a 16-byte content key and a 12-byte nonce. It adds the delimiter byte 0x02 and encrypts one record with `RECORD_SIZE` 4096. The body is salt (16 bytes), record size (4 bytes), key id length (1 byte), the sender public key, and the ciphertext.
4. Sign. The JWT has the header `{typ: JWT, alg: ES256}` and the claims `aud` (the origin of the endpoint), `exp` (now plus `JWT_TTL`, 12 hours), and `sub`.
5. Send a POST to the endpoint with `Authorization: vapid t=<jwt>, k=<public key>`, `Content-Encoding: aes128gcm`, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, `TTL: 86400` (`PUSH_TTL_SECS`), and `Urgency: high`. The client timeout is 20 seconds.

The outcome is a `SendOutcome`:

| Response | Outcome | Server action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2xx | `Delivered` | None. |
| 404 or 410 | `Gone` | Remove the subscription from the registry. |
| Other status | `Failed {status, message}` with the first 500 characters of the body | Log a warning. |
| Network error | `Failed {status: None}` | Log a warning. |
| Key or encryption error | `Err` | Log "push error". |

Sends run one after the other for each notice. They are best effort. Nothing is retried or queued. If a device is offline, the push service holds the message for up to the `TTL` of 24 hours.

The unit tests check the RFC 8291 test vector through `encrypt_with`. Run `cargo test --workspace` after any change to the encryption code.

## Limits

| Name | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` | 30 seconds |
| `RELIST_AFTER` | 30 seconds |
| `RETRY_AFTER` | 20 seconds |
| `LOGIN_TTL` | 600 seconds |
| `timeout_secs` default | 120 seconds |
| HTTP connect timeout | 15 seconds |
| Redirects | 5, same origin |
| `list_tools` pages | 50 |
| `MAX_RESULT` | 100 KiB |
| `STDERR_TAIL` | 4,096 bytes |
| Token refresh margin | 60 seconds |
| `MAX_PLAINTEXT` | 3,993 bytes |
| `JWT_TTL` | 12 hours |
| `PUSH_TTL_SECS` | 24 hours |
| Push client timeout | 20 seconds |

code_refs.note: Connection cache, fingerprint, status, OAuth login and callback, and `Stored` tokens.
Protocol versions, `initialize`, `list_tools`, `call_tool`, and redirect policy.
The stdio transport and process-tree termination.
The streamable HTTP transport and the 401 and 403 handling.
Discovery, registration, PKCE, endpoint check, and token requests.
Conversion of tool results to text with the 100 KiB cap.
VAPID keys, message encryption, and `send`.
The `notify` method that fans a notice out to subscriptions.

sections.title: Run, install, and extend the server
sections.summary: Lists the flags, the environment variables, the build and run scripts, the service installers for launchd, systemd, and Task Scheduler, and the Docker setup. Gives the steps to add a route, a WebSocket message, a service, and a setting.
sections.body:
## The problem this part solves

The server embeds the web build in its binary, listens on a network port, and runs agents with the rights of the user. A wrong build order, a wrong bind address, or a service that starts without the right environment causes a broken or an exposed server. This page lists how to build and run the server, how to install it as a service, how to run it in Docker, and where to add code.

The page covers:

- The flags and the subcommands.
- The environment variables.
- `build.sh`, `run.sh`, `install.sh`, and `install.ps1`.
- `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml`.
- The steps to add a route, a WebSocket message, a service, and a setting.

The topic "Build, run, and format" in the orientation pages gives the cargo commands for development: `cargo build --workspace`, `cargo test --workspace`, and `cargo fmt --all`. The page "Startup sequence, request guard, and sign-in" explains what the server does after it starts.

## Flags and subcommands

The command is `ostra [serve] [flags]`. The binary comes from the crate `ostra-server` and is `target/release/ostra`.

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--port <u16>` | The port. If you omit it, the server uses `server.port`, else it scans 7878 to 7897, then asks the OS for a port. |
| `--no-open` | Do not open the browser. |
| `--dev` | Also accept the host of the Vite dev server (`localhost:5173`, `127.0.0.1:5173`). |
| `--bind <addr>` | The listen address. The default is `127.0.0.1`. Use `0.0.0.0`, `::`, `all`, or `*` for every interface. The flag overrides `server.bind`. |
| `--allow-host <name>` | An extra host name that the browser can use, such as the domain of a reverse proxy. You can repeat it. The server merges the values with `server.allowed_hosts`. |

The other subcommands are `config`, `url`, `sessions`, `signout`, and `stop <session>`. The harness commands `hook` and `mcp-stdio` and the hidden command `sandbox-init` are not for users.

The `[server]` table of `config.toml` (`ServerConfig`) has four keys: `port`, `bind`, `allowed_hosts`, and `use_ip_host` (default `false`). The server fixes the listen address, the port, and the host list at startup. A change to them needs a restart. Most other settings apply without a restart, because `Shared::global()` reads the file on each call.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Read by | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_CONFIG` | `ostra-core` paths | The path of `config.toml`. The default is `<config dir>/ostra/config.toml`. |
| `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` | `ostra-core` paths | The data dir. The default is `<local data dir>/ostra`. |
| `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` | `master_key.rs` | A key file for credentials. Use it for a mounted Docker secret. |
| `OSTRA_LOG` | `main.rs` | The tracing filter. The default is `info`. |
| `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` | `prices.rs` | The URL of the model price catalog. An empty value turns fetching off. The refresh interval is 24 hours and the retry interval after a failure is 1 hour. The cache is `<data dir>/models-dev.json`. |
| `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` | `run.sh`, `install.sh` | A file whose `export NAME=value` lines the script applies. |
| `OSTRA_PREFIX` | `install.sh`, `install.ps1` | The install prefix. The default is `~/.local`. |
| `SKIP_BUILD` | scripts | Set it to `1` to skip the build. |

The server also reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `CODEX_HOME` to detect the login state of the harness CLIs. The variables `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_TOKEN`, and `OSTRA_HARNESS` are set by Ostra for hook and shim processes. Do not set them yourself.

The data dir holds `registry.db`, `master.key` (when used), `server.json`, `server.log`, `assets/`, `hidden-artifacts/`, and `models-dev.json`. On Unix, the server sets the data dir to mode 0700.

## Build and run scripts

The binary embeds `web/dist` at compile time with `rust-embed`. The web build must therefore exist before `cargo build` runs.

### build.sh

`./build.sh` does these steps:

1. If `node_modules` is missing, run `npm ci --no-audit --no-fund`.
2. Build the web UI with `cd web && npm run -s build` if `web/dist/index.html` is missing, or if any file in `web/src`, `web/public`, `web/index.html`, `web/package.json`, `design/src`, or `design/package.json` is newer than it.
3. Run `cargo build --release -p ostra-server`.

The toolchain is Rust 1.98.1 (`rust-toolchain.toml`, with rustfmt and clippy) and Node.js 24. The file `.cargo/config.toml` makes `ts-rs` write TypeScript types to `web/src/api/gen` during cargo builds and tests.

### run.sh

`./run.sh [ostra flags]` runs `./build.sh` unless `SKIP_BUILD=1`. If `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` names a file, it applies only the lines that match `export NAME=value`. Nothing else in the file runs. Then it runs `exec ./target/release/ostra "$@"`.

## Install as a service

The install scripts build the server, copy the binary, and register a per-user service that starts at login. Run the script from the repo root. The default listen address of the service is `127.0.0.1`.

### install.sh on macOS and Linux

Commands: `install` (the default, also used when the first argument starts with `-`), `restart`, `status`, `url`, and `uninstall`. Any other OS exits with "Use ./run.sh instead."

`install` does these steps:

1. Run `./build.sh` unless `SKIP_BUILD=1`.
2. Copy `target/release/ostra` to `$OSTRA_PREFIX/bin/ostra` through a temp file and a rename. A running server keeps its old binary, and macOS does not kill it for a changed image.
3. Write the launcher `$OSTRA_PREFIX/bin/ostra-service`. It exports the `PATH` of the installing shell, because service managers start with a minimal `PATH` and the harness CLIs need the real one. It exports `OSTRA_CONFIG` and `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` when you set them. It applies the `export` lines of `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` at each start, so a changed key needs only a restart and the secrets stay out of the service file. It runs `exec ostra serve --no-open`, adds `--bind 127.0.0.1` unless your flags contain `--bind`, and appends your flags.
4. Write the service definition and start it.
5. Wait up to 15 seconds (30 checks of 0.5 seconds) for a new `server.json`, then print the sign-in URL from `ostra url`. If the wait fails, the script prints the log paths and exits with 1.

| Item | macOS | Linux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Service | launchd agent `dev.ostra.server` in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` | systemd user unit `~/.config/systemd/user/ostra.service` |
| Restart policy | `KeepAlive` on an unsuccessful exit, `ThrottleInterval` 10 seconds | `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=5` |
| Stop | launchd | `KillSignal=SIGINT`, `TimeoutStopSec=20` |
| Error log | `<data dir>/service.err.log` | `journalctl --user -u ostra` |

The unit uses `KillSignal=SIGINT` because SIGINT is the signal for a graceful shutdown, and SIGTERM would stop the server in the middle of a write. The service sends stdout to `/dev/null` because the server already writes `server.log`. The data dir for the script is `$OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, else `~/Library/Application Support/ostra` on macOS, else `${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/ostra`.

After an install, the script warns in three cases: the bind is not loopback, `$OSTRA_PREFIX/bin` is not on `PATH`, and on Linux the user has no linger (`loginctl enable-linger` keeps the service running after logout). `uninstall` stops the service and removes the service file, the launcher, and the binary. It keeps the config file and the data.

### install.ps1 on Windows

The commands are the same. The script needs `npm` and `cargo` on `PATH`. It installs `ostra.exe` in `$OSTRA_PREFIX\bin`. It renames a running exe aside, because Windows cannot overwrite it. It registers the per-user Task Scheduler task `dev.ostra.server`. The task starts at logon, needs no administrator rights, and runs `conhost.exe --headless ostra.exe serve --no-open [--bind 127.0.0.1] <flags>`. The headless console gives `ostra.exe` a console and opens no window.

`conhost` exits with 0 however the server ends, so Task Scheduler never sees a failure to restart on. The task therefore repeats every 5 minutes with `MultipleInstances IgnoreNew`. The repeat starts a server that exited, and the setting skips the start while a server runs. The script stops with a message in these cases:

- `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` is set. The task runs `ostra.exe` directly and applies no credentials file. Save provider keys in the setup screen, or as user environment variables.
- `OSTRA_CONFIG` or `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` is set in the shell but not saved as a user environment variable. The task starts with the saved environment.
- Another server holds the data folder. The pid in `server.json` shows it.

The script waits up to 15 seconds for `server.json`.

### Caution about a public bind

Do not pass `--bind 0.0.0.0` unless you must. The server then serves plain HTTP on every interface, and anyone with a sign-in link can run commands as you. Use an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy and add its host name with `--allow-host`.

## Docker

Build the image from the repo root with `docker build -t ostra .`. The `Dockerfile` has four stages on `ubuntu:26.04`:

1. `web`: installs Node.js 24, runs `npm ci`, and runs `npm run build` in `web/`.
2. `rust`: installs the pinned toolchain with rustup, copies `web/dist`, and runs `cargo build --release -p ostra-server` with BuildKit cache mounts. It copies the binary out of the cache mount, because the mount is gone after the step.
3. `runtime`: installs `ca-certificates`, `git`, `openssh-client`, `curl`, and `bubblewrap`. It creates the user `ostra` with UID and GID 1000, and the folders `/data` and `/config`.

The image sets `OSTRA_DATA_DIR=/data` and `OSTRA_CONFIG=/config/config.toml`, exposes port 7878, and sets `STOPSIGNAL SIGINT`. The entry point is `ostra`. The default command is `--bind 0.0.0.0 --port 7878 --no-open`. The UID 1000 matches the first normal user on most Linux hosts, so a host folder that this user owns is writable without a `chown`.

The `web` stage copies `site/package.json`, and the root `package.json` lists `site` as an npm workspace. This checkout has no `site` folder. Create the folder or remove those lines before you build the image, or the build fails at the `COPY` step.

`docker-compose.yml` defines one service, `ostra`:

- It publishes `127.0.0.1:7878:7878` only. The server speaks plain HTTP. Reach it from another machine through an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy.
- It sets `stop_signal: SIGINT`.
- It mounts `ostra-data` on `/data`, `ostra-home` on `/home/ostra` (harness CLIs and their logins), `./config` on `/config`, and `/srv/ostra/projects` on the same path inside the container.

Before the first `docker compose up -d`, do these steps:

1. Create `./config` and set its owner to 1000:1000 with `sudo chown 1000:1000 config`. A folder that the Docker daemon creates belongs to root, and Ostra cannot write `config.toml` there, so it exits at start.
2. Replace `/srv/ostra/projects` on both sides of the mount with one absolute host folder that UID 1000 can write. Both sides must be the same path, because Ostra stores workspace and project paths literally.
3. Run `docker compose up -d` and open `http://localhost:7878`. Run `docker compose logs ostra` to read the sign-in link.

To keep the master key out of the data volume, mount a Docker secret and set `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` to its path.

## Extend the server

### Add a REST route

1. Define the request and response types in `crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs` with `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, TS)]` and `#[ts(export)]`. `.cargo/config.toml` exports them to `web/src/api/gen`.
2. Put the logic in a module of the server crate, as `files`, `skills`, `artifacts`, `commands`, and `repo` do. Declare the module in `lib.rs`. Return `Result<_, ApiErr>`.
3. Add a thin handler in `api.rs` with `State(app): AppState`, `Path`, `Query`, and `Json`. Resolve the workspace with `ws(&app, &id)?`.
4. Wrap work that must finish after the tab closes in `tokio::spawn`, as `git_op` and `clone_project` do.
5. Hold `start_work(&w)` when the route starts sessions. Use `w.work.try_write()` for a destructive change that must not race a starting session.
6. Register the route in `router()` with `.route("/api/...", get(h).post(h2))`. Use a path that starts with `/api/`. The guard then requires the host, the Origin and Sec-Fetch headers, and the session cookie, so the handler does not check sign-in.
7. Add `.layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(..))` to the route if a body can exceed 2 MB.
8. After the route changes state that browsers show, push a message: `app.push.send(Pushed {channels, msg})`. See `files::announce_git` and `git::workspace_updated`.

A route outside `/api/` and `/ws` gets no cookie check from the guard. The OAuth callback and `/internal/*` are the only cases. A new route outside `/api/` must authenticate itself. Prefer a path under `/api/`.

### Add a WebSocket message

1. Add a variant to `ClientMsg` or `ServerMsg` in `crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs`.
2. For a `ClientMsg`, handle it in the `match client` of `ws::run`.
3. For a `ServerMsg` from an engine notice, add an arm in `ws::route`.
4. For a `ServerMsg` that the server starts, send it through `app.push` with the channel names that must receive it.
5. Update the TypeScript client, because the generated types change.

### Add a service or a shared component

1. Put process-wide state in `Shared` in `app.rs` and construct it in `build`.
2. For a service that the engine calls for each workspace, add the method to the `ostra_engine::Services` trait and implement it in `ServerServices` in `services.rs`.
3. For a component that needs the `App` but exists before it (the executors are built first), use the `Default` plus `bind(&app)` pattern with a `OnceLock<Weak<App>>`, as `CodeTools`, `Management`, and `Coordination` do. Call `bind` in `build` right after the `App` is created.
4. For a background loop, take a `Weak<App>`, as `files::run_touches` and `nav::run` do. Spawn it in `build`.
5. If the component stores a credential, add its row prefix to `SECRET_KEYS` in `crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs`. Use `secret_get`, `secret_set`, and `secret_scan`. A row that is not in the list is stored in plain text.

### Add a setting

1. For a global setting, add a field with `#[serde(default)]` to `GlobalConfig` or `ServerConfig` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`.
2. Read it through `Shared::global()`, except for a value that the server fixes at startup, such as the bind address, the port, and the hosts.
3. For a CLI flag, add it to `ServeArgs` in `main.rs`, carry it in `ServeOptions`, and apply it in `app::bind_addr` or `app::access`. The order is: the flag, then the config, then the default, as `--bind` does.
4. For a workspace setting, add it to `WorkspaceSettings` (the file `workspace.toml`). `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}` edits it and returns 422 issues for a bad value.
5. For a project setting or a command, add it to `ProjectProfile` in `.ostra/project.toml`.
6. Do not put a credential in the config. Save it in the registry from a browser form, as `credentials.rs` does.

The page "Settings files and every setting" lists the existing settings.

## What happens when

- **You run `./run.sh` and the web build is stale.** `build.sh` rebuilds it because a source file is newer than `web/dist/index.html`.
- **`web/dist` is missing when you run `cargo build`.** The embed step fails. If `index.html` is missing at run time, the server answers 200 with the text "The web build is missing. Run `npm run build` in web/ and rebuild ostra."
- **You change the port while the service runs.** Run `./install.sh restart`, because the port is fixed at startup.
- **A service starts without your `PATH`.** The harness CLIs do not resolve. Install again from a shell with the right `PATH`, because the launcher records it.
- **You stop the server with SIGTERM.** Use SIGINT. The server shuts down gracefully only on Ctrl-C (SIGINT), so the unit and the container set SIGINT.

## Limits and defaults

| Name | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Default port | 7878 |
| Port scan | 20 ports |
| Service restart delay (launchd) | 10 seconds |
| Service restart delay (systemd) | 5 seconds |
| `TimeoutStopSec` | 20 seconds |
| Windows task repetition | 5 minutes |
| Wait for `server.json` after install | 15 seconds |
| Container UID and GID | 1000 |
| Request body default | 2 MB |

code_refs.note: The flags and the subcommands.
Flag handling in `bind_addr` and `access`.
Web build when stale, then the release build.
Build, apply export lines, and start the binary.
The launchd and systemd installer.
The Task Scheduler installer.
The four-stage image build.
Port, volumes, and the first-run notes.
The engine services that a new service extends.
The `[server]` settings.

sections.title: Console structure, routing, tabs, and the shell
sections.summary: Explains the boot sequence, the route table, resource ids, the tab model, layout persistence, the phone shell, mock and shot modes, the theme, and the bundle tools.
sections.body:
## What the console must do

The console is the React single-page app in `web/`. It shows sessions, executions, artifacts, project files, and documentation books side by side in tabs. After a reload, it must restore the same view. It must also open from a push notification that knows only a session id, work on a phone, and run without a server for tests and demos.

This page covers the boot sequence, the route table, resource ids, the tab model, layout persistence, the phone shell, mock mode, shot mode, the theme, and the bundle tools. A **screen** is a React component that fills the center pane for one resource id. The **shell** is the frame around the screens: the title bar, the sidebar, the tab strip, the quick-question dock, and the status bar. The page *REST client, socket manager, and live state* explains the data layer. The page *Design system: tokens, components, and focus rules* explains the components and the steps to add a screen.

## Folders under web/src

| Folder | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx`, `App.tsx`, `auth.ts` | The boot function, the route table, and the sign-in token code. |
| `api/` | The REST client (`client.ts`), the socket manager (`socket.ts`), the mock (`mock/`), and the generated types (`gen/`). |
| `lib/` | Logic without screens: resource ids, the tab reducer, shortcuts, palette data, live stores, the activity fold, gate answer builders, theme, install, push, and keyboard lock. |
| `shell/` | The desktop frame: `WorkspaceShell`, `TitleBar`, `Sidebar`, `QuickDock`, `StatusBar`, `Palette`, `ResizeHandle`, `Home`, `SignIn`, and the layout storage in `uiState.ts`. |
| `screens/` | One component for each resource type, with the subfolders `artifact`, `execution`, `project`, `session`, `setup`, and `workspace`. |
| `features/` | Units that many screens share: `gates`, `docs`, and `context`. |
| `components/` | `Markdown.tsx` for agent text and `monaco.ts` for the code editor setup. |
| `content/` | Static text in `stages.ts` and `agents.ts`. |
| `mobile/` | The phone shell and the phone screens. |

Tests sit beside the code. The web tree holds 48 test files. `App.test.tsx` renders each screen on mock data inside the shell.

## Boot sequence

`main.tsx` calls the `boot` function once. The function runs these steps in order:

1. Call `watchInstall()`. The browser fires `beforeinstallprompt` only once for each page load, so the listener must exist first.
2. Call `exchangeTokenFromUrl()` and wait for it. The first REST requests need the session cookie that the exchange sets.
3. Call `watchForTokens()`.
4. Call `registerServiceWorker()` without waiting for it.
5. Render `App` in `StrictMode` and pass the exchange error to it.

In mock mode, steps 2 to 4 do not run, because no server exists. If the exchange fails, `boot` still renders the app. The error text waits in `exchangeError`, and `App` shows it on the sign-in screen after the first request returns status 401.

### How the token exchange works

The `ostra` command prints a URL with `#token=<hex>`. The token works one time. `exchangeTokenFromUrl` in `web/src/auth.ts` does these steps:

- Read the token from the URL hash with the pattern `(?:^#|&)token=([^&]+)`. If no token exists, return `null`.
- Wait for the `prerenderingchange` event if the browser still prerenders the page. A background load must not spend the one-time token, because the real visit would then hold a used link.
- Return `null` if the page load already exchanged the same token. The module keeps a set named `exchanged` for this check.
- Call `history.replaceState` to remove the token from the address bar and the history. This stops the token from being copied with a link.
- POST `{ token }` to `/api/auth/exchange`. On failure, return the error message.

`watchForTokens` reloads the page when a later `hashchange` carries a token. When a user pastes a new link into an open tab, only the hash changes and the page does not reload. The boot code would then never see the token.

### Sign-in screen

`App` registers a listener with `onUnauthorized`. When any REST request returns status 401, `App` renders `SignIn` in place of the router. The screen accepts a whole sign-in link or a bare token of at least 16 hexadecimal characters (`tokenFromInput`). Other input gives the message: Paste the whole link the ostra command printed, or only the token after #token=. After a successful exchange, the screen calls `location.replace` with the path `/`.

The server sets the lifetimes. A sign-in link works for 15 minutes (`TOKEN_TTL_SECS`), and a session cookie lasts 30 days (`COOKIE_TTL_SECS`). The screen text tells the user to run `ostra url` for a new link. The page *Startup sequence, request guard, and sign-in* explains the server side.

## Route table

`App.tsx` exports the route table `routes`. All workspace paths share one parent route, and every child renders the same element, `RouteScreen`.

| Path | Element | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/_design` | Component gallery | Exists only when `import.meta.env.DEV` is true. It loads `@ostra/design/gallery` with a lazy import. |
| `/` | `Home` | Shows first-run onboarding when `api.onboarding()` reports no `onboarded_at`, 0 workspaces, and no skip. Otherwise it lists the workspaces. |
| `/w/:ws` | `WorkspaceShell` | The parent of all workspace screens. |
| `/w/:ws` children | `RouteScreen` | The index route and the paths `cost`, `settings`, `memory`, `skills`, `docs`, `b/:id`, `s/:id`, `x/:id`, `artifact`, `p/:key`, and `f/:key/*`. |
| `/w/:ws/projects` | `ProjectsRedirect` | Replaces the URL with `/w/:ws`, because projects now open as tabs from the sidebar. |
| `/w/:ws/*` | `RouteScreen` | The catch-all child. It serves `d/:key` and shows 'Nothing here' for unknown paths. |
| `/s/:id` | `SessionRedirect` | Finds the workspace of a session, then redirects. |
| `/x/:id` | `ExecutionRedirect` | Finds the workspace of an execution, then redirects. |
| `*` | `NotFound` | A link back to the workspace list. |

### Deep links that know only an id

A push notification cannot name a workspace. The server builds its URL as `/s/<session id>`. `SessionRedirect` calls `api.session(id)`, then replaces the URL with `/w/<workspace>/s/<id>` and keeps `location.hash`. `ExecutionRedirect` calls `api.execution(id)`, then `api.session` for the session of the execution, then replaces the URL with `/w/<workspace>/x/<id>`. If the execution has no session, the page shows 'This execution belongs to no session.' If a request fails, the page shows the error text. During the requests, the page shows a spinner and 'Loading…'.

### Which router the app uses

`App` creates the router once, at its first render. It uses `createBrowserRouter` in normal builds. It uses `createMemoryRouter` in shot mode, because the homepage shot lives at a static path inside the site and its routes must stay out of the address bar.

## Resource ids and URLs

A **resource id** is a string that names anything that can open in a tab. `web/src/lib/resource.ts` maps each id to one URL and each URL back to one id. Because the mapping is one to one, a reload or a shared link restores the same tab.

| Resource id | URL under `/w/:ws` | Screen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ws:overview` | `/w/:ws` | `WorkspaceScreen` |
| `ws:cost`, `ws:settings`, `ws:memory`, `ws:skills`, `ws:docs` | `/w/:ws/<page>` | `CostScreen`, `SettingsScreen`, `MemoryScreen`, `SkillsScreen`, `DocsScreen` |
| `session:<id>` | `/s/<id>` | `SessionScreen` |
| `exec:<id>` | `/x/<id>` | `ExecutionScreen` |
| `book:<id>` | `/b/<id>` | `BookScreen` |
| `artifact:<path>` | `/artifact?path=<path>` | `ArtifactScreen` |
| `project:<key>` | `/p/<key>` | `ProjectScreen` |
| `file:<key>:<path>` | `/f/<key>/<path segments>` | `FileScreen` |
| `dep:<key>:<uri>` | `/d/<key>?uri=<uri>` | `DependencyFileScreen` |

These rules apply to the mapping:

- `parseResource` splits an id at the first colon. Project keys never contain a colon, but a path or a URI can.
- `parseResource` returns `null` for an unknown type, an empty reference, an unknown `ws:` page, and a `file` or `dep` id without a key or without the rest.
- `resourcePath` encodes each path segment of a file separately, so slashes stay as separators.
- The `anchor` argument becomes the URL hash. The hash forms in use are `#gate-<id>`, `#setting:<dotted key>`, `#lesson:<key>:<id>`, and `#project:<key>`.
- The overview has no page segment. `resourceFromPath` returns `null` for `/w/:ws/overview`, for a `/d/` URL without `uri`, and for an `/artifact` URL without `path`.

### How a resource becomes a screen

`RouteScreen` calls `resourceFromPath` and then `ScreenFor` in `web/src/screens/index.tsx`. `ScreenFor` switches on the parsed resource type and renders the matching screen with `key={id}`. The key gives each tab fresh state when the user switches tabs. If the URL names no resource, `RouteScreen` shows 'Nothing here. Press the workspace name to go back to its overview.'

The function `selfScrolling` matches ids that start with `artifact:`, `file:`, `dep:`, `project:`, or `book:`. For these ids, the shell sets the center pane to `overflow-y: hidden`, because these screens scroll their own panes. All other ids get `overflow-y: auto`. The code editor (Monaco), the diff view, and the terminal (xterm) load with `lazy()`. Import them only through their lazy wrappers, because a direct import moves them into the main chunk.

## The shell and its tabs

`WorkspaceShell` reads `ws` from the URL and renders `MobileShell` when `useIsMobile()` is true. Otherwise it renders `Shell`. Both are keyed by `ws`, so tabs, stores, and dialogs never leak from one workspace to another.

The desktop `Shell` has this layout, from top to bottom: `TitleBar`, then a row with the `Sidebar`, the main column, and the optional `QuickDock`, then `StatusBar`. The sidebar has four left tabs: `sessions`, `files`, `artifacts`, and `git`. The main column holds the tab strip, a `PendingCommandsNotice` (hidden on `ws:settings`), and the center pane. The dock sends read-only questions to the `quick-answer` agent. 'Turn into task' copies a question into the New task form.

The shell provides `ConsoleContext`. It has three parts, and each part has a hook:

| Part | Hook | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Nav` | `useNav()` | `ws`, `activeId`, `tabs`, `open`, `close`, `keep`, `href` |
| `ShellActions` | `useShell()` | `openDock`, `closeDock`, `taskDraft`, `newWorkspace`, `addProject`, `runSetup`, `browseFiles`, `theme`, `toggleTheme` |
| `WorkspaceData` | `useWorkspace()` | `detail` and `reload` |

The phone shell provides the same context. Because of this, shared screens work in both shells. The option `OpenOptions` has four fields: `preview`, `anchor`, `beside`, and `push`. Desktop ignores `push`.

### The tab model

The tab model is a pure reducer in `web/src/lib/tabs.ts`. A `Tab` has an `id`, a `preview` flag, and a `pinned` flag. At most one tab is the **preview tab** (italic). The next preview open replaces it. **Pinned tabs** sit before all other tabs, are never the preview tab, and survive the bulk closes. The code sets no maximum number of tabs.

| Action | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `open` | If the tab exists, make it active. A normal open turns a preview tab into a normal tab. A new preview tab reuses the preview slot. With `beside`, a new tab goes after the active tab but never before the pinned group. Otherwise the tab goes to the end. |
| `keep` | Turn a preview tab into a normal tab. |
| `setPinned` | Pin moves the tab to the end of the pinned group. Unpin moves it to the start of the other tabs. Both clear `preview`. |
| `close` | Remove the tab. If it was active, the tab now at the same index becomes active, else the last tab, else `active` is `null`. |
| `closeMany` | Scope `others`, `left`, `right`, or `all`. Pinned tabs always stay. If the active tab closes, the given tab or else the first remaining tab becomes active. If nothing closes, the reducer returns the same state object. |
| `move` | Move a tab to an index. The index is clamped inside the group of the tab, pinned or not. A moved preview tab becomes a normal tab. |
| `activate` | Focus a tab. Add a normal tab at the end if it is missing. The shell uses this for deep links and history steps. |
| `restore` | Run `normalizeTabs` on a stored state. |

`normalizeTabs` drops duplicates and entries without a string id. It keeps only the first preview tab, puts pinned tabs first, and points `active` at an open tab, else at the first tab.

### Tab strip behavior

- A double-click on a tab keeps it. A double-click on the pane keeps the active tab.
- A middle click closes a tab.
- A right click, or the context-menu key, opens the menu 'Tab actions'. 'Close others', 'Close to the left', 'Close to the right', and 'Close all' appear only when they would close an unpinned tab. 'Close all' shows the hint 'Keeps pinned' when pinned tabs exist. 'Move left' and 'Move right' appear only where a move is possible. The last item is 'Pin' or 'Unpin'.
- A vertical wheel scrolls the strip sideways. The shell uses a native listener with `passive: false`, because the React `onWheel` handler is passive and cannot cancel the scroll.
- After each tab change, the shell calls `revealSelectedTab`. This function moves only the strip. `scrollIntoView` would also scroll every parent, including a page that frames the console.
- A tab of a session shows a status dot in place of its icon: `running` accent and pulsing, `waiting` warn, `completed` ok, `stalled` and `failed` bad.
- The design `Tabs` component also supports drag to reorder and Ctrl or Meta plus Shift plus an arrow key.

### Keep the URL and the active tab equal

Two effects in `Shell` keep the URL and `tabs.active` equal. The ref `shellNav` marks a URL change that the shell made itself. The ref `pendingAnchor` holds the hash that `open(id, { anchor })` asked for.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Shell as WorkspaceShell
    participant Reducer as tabsReducer
    participant Router as react-router
    User->>Shell: open session s_1 with anchor gate-g1
    Shell->>Shell: store pendingAnchor
    Shell->>Reducer: dispatch open
    Reducer-->>Shell: tabs.active is session s_1
    Shell->>Shell: set shellNav to session s_1
    Shell->>Router: navigate to /w/ws/s/s_1 with hash
    Router-->>Shell: routeId is session s_1
    Shell->>Shell: routeId equals shellNav, skip activate
```

When the user presses the Back button, the URL changes first. The shell dispatches `activate` for the new `routeId`, because `shellNav` does not match. If the target tab is already active and an anchor exists, `open` navigates at once, because the effect for `tabs.active` would not run. Opening a `file:` resource also sets `filesProject` to the project key of the file. The first tab state is the local copy, normalized, and then the route id activated.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  if (!routeId) return;
  if (shellNav.current === routeId) {
    shellNav.current = null;
    return;
  }
  dispatch({ type: "activate", id: routeId });
}, [routeId]);
```

## Layout persistence

The layout is the tabs plus five preferences. Without saved layout, a reload would close every tab. The shell saves the layout in two places. This table shows the preferences:

| Preference | Default | Values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `leftTab` | `sessions` | `sessions`, `files`, `artifacts`, `git` |
| `filesProject` | `null` | A project key |
| `sidebarOpen` | `true` | true or false |
| `dockOpen` | `false` | true or false |
| `theme` | `null` | `light`, `dark`, or `null` to follow the system |

The save steps are:

1. On every change, the shell writes the layout to `localStorage` under the key `ostra.ui.<ws>`.
2. After the first GET of `/api/workspaces/<ws>/ui` finishes, the shell sends a PATCH to the same route. It waits `PATCH_DELAY_MS` (800 ms) after the last change. A failed PATCH is ignored.
3. At start, the local copy wins. The shell applies the server copy only when this browser has no local copy. A second browser therefore restores the layout of the first.

`fromServerUi` returns `null` for an empty state: no tabs, no active tab, no left tab, and no theme. It also changes an unknown `left_tab` to `sessions`. The generated comment of `WorkspaceUiState.left_tab` lists only `sessions` and `files`, but the code accepts four values. If `localStorage` throws, `saveLocalUi` skips the write, and the server copy still restores the layout. If the GET fails, the shell sets `serverReady` anyway, so later changes still reach the server.

Panel widths are different. They belong to the browser, not to the workspace, because they depend on the screen. `usePanelWidths` stores them in `localStorage` under `ostra.panels`. The defaults are 264 px for the sidebar and 380 px for the dock. The limits are 180 to 640 px for the sidebar and 260 to 900 px for the dock. A drag on `ResizeHandle` changes the width. A double-click resets it. The arrow keys change it by 16 px, or by 48 px with Shift.

## The phone shell

`MobileShell` replaces the desktop shell when `useIsMobile()` is true. The hook tests the media query `(max-width: 720px)` (`MOBILE_QUERY`) and follows rotation and resize. It returns `false` in shot mode and during a server render. `Home` also switches to the phone onboarding (`MWizard`) and the phone list layout.

The phone shell has no tabs, no shortcut handler, and no palette. `nav.tabs` is an empty list, and `keep` does nothing. It shows one screen at a time under a header. These rules describe its navigation:

- The active resource comes from the URL. The default is `ws:overview`.
- Each pushed screen stores its depth in `location.state.depth`. Opening `ws:overview` without `push` resets the depth to 0. Any other open adds 1. Opening the active id again replaces the history entry unless `push` is true.
- Back closes the setup screen if one is open. Else it calls `navigate(-1)` when the depth is above 0. Else it replaces the URL with the overview. This last case gives a deep link, or a push notification, a way out.
- The header has Back, the title and subtitle, Search, 'Ask a quick question', and Menu. A screen can set its own title with `useMobileHeader`. Otherwise `mobileTitle` builds it from the id.
- Every screen change scrolls to the top unless the URL has a hash.

Three sheets open over the screen: Menu (workspaces, pages, theme, setup), Search, and Ask. The footer shows the connection state (Mock data, Live, Connecting, or Offline), the number of running executions, the number of waiting gates, and today's spend. A tap on the gate item opens the session. If a notice says that commands wait for approval, it links to settings. The notice does not show on the settings page or during setup.

`SearchSheet` is the phone replacement for the palette. It calls `useSearch(ws, query)` with the default debounce of 100 ms. It builds rows with `localItems` and `mergePalette`, and it uses `paletteCommands()` without `cmd:keyboard-lock`. Enter opens the first row. It supports only the commands dock, theme, new workspace, and add project. The constant `SEARCH_DELAY_MS` (250 ms) belongs to `MemoryScreen` and `MWorkspace`, not to the sheet.

`MobileScreenFor` in `web/src/mobile/screens.tsx` maps a resource to a phone screen. `DocsScreen`, `BookScreen`, and `DependencyFileScreen` are shared with desktop. `mobileFills` lists the ids that scroll themselves: `dep:` and `book:`. The phone shell keeps the theme in `localStorage` under `ostra.theme` through `lastTheme`. It does not save the layout to the server.

## Mock mode and shot mode

### Mock mode

Mock mode runs the console with no server. Set `VITE_MOCK=1` to start it. `npm run dev:mock` does this through the file `web/.env.mock`, and vitest sets the same value in `test.env`. `web/src/api/index.ts` and `web/src/api/socket.ts` load the mock with a dynamic `import`. The fixtures then stay out of the production bundle.

`mockApi` has the type `Api`, which is `typeof httpApi`. When a developer adds an endpoint to `client.ts`, the type check fails until `mockApi` implements it. These rules describe the mock:

- Every response resolves after 80 ms with a `structuredClone` of the value (`delay`).
- A thrown error in `attempt` becomes `HttpError` status 404.
- `createWorkspace` rejects with status 422 and issues after 400 ms, or resolves after 1500 ms.
- `answerGate` stores the answer with source `user` and sets the session to `waiting` or `running` from the number of open gates. It does not validate the answer.
- The mock socket opens 50 ms after creation. It streams the fixture deltas on `execution:<id>` every `STEP_MS` (1800 ms). It sends a terminal backlog 120 ms after a `term:<id>` subscribe, then live chunks. It echoes `term_input` with carriage returns changed to carriage return plus line feed.
- Under vitest (`MODE` equal to `test`), the mock socket never opens, so tests see no timers.
- The status bar shows 'Mock data' in place of the connection state.

### Shot mode

Shot mode is the console that the site shows on its homepage. Set `VITE_SHOT=1` (`vite --mode shot`, with `web/.env.shot`). It always runs with mock mode. The file `web/package.json` has no script for it. It differs from normal mode in these ways:

- The router is a memory router. It starts at the `path` query value of the iframe, and only if the value starts with `/w/`. Otherwise it starts at `/`.
- The shell starts with an empty tab strip. It does not read a saved layout and does not send the layout to the server.
- `useIsMobile()` always returns `false`.
- The Vite plugin `ostra-shot-csp` inserts a Content-Security-Policy `meta` tag at bundle time. A static host cannot send the header that the server sends.
- A `postMessage` bridge (`useShotBridge`) lets the parent page open tabs and set the theme. The console sends `ostra-shot-ready`, `ostra-shot-nav`, and `ostra-shot-theme`. It ignores a message from another source or another origin. It reports nothing before the first message of the page, so the startup of the shell does not stop the cycle of the page.

## Theme and live favicon

`resolveTheme(stored)` returns `light` or `dark` if the stored value is one of them. Else it returns `light` when the system matches `prefers-color-scheme: light`, else `dark`. `applyTheme` sets `data-theme` on the `html` element and writes `ostra.theme` to `localStorage`. Inside a workspace, the theme is part of the saved layout. `Home` and `SignIn` call `applyTheme` with `remember` set to `false`, so they read the last theme but never write it.

`useLiveFavicon` replaces the tab icon with the `LiveMark` of the active session. The mark has eight arcs, one for each lane from `research` to `docs`. `markState` rules: with no session, the mark is `IDLE`. For a completed session, or lane `done`, all arcs are `done` and the pearl is `ok`. Otherwise the arcs before the current lane are `done`, the current arc is `fail` (failed or stalled), `run` (running), or `wait`, and the later arcs are `off`.

## Build and development tools

`npm run dev` in `web/` starts Vite on port 5173. It proxies `/api`, `/ws` (with the WebSocket upgrade), and `/mcp/oauth` to `OSTRA_DEV_SERVER`. The default is `http://127.0.0.1:7878`. The OAuth redirect for MCP servers returns to the origin of the page, which is why the dev server proxies `/mcp/oauth`.

`npm run build` runs `vite build`. It writes `web/dist` (emptied first), with no source maps and `chunkSizeWarningLimit` 4000 KB. The Rolldown option `codeSplitting.groups` gives four library groups their own chunks, so a UI change keeps them cached: `react` (priority 40), `router` (30), `icons` (20), and `markdown-lib` (10). Monaco and xterm have their own chunks through `lazy()`.

The config resolves its root with `realpathSync.native`. On Windows, a path with wrong letter case made the workspace links resolve to another case, the optimizer saw two copies of React, and the page stayed blank. The real path gives one case.

These scripts exist in `web/package.json`: `typecheck` (`tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json`), `test` (`vitest run` with jsdom and `VITE_MOCK=1`), `lint`, `format`, `check`, and `check:fix` (Biome 2.5.14 with the root `biome.json`). `build.sh` runs the UI bundle only when `web/dist/index.html` is missing or older than a file in `web/src`, `web/public`, `web/index.html`, `web/package.json`, `design/src`, or `design/package.json`. The server binary embeds `web/dist`.

## What happens when

- **The URL names no resource.** `RouteScreen` shows 'Nothing here'.
- **The workspace cannot load.** `Shell` shows 'Workspace not available' and a button to the workspace list, because `api.workspace` failed and no data exists.
- **The user closes the last tab.** The shell navigates to `/w/:ws`, and the center pane shows the 'Nothing open' hint, because the pane renders `Outlet` only when a tab is active.
- **A deep link names a resource that is not open.** The shell adds a normal tab for it.
- **Two browsers use one workspace.** Each keeps its local layout. A browser without a local copy takes the server copy.
- **A redirect fails.** `SessionRedirect` and `ExecutionRedirect` show the error text in the page.
- **Service worker registration fails.** `registerServiceWorker` returns `null`, and the console continues without push.

## Limits and defaults

| Name | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PATCH_DELAY_MS` | 800 ms | `web/src/shell/WorkspaceShell.tsx` |
| Sidebar width | 264 px default, 180 to 640 px | `web/src/shell/ResizeHandle.tsx` |
| Dock width | 380 px default, 260 to 900 px | `web/src/shell/ResizeHandle.tsx` |
| Resize key step | 16 px, or 48 px with Shift | `web/src/shell/ResizeHandle.tsx` |
| `MOBILE_QUERY` | `(max-width: 720px)` | `web/src/mobile/useMobile.ts` |
| Mock response delay | 80 ms | `web/src/api/mock/mockApi.ts` |
| `STEP_MS` | 1800 ms | `web/src/api/mock/mockSocket.ts` |
| Dev server port | 5173 | `web/vite.config.ts` |
| `chunkSizeWarningLimit` | 4000 KB | `web/vite.config.ts` |
